statement: Structured analytic techniques help analysts challenge their own judgments, surface hidden mental mind-sets, stimulate creativity, and manage uncertainty when facing complex, ambiguous intelligence problems.

Adopt a systematic approach that considers a range of alternative explanations and outcomes so potentially relevant hypotheses and supporting information are not prematurely dismissed, reducing the chance of a missed warning.
Every analyst assimilates and evaluates information through experience-based mental models (frames or mind-sets) of assumptions and expectations about the world and specific domains.
Mental models bias perception: information that fits an analyst's unconscious model is more likely to be perceived and remembered than information that conflicts with it.

Mental models are indispensable for processing large volumes of information, yet they cause analysts to overlook, reject, or forget incoming or missing information that does not fit their assumptions.
Experienced analysts can be more susceptible to mind-set errors because past success entrenches their time-tested mental models.
condition: when relying on previously successful mental models

statement: The core risks of a mind-set are that analysts perceive what they expect, resist changing a formed perception, assimilate new information (sometimes wrongly) into the existing model, and dismiss conflicting information.
Analysts should be self-conscious about their reasoning process, examining how they reach conclusions rather than only the conclusions themselves.
Analysts should actively test the accuracy of their mind-sets by applying structured techniques that make mental models explicit and expose their key assumptions.

Perceptual biases distort analysis: analysts perceive what they expect (needing more unambiguous data to register the unexpected), resist changing a formed perception despite new evidence, and let an early ambiguous impression degrade later perception even after clearer information arrives.

Probability-estimation biases include availability (estimates driven by how easily an event is imagined or recalled), anchoring (estimates adjusted only incrementally from an initial value), and overconfidence, which is especially strong among experts.

Evidence-evaluation biases include over-trusting a small consistent dataset over a larger less-consistent one, difficulty judging the impact of missing information, and a perception persisting even after its supporting evidence has been discredited.

Causal-perception biases lead analysts to over-attribute rational, goal-maximizing intent to other actors (rejecting randomness, accident, or error) and to explain others' behavior by fixed disposition while explaining their own by circumstance.
Applying structured techniques does not guarantee analytic precision or accuracy, but it improves the sophistication, credibility, and policy usefulness of assessments.

Select the technique that best fits the specific analytic task; the primer groups techniques as diagnostic (make assumptions and gaps transparent), contrarian (challenge current thinking), and imaginative (generate new insights and alternative outcomes).

Major intelligence surprises have repeatedly followed strategic assumptions that were stated as near-certainties and never challenged, as in Pearl Harbor 1941, Chinese entry into Korea, Soviet missiles in Cuba, the Yom Kippur War, German unification, India's 1998 nuclear test, and Iraqi WMD in 2003.
Run a Key Assumptions Check to list and review the key working assumptions on which fundamental judgments rest.
Perform a Key Assumptions Check at the start of an analytic project, and re-check assumptions before finalizing judgments so the assessment does not rest on flawed premises.
condition: at project start and again before finalizing judgments

statement: A key assumption is a hypothesis accepted as true that forms the basis of an assessment; such assumptions are often held unconsciously, seldom examined, and almost never challenged.
The goal of a Key Assumptions Check is not to abandon assumptions but to make them explicit and identify what information or developments would demand rethinking them.

Execute the Key Assumptions Check in four steps: write down the current analytic line; articulate every premise (stated and unstated) it relies on; challenge each by asking why it must be true and whether it holds under all conditions; then keep only the assumptions that must be true and note what would break them.

When testing an assumption, ask how confident you are and why, what could undermine it, whether it is really a key uncertainty or key factor, whether it was true before but less so now, and whether being wrong would materially alter the analytic line.
Run a Quality of Information Check to evaluate the completeness and soundness of the sources underpinning analytic judgments.
Confidence in an analytic judgment should ultimately rest on how accurate and reliable its information base is.
Having multiple sources on an issue is not a substitute for good information that has been thoroughly examined.
Check information quality continuously and on a periodic schedule; otherwise judgments become anchored to weak information and prior caveats are forgotten or ignored.
Without knowing the context and conditions under which critical information was obtained, an analyst cannot properly assess its validity or set a confidence level.
condition: when the source's collection context is unknown

statement: For HUMINT, review the source's background, access, and motivation for providing the information before relying on the reporting.
Flag recalled reporting for other analysts and review any judgments built on it to determine whether that reporting was essential to those judgments.
A Quality of Information Check can expose adversary denial and deception, reveal intelligence gaps and new collection requirements, and tell policymakers how much confidence to place in judgments.
Treat over-reliance on a single, ambiguous source as an analytic error, and require sufficient, strong corroboration for critical reporting.
Maintain an Indicators or Signposts list of observable events or trends and review it periodically to track a situation, monitor targets, spot emerging trends, and warn of unanticipated change.
Build the indicators list from the observable events you would expect to see if a postulated situation (such as reform, military modernization, or instability) were actually developing.
When analysts are sharply divided, use an agreed indicators list to depersonalize the debate by shifting attention to an objective set of criteria.
condition: when views on an issue are sharply divided

statement: A published indicators list gives an objective baseline that instills rigor, enhances the credibility of judgments, and lets policymakers track developments themselves.

To apply indicators across rival explanations, identify the competing hypotheses or scenarios, build a separate list of expected activities, statements, or events for each, review and update the lists regularly, and infer the most likely hypothesis from how many of its indicators have changed.

Developing two indicator lists per hypothesis, one for signs a development is emerging and one for signs it is not, helps distinguish the cases and is particularly useful when arguing that an event is unlikely.
condition: when you must make the case that an event is unlikely, as in What-If analysis

statement: Use Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (ACH) to identify all reasonable alternative explanations and evaluate the evidence for its power to disconfirm rather than confirm each hypothesis.
ACH is most effective when there is a large amount of data to evaluate and when a small team can challenge each other's reading of the evidence.
condition: with a large body of data and a small challenging team

statement: ACH is particularly appropriate for controversial issues where analysts want a clear, reviewable record of which theories were considered and how the judgment was reached.
condition: on controversial issues that need an auditable analytic record

statement: Because ACH examines evidence systematically against every hypothesis, it is well suited to considering the possibility of denial and deception.

ACH counters three common forecasting mistakes: being unduly swayed by a first impression, failing to generate a full set of hypotheses at the outset, and relying on evidence that supports the preferred hypothesis while being equally consistent with others.
ACH forces analysts to work through all the possibilities to the best solution rather than accepting the first explanation that seems satisfactory.
In ACH, array the evidence against all hypotheses simultaneously rather than assessing the plausibility of each hypothesis one at a time.

The ACH process must give all information equal weight across hypotheses, prevent premature closure on one explanation, and protect against the tendency to discount information that does not fit the currently preferred explanation.

Run ACH by brainstorming hypotheses with diverse analysts, listing all significant evidence and arguments, building a matrix of hypotheses versus evidence marked consistent/inconsistent/not-applicable, refining and adding hypotheses as needed, and focusing on disproving hypotheses by tallying inconsistent versus consistent evidence to find the weakest and strongest.
A piece of evidence has diagnostic value only if it is consistent with a single hypothesis; evidence consistent with many or all hypotheses is unimportant for deciding which is more likely correct.
Test how sensitive an ACH conclusion is to a few critical items of evidence: if those items proved wrong, misleading, or the product of deception, assess how the explanation's validity would change.
Ask what evidence is not being seen but would be expected if a given hypothesis were true, and treat a conspicuous absence as a possible sign of denial and deception.
Report all ACH conclusions, including weaker hypotheses that should still be monitored as new information arrives, and establish the relative likelihood of the hypotheses.
Use Devil's Advocacy to challenge a single strongly held view or consensus by building the best possible case for an alternative explanation.

Devil's Advocacy is most effective for challenging a consensus or key assumption on a critically important question that cannot be gotten wrong, giving confidence the analytic line will hold up to scrutiny.
condition: on critically important judgments that cannot afford to be wrong

statement: When a group of analysts has worked an issue for a long time, assume a strong mind-set exists that deserves the closer scrutiny of Devil's Advocacy.
condition: when analysts have followed an issue for a long period

statement: Analysts have an obligation to policymakers to understand where their own judgments might be weak and open to future challenge.
The primary value of Devil's Advocacy is to check a dominant mind-set that makes contradictory evidence likely to be dismissed or given insufficient weight.

Conduct Devil's Advocacy by outlining the mainline judgment, assumptions, and supporting evidence, selecting the assumptions most susceptible to challenge, reviewing information for questionable validity or deception or gaps, highlighting evidence for an alternative, and presenting the flaws to the group.
Clearly identify any Devil's Advocacy product as such and lay out the conventional wisdom alongside it, so readers do not confuse the contrarian case with the current official view.

Use Team A/Team B, with separate teams building the best case for two or more competing views, when there are genuinely competing strong mind-sets, which distinguishes it from Devil's Advocacy that challenges a single dominant view.

Team A/Team B is warranted when at least two strong competing views exist in the office or policy community, for a longstanding issue, a far-reaching decision, or a dispute obstructing cross-agency cooperation, but because it is resource-intensive, weigh whether the issue merits it.
condition: when at least two strong competing views exist and the stakes justify the resource cost

statement: A Team A/Team B exercise can help opposing factions see merit in each other's perspective, reduce friction, narrow differences, and at minimum make each side feel its view received equal attention.
Policymakers often learn more from weighing well-argued conflicting views than from an assessment that masks substantive differences or is driven to the lowest common denominator.
Assigning analysts to advocate positions they normally do not support forces them to argue the other side and makes them more aware of their own mind-set.

Run Team A/Team B in two phases: an analysis phase that identifies competing hypotheses, forms teams to build the best case for each with explicit key assumptions, evidence, and logic, and identifies missing information; then a debate phase with parallel oral presentations judged by an independent jury of peers who question the teams and recommend further research and collection.

Use High-Impact/Low-Probability analysis to sensitize analysts and policymakers to unlikely events that would have major consequences, especially when everyone is convinced an event is improbable but has not thought through what its occurrence would mean.
condition: when an event is judged unlikely but its consequences are unexamined

statement: Mapping an unlikely but plausible event can uncover hidden relationships among factors and assumptions, expose oversights in the mainstream analytic line, and produce signposts that give early warning of a shift.

Conduct High-Impact/Low-Probability analysis by defining the high-impact outcome clearly, devising one or more plausible pathways to it, inserting possible triggers such as a natural disaster or a leader's sudden illness or an economic shock, identifying indicators for each pathway, and identifying factors that would deflect or encourage the outcome.
Use What-If analysis by assuming an event has already occurred and explaining how it might have come about, shifting attention from whether the event could occur to how it would.
What-If analysis resembles High-Impact/Low-Probability analysis but moves directly to explaining how the event could happen rather than dwelling on its consequences.
What-If analysis is particularly important when an analytic judgment rests on limited information or unproven assumptions.
condition: when a judgment rests on limited information or unproven assumptions

statement: A What-If analysis gives policymakers a thoughtful caution against accepting conventional wisdom without weighing the cost of being wrong, helping them hedge their bets even when they accept that the event is unlikely.

Run What-If analysis by stating the conventional line, assuming the event happened, selecting triggering events, building a chain of argumentation from logic as much as evidence, thinking backwards to specify what must occur at each stage, identifying one or more plausible pathways, generating indicators per scenario, weighing the consequences, and monitoring the indicators periodically.
Use Brainstorming as an unconstrained group process to generate new ideas and hypotheses; it can support virtually every other structured technique and is typically applied at the start of a project.

Group brainstorming lets analysts build on one another's ideas and exploit diverse perspectives for a modest time investment, whereas an individual brainstorming produces ideas free of others' egos and objections but loses those perspectives and may struggle to break free of personal cognitive biases.
Brainstorming maximizes creativity, forces analysts outside their normal mind-sets, surfaces a wider range of relevant factors, and prevents premature consensus around a single hypothesis.

Brainstorming is most productive when it is a structured process rather than an informal discussion, running a divergent phase to generate ideas followed by a convergent phase to group and organize them.

Never censor an analyst's idea during brainstorming no matter how unconventional; instead find out what prompted it, since it may contain the seed of an important connection to an unstated assumption.
Allow enough time for brainstorming, since it usually takes about an hour to set the rules and exhaust the conventional wisdom before the truly creative ideas emerge.
Involve at least one outsider who does not share the core group's educational background, culture, technical knowledge, or mind-set but has some familiarity with the topic.
Leave rank at the door and treat brainstorming as a democracy of ideas; senior experts may not cut off debate by citing seniority, and inviting junior officers can yield fresh-perspective ideas.
Ensure there is no official analytic line during brainstorming, because a long-held analytic line is one of the most significant blocks to new thinking.
Do not permit killer phrases such as 'that would not work' or 'that could not happen'; effective brainstorming begins with ideas and possibilities and defers tests of workability to later.
Keep a brainstorming session to roughly 60 to 90 minutes, after which the idea stream dries up and repetition and jokes replace creative ideas.
Record brainstorming ideas in a visible way, such as posted notes, so participants can react to earlier ideas and a written record survives for whoever writes the resulting report.

In the divergent phase, pose the problem as a one-sentence focal question, have each participant write key-word responses on notes, post them all and treat every idea equally, and continue until two or three pauses signal that conventional thinking is exhausted and divergent ideas emerge.

In the convergent phase, silently rearrange the notes into clusters by commonality (copying notes so an idea can sit in more than one group), label each cluster, flag notes that fit nowhere as either noise or a nascent idea, then vote to set priorities and next steps.
Use Outside-In Thinking to identify the full range of basic external forces, factors, and trends that would indirectly shape an issue.

Outside-In Thinking is most useful at the conceptualization of a project to identify critical external factors, and with modest effort it reduces the risk of missing important variables early in the analysis.
condition: at the conceptualization stage of an analytic project

statement: Most analysts think from the inside-out, concentrating on factors they control; thinking from the outside-in starts from external changes that could profoundly affect their field and recasts the problem in broader terms, making analysts more likely to uncover additional factors, dynamics, or alternative hypotheses.

Run Outside-In Thinking by writing a generic description of the problem, listing key social, technological, economic, environmental, and political forces you cannot influence, then the factors you can influence, assessing how each could affect the problem, and determining from the evidence whether each actually does.

Use Red Team analysis to model an adversary's behavior by replicating how the adversary would think, countering the mirror-image risk of imputing your own motives, values, and understanding to a foreign actor.

Foreign leaders often respond to events differently than the analyst would because of different cultural, organizational, or personal experiences, so do not assume they will act rationally in the analyst's own terms.

Red Team analysis deliberately places analysts in the adversary's cultural, organizational, and personal setting, transforming the analyst from an observer of the adversary into an actor operating within the adversary's milieu.

Red Team role-playing is especially useful for replicating the mind-set of authoritarian leaders, terrorist cells, or other non-Western groups that operate under very different codes of behavior or motivations.
condition: when modeling authoritarian leaders, terrorist cells, or non-Western groups

statement: Build a Red Team from experts with in-depth knowledge of the target's operating environment, personality, and style of thinking, including people who have experienced the culture, share the ethnic background, or have worked in a similar operational environment, not merely those who know the language.

Conduct Red Team analysis by having members react to stimuli as the target would, developing a set of first-person questions the adversary would ask, and drafting first-person policy papers that reflect the target's cultural and personal norms.
Red Team analysis cannot let analysts truly escape their own experiences and mind-sets, but it can at least prevent them from unconsciously falling into mirror-imaging.

Red Team products are drafted in first-person format, deliberately avoid caveats and qualifications, are rarely coordinated with other experts, do not purport to represent a consensus view, and give a prediction based on the target's special experiences rather than plotting all possible courses of action.

Use Alternative Futures (scenarios) analysis to systematically explore multiple ways a situation could develop when it is too complex or the outcomes too uncertain to trust a single-outcome assessment.
condition: when complexity or uncertainty is too high for a single-outcome assessment

statement: Alternative Futures analysis requires recognizing that uncertainty is high, being willing to consider a wide range of bearing factors, and being prepared to explore a range of outcomes without being wedded to a preconceived result.

Alternative Futures is a divergent-thinking technique that describes multiple plausible outcomes rather than predicting one, in sharp contrast to contrarian techniques that challenge an analyst's high confidence in a single event or trend.
Because it consumes significant time and resources, scenario analysis is best reserved for situations that could pose grave threats or otherwise have significant consequences.
condition: for high-consequence or grave-threat situations, given its cost

statement: Involving policymakers directly in the alternative futures exercise is the most effective way to communicate the results and sensitize them to key uncertainties, and participants often find the process as useful as the finished product.

Alternative Futures analysis helps weigh unknown factors and bound a problem, frames the costs, risks, and opportunities of different outcomes, anticipates surprises by challenging assumptions and considering wild cards, and generates indicators to monitor which future is becoming more or less likely.

Develop alternative futures by interviewing experts to frame the focal issue, brainstorming the forces and factors, selecting by consensus the two most critical and uncertain forces and converting them into axes with relevant endpoints, crossing the axes into a 2x2 matrix of four future worlds, and writing plausible stories and signposts for each.

After building the scenarios, have policymakers consider how current decisions or strategies would fare in each of the four worlds and identify alternative policies that are robust across futures or agile in the face of change.

At the start of a project, use brainstorming and a Key Assumptions Check to ensure important factors are not missed or taken for granted, and use Outside-In Thinking to place the project in a broader international context.
condition: at the beginning of an analytic project

statement: Indicators or Signposts and ACH are useful throughout a project and should be revisited periodically as new information is absorbed; ACH in particular helps prevent premature closure and highlights the most discriminating evidence.

During hypothesis testing, apply a contrarian technique to challenge the developing analytic line, use a Red Team effort to correct an overly rational-actor view of an adversary, and review intelligence gaps to gauge confidence in the information base.
condition: while hypotheses are being formed and tested

statement: As a final check before finalizing an assessment, re-review key assumptions as a logic sanity check, brainstorm to ensure no plausible hypothesis was dismissed, run Devil's Advocacy if a firm consensus has gone long unquestioned, and confirm a key-indicators list is included to track whether the judgments hold.
condition: as the assessment is being finalized

statement: Intelligence analysts should be self-conscious about their reasoning processes, thinking about how they make judgments and reach conclusions rather than only about the conclusions themselves.
Expertise itself is no protection from the common analytic pitfalls that are endemic to the human thought process; the analytic traps catch experts as much as anyone.
When experts fall victim to analytic traps, the effects can be aggravated by the confidence that attaches to expertise, both in the expert's own view and in others' perception.
Newly acquired information is too often evaluated and processed through the existing analytic model rather than used to reassess the premises of the model itself.

Information and expertise are a necessary but not sufficient means of good intelligence analysis; a comparable effort must be devoted to the science of analysis and how the mind processes information.

The cognitive pitfalls that affect analysts cannot be eliminated because they are part of human cognition; the achievable remedy is to train people to recognize them and develop procedures to offset them.
condition: the pitfalls are inherent to human mental processing and cannot be removed

statement: Analysts should distinguish clearly between what they know (fact or reliably reported information) and what they believe (opinion), and support opinion persuasively with evidence.
Analysts should seek the views of outside experts, including academic specialists and policy officials, rather than relying only on in-house judgment.
Analytic products should present alternative future scenarios rather than a single forecast.
Analytic judgments should be held to a show-me-your-evidence standard rather than accepted as unsupported assertions.
The key assumptions underlying an argument (linchpins) should be explicitly spelled out rather than left implicit.
Analysis should alert policymakers to changes in circumstances that would increase the likelihood of alternative scenarios.
Completely plausible premises based on solid expertise can support a logically valid forecast that turns out to be wrong because one premise, however plausible, was incorrect.
An erroneous analytic premise is often not empirically based but is itself a conclusion developed from the analyst's own model, sometimes called an assumption.

Analysis inevitably involves building mental models or filters of cause-and-effect relationships through which information is processed and interpreted, even when these models are not labeled as such.

The human mind is poorly equipped to deal with both inherent uncertainty (the natural fog of complex, indeterminate issues) and induced uncertainty (the man-made fog created by denial and deception operations).
Merely increasing awareness of cognitive and other unmotivated biases does little by itself to help analysts deal effectively with uncertainty.

Tools and techniques that gear the analyst's mind to higher levels of critical thinking (structuring information, challenging assumptions, exploring alternative interpretations) can substantially improve analysis of complex issues where information is incomplete, ambiguous, and often deliberately distorted.
Analytic products should clearly delineate their assumptions and chains of inference and specify the degree and source of the uncertainty involved in the conclusions.

A prudent analytic management system should emphasize procedures that expose and elaborate alternative points of view, such as analytic debates, devil's advocates, interdisciplinary brainstorming, competitive analysis, peer review, and elicitation of outside expertise.
Reliance on mental models or mind-sets to simplify and interpret reality is an unavoidable conceptual mechanism for intelligence analysts, often useful but at times hazardous.
Analysts should commit to challenge, refine, and again challenge their own working mental models, because doing so is central to sound interpretation of complex and ambiguous issues.

The orthodox prescription of more and better information is an inadequate remedy for weak analysis; greater attention should go to more intensive exploitation of information already on hand while continuously challenging and revising mental models.

Mirror-imaging is an unavoidable cognitive trap: no matter how much expertise is applied, when the hard evidence runs out the tendency to project the analyst's own mind-set onto a foreign entity takes over.
condition: when hard evidence about the foreign entity runs out

statement: To forecast a foreign leader's decisions the analyst must understand that leader's values, assumptions, and even misperceptions; without such insight, interpreting or forecasting foreign decisions is often little more than partially informed speculation.

Concluding that foreign behavior is irrational or not in its own best interest often indicates that the analyst has projected their own values and conceptual frameworks onto the foreign actor rather than understanding the logic of the situation as it appears to that actor.

Analysts should treat their calculations about foreign beliefs and behavior as hypotheses to be challenged, carefully considering alternative hypotheses, especially those that cannot be disproved on the basis of available information.

Analysis of Competing Hypotheses puts a series of plausible hypotheses into competition to see which survive a gauntlet of testing for compatibility with available information; surviving hypotheses that have not been disproved are then subjected to further testing.
Analysis of Competing Hypotheses will not always yield the right answer, but it can help analysts overcome cognitive limitations.

Analysts often reject the possibility of deception because they see no evidence of it, but this rejection is not justified, because well-planned and properly executed deception should not be expected to leave evidence readily at hand.
Rejecting a plausible but unproven hypothesis too early tends to bias subsequent analysis, because the analyst then stops looking for the evidence that might support it.
The possibility of deception should not be rejected until it is disproved or, at least, until a systematic search for evidence has been made and none has been found.
exception: unless the deception hypothesis has been disproved or a systematic search for evidence has found none

statement: Organizations should establish an environment that promotes and rewards critical thinking, for example analysis that considers in depth a series of plausible hypotheses rather than allowing the first credible hypothesis to suffice.

A basic finding of cognitive psychology is that people have no conscious experience of most of what happens in the mind; perception, memory, and information processing occur prior to and independently of conscious direction, and what appears in consciousness is the result of thinking, not the process of thinking.
Analytic thinking is a skill, like carpentry or driving, that can be taught, learned, and improved with practice, but it is learned by doing rather than by being told how to do it in a classroom.
Expert guidance may be required to modify long-established analytical habits toward excellence, just as regular running builds endurance but does not improve technique without expert coaching.

Under bounded rationality, because of limits in mental capacity the mind cannot cope directly with the world's complexity, so people construct a simplified mental model of reality and behave rationally within it, even though that model is not always well adapted to the real world.
Analysts do not approach their tasks with empty minds; they start with a set of assumptions about how events normally transpire in the area for which they are responsible.
The common-sense theory of knowledge, that accurate perception requires only opening one's eyes, looking at the facts, and purging preconceptions, is mistaken.

A mind-set can so color and control perception that an experienced specialist may be among the last to see what is really happening when events take a new turn; when faced with a major paradigm shift, the analysts who know the most about a subject have the most to unlearn.
Mind-sets also carry an advantage: they help analysts get production out on time and keep work going effectively between the watershed events that become chapter headings in history.

Collecting more information is often the reflexive organizational response even when analysts already have more than they can digest; what is usually needed is more genuinely useful information such as reliable HUMINT, or a more accurate mental model and better tools, not simply more data.

Perception is demonstrably an active rather than a passive process: it constructs rather than records reality, being a process of inference in which people build their own version of reality from sensory information.

Intelligence analysts must understand themselves before they can understand others; training should be directed inward toward the analyst's own thinking and reasoning processes, not only toward organizational procedures, methods, or substantive topics.
The circumstances under which intelligence analysis is conducted, with incomplete and ambiguous information, are precisely the circumstances in which accurate perception tends to be most difficult.
People tend to perceive what they expect to perceive.
It takes more information, and more unambiguous information, to recognize an unexpected phenomenon than an expected one.

Patterns of expectation become so deeply embedded that they continue to influence perception even when people are alerted to and try to account for data that do not fit their preconceptions; trying to be objective does not ensure accurate perception.

Events consistent with an analyst's expectations are perceived and processed easily, while events that contradict prevailing expectations tend to be ignored or distorted in perception through a subconscious process.

The tendency to perceive what one expects is more important than any tendency to perceive what one wants; evidence cited for wishful-thinking perception can generally be explained equally well by the expectancy thesis.

Expectations derive from past experience, professional training, and cultural and organizational norms, and are also shaped by the context in which perception occurs, since different circumstances evoke different sets of expectations.

Mind-sets are neither good nor bad but unavoidable, because people have no way to cope with the volume and complexity of incoming data without simplifying preconceptions about what to expect, what is important, and what is related to what.
There is no such thing as the facts of the case; what an analyst treats as facts is only a very selective subset of the overall mass of data to which the analyst has been exposed.

Objectivity is achieved not by avoiding preconceptions, which would be ignorance or self-delusion, but by making one's basic assumptions and reasoning as explicit as possible so that others can challenge them and the analyst can examine their validity.
Mind-sets tend to be quick to form but resistant to change.
Once an observer has formed an image, mind-set, or expectation about a phenomenon, that image conditions future perceptions of the same phenomenon.
New information is assimilated to existing images, which explains why gradual, evolutionary change often goes unnoticed.
A fresh perspective is sometimes useful, since a newcomer to a topic may generate accurate insights overlooked by experienced analysts; past experience can handicap as well as aid analysis.

The tendency to assimilate new data into pre-existing images is greater the more ambiguous the information, the more confident the actor is of the validity of the image, and the greater the commitment to the established view.
condition: strengthened by ambiguity of information, confidence in the image, and commitment to the established view

statement: To understand international interactions an analyst must grasp the situation as it appears to each opposing side and constantly shift back and forth between perspectives, one of the more difficult mental feats.
Initial exposure to blurred or ambiguous stimuli interferes with accurate perception even after more and better information becomes available.

The greater the initial blur and the longer the exposure to it, the clearer the picture must become before people can correctly recognize it, because early exposure builds confidence in an initial and perhaps erroneous impression.
The amount of information necessary to invalidate a hypothesis is considerably greater than the amount required to make the initial interpretation; established perceptions are difficult to change.
People form impressions on the basis of very little information, but once an impression is formed they do not reject or change it unless they obtain rather solid evidence.
Analysts should try to limit the adverse impact of impression persistence by suspending judgment for as long as possible as new information is being received.

The circumstances under which accurate perception is most difficult, namely highly ambiguous situations processed incrementally under pressure for early judgment, are exactly the circumstances under which intelligence analysis is generally conducted, a recipe for inaccurate perception.

The greater the ambiguity of the stimuli, the greater the impact of expectations and pre-existing images, so an intelligence analyst's own preconceptions are likely to affect the product more than in fields working with less ambiguous information.

Receiving information in small increments over time facilitates its assimilation into existing views, because no single item prompts a change of view and the significant cumulative message is attenuated when the information is not examined as a whole.

Intelligence analysts operate under strong pressure for premature closure, because customer demand for interpretive analysis peaks within two or three days of an event and forces an almost instant diagnosis based on preconceptions before adequate hard and background information is available.

Once an analyst commits an assessment in writing, both the analyst and the organization acquire a vested interest in maintaining the original assessment, and this organizational pressure for consistency reinforces perceptual bias.
A prudent management system should support analyses that periodically re-examine key problems from the ground up in order to avoid the pitfalls of the incremental approach.

Management should educate intelligence consumers about the limitations as well as the capabilities of analysis and define a set of realistic expectations as a standard against which to judge analytical performance.
Differences between stronger and weaker analytical performance are attributable in large measure to differences in how data and experience are organized in analysts' long-term memory.

Short-term memory has a severe physiological capacity limit of about five or six items that cannot be overcome, forcing a choice of where to focus attention between remembering earlier information and attending to incoming information.

Loss of detail as sensory stimuli pass from sensory storage into short-term and then long-term memory is the basis of selective perception and imposes irreversible limits: people can never retrieve what was actually there, only their stored interpretation of what they thought was there.
The more frequently a mental path is followed, the stronger it becomes and the more readily available the information located along it.

Once people start thinking about a problem one way, the same mental pathways get activated and strengthened, which aids retrieval but also forms mental ruts that make it difficult to reorganize the information to see it from a different perspective.

A schema is any pattern of relationships among data in memory that hangs together strongly enough to be retrieved and used as a single unit, and how knowledge is connected in memory critically determines what information is retrieved in response to a stimulus and how it is used in reasoning.

Concepts and schemata stored in memory exert a powerful influence on how perceptions are formed from sensory data, and if information does not fit what people know or think they know, they have great difficulty processing it.

The content of schemata in memory is a principal factor distinguishing stronger from weaker analytical ability, as illustrated by experiments with chess players and with physicians diagnosing illness.

Expertise in remembering meaningful patterns does not transfer to random data: chess masters reproduce real-game positions almost perfectly but do no better than novices on randomly placed pieces, because their skill is pattern and schema recognition rather than raw memory.
The master analyst's unique ability is attributable to the schemata in long-term memory that enable perceiving patterns in data that pass undetected by the average observer.

The key factor in transferring information from short-term to long-term memory is developing associations between the new information and schemata already in memory, not the duration held in short-term memory or the number of repetitions.
Continuous repetition or maintenance rehearsal is effective for holding information in short-term memory but is an inefficient and often ineffective means of transferring it to long-term memory.

The greater the depth of processing, meaning the effort, cognitive capacity, and associations forged with existing knowledge, the greater the ability to recall, and this holds regardless of whether people are told in advance that their memory will be tested.

Learning by assimilation, fitting new information into an existing schema, is a desirable method because it is learning by comprehension, but it can only be used for information that is somehow related to previous experience.
condition: only applicable when the new information relates to an existing schema

statement: Judgment is the joint product of the available information and what the analyst brings to it, and substantive knowledge and analytical experience determine the store of memories and schemata the analyst draws on to generate and evaluate hypotheses.

The key to strong analysis is not the simple ability to recall facts but the ability to recall patterns that relate facts to each other and to broader concepts, and to employ procedures that facilitate this process.

Working memory is limited to about seven plus or minus two items, which is why people have difficulty grasping a problem in all its complexity and cannot hold all the pros and cons in mind at once to weigh them.

The recommended technique for coping with the limits of working memory is externalizing the problem, getting it out of one's head and onto paper in a simplified form that shows the main elements and how they relate to each other.

A simple model of an analytical problem facilitates the assimilation of new information into long-term memory, defines the categories for filing and retrieving it, and acts as a mnemonic device providing the hooks on which to hang information so it can be found when needed.

If people lack an appropriate category for something, they are unlikely to perceive it, store it in memory, or later retrieve it; and if categories are drawn incorrectly, they perceive and remember things inaccurately.

Hardening of the categories, storing phenomena that differ in important respects under a single undifferentiated concept, is a common analytical weakness that causes errors, whereas fine distinctions among categories and tolerance for ambiguity contribute to more effective analysis.

Factors that influence what is stored in memory and its future retrievability include being the first-stored information on a topic, the amount of attention focused on it, its credibility, and the importance attributed to it at the moment of storage.

Memory rarely changes retroactively: analysts seldom reassess or reorganize memories in response to new information, so information once dismissed as unimportant because it did not fit expectations does not become more memorable even after the analyst's thinking changes.
Learning new schemata often requires unlearning existing ones, which is exceedingly difficult, because it is always easier to learn a new habit than to unlearn an old one.
The schemata in long-term memory that are essential to effective analysis are also the principal source of inertia in recognizing and adapting to a changing environment.

Unlike the chess master, whose rules and environment are stable so a good schema never needs changing, the intelligence analyst must cope with a rapidly changing world in which schemata valid yesterday may no longer be functional tomorrow.

Judgment is what analysts use to fill gaps in their knowledge; it goes beyond the available information, is the principal means of coping with uncertainty, and always involves an analytical leap from the known into the uncertain.
The intelligence analyst's function is to transcend the limits of incomplete, ambiguous, and often contradictory information through the exercise of analytical judgment.

Analytical strategies matter because they determine which data the analyst attends to, deciding where the analyst shines the searchlight, which inevitably affects the outcome of the analytical process.

Satisficing, choosing the first hypothesis that appears good enough rather than identifying all possible hypotheses and determining which is most consistent with the evidence, is a strategy too often used by intelligence analysts.
Analysts should be self-conscious about their reasoning process, thinking about how they make judgments and reach conclusions rather than only about the judgments and conclusions themselves.

Situational logic, the most common analytic mode, generates and analyzes hypotheses from the concrete elements of the current situation, treating it as one-of-a-kind to be understood by its own unique logic rather than as one example of a broad class of comparable events.

Situational logic commonly traces cause-effect or, for purposive behavior, means-ends relationships: the analyst identifies the goals being pursued and explains why the foreign actor believes certain means will achieve them.

A first weakness of situational logic is the difficulty of understanding the mental and bureaucratic processes of foreign leaders, which leads to partially informed speculation or mirror-imaging when the analyst substitutes their own values and frameworks.

A second weakness of situational logic is that it fails to exploit theoretical knowledge from similar phenomena in other countries and times, so the proximate causes it identifies are often only symptoms of more fundamental causal factors.
Situational logic may be the best approach for estimating short-term developments, but a more theoretical approach is required as the analytical perspective moves further into the future.
condition: short-term versus longer-range forecasting horizon

statement: A theory is a generalization based on many examples that specifies that when a given set of conditions arises, certain other conditions will follow either with certainty or with some degree of probability.

Theory economizes thought: by identifying the key elements of a problem it lets the analyst sort through less significant detail, see beyond transient developments, distinguish superficial from significant trends, and forecast developments for which there is currently little concrete evidence.

A common weakness of applying theory to political phenomena is that theoretical propositions frequently fail to specify the time frame within which developments should be anticipated, so the analytical question is often not whether but when or under what conditions an outcome will occur.

Elaborating a theory to identify early-warning indicators guides both intelligence collection and analysis and generates hypotheses about when or under what circumstances an anticipated event might occur.

Theory that enables the analyst to transcend the limits of available data can also provide the basis for ignoring evidence that is truly indicative of future events, as when broad assumptions about authoritarian regimes led Iran specialists to misjudge the Shah's fall.
When specific beliefs are embedded in broad and persuasive general assumptions, it takes far more evidence, including more unambiguous evidence, to overturn them than to sustain continued confidence.

Situational logic itself draws heavily on implicit theoretical assumptions, because the analyst cannot select the significant elements of a situation or identify its causes and consequences without an implicit theory relating outcomes to antecedent conditions.

Social science, unlike natural science, deals with a probabilistic environment, so the best that can be expected of a social-science theory is that the given conditions lead to the specified outcome most of the time, not with full accuracy.

Comparison with historical situations fills gaps by assuming that unknown elements of the present are the same as known elements of a historical precedent judged comparable, using a conceptual model built from one or a few cases rather than many.

A vivid and powerful historical precedent often imposes itself on thinking from the outset, conditioning the analyst to perceive the present primarily in terms of its similarity to the past, so historical analogies often precede rather than follow a careful analysis of the situation.

Reasoning by comparison is an implicit admission of insufficient information to understand the present situation in its own right and of a lack of relevant theory, so anyone using it should be aware of the significant potential for error.

Assuming two situations are equivalent in all respects because they are equivalent in some is a valid assumption only when based on in-depth analysis of both the current situation and the historical precedent confirming they are comparable in all relevant respects.
exception: only valid when in-depth analysis confirms comparability in all relevant respects

statement: Because of reasoning by analogy, policymakers tend to be one generation behind, pursuing the policies that would have been most appropriate in the previous historical situation but are not well adapted to the current one.

People ordinarily use history badly, seizing on the first analogy that comes to mind without researching more widely, analyzing the case, testing its fitness, or asking in what ways it might be misleading.

The greater the number of potential analogues an analyst has available and the greater the depth of knowledge, the greater the likelihood of selecting an appropriate analogue and of perceiving the differences as well as the similarities between two situations.
Even under the best of circumstances, inferences based on comparison with a single analogous situation are probably more prone to error than most other forms of inference.

The most productive uses of comparative analysis are to suggest hypotheses and highlight differences, not to draw conclusions; comparison should not form the basis for conclusions unless thorough analysis of both situations has confirmed they are indeed comparable.
exception: unless thorough analysis has confirmed the two situations are comparable in all relevant respects

statement: Information cannot speak for itself: the significance of information is always a joint function of the nature of the information and the context of assumptions and expectations in which the analyst interprets it.

Uncritical accumulation of information is an appropriate first step when dealing with a new and unfamiliar subject, but it is absorbing information, not analyzing it; analysis begins only when the analyst consciously selects, sorts, and organizes information according to assumptions.
condition: the uncritical accumulation step is appropriate only as an initial step on an unfamiliar subject

statement: The question is not whether an analyst's prior assumptions and expectations influence analysis, but only whether that influence is made explicit or remains implicit.

In medical-diagnosis research, physicians who stressed thorough data collection as their principal method were significantly less accurate than those who identified and tested hypotheses, and collecting additional data through greater thoroughness did not increase diagnostic accuracy.

Objectivity is gained by making assumptions explicit so they may be examined and challenged, not by vain efforts to eliminate them from analysis; suppressing recognition of one's own subjective input can leave the analyst with less valid input to make.

No single hypothesis-generation strategy is necessarily better than the others; it is desirable to employ theory, situational logic, and comparison together at the early hypothesis-generation phase in order to generate all relevant hypotheses.

The Intelligence Community is far stronger in situational logic than in theory, and intelligence analysts tend not to generalize enough, in part because available theoretical insights are often unknown to or unused by political analysts.

Higher-level policymakers who are not subject experts use far more theory and comparison and less situational logic than analysts, so analysts would do well to take this difference in perspective into account when writing for their consumers.

The ideal process for choosing among hypotheses is to generate a full set of hypotheses, systematically evaluate each, and identify the one that best fits the data, and scientific method requires seeking to disprove hypotheses rather than to confirm them.

Common less-than-optimal strategies for choosing among hypotheses include satisficing, incrementalism, consensus (including telling the boss what they want to hear), reasoning by analogy, and relying on a set of maxims to distinguish a good from a bad alternative.

Most intelligence analysis is conducted in a satisficing mode: the analyst identifies what appears the most likely hypothesis, collects and organizes data according to whether they support it, and accepts it if it seems to provide a reasonable fit.

The satisficing approach has three weaknesses: the selective perception that results from focusing on a single hypothesis, failure to generate a complete set of competing hypotheses, and a focus on evidence that confirms rather than disconfirms the hypothesis.

A tentative hypothesis functions as a perceptual filter: analysts tend to see what they are looking for and overlook what is not included in their search strategy, limiting the processed information to what is relevant to the current hypothesis.
If the single favored hypothesis is incorrect, information may be lost that would have suggested a new or modified hypothesis.

The difficulty of selective perception can be overcome by the simultaneous consideration of multiple hypotheses, which focuses attention on the few items of evidence that have the greatest diagnostic value in distinguishing among competing hypotheses.

Most evidence is consistent with several different hypotheses, a fact easily overlooked when analysts focus on only one hypothesis at a time, especially when they seek to confirm rather than disprove the most likely answer.

One may overlook the correct answer if it is not among the hypotheses being considered, and research on hypothesis generation shows performance on this task is woefully inadequate because people are unable or do not take the time to identify the full range of potential answers.
Analysts should take more time to develop a full set of competing hypotheses, drawing on all three strategies of theory, situational logic, and comparison.

Diagnosticity of evidence is the extent to which an item of evidence helps determine the relative likelihood of alternative hypotheses, and in the absence of a complete set of alternative hypotheses the diagnosticity of evidence cannot be evaluated.

Evidence that is consistent with all hypotheses, such as a high temperature that fits many illnesses, has little or no diagnostic value, and it is common to discover that most available evidence is not very helpful because it can be reconciled with all the hypotheses.

Scientific method rejects hypotheses and tentatively accepts only those that cannot be refuted, whereas intuitive analysis concentrates on confirming a hypothesis and gives more weight to supporting than to weakening evidence; analysts can and should adopt the conceptual strategy of seeking to refute rather than confirm their hypotheses.

People do not naturally seek disconfirming evidence, and when such evidence is received it tends to be discounted, because supporting information is accepted as valid while weakening information is judged unreliable or an unimportant anomaly, making it easy to confirm almost any hypothesis one already believes.

A hypothesis can never be proved by enumerating even a large body of evidence consistent with it, because that evidence may also be consistent with other hypotheses, but a hypothesis can be disproved by citing a single item of evidence that is incompatible with it.

In Wason's 2-4-6 rule-discovery experiment, subjects who sought confirming rather than disconfirming evidence almost always failed to find the rule on their first attempt, with only 6 of 29 correct and 0 of 51 in a replication.

Situations in which evidence is consistent with several different hypotheses are extremely common in intelligence analysis, as with early-warning indicators equally consistent with an impending attack and with a bluff, so seizing on one hypothesis and seeking to confirm it often leads analysts astray.

Intelligence evidence usually has only a probabilistic relationship to the hypotheses being considered, so it is seldom possible to eliminate a hypothesis entirely; the most one can say is that a hypothesis is unlikely given the evidence, not that it is impossible.
condition: the evidence has only a probabilistic rather than deterministic relationship to the hypotheses

statement: That intelligence evidence is probabilistic weakens the conclusions drawn from a hypothesis-elimination strategy but in no way justifies a strategy aimed at confirming hypotheses; an optimal strategy still requires searching for information that disconfirms one's favorite hypotheses.

In documented intelligence successes, the analysts used procedures that facilitated formulating and testing alternative hypothetical estimates of enemy intentions against each other, pitting competing hypotheses against the evidence.

Simultaneous evaluation of multiple competing hypotheses permits more systematic and objective analysis than focusing on a single most-likely explanation, but it entails far greater cognitive strain, which is why it is seldom used in intuitive analysis and requires simple supporting procedures.
The often-implicit assumption that lack of information is the principal obstacle to accurate intelligence judgments is questionable and deserves to be challenged.

Once an experienced analyst has the minimum information necessary to make an informed judgment, obtaining additional information generally does not improve the accuracy of estimates but does make the analyst more confident, to the point of overconfidence.

Experienced analysts have an imperfect understanding of what information they actually use, are unaware of the extent to which their judgments are determined by a few dominant factors, and use much less of the available information than they think they do.

These findings should not be accepted at face value, because there are circumstances in which additional information does contribute to more accurate analysis, and circumstances in which additional, particularly contradictory, information decreases rather than increases an analyst's confidence.
exception: additional information can improve accuracy in some circumstances, and contradictory information can reduce rather than raise confidence

statement: The pattern that more information raises confidence while accuracy stays flat has been confirmed across diverse expert fields including horserace handicapping, clinical psychology, medical diagnosis, stock analysis, and weather forecasting, reflecting basic human processes that affect analysis of any subject.
With only minimal information the horserace handicappers' confidence was well calibrated with their accuracy, but they became overconfident as additional information was received.

There is little relationship between thoroughness of data collection and accuracy of diagnosis, and the explicit formulation of hypotheses directs a more efficient and effective search for information.

Experts' self-insight into their own judgmental process is usually faulty: they perceive it as more complex than it is, overestimate factors that have only minor impact, and underestimate their reliance on a few major variables, so people's mental models are simpler than they think.

A mathematical model based on an analyst's actual decisions is invariably a more accurate description of that analyst's decisionmaking than the analyst's own verbal description of how the judgments were made.

Additional information an analyst receives falls into four types with different effects: added detail on variables already in the analysis, identification of additional variables, information on the value of variables already included, and information on which variables are most important and how they relate.

Additional detail on variables already in the analysis and information on additional variables that lack significant influence have a negligible impact on accuracy, yet they form the bulk of the raw material analysts work with and increase confidence because the conclusions seem supported by a large body of data.
New facts affect the accuracy of judgments when they concern changes in variables that are critical to the estimate.
condition: the new fact concerns a variable critical to the estimate

statement: The accuracy of an analyst's judgment depends on both the accuracy of the mental model, meaning which variables matter and how they relate, and the accuracy of the values attributed to the key variables in that model.

In data-driven analysis, given a correct and properly applied analytical model, accuracy depends entirely on the accuracy and completeness of the data, and because the model can largely be made explicit and taught, there are relatively objective standards for judging the quality of the analysis.
condition: the analytical model is correct and properly applied

statement: In conceptually-driven analysis there is no agreed-upon schema, so analysts interpret information with largely implicit mental models, the outcome depends at least as much on the conceptual framework as on the data, and different analysts may reach different conclusions from the same data.

Current political intelligence is often extremely concept-driven rather than data-driven, because the analyst must interpret the latest unexpected events from an implicit mental model of how events normally transpire, so accuracy depends almost exclusively on the accuracy of that model.

Beliefs of all types tend to resist change, especially the implicit assumptions and supposedly self-evident truths that play an important role in forming mental models, and a self-evident truth at one point in time may be regarded as an uninformed assumption years later.

Because the mind strives instinctively for consistency, information consistent with an existing mind-set is perceived and processed easily and reinforces beliefs, while inconsistent information tends to be overlooked, perceived in a distorted manner, or rationalized to fit existing assumptions, through subconscious processes.

Learning better judgment through experience requires systematic feedback on the accuracy of past judgments and the ability to link accuracy to the configuration of variables that prompted them; intelligence analysts get little systematic feedback and rarely know whether a foreseen event occurred for the reasons foreseen, so personal experience may be a poor guide to revising a mental model.

The mosaic theory of intelligence, that collecting enough small pieces of information eventually reveals a clear picture, distorts understanding of the analytic process and provides part of the rationale for large technical collection systems.

Analysts do not actually work mosaic-style: they typically form a picture first and then select the pieces to fit, and pieces often appear to fit many different pictures, so accurate estimates depend at least as much on the mental model used to form the picture as on the number of pieces collected.

Medical diagnosis is a more accurate analogy for analysis than the mosaic: observe indicators, use specialized knowledge to develop hypotheses, collect additional information focused narrowly on discriminating among the hypotheses, then diagnose, attributing more value to analysis and less to collection.

There are inherent practical limits on how much can be gained by improving collection, whereas an open and fertile field exists for improving analysis, the mental models analysts use and the processes for evaluating information, where even small improvements could have large benefits.

Major intelligence failures are usually caused by failures of analysis, not failures of collection: relevant information is discounted, misinterpreted, ignored, rejected, or overlooked because it fails to fit a prevailing mental model, and the signals are lost in the noise.

The nature of intelligence forces analysts to deal with issues at an early stage when hard information is incomplete, since an issue with no gaps or ambiguity would not be an interesting intelligence problem, and when information is lacking analysts must lean heavily on prior beliefs and assumptions.

New ideas result from the association of old elements in new combinations, and the ability to bring previously unrelated information and ideas together in meaningful ways is what marks the open-minded, imaginative, creative analyst.

Analysts need not be constrained by conventional wisdom, which is often wrong, by existing policies, which can sometimes be changed for good reason, or by the specific analytical requirement as given, and should not hesitate to go back up the chain of command with a suggestion to do something different from what was asked.
When analytical judgments turn out to be wrong, it usually was not because the information was wrong but because the analyst made one or more faulty assumptions that went unchallenged.

Because analysts cannot question everything, they should use informal sensitivity analysis to find the linchpin assumptions that drive the analysis and question those, asking what could make each assumption out of date and how they would know it had not already happened.

Analysts should try to disprove their assumptions rather than confirm them, and if an analyst cannot think of anything that would cause a change of mind, the mind-set may be so deeply entrenched that the analyst cannot see the conflicting evidence.

Analysts should identify alternative models, conceptual frameworks, or interpretations by actively seeking out individuals who disagree with them rather than those who agree, resisting the greater comfort of talking only with colleagues who share the same mind-set.

Peer review by highly accomplished analysts from other branches who lack specialized knowledge of the subject can better identify hidden assumptions and alternatives and judge whether the analysis supports its conclusions, because an analyst's own colleagues and supervisors share a common mind-set and are least likely to raise fundamental challenges.

Mirror-imaging, filling gaps in one's own knowledge by assuming the other side will act as the US would under similar circumstances, leads to dangerous assumptions because people in other cultures do not think the way we do, an error termed the everybody-thinks-like-us mind-set.

The US perspective on what is in another country's national interest is usually irrelevant in intelligence analysis; judgment must be based on how the other country perceives its own national interest.
When an analyst cannot gain insight into what the other country is thinking, mirror-imaging may be the only alternative, but analysts should never put much confidence in that kind of judgment.
exception: only as a last resort when insight into the other side's thinking is unavailable, and never with much confidence

statement: Techniques for seeing alternative perspectives share the general principle of coming at the problem from a different direction and asking different questions, which breaks the existing mind-set by causing the analyst to play a different and unaccustomed role.

In the thinking-backwards technique the analyst assumes an unexpected event has occurred and works back from the future to explain how it came about, which shifts the focus from whether something might happen to how, and often makes a previously unlikely event seem quite plausible.
Thinking backwards is particularly helpful for events that have a low probability but very serious consequences should they occur.
condition: the event is low-probability but high-consequence

statement: In the crystal-ball approach the analyst imagines a perfect source has said a key assumption is wrong and then builds a scenario explaining how that could be true; if a plausible scenario can be developed, the assumption is open to some question.

Role playing requires actually acting out and living the role rather than merely imagining how another leader will react, because only living the role breaks the analyst's normal mental set, and it generally requires group interaction with different analysts playing different roles.
exception: merely imagining how another actor will react is not role playing

statement: Useful political gaming does not require elaborate preparation; starting the game from the current known situation with just one notional intelligence report can produce a useful one-day game with almost no preparatory work.
Gaming yields no right answer but usually causes players to see things in a new light, because where you stand depends on where you sit, and changing roles frees the mind to think differently.

A devil's advocate defends a minority or opposing view as strenuously as possible to expose conflicting interpretations and show how alternative assumptions make the world look different, as in assigning someone to actually develop plans for attacking a facility rather than merely reviewing its defenses.
Some competition between conflicting views is healthy and must be encouraged, but all-out political battle is counterproductive.
exception: all-out political battle over the competing views is counterproductive

statement: As a general rule people are too slow to change an established view rather than too willing, because the human mind is conservative and resists change, continuing to apply assumptions that worked in the past long after they have become outmoded.

Successful senior managers counteract the mind's conservative bent by paying attention to feelings of surprise when a fact does not fit their prior understanding, highlighting rather than denying the novelty, and treating disconfirmation as friendly rather than denying, downplaying, or ignoring it.

Analysts should keep a record of unexpected events and think hard about what they might mean rather than disregarding or explaining them away, considering whether each surprise is consistent with an alternative hypothesis, since a pattern of surprises may be the first clue that their understanding is incomplete or wrong.

When estimates based on strategic assumptions conflicted with tactical indicators of an impending attack, the strategic assumptions always prevailed and were never reevaluated in light of the increasing flow of contradictory information.

Tactical indicators should be given increased weight, and at a minimum the emergence of tactical indicators that contradict a strategic assumption should trigger a higher level of intelligence alert, because it may indicate a bigger surprise is on the way.

Intelligence judgments require imagination to conceive possible causes and outcomes that are not given in the data, to reconstruct how a problem appears from a foreign government's viewpoint, and to question things that have long been taken for granted.

A person's intelligence as measured by IQ tests has little to do with creativity, but the organizational environment exercises a major influence, since new but appropriate ideas are most likely to arise in a climate that nurtures their development and communication.

The view that creativity is innate and cannot be taught is largely untrue: while native talent matters, with understanding, practice, and conscious effort analysts can learn to employ their innate talents more productively and produce more imaginative, innovative work.

Deferred judgment is the most important creativity principle: the idea-generation phase should be separated from the idea-evaluation phase, with evaluation deferred until all possible ideas have been brought out, because a judgmental attitude dampens the imagination.

New ideas are by definition unconventional and likely to be suppressed unless born in a secure and protected environment, so critical judgment should be suspended until after the idea-generation stage, for individual idea searching and group brainstorming alike.

Quantity of ideas eventually leads to quality, because the first ideas that come to mind are the most common and one must run through these conventional responses before arriving at original ones, so one should generate as many ideas as possible before evaluating any.
Thinking should be encouraged to range as freely as possible, freed from self-imposed constraints whether they stem from analytical habit, limited perspective, social norms, or emotional blocks.

Cross-fertilization of ideas is important: combining ideas forms better ones, and people generate more creative ideas when teamed with others because personal interaction stimulates new associations, induces greater effort, and helps maintain concentration.

The positive value of group process applies to brainstorming sessions with evaluation deferred, not to standard committee meetings or coordination processes that force consensus based on the lowest common denominator of agreement.
exception: does not apply to committee or coordination meetings that force lowest-common-denominator consensus

statement: Optimal creative results come from alternating between individual thinking, which is more structured and systematic, and team effort, and a diverse group that includes analysts who are not close to the problem is clearly preferable to a homogeneous one.

There are techniques for stimulating the flow of ideas but none for determining which ideas are best, though the ability to generate more alternatives aids evaluation by revealing more potential consequences and repercussions of any single idea or action.

A new idea is the beginning, not the end, of the creative process: it must be developed, evaluated, and communicated, passing many organizational hurdles before it is embraced as an organizational product.

Scientists with more creative ability produced more innovative work only under favorable conditions: perceived responsibility for initiating new activities, considerable control over their own decisions, professional security, a superior who stayed out of the way, small project size, and engagement in other stimulating activities.
condition: only under favorable organizational conditions

statement: The individual conditions for creativity matter little alone but their impact is cumulative, and under unfavorable conditions the most creatively inclined people produce even less innovative work than their less imaginative colleagues, so when a large organization conflicts with a creative individual the organization generally wins.

Innate creative talent may be a necessary precondition for innovative work but is unlikely to be of much value unless the organizational environment nurtures the development and communication of new ideas, or the creative impulse will find expression outside the organization.

Managers at all levels should strengthen analysts' perception that new ideas are welcome, and an analyst's immediate supervisor and colleagues are responsible for providing a sheltered environment where a frail new idea can be expressed and tested before exposure to public criticism.

A questioning attitude is a prerequisite to a successful search for new ideas, since any analyst confident that they already know the answer and that it has not changed recently is unlikely to produce innovative or imaginative work.

A problem defined too narrowly is hard to solve because unconscious self-imposed constraints, like the imaginary square around the nine dots, exist only in the mind of the problem-solver and are not specified in the problem definition.

When analysts cannot keep all relevant factors in consciousness at the same time, complex analytical problems should be handled with the two basic tools of decomposition, breaking a problem into its component parts, and externalization, getting the problem into a visible form that can be worked with.

The limited capacity of working memory is the source of many problems in analysis, because the number of possible relationships between variables grows geometrically as the number of variables increases, with four variables giving six interrelationships and eight variables giving twenty-eight.

Decomposition, dividing a complex whole into its parts, is the essence of analysis: decompose a complex problem into simpler problems, get one's thinking straight on each, then paste the analyses back together with logical glue.

Externalization means getting the decomposed problem out of one's head and onto paper or a screen in a simplified form that shows the main variables and how they relate, so one can manipulate one part at a time and often be more accurate than reasoning entirely in one's head.

Decision problems are difficult chiefly because people cannot keep all the reasons pro and con in mind at the same time, so the solution is to get them all out of the head and onto paper in a visible shorthand form where their respective weights can be estimated and compared.

Decomposition and externalization tools are not aids to be used only by weak analysts and not needed by strong ones, because basic limitations of working memory affect everyone, and it is the more astute and careful analysts who most recognize the value of these very simple tools.
