Neglecting valid stereotypes inevitably yields suboptimal judgments, so resisting stereotyping is a moral stance that carries a real accuracy cost, and denying that the cost exists is not scientifically defensible.
condition: The stereotype is statistically valid in the relevant population.

statement: Causal base rates that imply something about the individual case, such as a pass rate signaling a test's difficulty, are readily used in judgment, whereas purely statistical base rates about the sampling ensemble are neglected.

Through diffusion of responsibility people are far less likely to help when they believe others also heard the call for help, so even normal, decent individuals often fail to step forward when bystanders are present.

People readily infer a general rule from a surprising individual case but resist deducing the particular from a surprising general or statistical fact, quietly exempting themselves and those they know from statistical conclusions.

Learning a surprising statistical fact does not change a person's understanding of concrete situations; the real test of learning is whether situational judgment changes, not whether a new fact can be recited.

Statistics carrying a causal interpretation influence thinking more than noncausal statistics, but even compelling causal statistics rarely overturn long-held beliefs or beliefs rooted in personal experience.
Regression to the mean means that an extreme performance is partly the product of luck and is typically followed by a less extreme, more average one, with no causal cause required.

People routinely attach spurious causal stories to regression effects, as in the Sports Illustrated jinx or a commentator's account of a second ski jump, mistaking a statistical inevitability for a causal effect.

Because praise tends to follow an above-average performance that then regresses downward and criticism follows a below-average one that regresses upward, direct experience falsely teaches that punishment works and reward fails.

Regression appears symmetrically in both directions of time, so that predicting an earlier score from a later one shows the same regression, which demonstrates that regression has no causal explanation.
Regression to the mean occurs whenever the correlation between two measures is less than perfect, and the amount of regression is proportional to the deviation being predicted.

A control group, ideally receiving a placebo, is required to separate a treatment's real effect from the improvement that regression to the mean produces on its own, since an extreme group improves by regression regardless of treatment.
Regression effects are ubiquitous yet hide in plain sight, so even eminent researchers confuse them with causation and experienced scientists develop a healthy fear of unwarranted causal inference.

When forecasting an outcome from an extreme observed value, make a regressive prediction toward the mean rather than extrapolating the extreme, because the extreme was partly due to luck that will not repeat.

Intuitive predictions are nonregressive: they are as extreme as the evidence and match the impression instead of moving toward the mean, so they are systematically biased, over-optimistic for the best cases and over-pessimistic for the worst.

To correct an intuitive prediction, start from the baseline average, form the intuitive estimate that matches the evidence, then move from the baseline toward that estimate only by the fraction equal to the correlation between the evidence and the outcome.
The stronger the correlation between the evidence and the outcome, the smaller the regressive adjustment required, so weak evidence should leave the prediction close to the baseline.
Correcting intuitive predictions is effortful System 2 work that is justified only when the stakes are high and the person is especially keen not to make mistakes.
condition: The stakes are high and accuracy is important.

statement: Unbiased predictions permit forecasting a rare or extreme outcome only when the evidence is very strong, so with evidence of modest validity you will never legitimately predict an extreme case.

Freedom from bias is not always the goal: when one direction of prediction error is far costlier than the other, as in venture capital's fear of missing the next giant or a banker's fear of default, deliberately extreme or asymmetric judgments can be justified.
condition: The costs of the two directions of error are markedly asymmetric.

statement: Under the narrative fallacy the stories people find compelling about the past are simple and concrete, over-assign causation to talent and intention rather than luck, and focus on the few events that happened while ignoring the countless ones that did not.
A compelling narrative creates an illusion of inevitability and of understanding, so that a good story about a success makes people feel they have learned a general lesson that is largely illusory.

The ultimate test of an explanation is whether it would have made the event predictable in advance, so a retrospective story that could not have predicted the outcome confers no genuine understanding.
The more luck was involved in an outcome, the less there is to learn from it.
It is easier to construct a coherent story from less information, so the comforting conviction that the world makes sense rests largely on an ability to ignore one's own ignorance.

Avoid saying you knew a past event would happen when it merely turned out to be true, because such language falsely implies the world was more knowable than it was; an event that many informed people did not foresee was not in fact knowable.

People cannot accurately reconstruct past states of knowledge or belief: after changing their mind they retrieve the current belief by substitution and often cannot believe they once thought differently.
Under hindsight bias, once an outcome is known people misremember having assigned it a higher prior probability, overstating the accuracy of their own and others' earlier predictions.

Under outcome bias observers judge the quality of a decision by whether its outcome was good or bad rather than by whether the process was sound, which makes it nearly impossible to evaluate a decision on the information available when it was made.
Evaluate a decision by the soundness of its process and the information available at the time it was made, not by whether its outcome happened to be good or bad.

Hindsight falls hardest on agents who act for others, such as physicians, advisers, and executives, who are blamed for sound decisions that turned out badly and given too little credit for good moves that look obvious only afterward.
The worse the consequence, the stronger the hindsight bias, so after a catastrophe people are especially quick to judge the officials who failed to anticipate it as negligent or blind.

Accountability judged by hindsight drives decision makers toward defensive, bureaucratic, risk-averse behavior such as ordering unnecessary tests, which protects the agent more than the client, so increased accountability is a mixed blessing.
Hindsight also over-rewards lucky reckless risk-takers, crowning a leader who took a wild gamble and won with an undeserved halo of prescience while the sensible people who doubted them appear timid.
Firm success reflects luck to a large degree, so the quality of leadership and management practices cannot be reliably inferred from observed corporate success.

The halo effect makes the same leader and the same behaviors look flexible and decisive when a firm thrives and rigid and confused when it fails, reversing the causal arrow so that a firm's failure makes its CEO appear rigid rather than the reverse.

Be especially suspicious when highly consistent patterns emerge from comparisons of more and less successful firms, because in the presence of large randomness such regular patterns are largely mirages of luck.

The profitability gap between firms labeled excellent and their lagging peers shrinks toward nothing after the study period through regression to the mean, so business books that distill recipes for success impart little enduring value.

Under the illusion of validity, coherent and confident impressions can coexist with near-zero predictive accuracy, because subjective confidence tracks the coherence of the story rather than its actual validity.
Continuing to feel confident in an evaluation even after learning that it has no predictive validity shows that confidence is produced by System 1 coherence rather than by the evidence.
Individual investors on average lose by trading: the stocks they sell subsequently outperform the ones they buy by about 3.2 percentage points a year, beyond the substantial costs of trading.
The most active traders obtain the poorest results while those who trade least earn the highest returns, so more trading on one's ideas destroys value.
Individual investors tend to sell winners and hold losers, which is backwards because recent winning stocks tend to keep outperforming recent losers.

Across eight years the year-to-year correlation of financial advisers' performance rankings averaged about 0.01, so persistence of skill was effectively absent and the firm was rewarding luck as if it were skill.

The illusion of skill is sustained by professional culture, so facts that threaten livelihood and self-esteem, especially statistical performance data that clash with personal experience, are simply not absorbed.
Subjective confidence is a feeling generated by cognitive ease and associative coherence, not a reasoned judgment about accuracy.
A community of like-minded believers lets people maintain unshakable faith in a proposition however absurd, which reinforces professional illusions of skill.
The ease with which the past is explained fosters overconfidence in the ability to predict the future, because the illusion of understanding the past implies the future should be knowable.
Large historical outcomes are substantially determined by luck, which makes long-term developments far less predictable than compelling narratives of the march of history imply.
In a twenty-year study, expert political forecasters performed worse than a random assignment of equal probabilities and, even in their own specialty, were no better than nonspecialists.

Beyond a point reached quickly, more knowledge does not improve prediction but breeds overconfidence, and the most famous and in-demand experts tend to be the most overconfident and to make the most flamboyant forecasts.
Experts resist admitting error and, when forced to, offer excuses such as being wrong only on timing, an unforeseeable event intervening, or being wrong for the right reasons.

Forecasters who think like foxes, treating reality as the product of many interacting forces including luck, predict better than hedgehogs who fit events into one confident big theory, though even foxes forecast poorly.
Errors of prediction are inevitable because the world is genuinely unpredictable, so many forecasting failures are not the forecaster's fault.
High subjective confidence should not be trusted as an indicator of accuracy, and low confidence can actually be more informative.
Short-term trends and near-future behavior can be predicted with fair accuracy from prior behavior and achievements, even though far-future performance in a new domain cannot.
condition: The prediction concerns short-term continuation from established prior behavior.

statement: Simple statistical algorithms match or beat expert clinical judgment in about sixty percent of studies with the remainder tied, and a tie favors the far cheaper formula, with no exception convincingly documented across roughly two hundred studies.
In low-validity, uncertain environments a simple formula's accuracy equals or exceeds that of experts across many domains, from medical prognosis to credit risk to predicting wine prices.
condition: The environment is a low-validity one with significant irreducible uncertainty.

statement: A simple formula built from a few weather variables forecasts the far-future value of fine wine more accurately than the market prices of the young wines themselves, correlating above .90 with actual prices.

Experts underperform formulas partly because they try to be clever and consider complex combinations of features, which more often than not reduces validity, whereas simple combinations of features predict better.
Human judges remain inferior to a prediction formula even when they are handed the formula's output, because they wrongly believe their extra knowledge of the case justifies overruling it.
Under the broken-leg rule, override a valid formula only on a rare and decisive individuating fact, not on ordinary additional information about the case.
condition: The overriding fact is both rare and decisive for the outcome.

statement: Humans are incorrigibly inconsistent when summarizing complex information, giving different answers to the same case on separate occasions, as experienced radiologists contradict their own normal-versus-abnormal ratings about twenty percent of the time.
Unreliable, inconsistent judgments cannot be valid predictors of anything.

Judgment inconsistency arises from System 1's extreme context-dependency, so irrelevant momentary factors such as mood, weather, or time since the judge's last break shift decisions without the judge noticing.
A formula always returns the same answer for the same input, so where predictability is poor its perfect consistency confers a reliability that inconsistent human judgment cannot match.
To maximize predictive accuracy in a low-validity environment, leave the final decision to a formula rather than to a human's global impression.
condition: The environment is low-validity and a defensible formula exists.

statement: Conducting an interview and letting the interviewers make the final selection lowers the validity of the procedure, because overconfident interviewers overweight their personal impressions and underweight other information.

Formulas that assign equal weights to a set of valid, standardized predictors predict new cases as well as or better than optimally weighted multiple regression, because equal weights are not distorted by accidents of sampling.

To structure a selection or hiring decision, choose about six prerequisite traits that are as independent as possible, ask factual questions for each, score each trait separately on a fixed scale, and combine the scores by formula.
Collect and score the information for one trait at a time before moving to the next, and go through the traits in a fixed sequence, to prevent the halo effect from contaminating later ratings.

Do not simply trust intuitive judgment, your own or others', but do not dismiss it either: intuition adds value only after a disciplined collection of objective information and disciplined separate scoring of traits.

A holistic close-your-eyes intuitive rating can add predictive value roughly equal to the sum of separate trait ratings, but only when it is formed after the disciplined trait scoring rather than instead of it.
condition: The intuitive rating follows a disciplined, factual trait assessment.

statement: Intuition can be trusted only when the environment is regular enough to be predictable and the person has had adequate opportunity to learn its regularities through prolonged practice with feedback.
condition: Both a sufficiently regular environment and prolonged practice with feedback are present.

statement: When highly valid cues exist an expert's System 1 can answer correctly even though System 2 cannot name the cue, whereas in a zero-validity environment such as long-term political or stock forecasting failures reflect the basic unpredictability of events, not a lack of talent.

In wicked environments where feedback is misleading, professionals learn the wrong lessons from experience and can develop false confidence, as a physician who palpated tongues without washing his hands felt clinically infallible while actually spreading the disease he predicted.

Statistical algorithms outperform humans in noisy environments mainly because they detect weakly valid cues and apply them consistently, whereas if a strong predictive cue exists capable human observers will usually find it.

It is unfair to blame anyone for failing to forecast an unpredictable world, but fair to blame professionals for believing they can succeed at an impossible task, since in the absence of valid cues intuitive hits are due to luck or lies.
Emotional learning, especially of fear, is acquired very quickly, often from a single experience and even from words rather than direct experience.
Whether a professional can develop valid intuition depends essentially on the quality and speed of feedback and on sufficient opportunity to practice.
Expertise is not a single skill but a collection of skills, so the same professional can be highly expert at some tasks in a domain while remaining a novice at others.

Fast and unambiguous feedback, as in braking through a curve or anesthesiology, builds valid intuition, whereas delayed, sparse, or ambiguous feedback, as in a therapist's long-term outcomes or radiology, does not.
To decide whether to trust an expert's intuition, assess the regularity of the environment and the expert's learning history, and largely set aside the expert's own confidence.

Because substitution can produce a high-confidence answer to the wrong question that is subjectively indistinguishable from a valid judgment, subjective confidence is not a good diagnostic of accuracy.
To elicit information from a group, confidentially collect each member's judgment before any open discussion, because this uses the group's available knowledge better than starting with discussion.
The inside view builds a forecast from the specifics of the case at hand, whereas the outside view builds it from the statistics of a reference class of similar cases.
People who hold information about an individual case rarely feel any need for the base-rate statistics of the class it belongs to, even when they already possess that knowledge.

Pallid statistical or outside-view information is routinely discarded when it conflicts with a vivid personal impression of the case, so in competition with the inside view the outside view does not stand a chance.
The reference-class baseline prediction should serve as the anchor, to be adjusted toward case-specific evidence only in proportion to that evidence's validity.
Under the planning fallacy, plans and forecasts are unrealistically close to the best-case scenario and could be improved by consulting the statistics of similar past cases.

Reference-class forecasting cures the planning fallacy: identify an appropriate reference class, obtain its statistics to form a baseline prediction, then adjust for case-specific factors only when there is particular reason to expect more or less optimistic bias than usual.

Optimism is widespread, stubborn, and costly: about forty-seven percent of inventors told their project was hopeless continued anyway and doubled their losses, and self-employment yields mediocre average returns compared with equivalent employment.
Most people genuinely believe they are superior to most others on most desirable traits, the better-than-average effect.

Overconfident and optimistic CEOs take excessive risk, prefer debt to equity, overpay for target companies, and undertake value-destroying mergers, and the market often responds by downgrading the acquiring firm.

Firms with award-winning, celebrated CEOs subsequently underperform in both stock and operating terms while the CEO's pay rises and their attention shifts outside the firm, so business-press celebrity is costly to shareholders.
Executives take greater risks when they personally have more at stake, so their unsound bets stem from genuine overconfidence rather than from gambling with other people's money.
Chief financial officers' one-year forecasts of stock-index returns correlated slightly below zero with the actual outcomes, and the CFOs did not appear to know their forecasts were worthless.

People set drastically overconfident confidence intervals: CFOs' stated eighty-percent intervals captured the outcome only about a third of the time, so a properly calibrated interval is several times wider than the one experts volunteer.
Overconfidence is a manifestation of WYSIATI, because an estimate is built as a coherent story from the information that happens to come to mind, with no allowance for what is unknown or unretrieved.

Social and market pressures reward confident, even misleadingly confident, experts over honest truth-tellers who admit uncertainty, so a candid wide confidence interval is treated as an unacceptable confession of ignorance.

Overconfidence is endemic and encouraged by clients: physicians who were completely certain of a diagnosis were wrong about forty percent of the time on autopsy, yet disclosing uncertainty is censured as a weakness.

An unbiased appreciation of uncertainty is a cornerstone of rationality, but it is not what people and organizations want, so acting on pretended knowledge is often preferred, especially when the stakes are high.

Standard economic theory assumes agents are rational, selfish, and stable in taste (Econs), whereas real people (Humans) have a System 1, are bounded by WYSIATI, are often generous, and frequently do not know their own future preferences.
Prospect theory is a purely descriptive model whose goal is to document and explain systematic violations of the rationality axioms in choices between gambles.

In psychophysics the subjective intensity of a stimulus is roughly a logarithmic function of its physical magnitude, so equal ratios of the physical quantity produce equal increments of subjective experience.

Bernoulli held that the subjective value of wealth is a logarithmic function of wealth, so people evaluate income changes in percentage terms and a given absolute increment matters less to the rich than to the poor.
People do not evaluate gambles by their expected value: most prefer a sure eighty dollars to a gamble worth eighty-two in expectation, because they are risk averse for gains.

Bernoulli's error was to attach utility to absolute states of wealth rather than to changes, a flaw that remained unquestioned for more than two centuries, illustrating how an accepted model can hide its own defect.
Prospect theory defines outcomes as gains and losses relative to a reference point rather than as absolute states of wealth.

Evaluation is relative to a neutral reference point or adaptation level, usually the status quo but sometimes an expectation or entitlement, so the same objective outcome is experienced as good or bad depending on that reference.
Under theory-induced blindness, once a theory is accepted its flaws become nearly invisible, and a sign of genuine advance is being unable to reconstruct why the old error ever seemed sensible.

Under loss aversion the psychological cost of a loss outweighs the psychological benefit of an equal gain, so a coin flip that pays 150 for heads and costs 100 for tails feels unattractive despite its positive expected value.

Because disadvantages of a change loom larger than its advantages, changes for the worse are hard to accept, so unemployed workers' minimum acceptable wage averages about ninety percent of their previous wage and falls by less than ten percent over a year.
In negotiation the reference point is the existing contract or status quo, both sides frame demands as concessions relative to it, and making concessions hurts because of loss aversion.

The rationality assumption is a necessary and productive intellectual tool whose predictions are precise or good approximations in many contexts, so the human deviations of prospect theory matter only in particular contexts dominated by the immediate emotional impact of gains and losses.
condition: The context is one where behavior is driven by the immediate emotional impact of gains and losses.

statement: Prospect theory has flaws of its own and theory-induced blindness is not restricted to expected utility theory, so the same skepticism must be applied even to a favored model.

The classic indifference-curve map omits the individual's current reference point of income and leisure, implicitly and wrongly assuming the status quo and past are irrelevant to how a change is valued.

Under the endowment effect, owning a good raises the minimum price a person will accept to sell it well above the maximum they would pay to buy it, contradicting the standard assumption of a single value for the good.

The endowment effect is explained by loss aversion: giving up a good one owns is more painful than acquiring an equivalent good is pleasurable, because the value function is steeper in the domain of losses.

There is no endowment effect or loss aversion for goods and money held for exchange, such as a merchant's stock or a shopping budget, so the effect applies specifically to goods held for use and enjoyment.
condition: The good is held for use rather than for exchange.

statement: In the mug experiments sellers demanded about twice what buyers and choosers would pay for the identical item and trade volume was under half the standard prediction, and since sellers and choosers face the same options the gap is driven purely by the emotion of giving up something owned.

Loss aversion is built into the automatic evaluations of System 1, as shown by babies clinging to a toy and by brain imaging in which selling a good one would use activates regions associated with disgust and pain.

The endowment effect fades with trading experience and requires physical possession before trading is raised, and veteran traders eliminate it by asking the Econ question of how much they want the good compared with the alternatives.
The brain gives priority to bad news through a fast channel, detecting threats, angry faces, and bad words faster than good ones, with no comparably rapid mechanism for recognizing good news.
Even purely symbolic or verbal threats, such as bad words or an opinion one strongly disagrees with, are registered as threatening by System 1 within a fraction of a second.

Under negativity dominance bad is stronger than good: bad emotions, feedback, information, impressions, and stereotypes carry more weight, form faster, and resist disconfirmation more than their good counterparts, as one cockroach ruins a bowl of cherries but a cherry does nothing for a bowl of cockroaches.
Stable relationships require good interactions to outnumber bad ones by at least about five to one, and a friendship built over years can be destroyed by a single bad action.
The boundary between good and bad is a movable reference point set by circumstances and expectations rather than an absolute level, so the same state feels good or bad depending on what preceded it.

A goal can serve as a reference point so that falling short of it is felt as a loss and exceeding it as a gain, and by negativity dominance the aversion to falling short is stronger than the desire to exceed.
People reduce their effort once a short-term goal is reached, sometimes against economic logic, as cabdrivers with a fixed daily earnings target work longer on slow days and quit early on busy ones.

Loss aversion measurably degrades performance: professional golfers sink putts for par, which avoid the loss of a bogey, about 3.6 percent more often than birdie putts, which are only a foregone gain, at every distance from the hole.
A good theoretical concept is valuable because it generates precise, nonintuitive, testable hypotheses, as loss aversion did in predicting the par-versus-birdie putting gap.

In renegotiating an existing agreement the current terms are the reference point, so any proposed change is seen as a concession, and loss aversion makes each side value its own concessions more than the other's, which makes agreement hard to reach.
Negotiating over a shrinking pie is especially difficult because it requires allocating losses, whereas people bargain far more easily over an expanding pie.

Negotiators often feign intense attachment to a bargaining chip in order to communicate a reference point, and the norm of reciprocity makes a concession presented as painful demand an equally painful concession in return.

Because loss aversion makes people fight harder to prevent losses than to achieve gains, incumbents and territorial owners usually prevail, and prospective losers from a reform resist more fiercely than prospective winners support it.

Judgments of economic fairness are reference-dependent: it is not viewed as unfair for a firm to pass losses on to workers or customers when its profits are threatened, but it is judged unfair to impose a loss on others merely to increase profit.

Violating fairness norms carries real economic cost: employers who are unfair suffer reduced productivity, and customers who feel overcharged relative to a new lower reference price cut their future purchases, in one study by about fifteen percent.

Under the certainty effect, removing the last increment of risk to reach complete certainty is valued far more than an equal probability change in the middle of the range, producing choices that violate expected utility as in the Allais paradox.
When a widely adopted and useful theory is challenged by an anomaly, its adherents tend to note the anomaly and keep using the theory unchanged.
In the domain of losses people are risk seeking, the mirror image of their risk aversion for gains, so faced with a sure loss versus a gamble they tend to gamble.

Facing a high probability of a large loss, people take desperate gambles that likely make things worse for a small hope of avoiding the loss, so risk-taking of this kind often turns manageable failures into disasters, as with failing businesses and losing sides in war.

People assign an inordinately high decision weight to a minuscule probability of a vivid harm, and the resulting emotion is both disproportionate to and insensitive to the actual level of probability.

Under denominator neglect a low-probability event is weighted much more heavily when framed as a relative frequency such as one in one hundred thousand than as an abstract probability such as 0.001 percent, because the frequency conjures a concrete individual victim.

Frequency framing can make a smaller risk seem larger than a bigger one, as a disease killing 1,286 of every 10,000 was judged more dangerous than one killing 24.14 percent, though the first risk is only half as large.
Even experienced forensic psychologists and psychiatrists are swayed by whether a risk is expressed as a frequency or as a probability.
Choice from experience underweights rare events, the opposite of choice from description, largely because many decision makers have never actually experienced the rare event.

Narrow framing, evaluating each risky choice in isolation, combined with loss aversion is a costly curse, whereas aggregating several favorable independent gambles into one broad frame makes them collectively attractive even when each is rejected on its own.
Broad framing, or deliberately thinking like a trader who treats a choice as one of many, blunts the emotional reaction to losses and increases sensible risk-taking.

Individual investors should check their portfolios infrequently, about quarterly rather than daily, because frequent monitoring makes the pain of small losses exceed the pleasure of equal gains and raises loss aversion, whereas aggregated feedback yields less risk aversion, better decisions, and higher returns.
Committing not to change an investment position for several periods, effectively locking it in, improves financial performance by reducing reactive churning.

Adopt a standing risk policy applied routinely to every relevant choice, such as always taking the highest insurance deductible or never buying extended warranties, because a risk policy is a broad frame that aggregates many similar decisions.

The outside view and a risk policy are broad-frame remedies for two opposing biases, the planning fallacy's excess optimism and loss aversion's excess caution, and an organization that can eliminate both should do so.
A decision maker responsible for many independent bets should adopt a broad frame and accept each risk with positive expected value, relying on statistical aggregation to mitigate overall risk.
condition: The bets are numerous and roughly independent.

statement: Money often functions as a proxy for points on a scale of self-regard and achievement, so the ultimate reward or punishment for a choice is frequently emotional rather than economic.
Mental accounting is a form of narrow framing in which people segregate money and outcomes into separate accounts, sometimes usefully for self-control and sometimes foolishly.

Under the disposition effect investors sell winning stocks and hold losing ones in order to close each mental account as a gain, which is costly because recent winners tend to keep winning and realizing losses reduces taxes.
A rational agent evaluates the whole portfolio and sells whichever holding is least likely to do well in the future, without regard to whether it is currently a paper winner or loser.

Under the sunk-cost fallacy people invest additional resources in a losing account when better options exist, throwing good money after bad to avoid the humiliation of closing a failed account, as in driving into a blizzard because the tickets were already paid for.

Escalation of commitment to a failing project reflects the agency problem, because continuing serves the executive who owns it by postponing a permanent stain on their record even as it harms the firm, which is why boards replace a CEO wedded to prior decisions.
A fresh decision maker who does not carry the same mental accounts is better able to ignore the sunk costs of past investments when evaluating current opportunities.
The sunk-cost fallacy can be reduced by teaching: graduate students trained to recognize it in economics and business courses are more willing than others to walk away from a failing project.

The original purchase price of an asset does matter and should be considered even by a rational agent, because in the United States realizing a loss reduces taxes while selling a winner incurs them, so the correct move is often to sell the loser.
Departures from the default option, that is acting rather than doing nothing, produce more regret and blame than sticking with the default when the outcome is bad.
The asymmetric risk of regret biases people toward conventional, risk-averse choices, such as favoring brand names over generics and cleaning up unconventional holdings before year-end review.

Anticipated regret can distort even life-or-death decisions, because a physician who prescribes an unconventional treatment faces more blame for a bad outcome than one who follows the standard of care, making the potential cost outweigh the benefit.

Losses are weighted about twice as much as gains across choices between gambles, the endowment effect, and reactions to price changes, with the loss-aversion coefficient even higher in some situations.

In a taboo tradeoff people refuse to trade any increase in a protected value such as a child's safety for money, yet this all-or-nothing stance is incoherent and can harm those it means to protect, because a fixed safety budget is used better by accepting tiny risks where they are cheap to avoid elsewhere.
The precautionary principle, strictly interpreted, is costly and can be paralyzing because it would have blocked many beneficial innovations, reflecting enhanced loss aversion rooted in System 1.
In a preference reversal people choose the safer bet but price the riskier bet higher, because joint evaluation makes the riskiness salient in a way that single evaluation suppresses.

Single evaluation is dominated by the emotional intensity of System 1, whereas joint evaluation forces the more careful System 2 comparison, so joint judgments are generally more stable and more rational.

To elicit thoughtful and coherent judgments, give judges a broad comparative context rather than isolated cases, because single-case evaluation reflects emotional intensity and anchoring, as punitive-damage awards for a burned child and a defrauded bank reverse under joint evaluation.
Be wary of joint evaluation when the party who controls what you see has a vested interest, because salespeople manipulate the comparison context to steer preferences.
condition: The context of comparison is controlled by an interested party.

statement: A framing effect makes logically identical outcomes described as gains (lives saved) or as losses (lives lost) reverse risk preferences, from risk averse to risk seeking, even among expert decision makers.

When confronted with a framing inconsistency people have no stable underlying preference to appeal to and typically respond with embarrassed silence, because the original choices came from System 1 with no deeper basis.

A consequential quantity should be presented in the frame that supports correct comparison: miles per gallon misleads because it is nonlinear, so gallons per mile is the right frame for comparing fuel savings, and a bad frame misleads policymakers as much as consumers.

Default options powerfully shape important choices that people make thoughtlessly, so opt-out organ-donation forms yield participation near ninety to one hundred percent while opt-in forms in similar countries yield only about four to twelve percent.

Experienced utility, the moment-by-moment area under the curve of pleasure and pain, is the proper criterion for judging some decisions, so paying different amounts for the same gain of experienced utility is a mistake.

Under the peak-end rule the retrospective global evaluation of an experience is well predicted by the average of the pain or pleasure at its most intense moment and at its end, not by the integral over its duration.
Under duration neglect the length of an experience has essentially no effect on its remembered global evaluation.
Decision utility can diverge from experienced utility, so a person's preferences, even memory-based ones formed only minutes earlier, cannot be fully trusted to reflect their actual interests.

The remembering self represents an episode by its peak and its end and composes it into a story, which conflicts with the experiencing self's preference for long pleasure and short pain, an inconsistency built into the design of the mind.

Evaluations of whole lives show duration neglect and a less-is-more effect: adding pleasant but less-happy years to a happy life lowers its judged total happiness, because an average prototype is substituted for a sum.
People care about the narrative of a life, its having a good ending, more than about the sum of its experienced feelings, and are moved even by events that change the stories of those already dead.
Apparent counterexamples to duration neglect, such as longer labor being worse or a longer vacation better, actually reflect the changed quality of the end state rather than the duration itself.

The remembering self, not the experiencing self, typically drives the choice of vacations and experiences, as people plan for the story and memory they will store rather than for the moment being lived.

Experienced emotional well-being and remembered life satisfaction are distinct measures that can diverge, so a factor such as ill health, having children, or high income can affect one far more than the other.

Mood at any moment is determined mainly by the current situation and immediate factors such as time pressure, socializing, or the presence of a boss, rather than by global factors like status or benefits.

Emotional state is largely determined by what a person attends to, so pleasure from an activity requires attending to it, as women who ate without multitasking derived more enjoyment than those who combined eating with other activities.
Emotional pain is unequally distributed across a population: about half of people go through an entire day with no unpleasant episode while a small fraction does most of the suffering.
Being poor makes people miserable, and being rich raises life satisfaction but does not on average improve day-to-day experienced well-being.

Experienced well-being rises with income only up to a satiation level of roughly seventy-five thousand dollars in high-cost areas, beyond which the average gain is zero, plausibly because higher income reduces the ability to enjoy small pleasures.
Severe poverty amplifies the experienced effect of other misfortunes, so illness, divorce, and loneliness hurt the very poor markedly more than those who are more comfortable.

Under errors of affective forecasting, or miswanting, people mispredict how future circumstances will make them feel, so newlyweds discount the base rates of divorce and disappointment and life satisfaction typically declines after marriage.

Answers to global life-satisfaction questions are produced by substitution, with people replacing the hard question by a mood heuristic, so a trivial event such as finding a dime measurably shifts reported satisfaction with life as a whole.
The score a person quickly assigns to their life is determined by a small sample of highly available ideas rather than by a careful weighting of the domains of their life.

Goals set in youth have large lifelong effects: valuing money highly at eighteen predicts both higher adult income and a stronger dependence of life satisfaction on income, so those who wanted money and got it are more satisfied and those who wanted it and did not are more dissatisfied.
Setting goals that are especially difficult to attain is a recipe for a dissatisfied adulthood.

Under the focusing illusion nothing in life is as important as it seems while you are thinking about it, so attention to any single factor such as climate or income distorts its true weight in overall well-being.

People adapt to most new circumstances, good or bad, largely by thinking about them less, so adaptation is in large part the gradual withdrawal of attention, and paraplegics and lottery winners return toward their earlier mood.

The main exceptions with no adaptation are chronic pain, constant loud noise, and severe depression, because pain and noise are biologically set to compel attention and depression is a self-reinforcing cycle of miserable thoughts.

Observers mispredict others' well-being through the focusing illusion by failing to anticipate adaptation, estimating a paraplegic's bad mood a year after the accident far too high, while people who actually know a paraplegic estimate much lower.

The remembering self is subject to a massive focusing illusion, so colostomy patients report experienced happiness no different from a healthy population yet would trade away years of life to be rid of the condition.

The combination of duration neglect and the peak-end rule biases people to prefer a short intense joy over a long moderate happiness, to fear a short intense but tolerable suffering more than a long moderate pain, and to abandon a long happy period likely to end poorly.

Anticipated regret is the verdict of the remembering self, which people accept as final, but that perspective neglects duration, over-weights peaks and ends, and is susceptible to hindsight, so it is not always the correct guide.

A duration-weighted conception of well-being treats all moments alike, but it cannot be a complete theory because people identify with their remembering self and care about their story, so both the remembering and experiencing selves must be considered since their interests diverge.
Declarations that a moment will always be remembered or is deeply meaningful are predictions that are often false, since many things people vow to remember are forgotten within ten years.

Which of the two selves matters more has policy stakes in medicine and welfare, because the ranking of conditions by severity differs depending on whether one measures how much people fear a condition, the suffering they actually experience, or the sacrifice they would make for relief.

In economics rational means only internal logical consistency, so a rational agent may hold bizarre beliefs or preferences as long as they are coherent, a standard that real Humans cannot consistently meet.
Humans are not irrational; the heuristics-and-biases research shows only that they are not well described by the rational-agent model, so they should not be branded irrational.
When people act in ways that seem odd, first examine whether they have a good reason for it, and invoke a psychological bias interpretation only when the rational reasons become implausible.
Humans often need help to make better decisions, and well-designed policies and institutions can provide that help without curtailing freedom, an approach called libertarian paternalism or nudging.

Choice architecture, especially the default option, has a huge effect on outcomes because the default is perceived as the normal choice and deviating from it is an act of commission that requires more deliberation, carries more responsibility, and is more likely to evoke regret.

Effective nudges require no immediate change and convert losses into foregone gains while aligning System 2's laziness with long-term interests, as Save More Tomorrow ties automatic saving increases to future pay raises.

Because Humans routinely sign contracts without reading the fine print, firms can hide important information in plain sight, so consumers need contracts simple enough to actually read rather than mere full disclosure.
A market in which firms compete by offering better products is preferable to one in which the winner is the firm best at obfuscation.

System 2 articulates judgments and choices but usually endorses or rationalizes ideas and feelings generated by System 1, inventing presentable reasons for a System 1 judgment and then believing them.

System 1 is the origin of most of what people do right, not only of errors, because its rich associative model of the world and its repertory of practiced skills usually produce accurate, adequate responses.

Skill develops only given a regular environment, adequate opportunity to practice, and rapid unequivocal feedback, and when these conditions hold the intuitive judgments that quickly come to mind are mostly accurate.
condition: The environment is regular, practice is adequate, and feedback is rapid and unequivocal.

statement: System 1 registers the cognitive ease of processing but issues no warning when it becomes unreliable, so intuitive answers arrive quickly and confidently whether they come from genuine skill or from a heuristic, and System 2 has no simple way to tell the two apart.

Little can be done about biases without a considerable investment of effort, because System 1 is not readily educable and even an expert who studies these errors remains prone to overconfidence, extreme predictions, and the planning fallacy.

The realistic defense against System 1 errors is to learn to recognize situations where errors are likely, such as noticing that a number will act as an anchor or that a choice could change if reframed, then deliberately slow down and call in System 2.
The recognize-slow-down-and-check procedure is least likely to be applied when it is most needed, because questioning one's intuitions is unpleasant under the stress of a big decision.
It is far easier to identify a judgment error when observing others than when about to make it oneself, because observers are less cognitively busy and more open to information than actors.

Organizations avoid errors better than individuals because they think more slowly and can impose orderly procedures such as checklists, reference-class forecasting, and the premortem, supported by a shared vocabulary for spotting biases.

Treat an organization as a factory that manufactures decisions and apply routine quality control at the three stages of framing the problem, collecting the relevant information, and reflection and review, rather than only reviewing processes after a disaster.

A precise, shared vocabulary of biases such as anchoring, narrow framing, and excessive coherence is essential to constructive criticism, because a label is a hook to which everything known about the bias, its causes, effects, and remedies attaches, like the name of a disease.

People rely on a limited number of heuristic principles that reduce the complex tasks of assessing probabilities and predicting values to simpler judgmental operations, which are generally useful but sometimes lead to severe and systematic errors.

Under the representativeness heuristic the probability that A belongs to or originates from B is judged by how much A resembles B, so people order candidate categories by probability and by similarity in exactly the same way.

Intuitive posterior odds are dominated by the sample proportion and are essentially unaffected by sample size, and they are far less extreme than the correct values, a systematic underweighting of evidence known as conservatism.

People expect a random process to look random even within short subsequences, so a run that appears too orderly is judged non-random, and a locally representative sequence in fact deviates from chance by containing too many alternations and too few runs.

Under the gambler's fallacy people wrongly believe that after a run of one outcome the opposite is due, treating chance as self-correcting, when in fact deviations are not corrected as the process unfolds but merely diluted.

Under insensitivity to predictability, people make predictions as extreme as the favorableness of the description, ignoring the reliability of that evidence and the actual predictability of the outcome, as when a five-year forecast of a teacher equals the evaluation of a single trial lesson.

The extremeness and range of predictions should be controlled by predictability, so when predictability is nil the same value such as the average should be predicted for every case, and the range of justified predictions widens only as predictability increases.

Under the illusion of validity, confidence in a prediction depends on how well the chosen outcome matches the input rather than on the factors limiting accuracy, and this unwarranted confidence persists even when the judge knows the predictors are scanty or unreliable, as with selection interviews.

Internal consistency among redundant, correlated inputs raises confidence in a prediction, yet inputs of equal validity yield higher accuracy when independent than when redundant, so redundancy increases confidence while decreasing accuracy.

People fail to expect regression toward the mean where it must occur and invent spurious causal explanations when they notice it, because regression conflicts with the belief that the predicted outcome should be as extreme as the input.

Because behavior improves after punishment and deteriorates after reward by regression alone, people are systematically rewarded for punishing others and punished for rewarding them, a contingency they generally fail to notice, which leads them to overrate punishment and underrate reward.

Because size is judged by the availability of instances, a class whose instances are easier to retrieve, through greater fame, salience, or recency, is judged more numerous than an equally frequent class that is harder to retrieve.

Judged frequency depends on how easily a search set can be generated, so people judge words more likely to begin with a given consonant than to carry it in third position, because first-letter search is easier, even for consonants that are actually more common in third position.

When instances must be constructed rather than recalled, frequency or probability is judged by the ease of constructing them, so vividly imagining many failure contingencies makes a venture appear far more dangerous than it is, while dangers that do not come to mind make it appear safer.

Under illusory correlation people overestimate how often natural associates co-occur and rediscover unfounded lore, an effect so resistant to contradictory data that it persists even when the true correlation is negative and blinds judges to relationships that are actually present.

People overestimate the probability of conjunctive events, where every step in a chain must occur, because they anchor on the high probability of each elementary step and adjust insufficiently, producing unwarranted optimism that a multi-step plan will succeed on time.

People underestimate the probability of disjunctive events, where failure follows if any one component fails, so they underrate the chance that a complex system fails, and the direction of the anchoring bias can be read from event structure: chain-like conjunctions are overestimated and funnel-like disjunctions underestimated.

Assessed subjective probability distributions are far too tight, with true values falling outside the stated ninety-eight percent interval about thirty percent of the time, because people anchor on their best estimate and adjust insufficiently, and proper scoring incentives do not eliminate the miscalibration.

How a probability is elicited changes the answer, because asking for percentile values versus asking for odds at stated values invokes different anchors and yields systematically different, less or more extreme, distributions.

These cognitive biases are not attributable to motivation such as wishful thinking, because several of the severe judgment errors persist even when subjects are encouraged and rewarded to be accurate.

Experienced and statistically trained people commit the same heuristic biases when they reason intuitively, so sophistication removes elementary errors like the gambler's fallacy but not similar fallacies in more intricate, less transparent problems.

People fail to learn fundamental statistical rules such as regression toward the mean and the effect of sample size from lifelong experience because the relevant instances are not coded appropriately, since they do not attend to the variables that would reveal the pattern.

People cannot detect their own miscalibration because they do not naturally group their predictions by the probability they assigned, so they never discover that only about half of the forecasts they judged ninety percent likely actually came true.

Internal consistency is not sufficient for judged probabilities to be rational; they must also be compatible with the person's whole web of beliefs and knowledge, since a perfectly coherent set of gambler's-fallacy probabilities is still incompatible with knowing a coin has no memory.

Frame invariance cannot be expected to hold and a sense of confidence in a choice does not ensure the same choice would be made under another framing, so it is good practice to test the robustness of preferences by deliberately framing a decision problem in more than one way.

Decision weights are nonlinear and regressive with respect to stated probability: moderate and high probabilities are underweighted relative to certainty while low probabilities are overweighted, and very low probabilities are either grossly overweighted or neglected, making weights unstable there.

Under the category-boundary effect a change from impossibility to possibility, or from possibility to certainty, has a larger impact on decision weight than a comparable change in the middle of the probability scale.

Under the pseudo-certainty effect an outcome that is actually uncertain is weighted as if it were certain when a problem is framed in stages so that people ignore an earlier phase and treat a later contingent gain as sure.

People find probabilistic insurance distinctly unattractive because they undervalue a reduction of a hazard relative to its elimination, so halving a risk is not judged worth half the premium, and this applies to any protective action such as a checkup, new tires, or an alarm that reduces but does not eliminate a hazard.

Protection is more attractive when framed as fully eliminating a specific risk than as reducing an overall risk, even for identical actuarial effect, as a vaccine that cuts disease probability from twenty to ten percent is preferred when described as fully effective against one of two strains rather than as effective in half of cases.

A framer such as a physician or advisor can influence a decision without distorting or suppressing any information, merely by framing outcomes as gains or losses, and such formulation effects can occur fortuitously or be exploited deliberately, as labeling a price gap a cash discount rather than a credit surcharge exploits loss aversion.

People spontaneously frame decisions in topical mental accounts anchored to a local reference level, so willingness to travel to save a fixed amount depends on the item's price, with sixty-eight percent making the trip to save five dollars on a fifteen-dollar calculator but only twenty-nine percent on a one-hundred-twenty-five-dollar one, though the minimal and comprehensive accounts are identical.

Loss aversion produces a status quo bias, because the disadvantages of any alternative are weighted as losses and its advantages as gains, so the same difference in pay or conditions looms larger as a disadvantage than as an advantage and the decision maker favors retaining the status quo.

The instability of preferences produces a preference for stability, since once separated twins adopt their new environments as reference points each prefers to stay, and the combination of adaptation and loss aversion also buffers regret and envy by devaluing foregone alternatives and others' endowments.

Loss aversion and the endowment effect do not apply to routine commercial exchange, because a merchant nets costs and revenues over a period and a consumer treats money as a proxy for alternative purchases, so matching debits and credits cancel before evaluation.
condition: The transaction is a routine exchange rather than a good held for use.

statement: Framing not only anticipates experience but can mold it, so framing an expenditure as an uncompensated loss versus the price of insurance can change the actual experience of the outcome, even though a mortality-versus-survival frame changes choice without changing experience.

All analyses of rational choice incorporate the principles of dominance and invariance, yet human choices demonstrably violate invariance, so preferences that reverse under mere reformulation cannot be defended as simply reflecting different values.

By Bayes's rule in odds form the posterior odds equal the prior odds times the likelihood ratio, so even a fairly accurate test with a 25-to-1 likelihood ratio applied to a rare condition present in only one in six hundred cases yields a posterior probability of just about four percent.

Under the evaluability hypothesis, preference reversals between single and joint evaluation arise because some attributes become evaluable only in joint evaluation, so an attribute that cannot be judged in isolation drives the comparison once the options are seen together.
Loss aversion has a neural basis, since individuals with focal amygdala lesions show little or no loss aversion in their risky monetary choices.

Poverty can make economic behavior more realistic and in some respects more rational, because the poor are more likely to respond to real outcomes than to their verbal description and so are less swayed by framing.
Forecasting is not an innate 'you have it or you don't' talent; it is a skill that can be cultivated.
About 2% of a large pool of volunteer forecasters ('superforecasters') forecast geopolitical and economic events with accuracy far better than chance.
Media, corporations, and governments routinely produce and consume forecasts without ever measuring or reporting the forecaster's accuracy track record.
The forecasting accuracy of most high-profile pundits is never rigorously tested, so their real track records are unknown despite their public authority.
In a twenty-year study, the average expert predicted political and economic events about as accurately as random guessing on many questions.
condition: on many political and economic questions, especially longer-range ones
exception: 'many' does not equal all; short-range questions were beatable

statement: Expert forecasting accuracy declines as the time horizon lengthens: it is easiest to beat chance about one year out and falls toward the chance ('dart-throwing chimpanzee') level three to five years out.
In nonlinear, complex systems, tiny differences in initial conditions can amplify into large divergences (the butterfly effect), imposing hard limits on long-range predictability.
condition: in nonlinear/chaotic systems such as weather and geopolitics

statement: Accumulating more knowledge and data-crunching power does not necessarily increase the predictability of complex systems.
It is possible to foresee the future to a useful degree, and any intelligent, open-minded, hardworking person can cultivate the requisite forecasting skills.
condition: at least in some situations and to some extent
exception: there remain irreducible limits to foresight that cannot be surmounted

statement: How predictable something is depends on what you are trying to predict, how far into the future, and under what circumstances; predictability and unpredictability coexist.
Treating the future as simply 'predictable or not' (clocklike versus cloud-like) is a false dichotomy to be avoided.
Weather forecasts are typically reliable a few days ahead but grow markedly less accurate three to five days out, and beyond about a week are no better than chance.
As a general rule the further ahead one forecasts the harder it is to see, but there can be prolonged exceptions to that rule.
exception: prolonged exceptions exist, e.g. long bull markets or long-stable ecosystems that hold until an abrupt shock

statement: Forecasting skill improves only through a repeated cycle of forecast, measure accuracy, and revise; meteorology improves because forecasters make many forecasts and routinely check them.
Most forecasting does not improve because consumers of forecasts do not demand evidence of accuracy, so there is no measurement, without measurement no revision, and without revision no improvement.
To drive progress, set a clear goal and find a measure that tracks progress toward it; measurement is fundamental to improving performance.
Forecasts often serve goals other than accuracy (to entertain, advance agendas, impress, or comfort), and this unacknowledged jumble of goals obstructs measurement and improvement.
Foresight is a real, measurable skill: some people reliably judge how high-stakes events will unfold three months to about a year and a half ahead, better than chance.
condition: for time frames of roughly three months to eighteen months

statement: What makes superforecasters good is not who they are but what they do: foresight is the product of particular ways of thinking, gathering information, and updating beliefs that can be learned and cultivated.
A roughly sixty-minute tutorial covering basic forecasting concepts (the 'Ten Commandments') improved forecasters' accuracy by about 10% across the tournament year.
Even modest improvements in foresight, if sustained over time, compound into a large cumulative advantage.
The difference between forecasting heavyweights and amateurs is the ability to discriminate finely between probabilities, e.g. to tell a 60/40 bet from a 40/60 bet.
Commitment to self-improvement is the strongest single predictor of forecasting performance.

In the IARPA tournament the Good Judgment Project beat the official control group by 60% in year one and 78% in year two, beat university competitors by 30-70%, and outperformed professional intelligence analysts who had access to classified data.
Superforecasting requires only minimum levels of intelligence, numeracy, and world knowledge; above that threshold what matters most is how the forecaster thinks, not raw intelligence or arcane math.
condition: above a minimum threshold of intelligence, numeracy, and knowledge

statement: Superior judgment demands thinking that is open-minded, careful, curious, and above all self-critical, together with sustained focus.

When a well-validated statistical algorithm exists for the problem, use it: across more than two hundred studies statistical algorithms beat subjective judgment in most cases and tie in the rest, while being quicker and cheaper.
condition: when a well-validated statistical algorithm exists for the problem at hand

statement: Well-validated algorithms rarely exist for the specific problem at hand, so subjective human judgment remains necessary for most real forecasting.
Combining human judgment with computers (as in freestyle chess) can be more robust than either alone: the human draws on the computer's strengths but occasionally overrides it.
The desirable future model pairs a human expert with a computer to overcome the human's cognitive limitations and biases; the pure subjective-judgment 'guru' model is becoming obsolete.
Human thought is beset by systematic psychological pitfalls and biases, a fact only widely recognized in the last decade or two.

People are too quick to make up their minds and too slow to change them, and unless these mistakes are examined they persist for years (as when a specialist and patient both trusted a wrong cancer diagnosis without waiting for the pathology report).

Medicine advanced rapidly only once physicians accepted that experience and perception are unreliable for judging whether a treatment works and turned to scientific testing; forecasting needs the same measurement revolution.
The only alternative to a controlled experiment that delivers real insight is an uncontrolled experiment that produces merely the illusion of insight.
A single observed outcome cannot reveal whether an intervention helped, hurt, or did nothing, because too many confounding factors and alternative explanations are involved.
Randomly assigning subjects to treatment and control groups balances their differences so any outcome gap can be attributed to the treatment, provided enough people participate.
condition: with a sufficiently large number of participants

statement: People already inclined to believe an intervention works read ambiguous evidence in its favor, so strong evidence and rigorous experimentation are needed to overturn preconceptions.
Confidence untempered by doubt (the 'God complex' of trusting one's judgment as self-evidently true) blocks validation and causes stagnation.
'Cargo cult' science has the outward form of science but lacks what makes it truly scientific, namely doubt and rigorous testing.
The rate of scientific progress is set not by the rate of observation alone but, more importantly, by the rate at which one creates new things to test.

Even someone who champions the principle of not rushing to judgment can rush to judgment under pressure, as when the skeptic Cochrane accepted a wrong terminal-cancer diagnosis without waiting for the pathology report; understanding a bias does not immunize you against it.
Introspection can capture only a tiny fraction of the complex processes that actually drive our decisions.
Thinking runs on two systems: System 1 is fast, automatic, and always running; System 2 is slow, conscious, and effortful and is charged with interrogating System 1's answers.
In the standard decision routine System 1 delivers an answer first and only then can System 2 examine it, but whether System 2 actually engages is not guaranteed.

Most people, including very intelligent people, are not reflective: they accept System 1's first answer and write it down without checking, as the bat-and-ball item of the Cognitive Reflection Test shows.

Intuitive judgment is insensitive to the quality of the evidence it rests on: System 1 treats whatever evidence is at hand as reliable and sufficient, an assumption Kahneman labels WYSIATI (What You See Is All There Is).

Humans are creative confabulators, hardwired to invent coherent stories that impose order even when they do not actually know the cause, as split-brain experiments and after-the-fact stock-market narratives demonstrate.
The core error is moving too fast from confusion and uncertainty to a clear, confident conclusion without pausing on the intermediate step 'this is one possible explanation but there are others.'

Confirmation bias leads us to seize the first plausible explanation, gather supportive evidence without checking its reliability, and become 'motivated skeptics' who explain away evidence that undercuts our belief.

Treat an intuition as a plausible hypothesis, give alternative explanations a genuine hearing, and ask 'What would convince me I am wrong?'; the best evidence a hypothesis is true is often an attempt to falsify it that fails.
Set aside the feeling of certainty and replace it with finely measured degrees of doubt that can be reduced, though never to zero, by better evidence from better studies.

A coherent, tidy story that 'all fits' produces confidence, but coherence is not truth: high confidence mainly signals that a person has constructed a coherent story, not that the story is true, so admissions of uncertainty deserve to be taken seriously.

System 1's WYSIATI machinery was adaptive in the ancestral environment, where fast snap judgments from little evidence were sometimes essential to survival, even though it produces errors in modern analytic tasks.
Faced with a hard question we often unconsciously substitute an easier one and answer that instead (attribute substitution, or 'bait and switch'), letting the easy answer stand in for the hard one.
The availability heuristic and Kahneman's other heuristics are essentially bait-and-switch maneuvers carried out unconsciously by System 1.
System 1 cannot be switched off; the automatic 'tip-of-your-nose' perspective keeps running nonstop beneath conscious thought.
Intuition versus analysis ('blink' versus 'think') is a false dichotomy; the task is not to choose one but to blend the two as situations evolve.

Accurate intuition is pattern recognition: with training or experience people encode large numbers of patterns, and a competent expert immediately senses when something does not fit a familiar pattern.
Pattern-recognition ability comes at the cost of susceptibility to false positives, so intuition can fail as spectacularly as it can succeed.

Whether intuition yields insight or delusion depends on whether you work in a world of valid cues that can be learned; trust expert intuition more in high-validity environments (a fireground commander, a nurse) than in low-validity ones (stock picking).
condition: only in an environment that supplies valid, regular cues learnable through experience
exception: in low-validity environments such as stock picking, intuition is not trustworthy

statement: Valid intuition must be learned through opportunity and effort; without genuine opportunities to learn the cues, a seemingly valid intuition can only be luck.
Even where intuition is valid, double-check it with conscious thought when time permits, as the world chess champion respects his intuition yet still spends most of his time double-checking it.
If you have time before a big decision, think it through deliberately and be prepared to accept that what seems obviously true now may turn out to be false later.
condition: when there is time to think before deciding

statement: Tip-of-your-nose illusions are so persuasive that people routinely bypass deliberate analysis and go with a gut feeling, as when a columnist predicted an election result because 'the vibrations are right.'

Twenty-first-century forecasting resembles nineteenth-century medicine: theories, assertions, and confident well-paid figures but little experimentation or science, so we know much less than most people realize, and bad forecasts steer us subtly toward costly decisions.

To judge a forecast you must know exactly what it means and cannot fill in assumptions; vague terms leave a forecast too ambiguous to score right or wrong (as with Ballmer's undefined 'significant market share').
A forecast that omits a time frame can never be proven wrong, because one can always respond 'just wait, it's coming.'
A forecast hedged as a mere 'risk' (the event may or may not follow) is not falsified when the event fails to occur, so hedging words change what counts as an accurate forecast.

Highly informed, confident experts across the political spectrum failed to foresee Gorbachev and the Soviet turn, showing that agreement and confidence among experts are not evidence of predictive accuracy.
After a surprise, experts tend to downplay their predictive failures and sketch a retrospective arc of history that makes it appear they saw it coming all along.
Intelligence and integrity are not enough to guarantee good judgment; tip-of-your-nose delusions can fool anyone, even the best and brightest, perhaps especially them.
A forecast without a time frame is untestable: forecasters rely on an implicit shared timeline that erodes as memories fade, producing unresolvable disputes about the forecast's real meaning.
Forecasts that rely on implicit understandings of key terms instead of explicit definitions are untestable, and such vague verbiage is more the rule than the exception.

Vague probability words such as 'serious possibility' or 'fair chance' mean wildly different numeric odds to different people, creating dangerous misunderstandings, as when analysts who all wrote 'serious possibility' privately meant anything from 80/20 to 20/80.

Probability estimates should carry designated numerical meanings and be narrowed as much as the evidence allows; reserve the word 'possible' only for cases where no probability can reasonably be assigned.
The worry that a numerical probability implies false objectivity or exactitude is answered not by dropping numbers but by making clear that numbers, like words, express only a subjective estimate.

Expressing probabilities as numbers is superior to vague words because numbers are explicit and force forecasters to examine how they are thinking (metacognition), and with practice forecasters get better at distinguishing finer degrees of uncertainty.

The wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy is judging a single probabilistic forecast by which side of 50% it fell on: a '70% chance of rain' forecast is not wrong merely because it does not rain, and one probabilistic forecast alone cannot be judged accurate or inaccurate.

Vague language lets a forecaster exploit the wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy: 'a fair chance' can be retroactively stretched above or shrunk below 50% so the forecaster always appears right, a perverse incentive that rewards rubbery words over firm numbers.

Words like 'may' and 'might' are hollow because they assert only possibility and say nothing about probability, so a 'may' forecast can never be wrong; serious forecasts must instead use clearly defined terms, explicit timelines, and numbers.
A single probabilistic forecast cannot be judged, but a large number of them can be tabulated to determine a forecaster's track record.

Calibration measures whether stated probabilities match observed frequencies: a perfectly calibrated forecaster's '70%' events happen 70% of the time; forecasts above the diagonal are underconfident and those below it are overconfident.
Calibration calculations require many forecasts, so they are impractical for rare or one-off events; judging such forecasts demands patient data collection and cautious interpretation.
condition: only where enough forecasts of comparable events accumulate

statement: Resolution is the second facet of accuracy: decisively assigning high probabilities to things that happen and low probabilities to things that do not; good judgment requires both good calibration and good resolution, not calibration alone.

A sound scoring system rewards decisive correct calls and punishes overconfident wrong ones: hubris must be punished, so a forecaster who calls something a slam dunk should take a large hit when it fails, as in betting odds.

A Brier score measures the distance between what was forecast and what happened: 0 is perfect, 0.5 is chance-level or a hedged fifty-fifty call, and 2.0 is maximally wrong; like golf, lower is better.

A Brier score is meaningful only against a benchmark: what counts as good depends on the difficulty of what is being forecast, and a low score can reflect an easy environment rather than skill (always predicting 'hot and sunny' in Phoenix in June scores near zero).

The real test of forecasting skill is beating a mindless baseline such as 'predict no change,' not a raw hit rate: predicting 'no change' would have called 48 of 50 states in the 2012 US election, so 'called all fifty' overstates the skill involved.

Comparing forecasters fairly requires a level playing field of the same questions over the same period; dredging old forecasts from newspapers rarely yields apples-to-apples comparisons because real-world forecasters seldom predict the same developments over the same interval.

The rigorous way to study forecasting is to assemble many forecasters, ask large numbers of questions with precise time frames and unambiguous language, require numerical probability estimates, and wait for outcomes before scoring.

Intelligence and knowledge may improve forecasting only up to a point, with benefits tapering off quickly, so credentialed experts may be only slightly more accurate than attentive, well-informed lay readers.

In the EPJ study experts split into two statistically distinguishable groups: one no better than chance (worse than a dart-throwing chimp on long-range questions) and one that beat chance modestly, showing that some real political foresight exists.
What separated the more accurate forecasters was not credentials, access to classified information, or ideological leaning (what they thought) but how they thought.

Hedgehog thinkers organize everything around one Big Idea, force complex problems into a preferred cause-effect template, dismiss what does not fit, are unusually confident, and resist changing their minds even after a prediction clearly fails.

Fox thinkers are pragmatic, draw on many analytical tools chosen to fit each problem, gather information from many sources, speak in possibilities and probabilities rather than certainties, and more readily admit error and change their minds.
Foxes beat hedgehogs on both calibration and resolution, not merely by playing it safe with hedged probabilities; foxes had real foresight and hedgehogs did not.

A single Big Idea acts like tinted glasses that are never removed: it distorts reality, and additional information seen through the same lens increases the hedgehog's confidence without improving accuracy.
Hedgehogs' forecasting accuracy actually declined on the subjects they knew most about, because deeper expertise reinforced their one distorting Big Idea.

EPJ found an inverse correlation between fame and accuracy: the more famous an expert was, the less accurate his forecasts, because the media selects confident hedgehogs who tell simple, gripping stories.
