Simple, confident, one-perspective stories that declare things certain or impossible calm audiences and advance careers but impair foresight, whereas complex, caveated fox reasoning is bad media but good forecasting.

Aggregating the judgments of many people consistently beats the accuracy of the average group member and is often startlingly accurate, as when a fair crowd's average guess of an ox's weight was 1,197 pounds against a true 1,198.

The crowd average is not always more accurate than every individual, but individuals who beat the group tend to be different people each time, so consistently beating the aggregate reflects rare skill rather than luck.

Aggregation works because useful information is dispersed: valid pieces held by different people all point the same way and accumulate, while individual errors point in different directions and cancel out.

How well aggregation works depends on what is aggregated: pooling people who know nothing yields nothing, while pooling enough people who each know a little, especially about diverse things, produces the largest and most useful collective information pool.
condition: the contributors must collectively hold valid, diverse information

statement: Aggregations of aggregations, such as a poll of polls or combining polls with expert panels and quantitative models, can further sharpen forecasts.

Foxes forecast by deploying many analytical ideas and seeking many information sources and then synthesizing them into one conclusion; this inside-one-skull aggregation is in principle the same as a wisdom-of-crowds average.

Looking at a problem from only one perspective, even a logically sound one, produces error; the guess-the-number game shows you must combine the pure-logic view with the psycho-logic of how real, imperfect people actually behave.

Perspective-taking, imagining a situation from another's viewpoint (an opponent's likely cards, other contestants' reasoning), is essential but does not come naturally, because the tip-of-your-nose perspective insists it already sees reality correctly.

Actively aggregating many perspectives (the dragonfly-eye approach) is a key reason foxes forecast better than hedgehogs, and the fine-grained gradations this yields often separate good forecasters from great ones.

The fox/hedgehog distinction is a spectrum, not a dichotomy: people think differently in different circumstances and their thinking habits are not immutable, so one can deliberately shift modes with effort.
All models are wrong but some are useful: the fox/hedgehog model is a simplifying starting point for understanding forecasting styles, not a complete account of human thinking.

Judge a past judgment by whether it was reasonable given the information available at the time, not by whether the outcome turned out correct; this requires mentally traveling back and resisting knowledge of what later happened.
A judgment can be both reasonable and wrong: being wrong does not make a conclusion unreasonable, as with the intelligence community's sincere and defensible but false conclusion about Iraqi WMDs.

Replacing 'Was it a good decision?' with 'Did it have a good outcome?' is a pernicious bait and switch: a lucky good outcome does not make a foolish bet wise, nor does an unlucky bad outcome make a sound bet unwise.
Drawing lessons from outcomes alone rather than from the quality of the decision degrades judgment over time; good poker players, investors, and executives evaluate the decision, not just the result.

The intelligence community's WMD errors were correctable: better analysis would have made the conclusion less confident rather than different, and a 60-70% estimate instead of certainty might have changed the decision to invade.

Stating a conclusion in certainty language that admits no possibility of surprise ('Iraq has...') is hubris; the intelligence community was not merely wrong but wrong when it declared it could not be wrong.

The WMD analysis never seriously explored the possibility that it was wrong: there were no red teams, no devil's advocates, and no competing-hypothesis papers, and failing even to consider an alternative is worse than considering and rejecting it.

Analytical methods should be rigorously tested under realistic conditions rather than adopted for their intuitive appeal; the CIA's psychology-of-bias training manual, though sensible, has never been tested for efficacy.
Without accuracy metrics there is no meaningful way to hold forecasters accountable for accuracy; officials' claims of being right '80% or 90% of the time' are merely guesses.

Accountability for process (did you consider alternatives and look for contrary evidence) is not accountability for accuracy; ticking process boxes without ever checking whether forecasts come true is like ensuring physicians wash their hands but never checking whether the treatment works.

The most informative forecasting questions lie in a 'Goldilocks zone' of difficulty, neither so easy that any attentive newsreader gets them right nor so hard that no one can, which is the best place to find and cultivate talent.
Human cognitive systems cannot forecast turning points in the lives of individuals or nations several years into the future, and no amount of effort or talent search will overcome that hard limit.
condition: for turning points several years out

statement: The only way to know whether a forecasting intervention like training actually works is a controlled experiment: randomly give the intervention to one group of forecasters and not another, hold all else constant, and compare accuracy.

The Good Judgment Project's winning method identified the top forecasters, computed a crowd average that gave those top forecasters extra weight, and then 'extremized' the result by pushing it closer to 100% or 0%.

Extremizing works because each member of a crowd holds only part of the dispersed information; if everyone had all of it they would be more confident, so pushing the aggregate toward the extremes simulates full information-sharing.
condition: when relevant information is genuinely dispersed and diverse across independent forecasters

statement: A few hundred ordinary volunteers using simple aggregation methods beat professional intelligence analysts who had access to classified data, with superforecasters reportedly about 30% more accurate than analysts reading secret intercepts.
The IARPA tournament had forecasters continuously update their forecasts in real time, scoring each revision as a separate forecast, unlike one-shot forecasting studies.

The top ~2% of volunteers (superforecasters) had a collective Brier score of 0.25 versus 0.37 for other forecasters, outperformed regulars by more than 60% by year four, and could forecast about three times further out (300 days as accurately as regulars at 100 days).

Publicly testing forecasting accuracy threatens organizational insiders, because individuals' interest in preserving a comfortable status quo conflicts with the organization's interest in accuracy, which is why forecasting tournaments are rare.
Superforecasting is a reproducible skill rather than a unique oracle's gift: dozens of ordinary volunteers independently reached the top of the rankings.

Randomness is easily mistaken for skill: among thousands of people each making many coin-toss calls, some will appear highly accurate by pure luck, so extreme results in a large group say nothing about the skill of those who achieve them.
People have no intuitive feel for randomness; it is invisible from the tip-of-your-nose perspective and can be seen only by deliberately stepping outside oneself.

An early run of purely random hits creates an illusion of control and prediction, making even elite students sincerely believe they can predict random outcomes, as Langer's rigged coin experiment showed.

A cited track record of dramatic forecasting successes tells you almost nothing about a forecaster's accuracy, because a chimp throwing enough darts hits bull's-eyes and anyone can 'call' a crash by perpetually predicting one.

Showing that one person's success was individually improbable and concluding it cannot be luck ignores how many others were trying; with thousands of attempts, someone getting that lucky becomes likely, just as a lottery winner is not a skilled ticket-picker.
Business success stories rarely provide solid evidence that the highlighted qualities caused the outcome or that copying them will reproduce it, and they rarely acknowledge the role of luck.
Skill versus luck is a false dichotomy: most performance mixes both in varying proportions, from almost all luck to almost all skill.

Regression to the mean: because extreme results are partly luck, a later measurement tends to move toward the average, as father-son heights (correlation about 0.5) predict a tall father's son to be only halfway to the population mean.

Regression to the mean explains why a treatment sought when a fluctuating symptom is at its worst appears to work: you would probably have improved anyway, and forgetting this underlies many things people wrongly believe.
The speed of regression to the mean diagnoses the luck-versus-skill mix: slow regression indicates a skill-dominated activity while fast regression indicates a chance-dominated one.

Superforecasters did not regress to the mean in years 2 and 3 but increased their lead, evidence of skill rather than luck; the offsetting cause was being recognized as 'super' and placed on teams of strong colleagues.

The year-to-year correlation of individual forecasting performance is about 0.65: roughly 30% of superforecasters fall from the top 2% each year while 70% remain, a consistency near-impossible for luck (about 1 in 100 million) but likely (about 1 in 3) at that correlation.
Do not treat any year's top forecasters as infallible, since luck ensures even superstars will occasionally have an ordinary year, yet their results overall reflect genuine skill rather than luck.
Some questions carry irreducible uncertainty, resolved by quirky last-minute events or nonlinear interactions among many variables (such as the price of oil) that no forecaster could foresee.

Intelligence and knowledge help forecasting but add little beyond a threshold: the large gap is from the general public to forecasters, not from forecasters to superforecasters, who score around the 80th percentile rather than genius level.
condition: beyond a threshold level of intelligence and knowledge

statement: Requisite intelligence and knowledge are necessary but not sufficient for good forecasting: many clever, informed forecasters fell short, and brilliant officials such as those who escalated the Vietnam War made disastrous forecasts.

A critical forecast should rest on serious analysis of its underlying assumptions; the Vietnam domino-theory forecast was held with certainty yet never critically analyzed until years after the escalation decisions, a failure to examine assumptions.
Ultimately it is not raw mental crunching power that determines forecasting accuracy but how that capacity is used.

Fermi-ize a hard question by breaking it into sub-questions ('what would have to be true?', 'what information would let me answer this?') to separate the knowable from the unknowable and bring the guessing into the open, which usually yields a more accurate estimate than a black-box hunch.
Decomposing a question into estimable parts and combining crude guesses can produce a surprisingly accurate answer from little or no data, as in estimating the number of piano tuners in a city.
When estimating an unknown quantity, set a 90% confidence interval (a range you are 90% sure contains the true value) and reason to a defensible point within it rather than blurting a single number.

Faced with a hard question, System 1 substitutes an easier related question that is not actually responsive, so reread the exact question to catch the swap (the Arafat question asked whether inquiries would find polonium, not whether Israel poisoned him).

Enumerate the distinct pathways by which an event could occur: each additional independent way it could happen raises its overall probability (Arafat could have been poisoned by Israel, by Palestinian enemies, or contaminated after death).

Begin an estimate with the outside view (the base rate: how common the outcome is in a broader reference class) before considering the specifics of the particular case, for example starting from the 62% of households that own a pet.

The inside view (concrete, story-rich specifics) is seductive, so even smart people neglect the outside view and read illusory meaning into unsurprising facts, as when a pundit found deep significance in a former president's approval rating rising, though such ratings always rise after leaving office.

Refine the outside view by narrowing the reference class to match the specific case more closely, such as using the pet-ownership rate of single-family detached homes (about 73%) rather than of all households.

When no ready base rate exists, construct an outside view Fermi-style by bounding the probability above zero and below 100% and reasoning to a range and midpoint, rather than skipping straight to the inside view (Arafat: bounded to 20-80%, start at 50%).

The outside view must come first because of anchoring: starting from the inside view risks anchoring on a meaningless number, whereas the outside-view base rate provides a meaningful anchor to adjust from.

Anchoring biases estimates toward whatever starting number is in mind, even an obviously irrelevant one, and people typically underadjust away from the anchor, so a bad anchor easily produces a bad estimate.

Explore the inside view in a targeted, purposeful way, as an investigation rather than an aimless amble, by structuring each pathway to a 'yes' as a hypothesis and researching evidence for and against it.

Merge the outside and inside views into one synthesized estimate, as one demonstration did by starting from a base rate of Islamist attacks (1.2/year), adjusting for a heightened ISIS threat and increased security to 1.8/year, and scaling to the forecast window to reach 34%.

Adjust the base rate for case-specific developments, but weigh opposing factors against each other and move the estimate only as far as the net evidence warrants rather than overreacting to the most salient change.
A synthesis of outside and inside views is a good beginning, not the end; strong forecasters keep seeking additional perspectives from teammates and experts to fold into their estimate.

The 'crowd within': asking yourself to assume your first judgment is wrong, consider why, and make a second independent estimate, then averaging the two, improves accuracy almost as much as consulting a second person; letting several weeks pass before the second estimate has a similar effect.
Writing a judgment down and critiquing it as if you were someone else creates distance from it so you can scrutinize it for holes, asking 'Would I be convinced by this if I were somebody else?'

To counter confirmation bias, flip the question's wording (from 'Will they grant the visa?' to 'Will they deny the visa?'), which tilts your evidence search in the opposite direction and surfaces reasons you would otherwise overlook.
Knowing about confirmation bias, deliberately seek out evidence that cuts both ways rather than only evidence that supports the way the question is framed.
Fermi estimation, once practiced, can become a natural habit of thought that gives a forecaster a large advantage in breaking apart otherwise intimidating questions.

Dragonfly-eye forecasting requires sustained point-counterpoint reasoning ('on the one hand, on the other, on the third hand') that synthesizes many dissonant perspectives, continued well past where most people would give up.

Because people naturally gravitate to like-minded sources, deliberately cultivate exposure to diverse and ideologically varied information, as one superforecaster did by building a tagged source database and a program that selects readings to maximize diversity.

Active open-mindedness means treating beliefs as hypotheses to be tested rather than treasures to be guarded: taking seriously evidence against your beliefs, attending to those who disagree, and treating a change of mind as a strength rather than a weakness.

An appetite for questioning basic, emotionally charged beliefs (self-critical thinking) matters more than raw intelligence: a less brilliant but more self-critical person will often out-forecast a smarter person who lacks that capacity.

Superforecasters score high in 'need for cognition' (enjoyment of hard mental work) and openness to experience (curiosity and preference for variety), often reframing an unfamiliar question as an opportunity to learn something new.

Superforecasters are almost uniformly highly numerate, yet they rarely use explicit math models; the great majority of their forecasts come from careful thought and nuanced judgment rather than arcane calculation.
Numeracy helps forecasting not because it unlocks arcane predictive math but for a subtler reason tied to comfort with probability, so advanced mathematics is not a prerequisite for superforecasting.

Universal agreement among people asked to judge a hard problem independently is a warning flag of groupthink, not reassurance; a spread of judgments is welcome evidence that people are thinking for themselves.
When independent advisors give a range of estimates, synthesize them (by simple or respect-weighted averaging) rather than demanding consensus, applying dragonfly eye at the group level.
A leader should encourage advisors to say what they truly believe rather than what the leader wants to hear, treating the gathering and presentation of diverse views as a critical part of the job.

A claim can be 'right but unreasonable', the mirror image of 'wrong but reasonable': a correct conclusion stated more extremely than the evidence supports (100% certainty that bin Laden was in the compound) is still poor judgment, and the lucky outcome does not redeem it.

Even a highly probable conclusion is not certain: explicitly enumerate the alternative explanations, since several individually tiny possibilities add up to a non-trivial residual probability, and these fine distinctions matter (as the WMD failure showed).

People often say '50/50' to mean 'I'm not sure' rather than a literal probability; retreating to a 50% ignorance prior because advisors' estimates disagree discards the real information contained in their collective judgment.
Most people operate a coarse three-setting mental dial for uncertainty ('gonna happen', 'not gonna happen', 'maybe') rather than fine-grained probabilities.

The coarse mental dial is an evolutionary adaptation: fine probability distinctions were rarely needed and could be dangerously slow against ancestral survival threats, so humans ignore small chances and default to binary judgments.
Certainty (0% and 100%) weighs far more heavily in the mind than probability theory says it should: people will pay disproportionately more to eliminate the last of a risk than to halve it.

Confidence and accuracy are positively correlated, but people exaggerate the size of that correlation and equate confidence with competence, trusting more confident advisers even when track records are identical and dismissing forecasters who give middling probabilities as incompetent or lazy.

Probability is deeply counterintuitive: grasping 'a 70% chance of rain' requires understanding that rain should occur on 70% of such days, which is alien to the native 'it will or will not rain', so even sophisticated people make elementary probability errors.

People routinely translate a high probability such as 80% into a certainty that the event will happen, so communicators must actively insist that '80% it will' also means '20% it will not'; only near even odds (about 60/40) do people readily grasp the uncertainty.
All scientific knowledge is tentative: scientists treat certainty as illusory and there is always an invisible asterisk on any assertion that something is true.
Uncertainty is an ineradicable element of reality; it is the dream of total certainty, not uncertainty itself, that is an illusion.
Because nothing is certain, the yes/no settings of the two- and three-setting mental dials must be discarded and the remaining 'maybe' must be subdivided into fine degrees of probability.
Express probability as numbers subdivided as finely as you can manage, but only so far as the granularity captures real distinctions (an 11% event must actually occur less often than a 12% one).
condition: only where the finer scale reflects genuine differences in frequency

statement: Probabilistic thinking rejects certainty and treats everything as a matter of probability sought with as much precision as possible, replacing an answer like 'absolutely' with a specific figure such as '60%'.

Distinguish epistemic uncertainty (unknown but in principle knowable, a clocklike problem) from aleatory uncertainty (unknowable even in theory, an irreducibly cloud-like problem that guarantees surprises).

When a question is loaded with irreducible uncertainty, be cautious: keep initial estimates inside the 35-65% shades-of-maybe zone and move out only tentatively, because the cloudier the outlook the harder it is to beat chance.
condition: for questions dominated by aleatory (irreducible) uncertainty

statement: Frequent use of exactly 50% signals three-setting thinking, where it stands in for 'maybe', and frequent 50%-users are measurably less accurate; a careful probabilistic thinker is no more likely to say 50% than 49% or 51%.

Granularity predicts accuracy: forecasters who use single percentage points are more accurate than those who use fives, who beat those who stick to tens, and rounding superforecasters' estimates even slightly degrades their Brier scores.

Impressive-sounding precise probabilities can be empty 'bafflegab', but the tournament data show that superforecasters' fine-grained distinctions genuinely improve accuracy rather than merely impressing.

Precision at the extremes matters when consequences are large: distinguishing 'extremely improbable but possible' from 'categorically impossible' can be decisive, as with a rare disease outbreak or funding a rare breakout success.
condition: when the payoff or harm of the improbable event is very large

statement: Elementary probability is an essential if mildly unnatural skill; without it, one is at a severe disadvantage in navigating an uncertain world.

Even sophisticated organizations use only coarse five- or seven-degree probability scales, short of what committed forecasters can achieve; organizations could obtain finer, more accurate results if they valued and encouraged granularity.
Science addresses 'how' (causation and probabilities) rather than 'why' (purpose); probabilistic thinking and 'it was meant to be' fate thinking are in tension and cannot be mixed.
Counterfactual thinking, imagining how events might have turned out differently, causes people to imbue those events with more meaning and to see them as fated.

Probabilistic thinkers take the outside view even toward identity-defining events, seeing them as quasi-random draws from once-possible worlds; the reasoning 'it was so improbable, but it happened, so it was 100% meant to be' is incoherent.

Superforecasters score lowest on belief in fate, and across forecasters the more one embraces 'it was meant to happen' thinking the less accurate one's forecasts, so probabilistic thinking is positively correlated with accuracy.
Finding meaning in events correlates positively with psychological wellbeing but negatively with forecasting accuracy, an unresolved tension between being happy and being accurate.

The repeatable superforecasting process is: unpack the question into components; separate the known from the unknown and scrutinize every assumption; take the outside view first, then the inside view; compare your views with others' and with crowd-wisdom methods; synthesize them dragonfly-style; and express the judgment on a finely grained probability scale.

A forecast is a judgment based on current information that should be updated as information changes; an updated forecast is likely closer to the truth than a stale one, so when the facts change, change your mind.
Superforecasters update their forecasts much more frequently than regular forecasters, monitoring developments closely with tools like news alerts, which contributes to their accuracy.

Superforecasters' skill is not merely a product of frequent updating: their initial forecasts, before any updating, were at least 50% more accurate than regular forecasters', so they would have won even with no updating allowed.
Good belief updating is not mindless reaction to the latest news; it demands the same skills used to make the initial forecast and can be even more challenging.
Reacting correctly to obvious news that everyone already sees gives no forecasting edge; superior forecasts come from identifying and responding to subtler, diagnostic information faster than others.

Smart updating means spotting subtly diagnostic evidence and nudging the forecast in the right direction before others do, as when a delayed lab announcement was read as a sign the test had found what was sought.

A forecaster faces two symmetric updating dangers: underreaction (giving too little weight to new information) and overreaction (treating new information as more meaningful than it is and adjusting too radically); both can destroy a good forecast.

An updating failure can stem from a bait and switch: having unconsciously answered an easier substitute question, a forecaster dismisses genuinely relevant new evidence as irrelevant to that replacement question.

Belief perseverance makes people intransigent and prone to rationalizing away information that upsets settled beliefs, even reading the absence of expected evidence as confirmation ('no sabotage yet proves sabotage is coming').

When forced to acknowledge undeniable facts, people usually budge only grudgingly and change their beliefs less than they should, because the brain works to keep its orderly model minimally disturbed.
Publicly committing to a belief freezes it in place and makes it resistant to change, and the stronger the commitment the greater the resistance.

Beliefs are stacked like a Jenga tower: a peripheral belief that supports nothing else is easy to revise, but a belief near the core of one's self-perception cannot be pulled out without threatening others, so people resist updating it.

Judgments about contested risks are driven less by weighing evidence than by identity, so logically unrelated issues correlate and people refuse even to imagine evidence that would overturn an identity-linked belief.
The deeper a belief sits in one's identity, the more extreme the reluctance to admit error, because conceding it would take a sledgehammer to a large part of one's mental structure.

Having little ego invested in a forecast is an advantage: it makes admitting the forecast is off-track and adjusting far easier, whereas experts and pundits with reputations on the line resist updating.

The dilution effect: adding clearly irrelevant information about a case weakens a judgment that rested on a diagnostic cue, causing people to sway at the mercy of meaningless noise, a form of overreaction.
Overreaction is common and costly: much of the volume and volatility of stock trading comes from traders overreacting to ephemeral, non-significant information.

Investors who trade frequently earn worse returns than buy-and-hold investors, as one study of tens of thousands of households found the most active traders earning 11.4% against a 17.9% market return.
An absence of commitment enables overreaction: forecasters or traders not emotionally connected to their positions freely overadjust to information of ephemeral, non-significant character.
Good updating finds the middle passage between the twin hazards of underreaction and overreaction, steering between them like Scylla and Charybdis.
Even the best updaters make both kinds of error, underreacting to a discounted signal or overreacting to a single stale but convincing report, so vigilance against both is continuous.
Superforecasters update their forecasts often but in small increments ('units of doubt'), and this pattern of many tiny updates threads the middle between underreaction and overreaction.

Carefully balancing old and new information captures the value of both: ignoring new evidence forfeits its value, while basing a forecast entirely on the latest evidence forfeits the value of the prior, so update frequently but bit by bit.
The Bayesian core insight is to get gradually closer to the truth by constantly updating a prior belief in proportion to the diagnostic weight of new evidence.
Experienced forecasters begin from the base rate as their 'prior' before folding in case-specific evidence, as when a Senate-confirmation base rate of about 96% anchored a nomination forecast.
New evidence should move a forecast in proportion to its diagnostic value, judged by how much more likely that evidence is if the hypothesis is true than if it is false.

You need not memorize or explicitly compute Bayes' theorem to forecast well; what matters is the Bayesian spirit of updating in proportion to the evidence, so most superforecasters are 'Bayesians who do not use Bayes' theorem'.

'Many small updates' is not a universal rule: when a forecast rests on a single piece of evidence that turns out to be failing or wrong, ditch it and build a fresh forecast rather than nudging gradually.
condition: when a forecast is propped up mainly by one piece of now-discredited evidence

statement: There are no fail-safe forecasting formulas, only broad principles with many caveats whose application requires nuanced judgment; it is better to break a rule than to make a barbarous forecast.
The craving for fail-safe rules and guaranteed certainty is the source of people's fatal attraction to overconfident hedgehog pundits.

A growth mindset, the belief that ability is largely the product of effort and can be developed, is essential to top-flight forecasting, whereas a fixed mindset ('I'm bad at this') becomes self-fulfilling by discouraging effort.
People with a fixed mindset attend only to whether they were right or wrong and ignore feedback that could improve them, while only growth-mindset people prioritize learning from that feedback.
Treat failure as an opportunity to learn by cycling through try, fail, analyze, adjust, and try again, and take pride in promptly admitting mistakes rather than reaching the limits of one's ability.
Prompt acknowledgment of error is valuable and should be cultivated: there is no harm in being sometimes wrong, especially if the mistake is promptly found out and corrected.
Skills are learned by doing and improved by doing more, even the most demanding ones: classroom instruction and simulators alone cannot produce a qualified pilot, who needs hours in the air.
Much expert knowledge is tacit and cannot be fully captured in words (as a precise physics of bicycle-riding still cannot teach someone to ride); it is acquired only through hands-on experience.
Learning to forecast requires actually trying to forecast: reading books about forecasting is no substitute for the practice, feedback, and correction of doing it.

Not all practice improves skill; it must be informed practice guided by knowing which mistakes to avoid and which best practices truly work, and book knowledge and practice reinforce each other so that each amplifies the other's benefit.

Effective practice requires clear and timely feedback; experience without feedback does not build skill, as police officers do not get better at detecting lies with experience because feedback is delayed or absent.
Without clear feedback, confidence grows faster than accuracy, so accumulated experience breeds overconfidence rather than genuine skill.

People are generally overconfident, with confidence exceeding accuracy, but overconfidence is not immutable: those who receive clear, prompt feedback, such as meteorologists and bridge players, become well-calibrated.
To learn from failure you must know when you fail; unambiguous knowledge of a failure is what lets you analyze what went wrong, adjust, and try again.
Ambiguous language destroys feedback: vague terms like 'probably' or 'significant' can mean almost anything, so neither an observer nor the forecaster judging herself can extract meaningful lessons.

The Forer effect shows vague language is elastic and gets stretched to fit whatever the reader wants, so forecasters who judge their own vague forecasts fool themselves into seeing accuracy that is not there.
Long time lags destroy feedback: when a forecast spans months or years, ordinary forgetfulness and hindsight bias distort recall of what was actually predicted.

Hindsight bias, the 'I knew it all along' effect, makes people misremember a prior estimate as closer to the known outcome; experts recalled their pre-collapse Soviet estimates about 31 percentage points higher than what they had actually said.
Numeric, unambiguous forecasts produce clear feedback that cannot be dodged by vague language or hindsight bias, giving the forecaster a genuine chance to learn from a bad result.

Judgment calibrated in one domain transfers poorly to another, so to improve at a given type of forecasting you must practice that same type repeatedly with good feedback and a willingness to say 'I got that wrong, let me learn why.'
Periodically reexamine your assumptions and consult real experts rather than assuming your own expertise, because unexamined shared assumptions cause forecasting failures.

Superforecasters run careful, self-critical postmortems and prepare for them by leaving detailed comments explaining why they made each forecast, so they can later reconstruct and critique their reasoning.
A good outcome does not prove a good decision: honestly acknowledge when you 'lucked out', because assuming a good outcome means a good decision blinds you to flaws in your thinking.
People show a self-serving asymmetry, welcoming 'I was almost right' counterfactuals while dismissing 'I was almost wrong' ones; superforecasters resist this and give honest credit to luck.

Chance plays a larger role in forecasting than in a skill like cycling, so following best practices improves the odds of a good outcome but less reliably than in low-chance domains, and forecasters should therefore remain tentative.

Grit, the passionate perseverance of long-term goals despite frustration and failure, married with a growth mindset, is a potent force for improvement, and caring more about learning than about scores sustains it.

In philosophic outlook superforecasters tend to be cautious (nothing is certain), humble (reality is infinitely complex), and nondeterministic (what happens is not meant to be and need not have happened).

In thinking and method superforecasters tend to be actively open-minded, intelligent and curious (high need for cognition), reflective and self-critical, numerate, pragmatic, analytical, dragonfly-eyed, probabilistic, thoughtful updaters, and good intuitive psychologists alert to their own biases.

Perpetual beta, the commitment to continual belief updating and self-improvement, is the strongest predictor of becoming a superforecaster, roughly three times as powerful as intelligence, making superforecasting about 75% perspiration and 25% inspiration.
No level of intelligence compensates for a lack of dedication to continually developing one's skill, though there are many paths to success and a strength in one area can offset a deficit in another.

Teams are dual-edged: they can cause terrible mistakes through groupthink but can also sharpen judgment and accomplish what no individual can, so managers must attend to both the negative and positive potential rather than only one.

Groupthink arises when a cohesive group that gets along too well develops shared illusions that interfere with critical thinking, so everyone agrees and the very fact of agreement is tacitly taken as proof the group is right.
The same team can produce both a fiasco and a triumph depending on its decision-making process rather than its membership, as the Kennedy team did across the Bay of Pigs and the Cuban missile crisis.

Guard against groupthink by redesigning the process: instill skepticism, license every participant to question anything as a generalist, appoint devil's advocates or intellectual watchdogs, and set aside protocol and hierarchy that impede free debate.

A leader should sometimes leave the room and withhold his own initial preference so the group deliberates freely, because there is less genuine give-and-take when the boss is present and his view is known.

Aggregation improves accuracy only when judgments are formed independently so that errors are random and cancel out; when group discussion destroys independence (through a dominant, bullying, or credentialed voice), errors compound instead of canceling.
condition: only when members form judgments independently before pooling

statement: Loss of independent judgment is the root of collective folly such as speculative bubbles, but it is not inevitable: a group that keeps questioning itself and welcomes vigorous debate can become more than the sum of its parts.
Teams risk cognitive loafing (free-riding on others' effort) as well as groupthink, and these two tendencies can reinforce each other into self-righteous complacency.

Effective team norms are to be cooperative but not deferential, to treat neither consensus as always good nor disagreement as always bad, to never take agreement itself as proof of being right, and to keep asking pointed questions.
The opposite danger to groupthink is rancor and dysfunction, so team members must disagree without being disagreeable, practicing constructive confrontation.

Precision questioning surfaces the reasoning behind a vague claim so it can be tested: instead of a personal shot or a vague 'what do you mean?', zero in with questions like 'What do you mean by that term?' and 'What evidence, over what time frame?'

Precision questioning that probes a plan's assumptions could have exposed the Bay of Pigs contingency-plan flaw (an 80-mile swamp between landing and refuge), which is exactly the scrutiny cohesive groups tend to skip.
On average, forecasters working in teams were 23% more accurate than forecasters working alone.

Success can breed hubris that undermines the very habits of mind that produced it ('CEO disease'): being told one is exceptional can lead a person to think a judgment must be right simply because it is theirs.
Excessive politeness ('dancing around') hinders the critical examination of views, so teams improve by explicitly inviting push-back and thanking members for constructive criticism.
A premortem, in which the team assumes a planned course of action has already failed and explains why, makes members feel safe to voice doubts they have about the leader's plan.
A team without formal structure can be built by leading from behind, explaining one's own reasoning in detail, inviting comment, and organizing shared work without appearing to take over.
The best teams have psychological safety in which members feel free to correct higher-ups, and a shared purpose signaled by talking about 'our' work more than 'my' work.
When a forecaster who had earned superforecaster status was placed on a team of other superforecasters, that person became about 50% more accurate.
A committed team gathers far more information than any individual could, even one with unlimited hours, because different members bring different research styles and cover more ground.

Markets aggregate widely dispersed information into a price through trading incentives, but the strong efficient-market hypothesis is untenable because markets make mistakes and sometimes lose their collective minds, even though they remain hard to beat consistently.
In the tournament, teams of ordinary forecasters beat the crowd average by about 10%, prediction markets beat ordinary teams by about 20%, and superteams beat prediction markets by 15% to 30%.
A team's collective active open-mindedness correlates with its accuracy and is an emergent property of the group's communication patterns, not merely the sum of members' individual open-mindedness.

A group of open-minded people who do not engage one another is less than the sum of its parts, whereas a group of opinionated people who engage each other in pursuit of the truth is more than the sum of its parts.
A culture of sharing driven by 'givers' who contribute more than they take improves others' behavior to everyone's benefit, and contrary to the 'chump' intuition givers tend to come out on top.

Diversity of perspectives, not raw ability alone, drives the gains from aggregation, because combining uniform perspectives merely produces more of the same; the real task is tuning the mix of ability and diversity rather than choosing between them.

Extremizing's effectiveness depends on diversity: a team whose members already share all their information gains little or nothing from extremizing, while a diverse pool that has not pooled its information gains greatly from it.
condition: only where forecasters hold diverse, unshared information
exception: a team of clones who all know the same things should not be extremized

statement: Aggregating a team of advisers' independent estimates yields a hard-to-beat 'wisdom of the crowd' figure that deserves more respect than leaders often give it, as with the roughly 70% median estimate that the man in the compound was bin Laden.

The leader's dilemma is that the qualities leaders are expected to display (confidence, decisiveness, vision, and relentless determination) appear to conflict with the superforecaster's traits (nothing is certain, slow self-critical thought, readiness to change one's mind, and humility).
Cheap, accurate aggregate-forecasting tools will not and should not replace human analysts and decision-makers, but the inexpensive forecasts they generate should be on decision-makers' desks.
Never entirely trust your plan: no plan extends with certainty beyond first contact with reality, so improvisation is essential because no two situations are exactly alike.
Train subordinates in critical thinking through debate where disagreement is expected and even superiors' views can be challenged, rather than by having them memorize a single supplied right answer.
An imperfect decision made in time is better than a perfect one made too late, and waiting for full information in a tense situation is more often a sign of weakness than of strong leadership.
Draw a sharp line between deliberation and implementation: while deciding, weigh uncertainty and complexity, but once the decision is made, set doubt aside and act with resolute confidence.

A leader must combine unwavering determination to accomplish a goal with openness to abandoning the plan when circumstances demand, and the art of leadership is recognizing the moment a new decision is required.
exception: a course of action should not be abandoned without overriding reason, yet inflexibly clinging to it can also cause failure

statement: Mission command (Auftragstaktik) pushes decision-making power down to those on the ground who first meet surprises, telling subordinates what goal to achieve but not how, thereby blending strategic coherence with decentralized execution.
Give subordinates the goal and the intent behind it (the why), so they can improvise appropriately when reality differs from what headquarters expected instead of freezing and awaiting new orders.
Rigid top-down command shakes subordinates' trust and leaves them uncertain and rattled when events unfold differently from what higher orders presumed.

Cultivating flexible, independent-thinking subordinates requires a culture that welcomes unwelcome words and deliberately preserves and promotes iconoclasts, since punishing dissent (as was done to the young Eisenhower) is a serious mistake.

Develop flexible thinking by pushing people out of their intellectual comfort zone through training with genuine surprises rather than scripted exercises and through exposure to bright people who hold very different basic assumptions.
A cool, assured outward appearance spreads confidence and boosts morale better than false claims of certainty, so a leader can privately hold doubt while outwardly projecting steadiness.

The divide between doers and thinkers is a false dichotomy: a leader must be both, figuring out the right move and then executing it boldly, since the bold move is the right move except when it is the wrong move.

Mission command applies beyond the military: successful businesses tell people what to accomplish but not how (as at 3M) and institutionalize respectful dissent followed by full commitment ('have backbone; disagree and commit').

The humility required for good judgment is intellectual humility, a recognition that reality is profoundly complex and judgment error-prone, and it is distinct from self-doubt, so it can coexist with high self-regard and confidence in one's abilities.

Intellectual humility compels the careful reflection needed for good judgment while confidence in one's abilities inspires determined action, so combining the two is fruitful rather than contradictory.

A confident expert should distinguish what she is confident about from what she is not, holding humility toward the irreducible complexity of the problem as distinct from her confidence relative to opponents.
Successful people are tempted by a dangerous shortcut, 'I have good judgment, so my believing my judgment is correct proves it is', which amounts to seeing reality only from the tip of one's nose.

Separate factual judgments from moral feelings: assuming that moral and cognitive weakness run together is an illusory correlation that leads forecasters to underestimate a despised opponent, the most serious forecasting error in a conflict.
There is no necessary link between morality and competence, so a forecaster who assumes vicious regimes or groups must be inept will fail when accuracy matters most.

Letting values such as loathing or hope contaminate a factual forecast produces wishful, biased conclusions, and even strong self-critics do this, as when a forecaster's hatred of a regime led to a wishful prediction that the rebels would win.

Even accomplished experts fall for WYSIATI, drawing sweeping conclusions from the salient evidence in front of them without checking easily available data, because a conclusion that feels true does not feel like an assumption to be tested.

Cognitive illusions cannot be switched off even when you know they are illusions, just as the Muller-Lyer lines still look unequal after you measure them; you cannot turn off the tip-of-your-nose perspective, only monitor its outputs and check them against a 'ruler' when time allows.

What makes superforecasters good is less what they are than what they do: the hard work of research, careful thought and self-criticism, gathering and synthesizing perspectives, granular judgment, and relentless updating.

Continuous self-scrutiny, using deliberate System 2 thought to catch System 1 errors, is exhausting and the feeling of knowing is seductive, so anyone can slip back into easy intuitive thinking and blow a forecast; the skill is fragile.

Scope insensitivity makes people answer 'how bad does this make me feel?' instead of the actual scaled question, so their willingness to pay barely changes whether 2,000 or 200,000 birds die, a bait and switch driven by an affective prototype.

In forecasting the time frame is the scope of the question, and the probability of an event must scale with the length of the window; ignoring this leads to scope-insensitive answers, as when regular forecasters gave about the same probability for a regime falling in three months as in six.

Superforecasters resist scope insensitivity by calibrating probability to the time frame (assigning 15% over three months but 24% over six months to the same event), thinking about how the answer would change under other time frames.

Stress-test your mental model by running thought experiments that vary the question's parameters (the cutoff date, a target threshold) to check whether your answer moves appropriately and stays scope sensitive.

Deliberate practice can turn effortful System 2 corrections, such as stepping back to take the outside view, into habitual automatic System 1 operations, lightening the cognitive load as a skill becomes second nature.
Superforecasting remains fragile hard work: those who do it well appreciate the fragility of their success, expect to stumble, and when they do get up, draw the right lessons, and keep forecasting.
Smart, dedicated people can inoculate themselves to some degree against certain cognitive biases through training, so organizations gain from recruiting and training talented people to resist biases.
Adversarial collaboration, deliberately working with those who hold opposing views to find common ground and resolve disputes, is a valuable route to better understanding.

'Forecasting works if you follow my formula' versus 'forecasting is bunk' is a false dichotomy; a tournament of short-horizon questions tells us nothing about the ability to spot rare, high-impact events, and we should not pretend it does.

Many events called 'black swans' are actually gray, imaginable and even anticipated beforehand (airplane-as-weapon scenarios before 9/11, a decade of great-power war fears before World War I), so if a black swan must be literally inconceivable they are far rarer than claimed.

History both jumps through rare big events and crawls through slow incremental change such as rising life expectancy and compounding economic growth, and that slow change can be profoundly important, so short-horizon forecasting matters even if one believes only rare events 'make history'.

A rare event becomes a 'black swan' through its consequences, which unfold over time through many contingent, forecastable steps, so the wider you draw the event's boundary the more of it is composed of sub-events that can in fact be forecast.

Two legitimate strategies under deep uncertainty are black-swan investing (spread many bets expecting most to fail while hoping for a rare huge win) and edge-forecasting (beat competitors by being slightly more accurate for frequent modest returns); neither is superior, they are simply different.

No geopolitical or economic forecaster can reliably predict anything about ten years out beyond the excruciatingly obvious, and accuracy declines toward chance around five years out, yet institutions still commission twenty-year forecasts.
condition: for open, nonlinear geopolitical and economic systems

statement: When you must plan beyond the forecasting horizon, plan for surprise by building adaptability and resilience and imagining specific shocks and how you would respond, because plans may be useless but planning is indispensable.

Preparing for surprises through resilience or antifragility is costly, so it forces priority-setting, which puts you back in the forecasting business; probability estimates are at the heart of all long-term planning, as with earthquake building codes or a two-war military doctrine.

The probability judgments underlying plans should be made explicit so their accuracy can be examined, and if a judgment is only a guess you should say so, because knowing what you do not know is better than thinking you know what you do not.

Hindsight bias is the cardinal forecasting sin: brushing off surprises makes the past look more predictable than it was, which fuels the false belief that the future is much more predictable than it is.

Many important quantities follow fat-tailed rather than bell-curve distributions, permitting far more extreme outcomes than a normal distribution would, as the existence of hundreds of billionaires shows wealth is fat-tailed.

Historical possibilities are distributed with fat tails like wealth rather than like height, so the world is far more volatile than most people realize and we risk grave miscalculation by assuming a normal distribution of outcomes.

Using a realistic fat-tailed distribution makes extreme catastrophes thousands of times more probable than a normal-distribution assumption implies, which should change how hard decision-makers work to avert them.

The world we inhabit is one quasi-random draw from a vast population of once-possible worlds: the past did not have to unfold as it did and the future is wide open, as illustrated by the roughly 12.5% chance that three pivotal twentieth-century dictators would all be born male.
Immersion in counterfactual, what-if history gives a visceral feel for radical indeterminacy and instills a profound humility about the limits of foresight.
Humility about the smallness of human foresight should not obscure the fact that people can, with considerable effort, make accurate forecasts about at least some developments that really do matter.

Hindsight-tainted post-hoc analyses of events (such as 'economics trumped nationalism') are a dead end that leave too much out and are worse still when generalized to other cases, though every event is an opportunity to improve one's mental models.
Learning from experience requires clear feedback, which requires unambiguous, scorable forecasts, so a forecaster should make a clear prediction with an explicit confidence interval and keep score.

Vague expectations about indefinite futures are useless because fuzzy thinking can never be proven wrong; only being clearly proven wrong forces us to adjust our mental models toward reality, which is why the forecast-measure-revise cycle is the surest path to seeing better.

Consumers of forecasts should stop being gulled by good stories and credentials and instead demand a track record and rigorous testing of accuracy before heeding a forecaster, just as we demand tested medicines.

Accuracy is often only one of a forecast's goals and is sometimes irrelevant, because forecasts are frequently judged by whether they advance the forecaster's or tribe's interests (kto-kogo) rather than by whether they come true.
The same forecaster with the same track record can be hailed or reviled depending only on whether the forecast aligns with the audience's partisan purposes.
An inaccurate forecast can still succeed at its real purpose, such as rousing action or advancing power, so evaluating a forecast requires knowing which goal it was actually meant to serve.

Scorekeeping and evidence-based evaluation can overcome entrenched interests through reason and a relentless focus on the goal, as the End Result System and evidence-based medicine eventually won despite threatening the medical hierarchy.

Evidence-based thinking (score, analyze, learn what works) is spreading across medicine, public policy, philanthropy, and sports, catalyzed by information technology, so an evidence-based forecasting movement would continue that broad shift rather than be an anomaly.

The blame-game reflex of swinging to the opposite extreme after each publicized error does nothing to improve forecasting and blocks the long-term investment needed to get better, as the intelligence community did after failing to warn of 9/11 and then over-warning on Iraqi WMDs.

The wrong-side-of-maybe fallacy makes numeric forecasts risky for organizations, since a probabilistic call can be unfairly blamed when the less likely outcome occurs, which is why fuzzy language persists as protective cover and blocks scorekeeping.

Numbers are tools, not sacred totems: a metric's quality ranges from wretched to superb and must be constantly scrutinized and improved, since a crude survival metric can let a hospital boast a 100% rate by turning away the sickest patients; progressive improvement is attainable but perfection is not.

A scoring rule should be tuned to the decision's real stakes: because a plain Brier score penalizes false alarms and misses equally, forecasters can be told the ground rules in advance (for example that a false positive costs a fraction of a false negative) so they adjust their judgments accordingly.

A scoring system that still needs tweaking can nonetheless be a large improvement over the status quo, just as imperfect credit scores are far better than whimsical loan-officer decisions and Brier scoring is better than judging a forecaster by titles, confidence, and book sales.
There is a real dilemma that the big question ('how does this all turn out?') is what matters but is too vague to score, while the scorable small question matters less on its own.

Bayesian question clustering resolves that dilemma: decompose an unscorable big question into many small, pertinent, scorable questions whose cumulative answers close in on the big answer, the way pointillist dots that each add little together form a picture.
Accurate forecasting is only one element of good judgment; other elements, such as moral judgment, cannot be counted or run through an algorithm.

Asking good questions is a critical dimension of good judgment, since a farsighted forecast cannot happen until someone poses the question; a good question passes the smack-the-forehead test, prompting 'if only I had thought of that' when read after the fact.

Superforecasting and superquestioning are likely different skills with different psychological recipes: superb question generation often accompanies a hedgehog-like Big-Idea confidence, unlike the foxy, uncertainty-sensitive eclecticism of superb forecasting.

A vague pundit 'forecast' is often better read as a question that draws forecasters' attention to what they should think about than as an answer, and forecasters and questioners have complementary strengths that each should use rather than treating them as a dichotomy.

Public policy debates routinely fail as a learning process: parties state vague, unfalsifiable positions and years later no one changes their mind, each side merely hunting the other's failures instead of adjusting.

Rationalizing away a failed forecast by pointing to a different measure or to the hedge words ('note the word risk, note the absence of a date') is exactly what makes public debate unproductive; forecasts must be pinned to unambiguous terms to enable learning.

Adversarial collaboration can be applied to polarized debates: opposing figures, with a trusted moderator, jointly design precise, benchmarked, time-bound forecast questions that would meaningfully test their disagreement, reducing ambiguity to a minimum.

A single forecast cannot resolve a complex dispute, so it takes many questions and clusters; a split decision in which each side is right on some points is a feature, not a bug, revealing that reality is more mixed than either side thought, which is progress if learning rather than gloating is the goal.

Adversarial collaboration presumes good faith, wanting the truth more than wanting to be right; strident public voices will not engage, but quieter reasonable ones will, and public scorekeeping imposes a reputational price on those who rationalize away failure.

Use pundits as inputs rather than oracles: good pundits argue the case for their forecasts like lawyers, so weigh everyone's arguments, dig further, and form your own forecast as a weighted synthesis, while discounting those who assert with no supporting arguments or only anecdotes.

Forecasting slumps are inevitable because history passes through phases of irreducible uncertainty where luck trumps skill, so even a strong forecaster should expect regression to the mean and respond by becoming more cautious and less prone to extreme forecasts.

Triage your forecasting effort toward Goldilocks-zone questions where work pays off, avoiding both easy clocklike questions that rules of thumb already answer and impenetrable cloud-like questions that even statistical models cannot beat chance on.

Break seemingly intractable problems into tractable sub-problems by decomposing them into knowable and unknowable parts, flushing ignorance into the open, exposing and examining assumptions, and daring to make explicit best guesses rather than hiding behind vague verbiage.

Strike a balance between the outside and inside views: because nothing is entirely unique, search for comparison classes even for seemingly one-off events and ask 'how often do things of this sort happen in situations of this sort?' before adjusting for specifics.
The planning fallacy leads people to underestimate how long a task will take, often by a factor of two or three, and it can be corrected by taking the outside view of such estimates.

Balance under- and overreaction to evidence by updating incrementally as a habit, teasing subtle signals from noisy news and hunting non-obvious lead indicators (what would have to happen before X), while resisting wishful thinking yet still moving fast on genuinely diagnostic signals.

Look for the clashing causal forces in a problem: for every good argument acknowledge the counterargument, list in advance the signs that would nudge you toward the other side, and synthesize the opposing views into a nuanced hybrid position rather than a cookie-cutter stance.

Distinguish as many degrees of doubt as the problem permits but no more, using a finely graded uncertainty dial, and apply the same probabilistic rigor to serious decisions that seasoned gamblers apply to sports rather than reserving rigor for trivial pursuits.

Balance under- and overconfidence, managing the trade-off between decisiveness and prudence, since long-term accuracy requires good scores on both calibration and resolution and creative ways to reduce both misses and false alarms, not merely avoiding the most recent mistake.

Look for the errors behind your mistakes with unflinching postmortems that own the failure and find the exact error, beware hindsight bias, recognize you can learn too little or too much from a failure, and also run postmortems on successes because a good outcome may hide offsetting errors or luck.

Bring out the best in others by mastering perspective taking (reproducing the other side's argument to their satisfaction), precision questioning (helping others clarify their arguments), and constructive confrontation (disagreeing without being disagreeable).

Superforecasting is the product of deep, deliberate practice with unambiguous feedback, not of reading manuals or casually tossing out probabilities, so each guideline must be learned by doing while balancing opposing errors.
Do not treat guidelines as binding rules, because no two cases are ever exactly the same; the commandments require constant mindfulness, especially when you are dutifully trying to follow them.

Remarkably good probability estimates can arise from a remarkably crude series of decomposed assumptions and guesstimates, so Fermi-izing an apparently unquantifiable question is worthwhile even when each input is rough.

The heuristics-and-biases account of judgment is contested (System 1 is often strikingly accurate and it is disputed how often heuristics mislead), but it still provides the best first-order approximation of the errors real-world forecasters make and the most useful guidance for reducing them.

A proper scoring rule such as the Brier score rewards a forecaster for reporting true beliefs and resisting political pressure by tying reputational penalties for overconfidence to the losses a gambler would incur; a practical test is that if you would not bet at the odds your probability implies, you should rethink the estimate.

Superforecasters probably outperform professional analysts not because they are smarter or more open-minded but because they treat forecasting as a cultivatable skill, whereas analysts work inside organizations that treat prediction as a sideshow rather than the real job.

Everyone makes predictions constantly, since analysis and policy advocacy embed implicit forecasts (a historical analogy carries a conditional prediction), and it is hard to get better at something you do not even recognize you are doing.

The fundamental attribution error leads us to attribute our own behavior to situational factors while attributing others' behavior to their character, so stepping outside ourselves to see a situation as others do is hard.

The skill-to-luck ratio of active superforecasters is substantial, plausibly between 60/40 and 90/10, and about 90% of active superforecasters (those answering at least fifty questions a year) stayed in the top 20% of performers, so when they fell they rarely fell far.

Inside-view probability estimates can be assembled with targeted questions about the key players, how powerful each is, what each wants, and how much they want it, then testing possible coalitions, ideally pooling answers from multiple experts.

Open competition with public leaderboards produced markedly less overconfidence among forecasters than earlier research that guaranteed anonymity, and it also made the hedgehog-fox distinction matter far less.

Because remarkably good forecasts often rest on many arbitrary decomposed assumptions, the real choice is not whether to engage in crude guesswork but whether to do it overtly, where it can be inspected, or covertly.

Under reason-based choice, a shift in probability matters to a decision only when it crosses a threshold that makes a factor become (or cease to be) a good reason to act, so a decision-maker's 'fifty-fifty' may signal only that nothing yet moved the dial past the action threshold.

Ambiguity aversion (the Ellsberg paradox) makes people prefer a known risk to an unknown one and can even make them prefer the certainty of a bad outcome to the mere possibility of one, a bias that distorts decisions under uncertainty.

Being able to anticipate unpredictability (volatility) is a major advantage, since an aggregation method that knew when to throttle back its extremizing would avoid heavy penalties; superforecasters still outperform in turbulent periods, but their margin of victory shrinks.

Do not default to 0.5 just because you feel you know nothing: doing so across unpacked sub-possibilities assigns incoherent probabilities that sum above 1.0, and in fact you almost always know a little, which should tip you away from maximum uncertainty.

When all you know is how long a phenomenon has already lasted, adopt Copernican humility and assume you are at no special point in its lifespan, which lets you build a crude confidence interval for how much longer it will last from the elapsed duration alone.
condition: when the only information available is the elapsed duration of the phenomenon

statement: The 'I made the right mistake' defense, deliberately erring toward caution because underestimating a threat is costlier than overestimating it, is sometimes legitimate, but it collapses when the forecaster refuses to update even long after the feared threat fails to materialize.
condition: when the asymmetric costs of the two errors genuinely justify caution
exception: it is not a valid defense if you cling to the position after disconfirming evidence accumulates

statement: The correlation between raw intelligence and forecasting accuracy declined over the course of the tournament, which implies a shrinking role for intelligence and a growing role for skill, evidence that practice really does make forecasters better.

Overconfidence in one's stock-picking skill is expensive: because no active fund consistently beats passive index funds and active funds charge higher fees, the humbler passive strategy wins over time, and even superforecasters are unlikely to beat deep, liquid markets though they can beat shallower, less liquid ones.
exception: superforecasters can outperform shallower, less liquid prediction markets

statement: A correct forecast produced by individually wrong judgments that happen to cancel out is luck, not a validated method, so declaring 'nailed it' and reusing the same method sets you up for failure; unpack even your successes to check the reasoning.

Ability is a product of nature and nurture together, not one or the other: genetic endowment sets outer limits, but within those limits a vast range of outcomes depends on the opportunities one has and one's readiness to seize them.

When judging a forecaster, do not confuse judgments of foresight with judgments of character (functionalist blurring): forecasting accuracy is a separate question from whether you admire or despise the person, and even a repugnant figure can sometimes see a situation more clearly than others.

Even for rare, once-in-decades events, forecasters can be partly evaluated by a logical-consistency test (they should not assign the same probability to a rare event over one year as over ten) and by scoring their calls on early-warning indicators, which beats embracing an extreme precautionary principle that rejects any change for which someone can imagine a plausible worst case.

Adjust the outside view for known systematic measurement biases, such as the social-desirability effect that makes some voters shy about telling pollsters they favor the 'boring' side, which lets forecasters correctly discount poll surges (as superforecasters did on the Scottish independence referendum).

Institutions cling to vague language partly because the public misreads belief updating as a sign of confusion rather than rationality, so the barrier to explicit probabilistic forecasting is often political rather than scientific.

Anointing an official performance metric creates incentives to game it (for example rejecting very sick patients to boost a survival rate), but the remedy is not to abandon metrics but to resist overinterpreting them.

Public tournaments with posted results create a form of accountability that makes forecasters more open-minded and better calibrated than anonymous forecasting, by attuning them to the possibility that they might be wrong.

Preparing for genuinely unprecedented high-impact events requires relaxing the usual guidelines, relying less on historical base rates and accepting more false alarms, because you cannot raise the hit rate on rare events without also raising false positives, so the aim is to keep false positives low and hedge against events others failed to imagine.
condition: when preparing for rare, high-impact, hard-to-imagine events

statement: Track expert judgment against explicit, pre-declared benchmarks of accuracy and rigor rather than letting experts keep their own scorecards.
How experts think (their cognitive style) predicts forecasting accuracy far more than what they think (their ideology or specific content knowledge).
condition: forecasting real-world political outcomes

statement: In long-run political forecasting, foxes — thinkers who know many small things, draw on many traditions, and tolerate ambiguity and contradiction — forecast more accurately than hedgehogs, who know one big thing and apply it formulaically.
condition: long-run political forecasting
exception: hedgehogs can match or beat foxes on some short-term forecasts inside their domain of expertise

statement: Forecasters' confidence in how well they are doing is often inversely related to their actual accuracy.
The most accurate forecasters and the quickest belief-updaters share a self-critical, self-deprecating cognitive style that spares them the largest mistakes.
Political partisans rarely admit error even when confronted with strong disconfirming evidence.
Elicit testable, falsifiable predictions in advance, score their accuracy against realized outcomes, and check whether forecasters revise their beliefs when they are wrong.

Measure judgment on two distinct axes: correspondence (how close forecasts come to observed outcomes) and logical process (whether the forecaster reasons fairly with evidence and honors reputational bets by updating).
Design forecasting-accuracy measures to withstand the objections forecasters raise when high-probability events fail to occur or low-probability events do occur.
Preserve a verbatim record of each original forecast, because absent a reminder of what they once predicted, people drift into self-serving revision of what they claim to have believed.
The close-call counterfactual defense ('I predicted x, x did not happen, but it almost did') is a recurring belief-system defense that inaccurate forecasters use to rescue failed predictions.
The 'right-mistake' defense ('I erred, but mine was the prudent error to make') is a recurring belief-system defense used to deflect a failed forecast.
Hindsight bias leads observers to believe they foresaw an outcome that they did not in fact predict.
Study the link between reasoning style and forecasting outcomes at the level of cognitive variables, not by naming and shaming individual forecasters.
Judge forecasters by the quality of their reasoning process, not solely by whether a single prediction happened to come true.
Urgently wanting an answer does not guarantee the question is empirically answerable; treat a forecasting problem as scientifically tractable only when its outcomes can actually be scored.
Standard causal methods (experimental and statistical control) cannot readily explain or extrapolate the non-occurrence of a unique event that has never happened.
condition: the event is sui generis and has never occurred

statement: Influential experts routinely offer confident yet mutually contradictory assessments that are impervious to the opposing side's arguments.
Set standards for judging judgment that can command assent across the full spectrum of reasonable opinion, so that scoring is not dismissed as a partisan maneuver.

Hold forecasters to two independent tests: correspondence (do their beliefs match the observable world?) and coherence/process (are their beliefs internally consistent and updated in response to evidence?); a good judge must both get it right and think the right way.
Base correspondence tests on future predictions rather than present or past facts, because sophisticated experts rarely make the crude factual errors about the present that lay partisans make.
condition: assessing sophisticated experts rather than lay partisans

statement: Benchmark every forecaster against simple statistical baselines such as always predicting the base-rate outcome, because accurately predicting very rare or very common events is trivial and inflates apparent skill.
A forecaster who always predicts the higher-base-rate outcome can reach near-perfect accuracy on very rare or very common events with no real skill, like a stopped clock that is right twice a day.
condition: the outcome has a very high or very low base rate

statement: Score forecasts across all four prediction-outcome cells — hits, false alarms (overprediction), correct rejections, and misses (underprediction) — not by counting hits alone.
High hit rates can be manufactured by indiscriminately attaching high probabilities to an outcome, which simply trades hits for a higher false-alarm rate.
Do not reduce forecasting skill to maximizing aggregate accuracy; make explicit the trade-off each forecaster strikes between overprediction (false alarms) and underprediction (misses).
Give early-warning forecasters extra credit for seeing a development before others, and penalize those who recognized an obvious development only long after it became clear.
Pin down elusive constructs through multimethod triangulation, and raise confidence in a claim only as independent methods and diverse sources converge on it.
Pursue nomothetic knowledge (who tends to be right across many times and places) rather than idiographic knowledge (who was right in one particular case).
Aggregate judgments across many experts, many questions, and many cases so that idiosyncratic case-specific noise cancels out and stable properties of good judgment emerge.
Apply identical, no-favoritism scoring rules to every forecaster's answers.

Test how sensitive your conclusions are to defensible scoring adjustments — value (the 'right mistake'), difficulty, controversy, and fuzzy-set partial credit — and trust only conclusions that stay robust across them.
Judgments about the quality of political judgment can never be rendered fully uncontroversial, because they rest partly on hard-to-refute counterfactual and moral claims.

Political disputes hinge not only on ascertainable facts but on hard-to-refute counterfactual claims and impossible-to-refute moral claims, which partisans use to shield their positions from falsification.
Political belief systems tend to evolve into self-perpetuating worldviews with their own self-serving scorekeeping criteria, favored historical analogies, and pantheons of heroes and villains.

To convincingly indict a leader's judgment, show not only that they misread the situation but that the misreading put events on a manifestly worse path that due diligence on the available information could have avoided.
Do not let the relativist critique paralyze measurement: failing to capture every facet of good judgment is not a reason to abandon objective standards of empirical accuracy and logical coherence.
Across a wide range of forecasting tasks foxes outperform hedgehogs, with one key exception where hedgehogs hold the advantage.
exception: the exception is the task class where hedgehogs outperform, later identified as short-term forecasts within their domain of expertise

statement: Elicit forecasts as numerical probabilities rather than vague verbal terms, because words like 'likely' or 'remote chance' are interpreted across a huge range and cannot be reliably scored.
Only probability judgments of 0 (impossible) and 1.0 (inevitable) are individually falsifiable; every intermediate probability can be evaluated only in aggregate across many forecasts.

Assess probabilistic forecasts on two aggregate dimensions: discrimination (assigning higher probabilities to events that happen than to those that do not) and calibration (events assigned probability p occurring about p of the time).

Define each predicted outcome precisely enough to pass a clairvoyance test — a clairvoyant who knew the future could score it with no request for clarification — which rules out vague, oracular pronouncements.
Frame forecasting questions around unadorned facts before rhetorical spin, such as 'defense spending as a percentage of GDP' rather than 'reckless warmongering' or 'prudent precaution'.
Prediction and explanation are decoupled: one can explain without predicting, and predict without explaining.
A forecast can fail even from a sound theory when the antecedent conditions for applying it are unknown, as physics explains why a radiator freezes below freezing but not how cold tonight will be.
A forecast can fail even with a sound theory and known antecedents when the outcome is subject to chaotic oscillation, as earthquakes are understood and monitored yet remain unpredictable.

Forecasters invoke 'explanation is possible without prediction' when their own side's predictions fail, and 'prediction is possible without explanation' when rivals' predictions succeed — a self-serving asymmetry.

Treat forecasting accuracy as a fallible but far-from-useless indicator of how well a viewpoint grasps causal mechanisms; over many forecasts, confidence in a viewpoint should rise and fall with its predictive record.
