Systemic thinking includes modeling strategic interdependence between players and two-level games, in which a move in one arena such as international negotiation is simultaneously a move in another such as domestic politics.

Check your coherence about a past or future by drawing paired curves — an inevitability curve tracing how the likelihood of the actual outcome rose over time and an impossibility curve tracing how the likelihood of alternatives fell — since the two should complement to one and any gap exposes incoherence.
Counterbalance the order in which you consider an outcome versus its alternatives, because the order of elicitation can itself bias which one seems more likely.

Score a probabilistic forecast with the Brier probability score, the mean squared difference between each assigned probability and the realized outcome coded one or zero, where the ideal score of zero requires assigning one to everything that happens and zero to everything that does not.

For a forecast over mutually exclusive and exhaustive outcomes, compute the probability score by summing the squared deviations between assigned probability and realized outcome across all the outcomes.

Decompose an overall accuracy score into its components of variability, calibration, and discrimination, because the aggregate alone hides whether a forecaster is playing safe, discriminating well, or facing a hard task.

Measure the hedgehog-fox cognitive style with a short need-for-closure scale plus direct self-classification, capturing tolerance for ambiguity, openness to opposing views, and preference for parsimony versus case-by-case improvisation.

Covering-law beliefs about world politics — such as neorealist balancing, the robustness of nuclear deterrence, and the survival-of-the-fittest view of civilizations — strongly shape which historical counterfactuals a scholar will accept or reject.

Decompose a probability score into three parts — variability (how unpredictable the environment is), calibration, and discrimination — because a single score cannot tell you whether a poor result reflects a hard task, miscalibration, or weak discrimination.

Environmental difficulty is set by the base rate: an outcome with a base rate near zero or one is easy to predict, while a base rate near one-half is the hardest, where the base rate offers no more guidance than chance.
Diagnose which calibration failure you have: systematic overprediction, systematic underprediction, over-extremity (too bold in both directions), or under-extremity (too timid in both directions).
Distinguish self-aware forecasters from fence-sitters: good calibration with poor discrimination signals someone who never strays from the base rate, so demand both calibration and discrimination.

Discrimination is squared and so insensitive to direction: a forecaster can earn a perfect discrimination score by being perfectly but consistently wrong, which is why discrimination must be read alongside calibration.

To show real overconfidence rather than a regression-to-the-mean artifact, demonstrate that the average probability judgment differs significantly from the average objective frequency for well-specified event classes and that the gap grows predictably with drivers like cognitive style and extremism.

Formal statistical models beat human forecasters but not by massive margins, because many real-world variables follow a near-first-order autoregressive process that a simple persistence-plus-reversion rule captures well.

In significance testing treat the forecaster, not each individual forecast, as the unit of analysis, because one person's many predictions are not statistically independent and treating them as such inflates significance.

Five legitimate objections map to five scoring adjustments: task-difficulty, value for error-avoidance priorities, controversy over what actually happened, fuzzy-set over what almost or might yet happen, and probability-weighting for the nonlinear treatment of probabilities.
Judge forecasting skill by whether it beats a base-rate strategy, not by raw accuracy: a skill score of zero means the forecaster told you nothing you could not have gotten from the base rate.

A skill score rewards the courage to deviate correctly from the base rate, assigning above-base-rate probabilities to uncommon events that occur, and punishes mindless base-rate reliance that misses rare events.

Beware that difficulty-adjusted skill scoring, by rewarding deviation from the base rate, can also reward specious pattern-hunting in randomness, and the right reference population for a base rate is often disputed where no well-established laws exist.

The best simple value adjustment for an outcome equals the average forecast for it minus its base rate, correcting each estimate by however much it systematically strayed from reality, and it should be interpreted only at the aggregate level.

Prefer specifying your error-avoidance priorities in advance over fitting adjustments to the mistakes you actually made, because an adjustment tuned to your realized errors gives you the most self-serving benefit of the doubt.

Do not apply separate value adjustments for over- and underprediction, because doing so makes a broken-clock forecaster look perfectly calibrated and falsely assumes the forecaster knew in advance which kind of error they would make.
Giving a forecaster the benefit of the doubt through a value adjustment improves their score only by improving calibration, never discrimination.
Test a group difference across a wide range of plausible weightings of false-alarm versus miss penalties, and trust the difference as real skill only if it survives every plausible weighting.
Collapsing the probability scale toward its endpoints treats every maybe from .1 to .9 as equivalent, so scoring then depends only on accuracy at the extremes of impossible and inevitable.

Nonlinear probability weighting rewards confident endpoint calls that come true, punishes confident endpoint calls that fail, and treats a wrong-direction move at the extremes as more serious than the same move in the middle of the scale.

When the outcome itself is disputed, bracket a forecaster's score with lower and upper bounds by recomputing under the reality classification least and most favorable to them, and trust only conclusions that survive both bounds.
Penalize the 'I was almost right' excuse in proportion to its asymmetry: discount it by how rarely the same forecaster admits they were almost wrong or merely lucky when they got something right.

Because skill estimates rest on assumptions about both the world (base rates and what counts as the outcome) and the forecaster (their values and use of probabilities), test the robustness of any conclusion across a wide range of scoring adjustments.
Use Monte Carlo simulation to treat your dataset as one case among a vast space of possible environment and response-style parameters, revealing how special or contingent your result is.

Good judges should respect four formal coherence rules: the additive rule for exclusive events, the multiplicative rule for independent events, the total-probability form of Bayes's rule, and Bayesian updating on new evidence.

In a scenario chain where A probably leads to B leads to C, the probability of the whole chain falls off fast — even at .7 per link the joint probability is only about .34 — usually faster than forecasters' estimates, producing conjunction and sub-additivity errors.

The egocentricity gap, assigning your favored outcome more probability than a full accounting of rival hypotheses would justify, grows largest when you make extreme likelihood judgments while holding cautious priors about your own theory.
Recognize sub-additivity as a violation of the additive rule: when a whole set of exclusive, exhaustive outcomes is judged less likely than the sum of its parts, coherence has broken down.

Compute how much to update in three steps: form the likelihood ratio (probability of the outcome under your view divided by its probability under the rival view), form the prior-odds ratio (your confidence in your view divided by your confidence in the rival), and multiply them to get the posterior odds.

How much you should revise a belief depends on the evidence's diagnosticity and your starting prior: strongly diagnostic evidence moves beliefs fast, weak evidence near a likelihood ratio of one moves them slowly, and a low prior has more room to rise than a high one.

Never hold a probability of exactly one in your own view or zero in a rival's, because the odds ratio then becomes undefined and no evidence can ever move you; cap extreme confidence at values like .95 and .05 to stay updatable.
Repeatedly presented probative evidence eventually converges competing beliefs, and convergence is fastest when the prior is strong and the evidence is diagnostic.
The egocentricity gap is larger for more aggressive forecasters, because it grows with the extremity of the likelihood ratio, and hedgehogs offer more extreme likelihood ratios than foxes.

Discount a losing forecaster's 'it almost happened' excuse by the ratio of how often they invoke such reasoning when right versus wrong; if they claim it nine times more often after failures, grant only a ninth of the credit.

Judge an effort to measure judgment not against methodological perfection but against a realistic standard: whether it provides a starter framework for drawing cumulative lessons about the accuracy of expert judgment.
Treat the measurement of good judgment as beginning a conversation rather than ending it, acknowledging the fallibility of any analytical apparatus while still pursuing cumulative improvement.

Critics of deterrence argued that U.S. Cold War policy produced a self-fulfilling prophecy: misperceiving the USSR as aggressive and acting on that belief led the Soviets to see the U.S. as a threat and to arm, so each side's effort to gain security made the other less secure (a security dilemma).

Deterrence theorists and policymakers often assume rather than demonstrate an adversary's hostility, and should at minimum state that hostility explicitly as an assumption rather than treat it as established fact.

Apparent disagreements about the general efficacy of deterrence often reduce to disagreements about the adversary's nature: its goals, risk-taking propensity, how it can be influenced, and how it perceives you.

It is important to separate a state's intentions from its motives, because an expansionist move driven by a quest for domination differs, for both theory and policy, from one driven mainly by a search for security.
Access to documents can settle particular factual disputes but rarely resolves broader disputes about an adversary's motives, intentions, and the sources of its behavior.

A recurring misperception pattern is that leaders exaggerate the threat from an adversary while failing to see how their own behavior, such as alliance-building, contributes to that adversary's insecurity.
Appeasement of an adversary can rest on the faulty belief that the adversary can be conciliated.

Elite foreign-policy decision-makers differ from the mass publics studied in mainstream political psychology: they face high-stakes matters that fully engage their attention and expertise, so a better analogy is how people reason in domains of great personal concern than how they cast peripheral votes.
Experimental findings drawn largely from college-student samples may not generalize to political leaders or other populations.
Signaling (how a state tries to convey desired images of its intentions) and perception are two sides of one process, and treating them in separate literatures harms the understanding of both.
A leader's incentive to 'get it right' can be driven by domestic political survival rather than by foreign-policy accuracy.
Historians came to regard misperception as a central cause of both world wars.
Inferring other actors' intentions and motives is crucial for setting foreign policy, except in the rare case where the state has a dominant strategy that is best no matter what the other side does.
exception: when the state has a dominant strategy (a best response regardless of others' actions)

statement: Strategy must be matched to the adversary's type: trying to conciliate an aggressor makes things worse, while relying on threats against a state that seeks security and already fears you also makes things worse.
condition: the choice depends on whether the adversary is an aggressor or a security-seeker

statement: Forming an accurate perception of another actor is very difficult because the other's behavior is usually ambiguous and deception is an ever-present possibility.
Debates about an adversary's intentions are rarely resolved except by extraordinary, unambiguous actions, such as Hitler's 1939 seizure of the rump of Czechoslovakia.

A state must not only perceive its environment accurately but also understand how others perceive it, along the dimensions of menacing-versus-reassuring, weak-versus-strong (in both capability and resolve), and steadfast-versus-changeable, because the other's response depends on those perceptions.

Effective policy toward another actor must take that actor's perceptions as its starting point even when those perceptions are factually wrong; one may try to change them, which itself requires understanding them, but if change is impossible policy must be based on that reality.

Claiming that perceptions matter does not mean they are invented from nothing or that other levels of analysis can be ignored: domestic sources enter foreign policy not only as a separate variable but also as a source of beliefs and perceptions.
Some ways of thinking are so deeply ingrained and shared within a country that people are largely unaware that alternatives exist or that these frames vary across time and culture.

Left-wing and right-wing governments often perceive the external environment differently, so a country's perceptions and policies can change when the party in office changes, in nondemocracies as well as democracies.
Actors with a stake in continued good relations with another country are likely to perceive its leaders, society, and foreign policy as relatively benign.
Needs produced by the exigencies of domestic politics can generate perceptions that cannot be justified by the available information.

Treating incorrect perceptions and failed policies as irrational while treating accurate perceptions and successful policies as rational (and therefore not needing explanation) is a fallacy driven by hindsight bias.

Because the world is probabilistic and much information is hidden from actors, it can be rational to pursue a policy that in fact turns out badly, and the best-grounded inferences can turn out to be wrong.

There are few firm guidelines for what counts as rational processing of complex information; the label 'irrational' is often merely applied to people who disagree with us and appear to ignore disconfirming evidence.

Bounded-rationality accounts that invoke the costs of acquiring and processing information can be stretched to rationalize almost any heuristic, putting a rationalist gloss on biases instead of probing how people actually think.

Inferring that another actor's behavior reflects a deliberate plan, rather than accident or bureaucratic maneuvering, is attractive because it is parsimonious and saves the costly and often impossible search into the inner workings of the other's government, which is why the inference is common even when wrong.

When searching for evidence there is an almost inescapable tendency to examine cases of conflict, surprise, and error, which biases causal inference because analysts lack comparison with better-outcome cases and may attribute failure to factors that are constants rather than variables.
Analysts must distinguish the claim that a perceptual process is common from the claim that it is likely to lead actors astray, because the two are not the same.
Concentrating on errors and conflict gives an unbalanced picture of world politics and of leaders' skill, so successes in perception and signaling also need to be studied.

People are prone to draw on analogies from cases that were important to them or their country, especially events that occurred when they first became politically active or first held positions of responsibility.
Realist theory predicts that international anarchy and the resulting preoccupation with security make decision-makers highly sensitive to threats and prone to over-perceive them.
condition: under international anarchy where security is the driving concern

statement: Human beings are psychologically disposed to divide the world into in-groups and out-groups, to disfavor the out-group, and to find it hard to empathize with them.
Leaders and the mass public tend to be self-righteous and to have difficulty understanding the hopes and grievances of others, which worsens international relations.

Because liberalism traces foreign policy to regime type, institutions, and societal interests, analysts should expect dictatorships and democracies to differ significantly in how they view international politics and the images they hold of others.
condition: when comparing regimes of different types

statement: Democratic leaders are prone to believe that compromise and lasting agreement are possible, at least with other democracies.
condition: at least with other democracies

statement: The perceptions of a highly ideological regime are better understood by examining its ideology than by examining the actual external environment.
condition: for highly ideological regimes

statement: A regime's specific perceptions are shaped by ideas derived from its core ideology, so ideology can drive systematic misjudgment of others (e.g., Stalin over-estimated the chance of a postwar U.S. loan because his ideology held the capitalist economy required it).
A state's unusual national history and founding can leave it poorly equipped to understand other countries.
Government organizations carry their own perceptual predispositions: diplomats favor negotiation and compromise, while militaries treat threats and military power as central tools of foreign policy.
Militaries tend to judge other states' intentions by their military postures rather than by other signals.

Confining analysis to individuals' internal cognition misses that ideas and attitudes are formed through social interaction, so political perceptions cannot be explained by looking only inside people's minds.

Preexisting beliefs and expectations powerfully shape how people see new information; expectations and psychological or political needs are the two strongest and most general influences on perception.
Most information about the world is ambiguous, which is why perception depends so heavily on the observer's prior ideas.

Facts never speak for themselves: what is treated as evidence, and whether something is seen as evidence at all, depends on the observer's theories, so no one can be a naive empiricist even in the physical sciences.
Perception is more accurately described as 'I'll see it when I believe it' than 'I'll believe it when I see it', because expectations drive what is perceived rather than the reverse.
When expectations of hostility are widespread, they tend to be self-confirming: a suspicious atmosphere produces events and readings that seem to confirm the suspicion.
condition: when hostile expectations are already widespread

statement: Untrained people are prone to confirmation bias, searching for information that supports their existing views rather than information that might undermine them.

Intelligence organizations are vulnerable to confirmation bias and may fail to vigorously seek disconfirmation of their own hypotheses, as when the CIA under-tested its belief that Iraq was pursuing WMD.
Exposure to belief-contradicting information can backfire: people rehearse why the reports are wrong and marshal supporting arguments, ending up even more certain than before (the backfire effect).
condition: when the information is recognized as discrepant with the person's beliefs

statement: People are largely theory-driven and closed-minded, because the brain is disposed to make sense of stimuli as fast as possible when evidence alone cannot yield a coherent picture.
Human beings are sense-making animals who work from a coherent overall picture down to the details rather than building the picture up from details.

The same information is interpreted differently depending on the general framework applied, and specific beliefs make sense only within the appropriate framework (e.g., pre-modern bleeding and purging followed naturally from viewing the body as a system of intake and outgo that had to stay in balance).

Perceiving another country requires general ideas to interpret specifics, so individual pieces of information tend to confirm the already-established picture rather than overturn it, as with the widely shared pre-2003 belief that Saddam Hussein possessed WMD.

Induction alone cannot overturn an established interpretation: without an alternative framework that casts the information in a different light, discrepant details are absorbed into the prevailing narrative, and the most a careful observer can do is note that not all the information fits.

Intelligence can fail when a salient alternative concept is missing: the A. Q. Khan proliferation network was misread because transnational seller-networks were not salient and the prevailing worldview cast Pakistanis as buyers of nuclear material rather than sellers.
Theories and the expectations they generate drive perception at every scale, from broad implicit beliefs about human motivation to narrow propositions about specific individuals and cases.

Expectations bias threat perception in ambiguous situations, so observers read identical ambiguous movements as more threatening depending on the actor (for example young men versus senior citizens, or by racial stereotype).

Training can rapidly reshape perception: a crew drilled to expect attack misread an ascending airliner as a descending attacker (USS Vincennes, 1988), while an untrained nearby ship read the same radar correctly.
Expectation effects can be self-reinforcing through positive feedback: once an event primes observers, previously-ignored evidence is 'detected' as confirming, as in the 1987 preschool-abuse panic.

The drive to build a coherent story can override logic, as in the Linda problem where people rate a conjunction (librarian and activist) as more probable than one of its conjuncts (librarian), violating probability because the conjunction tells a better story.

Once a conclusion is formed from evidence, people tend to keep the conclusion even after learning the evidence was false, because they forget the basis of the belief (belief perseverance / on-line processing).

Labeling quick cognitive closure as 'premature' is not always right: one must weigh the costs of delaying judgment against those of jumping to a conclusion, since many problems are best handled early and hesitation can carry domestic-political costs.
condition: the balance depends on the relative costs of delay versus early error in the specific situation

statement: Uncertainty is mentally costly and often painful, so forming beliefs quickly can be a rational economy of limited cognitive resources rather than a defect.

Images and beliefs form quickly, long before full information is available, and once they take hold are hard to displace, so later discrepant information persuades the uncommitted but is downgraded or misperceived by those who have already taken a position (e.g., the CIA analyst on the Iraqi aluminum tubes).

First reports of any crisis are incomplete or misleading, yet the pressure to act and a leader's need to appear confident make it psychologically hard to hold a tentative belief while signaling readiness to revise it, as in the initial misreading of the 2012 Benghazi attack.

Being strongly theory-driven degrades forecasting: Tetlock found that 'hedgehogs' who hold one big idea predict political events worse than 'foxes' who are less wedded to strong expectations, partly because hedgehogs cling to theory-derived predictions too long.

Accountability and instructions to keep an open mind can reduce premature closure but are not foolproof, and accountability can backfire by pushing people to be decisive and therefore to close prematurely.

Perseverance past disconfirming evidence is sometimes valuable, since many scientific breakthroughs required years of persistence, so an organization benefits from containing individuals who range across the stubbornness-to-openness spectrum even though a state ultimately needs a single policy.

The general frame brought to an issue strongly shapes the conclusions drawn from identical evidence, as when framing health insurance as individual choice versus a human right predisposes people to opposite positions.
Applying the wrong analogical frame to a new problem produces error, as when experts viewed biological weapons through the frame of chemical weapons despite crucial differences between them.

An institution's initial frame delays recognition of a developing situation: UN staff were slow to grasp the 1994 Rwandan genocide partly because they had framed the danger as a civil war before the massacres broke out.

Framing an issue in terms of a value the target already endorses can shift their position (Gorbachev's resistance to German unification weakened once it was framed as self-determination), while framing an issue as national security ('securitization') sharply narrows the room for debate.

A dominant frame and the expectations it generates can turn ambiguous evidence into violence, as when German soldiers in 1914, primed by memories of franc-tireurs, read ambiguous signs as guerrilla fire and committed atrocities.

Political actors compete to establish the frame in which their actions are seen, and naming is a key tool: proponents rush to attach a resonant label to their position before opponents can attach an unattractive one.

In real politics, unlike experiments with naive subjects, the causal direction between a frame and a view is hard to establish because participants choose their own frames from prior predispositions, so the frame may be an effect of prior beliefs rather than an independent cause.
People often choose the frames they use because of their existing views rather than passively accepting a frame offered to them.
Real political issues almost always come with competing alternative frames on offer, unlike many laboratory experiments, because they connect to preexisting values that divide people.

Framing effects usually work by making different considerations, values, or feelings salient rather than by changing a person's substantive theory of how the world works, as in Prospect Theory, where identical choices elicit more risk-taking when framed as avoiding losses than as making gains.
People usually do not realize that their interpretation of incoming information is strongly shaped by what they already believe.

Because they do not see the role of their prior beliefs, disputants argue heatedly over specific pieces of information when what really divides them is their differing beliefs, so time is wasted failing to address the real source of disagreement.
Failing to see the role of prior beliefs, each side comes to regard the other as not merely wrong but unreasonable, because the specific evidence seems obviously to count against the other's view.

Not recognizing the influence of prior beliefs makes people more confident, because they see ambiguous information as less ambiguous than it is and treat it as independent confirmation, which is a major source of overconfidence.

In the Iraq WMD case, both producers and consumers of intelligence grew more confident that active programs existed because they failed to see that they read new information (much of it fabricated) as confirming only because prior beliefs about Saddam already pointed that way.

The irrationality in belief-driven interpretation is not that the evidence is inconsistent with the belief, but that people treat the evidence as confirmation that any reasonable observer would read the same way regardless of their starting point.

People probably cannot avoid assimilating new information to prior beliefs, since the extreme injunction not to would make functioning impossible, but greater self-awareness can reduce undue confidence, improve understanding of how others read the evidence, and focus attention on the important questions.
condition: self-awareness reduces but cannot eliminate assimilation to priors

statement: A practical debiasing step is to recognize when a conclusion rests mainly on the prior plausibility of the general picture rather than on the specific new evidence, to ask whether that evidence is equally consistent with alternative explanations, and to consider how it would look under a different framing.

How much and in which direction you should revise a belief depends on how confident you are in your prior and on how diagnostic the new information is, that is, how well it discriminates between your view and the alternatives.

The updating rule cuts both ways: a well-established belief can be overturned by sufficiently disconfirming evidence, but a firmly grounded prevailing view need not change for some discrepant evidence, which may be an outlier.
Being slow to change your mind in the face of discrepant information is not necessarily irrational, because extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.

Two people can rationally respond differently to the same new information without either violating the norms for handling evidence, because they hold different priors and different judgments of the evidence's diagnosticity.

What matters is not only whether information is consistent with your view but whether it clashes with and discriminates among alternatives, yet even sophisticated analysts are much quicker to note that events fit their expectations than to test whether the same events also fit alternative theories.

Evidence consistent with a favored hypothesis is often equally consistent with alternatives (Iraqi behaviors read as WMD concealment could equally reflect corruption, standard operating procedures, or currying favor), so analysts must actively seek evidence that discriminates between hypotheses.
Seeking evidence that discriminates between hypotheses is not intuitive and has to be explicitly taught, so untrained people tend to stop searching once the evidence merely fits their view.

Divergence or even polarization of beliefs in the face of a common stream of information is not automatically evidence of irrationality, because it can arise from different priors or different judgments of how diagnostic the information is.

Reacting to discrepant evidence by becoming more committed is not necessarily irrational, since a Bayesian may legitimately discount the evidence by distrusting its source when it contradicts a well-established position.

Bayesianism's practical limitation is that the confidence in a prior and the diagnosticity of evidence are not objective and must be supplied by hand, so the rule cannot tell you how certain to be or how far, or even in which direction, to move.

In experiments and medical trials evidence can often be judged independently of priors, but few political judgments are that clear: political information does not speak for itself and its interpretation is inevitably shaped by prior beliefs.

Because priors and diagnosticity judgments are not independent in political cases, the same behavior is read oppositely by hawks and doves, with a dove seeing willingness to compromise where a hawk sees an attempt to lure the country into complacency.

Expectation can cause outright misperception of what an actor said or did, as when Kissinger misheard Chinese signals before the 1971 Bangladesh crisis, so even someone trying to update rationally moves in the wrong direction because the input itself was distorted.

Often an analyst cannot even describe what the other actor did without reference to the disputed beliefs, as when Malenkov's peaceful-resolution statement or Khrushchev's army cuts were read either as genuine conciliation or as maneuvers for advantage.

A conciliatory act is a legitimate diagnostic clue because it is more likely when intentions are benign than malign, but the same act can be explained away (Dulles argued Khrushchev cut forces to reallocate resources for a graver threat), and the updating rule alone cannot adjudicate which reading is correct.

A prior belief can flip the reading of the very same event into confirmation: intercepted Iraqi orders to destroy indications of WMD were taken as proof of concealment and only later, once it was known there were no programs, re-read as innocent removal of old traces.

The meaning of even direct evidence such as video footage depends on prior beliefs about the actors, so the same recording can support opposite inferences depending on one's general beliefs about how people behave (the Ferguson shooting tape).

It does not make strict sense to ask whether political actors are good Bayesians; the useful questions are whether they neglect their priors (drifting like driftwood) or ignore new information (flying straight like a bullet).

Because diagnosticity cannot be fully separated from priors, theory-driven perception cannot be dismissed as irrational; the irrationality lies mainly in the cases where people do not realize they are inferring this way, and that lack of self-awareness inflates their confidence.

Much of the brain's work, including thinking, judging, and concluding, is unconscious, and people are unaware of these processes, as shown when the motor signal to act preceded the reported decision to act.

People lack privileged access to their own mental processes: they explain their own behavior with the same inference they apply to others, then adopt the inferred goals and beliefs as a basis for future action, as Truman did in forming his image of the USSR after acting.

Judgments are contaminated by the welcomeness of a message without the person's awareness: listeners rated a speaker's style and competence by whether they agreed with his message, not realizing the content had driven their supposedly stylistic judgment.
The reasons people give for their judgments and decisions may be post-hoc stories rather than the actual causes, so introspective self-reports about how a conclusion was reached can be unreliable.
It is very likely that the reasons leaders give for their views and decisions, even when sincere, do not reflect the actual considerations at work.

Because officials may be unaware of the real forces behind their conclusions, analysts and historians who rely on documents in which officials lay out their arguments must treat even sincere explanations as unreliable evidence of true motivation.
Stimuli that never reach consciousness, and stimuli whose influence goes unrecognized, can significantly shape perception and judgment through priming.

Priming can affect even moral and political judgments through incidental factors such as an unpleasant room, an uncomfortable chair, cleanliness reminders, or the type of polling place, so in some cases voting behavior can be predicted before the voter is aware of deciding.

The implications of implicit and priming findings for elite foreign-policy judgments and leaders' images of other countries remain obscure and warrant skepticism, because such an effect must survive a long, multi-participant governmental process.
condition: the impact may be greatest in personalistic regimes where one dominant individual can act quickly

statement: There is an inherent tension in claiming that short-lived extraneous stimuli have long-term effects, since later influences of the same kind should reverse the initial effect, so lasting effects are the exception rather than the rule.
exception: unless path-dependence locks in an initial perception or a temporary impression triggers an immediate irreversible action

statement: Decision-makers, like everyone, are influenced by factors they are unaware of and would deny, such as early experiences with a country and socialization, and they wrongly believe their deep beliefs arose from careful thought rather than upbringing.

The mind works on two tracks: System 1 is fast, automatic, unconscious, and heuristic-laden and is the default, while System 2 is slow, explicit, and effortful; assimilating new information to prior beliefs is System 1 at work.
System 1 is efficient and serves people well most of the time, but it sometimes produces misperceptions and the illusion that new information is independently confirming one's existing views.

System 2 is engaged only under prompting because it is mentally costly, people overestimate how much System 2 governs their lives, and even when System 2 operates System 1 still feeds it many of its inputs.

Because intuition is not schooled by careful methodology, System 1 is over-impressed by first-hand and vivid evidence, mistakes correlation for causation, builds simple stories, and over-attributes others' behavior to personal characteristics while underplaying situational factors.

Intuition, though not grounded in deliberate reasoning, can still reach valid conclusions, as with Truman's decision to stay in Berlin and Reagan's sense of Soviet weakness, both of which proved correct.

Initial reactions to a crisis tend to reach extreme responses, while peaceful resolutions require ingenuity and skill that take time to develop, so leaders reconsidered when time allowed in 1962 but leapt to extreme measures in 1914.

The virtues of quick intuitive judgment are greatest where people get repeated exposure to similar situations with accurate feedback, conditions that foreign policy does not meet because the important cases are few and feedback is weak.
condition: intuition is most trustworthy in domains with repeated similar cases and prompt accurate feedback

statement: Judging whether deliberation improves decisions is confounded by selection effects, since the issues subjected to prolonged deliberation are the hardest ones, so heavily deliberated decisions turning out badly may reflect problem difficulty rather than the process.

The System 1 versus System 2 distinction may be overdrawn, because crises trigger both time pressure and high stakes, and real foreign-policy decisions often show System 1 biases even amid full attention and elaborate staff deliberation.

Careful conscious deliberation does not automatically free a person from System 1's grooves: assimilation of new information to prior beliefs occurs even when people proceed slowly and carefully, and since even System 2 is error-prone, better results require more explicit methodological self-consciousness than System 2 normally supplies.

A strong influence of genes or biology on behavior does not amount to determinism, because the same biological factors can produce different outcomes depending on how they interact with other factors.

Human beings are distinguished from other mammals by their facility for cooperation, and since success in international politics depends on the ability to cooperate with many actors, it is a mistake to believe evolution has selected humans for brutality.

Leaders often attribute others' trusting or mistrustful stance to their own beliefs about human nature, and a core difference among ideologies is how far human nature is believed to guide and constrain behavior and societal possibilities.
The belief that people can be remade into a form specified by a ruling group has always led to disaster.

Ideological differences may produce differences in the propensity to perceive threat and to see possibilities for cooperation, but strong evidence, especially for elite foreign-policy behavior, is hard to obtain because cases confound a leader's ideology with the adversary's own characteristics.
condition: evidence is confounded when ideology co-varies with the adversary's characteristics

statement: Inferring a stable threat-perception disposition from stylized facts is unreliable: Cold War conservatives' hard line toward the USSR is weak evidence of a general trait because they were also more ideologically hostile, and toward right-wing dictators the pattern reversed, with conservatives favoring cooperation.

Analysts should beware attributing survival functionality to any existing trait, because the fact that a bias is prevalent and compatible with survival does not show it was generated or maintained for its particular survival value.

Dispositions toward authority, sensitivity to threat, tolerance for ambiguity, which strongly affects the ability to delay cognitive closure, and taste for novelty are partly innate and do affect political orientations and perceptions.

The style of a person's beliefs, such as being vehement and unqualified, can persist even when the content of those beliefs changes radically, as with activists who reversed their Vietnam positions while keeping the same absolutist manner.

Threat perception tends to be trait-like and stable across eras: those very suspicious of the USSR during the Cold War now tend to be most alarmed by Islamic fundamentalism, China, and Iran, while former doves take a more relaxed stance on all of them.

The strongest evidence that significant aspects of personality, including basic political orientation, are innate comes from studies of identical twins raised apart, though nature and nurture interact so that the magnitude and even direction of gene effects vary with environment.

The struggle for leadership selects atypical people who tend to be extreme in energy, ambition, and self-regard, so leaders should not be modeled as psychologically average, and the selecting traits may differ from one kind of society to another.
Many stimuli activate the amygdala, the seat of emotion, before they reach the brain areas associated with deliberation.
Emotions are not separate from or opposed to cognition; they saturate thinking and provide the driving force for action, and without them people would struggle to make any decisions at all.
Because leaders believe they are supposed to shun emotion, they tend to be slow to recognize their own feelings at work, as Nixon was with his hatreds.

Even nuclear deterrence rests on emotion rather than pure calculation: retaliating after one's own state is destroyed serves no rational purpose, so vengeance is the only explanation, yet neither side ever doubted the threat's credibility.

Almost every cognitive process, including attention, evaluative judgment, probability estimates, risk perception, out-group bias, and moral judgment, is shaped by momentary emotions in systematic and profound ways.

One cannot make simple generalizations linking a specific emotion to a specific perception or response, because the relations are reciprocal (stimuli must be detected to trigger emotions, and emotional states shape how stimuli are perceived) and vary across person and situation.

An analyst can rarely move directly from the external situation to an actor's response without considering emotions, since the same hostile move can make one person angry and another fearful, with quite different responses, and passing mood can prime either.

Anger usually leads to action while fear favors restraint, so an angry crisis response pushes toward force whereas a shift toward fear makes slower, more restrained, cooperation-permitting policies more attractive, as when Kennedy's team moved from an impulse to bomb toward blockade during the Cuban Missile Crisis.

Emotions are often triggered before cognitive processing and strongly influence it, so people judge policies partly by whether they feel right, as when austerity felt right because a government seems obliged not to spend beyond its means.

It can be very difficult to alter hostile relations without first shifting the emotional valence, which is why leaders use emotional appeals, as Gorbachev did by admitting past mistakes and Kennedy did by honoring Soviet wartime sacrifices in his American University speech.

Emotions can legitimize otherwise reprehensible acts, since a violent response to an insult is more accepted when seen as spontaneous anger than as calculation, so timing matters, as the Germans understood in expecting Austria to avenge the Archduke immediately before sympathy faded.

All reasoning is motivated in the trivial sense that something prompts it, but the label 'motivated reasoning' properly applies only when the driving motives are something other than accuracy, and these are often tied to emotions and needs.

People hold beliefs not only to understand their environment but to meet personal, social, and political needs, and the need to live comfortably with oneself strongly influences belief, so needs stand alongside expectations as the two main drivers of perception.

A strong motive to scrutinize a disagreeable claim is not motivated bias as long as the completed evaluation is fair; motivated reasoning occurs only when evidence pointing in different directions is treated differently, crediting sources when they confirm and discrediting them when they disconfirm.

Failing to change your view after not finding flaws in a contrary study is not necessarily motivated, because on Bayesian grounds strong prior grounds can rationally lead you to distrust a single contrary study and even to conclude it must be flawed though you cannot locate the flaw.

The operational signature of motivated reasoning is judging as fatal flaws in an opposing argument exactly the features you would accept, or even admire, if they were deployed in service of your favored conclusion.

Motivated and unmotivated bias are clear in principle but extremely hard to separate in practice, because there are many paths to any conclusion, so the best chance to distinguish them is to find cases where expectations and needs pull in opposite directions.

Motivated reasoning is likely when a person heavily invested in a policy is slower than less-invested colleagues to see evidence that undermines it, as Bethmann Hollweg was slow to see that Britain would intervene in 1914.

Motivated reasoning is likely when a person suddenly embraces previously rejected ideas because doing so yields a comforting conclusion, as when Allen Dulles credited the 1956 Hungarian uprising to Soviet repression rather than the Western broadcasts he had long championed.

Some perceptions exceed what theory-driven bias explains, because people may ward off perceptions that would cause them great pain (willful blindness), and one need not accept Freudian repression since implicit pre-conscious filtering can screen out unbearable stimuli.

A clue that motivated reasoning is operating is the failure to ask questions one would normally expect, as when officials confident of winning in Vietnam never asked why, if the communists were losing, they were unwilling to negotiate.

An analyst should be suspicious when plans proceed despite the removal of a condition that had been treated as essential from the start, as when Castlereagh went ahead with operations in 1809 after Austria pulled out of the war against Napoleon.

People may sincerely believe they exercised adequate care yet still be biased, which is why the law imposes a 'should have known' standard to counter the incentive not to see, as in industrial-accident liability.

The needs that produce motivated bias divide into two related kinds: those that push a person to establish or maintain a preferred belief, and those that require painful value trade-offs not be directly confronted.

Under strong motivation to reach a conclusion, the evidence a person selects, the interpretations given, the way conflicting considerations are balanced, and the images formed of others may be rationalizations of a desired view rather than disinterested deliberation, so analysis and even deeply held beliefs can be rationalizations more than rationales.

Unflattering characterizations of an adversary are often a byproduct of a failed relationship rather than its root cause, as British diatribes about Mossadeq and Iranian culture followed rather than caused the collapse of the 1951 oil negotiations.

Before attributing great causal power to ideas and beliefs, ask what produces them and why people accept them, because ideas do not float freely and convenient beliefs often shift in sync with material interests and circumstances.

A clue that reasoning is motivated is that the person's conclusion in one domain violates the general principles they apply elsewhere, as when social conservatives treat homosexuality as chosen while stressing biology in other areas, or media-effects beliefs flip neatly along partisan lines.

Motivated reasoning is often produced by having an interest, frequently monetary, in believing something to be true, since it is hard to get someone to understand something when their income depends on not understanding it, as when S&P raised ratings after losing market share.
It is rational to weigh cost in deciding what to do, but only motivated reasoning can explain why the perceived magnitude of a danger would vary with the cost of dealing with it.

The interest driving a motivated belief need not be monetary, and a belief can be a fairly direct product of difficult circumstances, as Gorbachev's New Thinking may have been powerful yet not autonomous, serving as a rationale for concessions forced by Soviet economic collapse.

A perception can be driven by the need to justify a course of action rather than by new evidence, as Gorbachev's belief at Reykjavik that Reagan was sincere is hard to explain by Reagan's unchanged behavior and better explained by Gorbachev's need for a rationale to move toward the U.S. position.

The political relationship drives cultural and racial portrayal more than the reverse, so adversaries are depicted as darker and more animalistic as relations worsen, as with images of the Japanese from the 1920s to the 1930s and of American Indians shifting with their alliance to Britain.

Even more powerful than the need to discredit adversaries is the need to think well of oneself, and this self-flattering self-deception increases conflict, as Adam Smith observed that people turn their view away from whatever would judge their own conduct unfavourably.
People tend to avoid perceiving painful value trade-offs, convincing themselves that a trade-off is minor or nonexistent even when it is actually severe.

People oversell their policies to themselves as well as to others, because doing so smooths away doubts and builds the self-confidence needed for dangerous and prolonged ventures, so that second thoughts become as psychologically crippling as they are politically.

On a contested policy, advocates tend to believe every consideration lines up on their side (a favored policy is judged both low-cost and high-benefit) while opponents believe every consideration lines up against it, and almost no one holds the mixed view, as in the debates over immigration reform and the Iraq War.

Realism's teaching that a leader may need to behave immorally to serve the country has the virtue of letting the leader see more clearly how others will respond and what the costs will be, so that mitigating steps can be taken.

Avoidance of trade-offs shows up when a person changes a long-held belief to fit a course of action already chosen, as when Cheney moved from expecting that overthrowing Saddam would bring chaos and costly occupation to expecting troops to be greeted as liberators.

A comforting perception can arise that contradicts a person's own well-established views, as when Nixon believed a troop withdrawal would show North Vietnam he wanted peace despite his standing conviction that he had to appear tough, while a subordinate without ultimate responsibility saw the trade-off more clearly.

The mechanism of trade-off avoidance is that a person fixes on one dominant value and, without realizing it, draws all other considerations into line so they point the same way, which is why overconfidence in hard cases often appears only after the decision is made.

Leaders rarely acknowledge conflicts between their most deeply held values, instead proclaiming that national interests and values do not conflict, that security need not be bought at the price of civil liberties, and that deterring an adversary carries no risk of an unnecessary hostility spiral.

When the risks and sacrifices of a decision cannot be submerged, leaders often come to believe the fateful choice was dictated by forces beyond their control and attribute the choice to the adversary, as Europe's leaders in 1914 uniformly felt war was forced on them while only their adversaries had freedom of choice.

A belief that one has a dominant strategy relieves a decision-maker of the hard task of ascertaining others' fears and intentions and of considering that one's own actions could worsen the situation, as many 1914 decision-makers believed their course was best no matter what the other side did.

A related comfort-belief that eases a risky course is that a more cautious path would be no safer, as officials urging belligerence at the start of the Berlin Blockade argued that nothing the West did could either provoke or conciliate the Soviets.

Leaders who take great responsibility seek ways to lift some of the psychological burden, so they are prone to see the most consequential choices as required by circumstances rather than as genuinely chosen.

The belief that a policy is best on every value dimension boosts confidence and aids implementation but slows the recognition that the strategy may be failing and needs re-examination, because undermining one or two of many reasons will not reverse it.

The need to justify a policy can elevate initially subsidiary goals to primary ones, as the Bush administration came to believe more strongly in making Iraq a democracy after learning that Saddam had no active WMD programs.

It is hard to shake off earlier ideas even without any motivation, because a person is prone to interpret new research in the terms already set out, and coming at material with fresh eyes has real limits.

Useful debiasing habits for an analyst are to be slower to treat new information as independent confirmation rather than mere non-disconfirmation, to look for the core differences underlying competing views since surface arguments about recent events are usually driven by deeper long-standing beliefs, and to grow suspicious whenever multiple independent considerations are said to point to the same policy.

Understanding perception can correct errors, but the incentive structure and organizational culture of an intelligence agency can matter as much as psychological factors, as the CIA's incentives and culture were at least as important as psychology in its slowness to see that the Shah of Iran might fall.

A key intelligence failure mode is neglecting negative evidence, the dogs that did not bark, meaning things that should appear if the prevailing hypothesis were true but are absent, because absent events make far less impact than present ones and overcoming this requires training and discipline.

Longstanding background beliefs can blind analysts to real possibilities, as analysts could not shake the belief that religion could not be a driving force in a modernizing state, delaying recognition that the Shah's regime might be overthrown.

Debiasing has limits, because even the best procedures and most careful analysis can yield incorrect answers, and hindsight bias wrongly makes people assume that a wrong answer proves serious cognitive or motivated error, when the pre-2003 view that Saddam sought WMD was actually more reasonable than the truth.

Perceptions of the world and of other actors diverge from reality in patterns that can be detected and for reasons that can be understood, so misperceptions are not random accidents but a patterned phenomenon usable to explain decisions, account for interaction, and improve understanding of international relations.

Prior work on perception in international relations over-focuses on emotional and motivated distortions such as wishful thinking to the neglect of cold cognitive factors, namely how even a perfectly unemotional and careful person draws inferences from highly ambiguous evidence.

Applying laboratory findings to statecraft is limited, because few experiments give subjects incentives to perceive accurately even though accuracy is the prime concern of real decision-makers, and it is hard to know whether lab influences are strong enough to show up amid the other powerful variables of political decisions.

Beware over-psychologizing: many critical psychological explanations are offered for behavior that political analysis explains more convincingly, such as the way the absence of a sovereign in the international realm gives even highly rational decision-makers reason to be extremely suspicious and mistrustful.

Bias analysis must be applied symmetrically to all sides: it is a fault to scrutinize hard-line or unsympathetic views for emotional and cognitive distortion while exempting the conciliatory views one happens to agree with.

Theories validated on trivial beliefs may not transfer to high-stakes expert judgment, since most psychological theories were built around beliefs unimportant to the person with only minor consequences, and consistency theories explain the young, impaired, frightened, or emotionally overwhelmed rather than competent adults making important non-crisis decisions.

A useful test of a decision theory is whether the proponent would admit it resembles how he himself makes serious decisions, such as his own research, so if a psychologist's account of how decision-makers draw inferences is wildly different from how he handles his own professional data, the theory deserves skepticism.

Absent contrary evidence, model political decision-makers as no less rational, sophisticated, or motivated to understand their environment than scientists, recognizing that they face harder problems with more limited tools rather than perceiving in ways a scientist would be ashamed of.

Drawing on diverse psychological subfields risks mixing incompatible assumptions, but the convergence of explanations across very different realms such as attitude change and visual perception gives greater confidence in them.

There is no easy way to determine the accuracy of a perception, because it is hard to know what a person's perception was and harder to know whether it was correct, as even the once-settled judgment that Churchill read Hitler rightly and Chamberlain wrongly is now disputed.

To mitigate the difficulty of judging accuracy, draw most heavily on cases with extensive evidence and broad historian agreement, note the existence of alternative historical explanations, and treat some cases as plausible though perhaps hypothetical examples that at least show a perception was held and could easily have been wrong.

Rather than asking whether a perception was correct, it is often more fruitful to ask how it was derived from the available information, explaining accurate and inaccurate perceptions with the same general theory, just as optical illusions are explained by a broader theory of vision.

Comparing different actors' perceptions of the same object or situation lets an analyst locate systematic differences traceable to different information-processing, different prior images, or different specific experiences, which is especially valuable for explaining a person's perceptual predispositions.

Because many perceptual errors are random and an instance of almost any misperception can be found, single cases cannot show which errors are most frequent or which antecedent conditions they accompany, so one must study many cases, analyze only high-frequency misperceptions, and search for cases that would contradict the proposed explanation.

Studying patterns of misperception that occur within a shared culture and largely independent of personality shows that even actors with much in common can easily misperceive each other and that important causes of misperception trace to general cognitive processes rather than to a disturbed psyche.

Knowing an actor's interests does not tell you how he will perceive his environment or how he will select routes to his goals, so interest alone cannot answer process questions such as when a statesman thinks others are aggressive or how discrepant information is handled.

At the highest levels, where the cost of inaccuracy is heavy, interest-based analysis fails, since it was not in Chamberlain's interest to see Hitler as appeasable nor in Acheson's interest to believe China would stay out of Korea; those misperceptions ran against the actor's interest.

Beliefs act as switchmen: interests may drive conduct, but the world-images created by ideas determine the tracks along which interest-driven action runs, so once a belief such as the domino theory is taken as given, interest can explain the policy while the belief itself is doing crucial causal work.
Bureaucratic role shapes perception, as military officers seem quicker to detect threats than political leaders, though the causal relationships are often hard to establish.

Proposals to minimize misperception aim to increase explicit, self-conscious judgment and to reduce the extent to which decision-makers reach conclusions without being aware of the alternatives they are rejecting.

Perceptual and decision errors will always be common given the complexity and ambiguity of international information, but steps can increase the degree to which disciplined intelligence is brought to bear on a problem.

Whether perceptions matter is an empirical question, and one can distinguish the psychological milieu, the world as the actor sees it, from the operational milieu, the world in which the policy is carried out, while recognizing that the 'why' questions behind state action require decision-making analysis.
Fully-linked, high-density causal theories have no privileged status, because explanation need not fill in every link between cause and effect and one can always ask for the links between the links.

The intuitive comfort of 'if that is how the statesman saw it, no wonder he acted so' can mislead, because studying decision-making is warranted only if variations in how people see the world actually affect how they act.

The specifics of a triggering event often cannot explain an outcome when many other probable events could have substituted for it, as the Viet Cong attack on Pleiku only affected the timing of U.S. bombing of North Vietnam.
Which level of analysis to focus on is not arbitrary or a matter of taste but reflects beliefs, often only hunches, about which variables drive the phenomenon of concern.

Decision-makers rarely rely on pure vicarious identification (asking how they themselves would act in the other's shoes), because they believe others may not behave as they would and that officials within the other state differ among themselves, so they seek detailed information on each significant person.

In perceiving others, people over-attribute behavior to personality and underestimate the situation, yet when explaining their own behavior they attribute it to the requirements of the situation rather than to their own dispositions.

There is unlikely to be a single most-important level of analysis, because the importance of each level varies by issue area, by how rich an answer is sought, and by the stage of the decision, with domestic politics setting the occasion, bureaucratic bargaining shaping the options, the leader's predisposition driving the choice, and bureaucratic routines governing implementation.

The same variable can have opposite effects at different stages of a decision, as conflict among subordinates increases the variety of information and decision opportunities reaching the top leader while decreasing his ability to ensure his decisions are faithfully implemented.

The importance of variables at one level varies with the state of variables at other levels, so the influence of other levels decreases when variables at one level are in extreme states, as bureaucratic maneuvering matters more when top decision-makers are inexperienced or preoccupied.
States tend to behave alike under extreme danger or extreme opportunity, but under less severe environmental constraints their behavior diverges and must be explained at the decision-making level.
condition: behavior converges only under extreme external compulsion

statement: The claim that an overwhelming situation makes decision-making analysis unnecessary is flawed, because if a situation truly compelled everyone to act alike there would be no hesitation, no sense of being torn, and no elite debate, yet easily-reached consensus decisions like the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan stand out precisely because they are rare.

Whether one faces extreme danger is itself often bitterly contested rather than self-evident, since for Churchill the house was burning soon after Hitler took power, for Chamberlain only after March 1939, and for others never, and decision-makers may even agree their state is threatened while disagreeing about the source.

Even an unambiguous threat such as a large armed attack does not determine all aspects of the response, because there are several exits from the burning house, as the U.S. had no choice but to declare war after Pearl Harbor yet its choices to fight Germany first and demand unconditional surrender were far less compelled.

Even if all states respond similarly to a high threat, an analyst must still explain how the threat arose and why the adversary was aggressive, which may require examining variables at other levels of analysis.

One cannot prove that the external environment determined a response merely by showing that the decision-makers believed so, because the subjective feeling of necessity, while it may lead them to restrict their search for alternatives, does not show that others in the same situation would have felt the same compulsion.

Cognitive-consistency and dissonance dynamics lead decision-makers to avoid psychological conflict by convincing themselves they had no choice, so a situation that appears overwhelming in retrospect may partly be an artifact of the decision-makers having claimed it was.

Pre-office promises of new policies are often neglected once a leader takes power, so a government's foreign policy frequently ends up resembling its predecessor's more than its own campaign rhetoric, as with Eisenhower and Gladstone.

Incoherent or contradictory state behavior is not sufficient evidence for bureaucratic or multi-actor causation, because normal individual decision-making under multiple goals and highly ambiguous information also produces contradictory and badly-fitted policy.

Bureaucratic-politics explanation rests on two claims: that bureaucrats' policy preferences are determined by their position (where you stand depends on where you sit), and that state policy is formed by bureaucratic bargains and routines.

For bureaucratic interest to be more useful than national interest, one must be able to specify the bureaucratic position in advance, and where there is substantial disagreement within an organization, decision-making analysis must be applied at the bureaucratic level too.

Even if bureaucratic preferences track position, that matters only if the preferences explain outcomes, and since the distribution of bureaucratic power is often set by past decisions of top leaders and wider publics, explaining outcomes purely by bureaucratic maneuvering is superficial at best.

Role does shape preferences on parochial issues such as military hardware and doctrine, and officials often reverse their positions when they change offices, as Marshall did between Chief of Staff and Secretary of State and Churchill did between the Home Office and the Admiralty.
condition: most clearly for routine, hardware, and doctrine issues

statement: Organizational perspective matters less when issues are unusual rather than routine, require relatively quick decisions, and involve important widely-shared values, so beliefs on the biggest war-and-peace questions are usually unrelated to bureaucratic roles.
condition: for unusual, high-stakes, value-laden decisions rather than routine ones

statement: On the major decisions of U.S. foreign policy the striking feature is either broad unanimity or that the key disputes, such as hawks versus doves on Vietnam and the Cuban Missile Crisis debate, did not track bureaucratic roles, with leading officials espousing views unrelated to their positions.

To claim that policy is explained by bureaucratic maneuvering, one must specify in advance the relationship between the array of bureaucratic positions and the outcome, because it is not enough to show that an outcome can be described as a compromise, since almost any outcome fits that description.

A clash of bureaucratic stands can often be more fruitfully viewed as a clash among values widely held in society and within the decision-makers' own minds, because different bureaucratic units serve the divergent values that the leader seeks to further.

Without a theory specifying how policy is formed from conflicting bureaucratic preferences, one cannot tell whether any outcome is explained at the bureaucratic level, because there is no basis for claiming that a different constellation of interests, or no bureaucracies at all, would have produced a different result.

Internal elite disagreement among people who could hold power without a regime change reveals the limits of both domestic politics and the international situation as determinants, though such disagreement does not prove the dissenter would have acted on his views in office, since his opposition may reflect his role, lack of information, or political expediency.

Personalistic leaders defeat bureaucratic prediction, as the British WWII unit that recreated the German perspective predicted the positions of parts of the German bureaucracy well but could never predict when Hitler would side with a faction or impose his own solution.
Decision-makers' beliefs and images of others are part of the proximate cause of their behavior, so variables at the other levels of analysis cannot by themselves tell you what the behavior will be.

Even if everyone behaves the same way in the same situation, studying decision-making is worthwhile when there are constant gaps between decision-makers' perceptions and reality, because the shared behavior would otherwise puzzle an observer by being self-defeating or based on incorrect beliefs.

A mediated two-step model treats the actor's perceptions as an immediate cause of behavior, which lets cases of differing accuracy be grouped together, as Britain and France feared German threat before both world wars though mistaken in the first case and correct in the second.

What an analyst believes about an actor's perceptions changes the questions worth asking, so once the Pentagon Papers showed U.S. leaders had a fairly accurate view of the odds in Vietnam, the key question shifted from why they were over-optimistic to why saving Vietnam was thought worth the high expected price.

Reframing a puzzle through the actor's likely perception is often more fruitful, so the central Cuban Missile Crisis question is probably not what Soviet risk propensity explains the bold step but how the Soviets so badly misestimated the probable American response.

Having the same perceptions does not guarantee the same response, but responses are often the same, and when actors with different images of an adversary agree on a response, that agreement tends to be short-lived.
The roots of many important policy disputes lie in differing perceptions, and when the actors do not realize this they misunderstand their disagreement and debate unenlighteningly.

The second step of analysis relates the images held to the information available to the actor by asking how statesmen develop images of others, what evidence they weight most, what makes them perceive threat, when they see a hostile actor as having only limited objectives, and what kinds of behavior change an established image.

Propositions about the causes and effects of images can only be probabilistic, because too many variables are at work, so important perceptual predispositions can be discovered but will often not be controlling.
To decide intelligently how to act, a person must predict how others will behave, and to influence them he must estimate how they will react to each alternative policy he could adopt.

If an analyst believes another's behavior is situation-determined, he can predict it from the external stimulus by imagining what he would do, but if any inside-the-state level matters he must use a rough hypothetico-deductive method to ask what constellation of forces, beliefs, and goals could explain the state's behavior.

No piece of behavior is self-explanatory or has only one plausible implication for the actor's future conduct, so understanding consists largely of perceiving an action and deducing the internal processes of which it is the end result.

Reconstructing another's internal processes lets an analyst respond differently to the same behavior depending on why it occurred, since attributions about whether the act was controllable, understood, or done under duress change predictions of future behavior and therefore one's own response.

People react less to the actual harm inflicted on them than to what they believe the other intended, growing angry and retaliating in proportion to perceived intent largely regardless of how much harm was actually done.

Statesmen infer intentions the same way, as when many U.S. officials read Soviet demands on Eastern Europe as arising from fear of a postwar American withdrawal, concluded the demands could be eased by guaranteeing Soviet security through a strong UN, and then inferred a Soviet threat once that reassurance failed.

The inferred motive behind an act dictates the scale of the response, so Acheson read the Korean War as proof that communism would use armed aggression whenever it thought it could win and inferred the need for broad rearmament, whereas reading it as exploitation of an area outside the declared defense perimeter, or as driven by security fear, would have implied a smaller response.

The same act supports very different predictions depending on the inferred motive, as Kennedy read the Cuban missiles as evidence the Soviets would run high risks even where their interest was marginal and would be more aggressive elsewhere, whereas reading them as emotional commitment to Castro or as unrecognized provocation would have implied different futures.

To interpret another actor's behavior, first separate the situational (external) factors from the internal ones that produced it, building interactive models where needed and recognizing that internal processes may vary with context and over time.

An analyst learns little about an actor's internal processes when the actor behaves as anyone would in that situation, because when the situation fully determines the response no characteristics can be attributed to the actor, so a weak actor conceding a minor issue to a stronger adversary reveals almost nothing about his goals, beliefs, or risk tolerance.

An analyst learns most about an actor's internal processes when the actor behaves unusually, not as the situation seems to dictate, as costly Russian railroads toward Afghanistan were read as hostile because their expense was justified only by an intent to bring military pressure against England.
A costly act that lacks an economic or other non-hostile rationale is attributed to hostility, whereas a cheap or self-benefiting act need not be, even when the strategic effect is identical.

People reverse the inference to read the situation from the actor, so when a powerful person complies with a request observers attribute it to his own values and desires, but when a weak person complies they infer compulsion from the environment.

Before predicting an actor's behavior, ask whether the external stimuli were so compelling as to determine his action, because behavior produced under external compulsion is not expected to recur once the compulsion is removed.

If another's hostile behavior is externally compelled and the compulsion is temporary, the right move is to ease the external constraint and build good relations rather than respond with hostility, because a hostile response does no good while the other cannot defect and at worst creates a new dispute that outlasts the original cause.
If the other's dependence or compulsion is permanent, an actor need not care whether the resulting hostility was freely chosen, because its harmful effect on him is the same either way.
condition: only when the compulsion on the other is permanent rather than temporary

statement: A commitment or peace treaty signed by a totally defeated country is a weaker index of its future behavior than one signed under less dire circumstances, because unless the victors keep it permanently weak it has no reason to abide once it recovers.

Knowing only that an actor is not behaving as anyone would in that situation is not enough, because the analyst must determine which internal process explains it, since a person may fail to flee a burning house from abnormal goals (wanting to die) or from abnormal perceptions (not sensing the danger).

A target's response to harm is mildest when it believes the other did not expect, intend, or approve the harmful outcome, so good motives can partly rescue a bad policy, and a state that unintentionally harmed another should show it was upholding shared values and would act differently once aware of the impact.

A target responds more strongly but still with restraint when it believes the other sought a goal that conflicted with its interest but does not generally seek to harm it, so to limit the other's hostility a state should show its action served values very important to it, that its gains exceeded the other's losses, and, if the harm came from a bargain with a third party, that it did its best to limit the costs imposed on the other.

A target responds most extremely when it believes the other intended the harm and sought it as a positive good to weaken or destroy it rather than as a by-product of a specific conflict, an inference drawn when the other uses inappropriate tactics, excessive force, or inflicts injury without due cause.

It is dangerous to pay a very high price for a marginal advantage or to refuse to be conciliatory on an issue known to matter more to the adversary, because the adversary reads gratuitous or disproportionate hostility as evidence of a desire to harm and reacts strongly even when the immediate injury is slight.

A threat of overwhelming force can be used to let the other side concede without loss of honor, as Britain arranged an overwhelmingly large fleet in the Dogger Bank incident so there could be no dishonor to the Russians in yielding.
exception: overwhelming force is escalatory except when deliberately sized to let the other yield without humiliation
