statement: Reaction to assistance, like reaction to harm, depends on the inferred explanation, so a helper is not automatically assumed to be a friend, and help given freely impresses more and is more likely to be reciprocated than help given under compulsion or by accident.

Aid that also benefits the giver is not read as a sign of goodwill, but when the other gives more than needed or takes less than he could exact, the actor infers the other has a positive stake in his well-being and expects friendly behavior in future.

Generosity, defined as a state declining to exploit another's weakness, and gratitude, defined as the beneficiary later responding with similar restraint, can describe state behavior without altruism, because forbearance signals common interest and the beneficiary reciprocates partly to avoid strengthening a nation that might later turn against it.

When a state forbears from exploiting the other and the other keeps exploiting, the state infers that the other either does not grasp that relationships rest on mutual concession or sees few common interests, and concludes it must defend itself against continued hostility.

Nation A trusts B when it believes B will not further its own interests at A's expense, usually because A believes B values the prospects of long-run cooperation more than the short-run gains it could get by exploiting its immediate power over A.

To demonstrate trust, an actor may deliberately allow, and even seek, situations in which the other could harm it, showing it recognizes the other as trustworthy and that they share dominating common interests, thereby laying the basis for a relationship not preoccupied with short-run gains or fear of a double-cross.

Accepting military risks that would never be run in real war, such as letting the victim fire first or suffering his fire without replying, is a costly signal that an act of violence is meant to stay strictly limited.

Three questions make correct assessment of the other's goals and beliefs decisive: can the issue in dispute be treated in isolation, how will the other carry out its undertakings, and what threats and promises will be most effective.

An actor must decide whether a dispute is situation-bound or a symptom of a deeper continuing disagreement, because if it is the latter, dealing with it on its merits is ineffective and concessions warranted by the immediate case may only invite further demands, so it is better to reset relations on a cooperative footing than to negotiate the narrow issue.
condition: when the underlying conflict is severe and cannot be dissipated by conciliation

statement: In negotiation an actor must look beyond the other's demands and promises to how the other will behave under various settlements, because no contract can cover every situation and much depends on the attitude each side adopts during the life of the agreement, so a negotiator must assess not only how much he can get but how much he needs to get.

The greater a party's fear and mistrust, the more detailed a contract it demands and the more guarantees it exacts, and in the extreme case where a party fears for its existence, changing the other's attitude matters more than winning advantageous provisions, since clauses are worthless if the other will evade them at the first opportunity.

A party will refuse any settlement with an adversary it believes will renege when convenient, no matter what terms are offered, as most British decision-makers would not consider peace with Hitler after September 1939 because they thought he would renew the war when it suited him.

The accuracy of an actor's estimate of the adversary's goals and beliefs determines whether his threats, concessions, and assurances succeed, because a threat backfires when the target actually welcomes the threatened action and assurances are wasted when aimed at a fear the other does not hold, as the U.S. reassured China about the Yalu power stations while China actually feared invasion.

An accurate understanding of the beliefs and goals behind an adversary's unacceptable proposal can open room for an arrangement that meets the other's objectives without sacrificing what you value most, achieving integration that upgrades common interests rather than merely splitting the difference.
condition: when the incompatibility between the two sides' goals is limited

statement: Integrative bargaining requires understanding one's own means-ends chain rather than pursuing goals without regard to why they were originally sought, since the skilled negotiator finds new alternatives that connect to the underlying objective, as the auto industry met a guaranteed-wage demand through supplementary unemployment benefits.

Pursuing established subgoals without knowing why they are valued blocks creativity, a problem compounded in large organizations, so superiors reduce organizational creativity when they issue specific directives without explaining their broader aims, leaving subordinates unable to design policies that exploit changing circumstances.

Explaining your true reasons to an adversary is useless or worse if those reasons involve goals and beliefs the other finds implausible, as U.S. technical explanations for lend-lease revisions made Soviet officials suspect a hidden motive and delay, so it was sometimes better to frame decisions in terms a Marxist would accept as sincere.

An accurate account of your motives can create rather than clear up conflict when the other cannot credit it, so a credible self-interested rationale can work better than a true altruistic one, as the Soviets would have returned liberated U.S. troops faster if told they were needed against Japan than told the motive was humanitarian.

For prediction, separating the internal from the situational components of behavior is a prelude to recombining them, since the inferred internal processes and the situation the other is expected to face must be considered jointly through the concept of intentions.

An actor's intentions are best defined as the actions he will or would take under given circumstances, rather than what he plans or hopes to achieve, because that is what others are trying to predict, which means intention cannot be separated from resolve and willingness to run risks.

A state's 'utopian intentions' are what it would do absent any external constraint, and examining them highlights characteristics of a state and a historical era, since what states want others to do varies across eras and states.

A state might refrain from aggression even under ideal conditions for reasons other than satiation, such as moral opposition to force or instrumental pacifism (the view that force is ineffective or counterproductive for the goal), though professed instrumental pacifism is hard to verify and may not survive if restraints are lifted.

Classifying states by whether they would change the status quo if it were easy makes almost all states look aggressive and is unhelpful, so an analyst should instead judge a state's 'basic intention' by the costs and risks it is willing to tolerate.

Two states can share the same utopian intention, such as spreading their political systems, yet have very different basic intentions because they differ in willingness to run risks and make sacrifices, just as status-quo powers differ in the price they will pay to preserve what they hold.

The decisive claim in reading an adversary is often not that it would expand but that it would expand even when the risk is high, and such a conclusion may rest on a shaky premise, as Acheson inferred Soviet aggressiveness from Korea by assuming Russia knew the U.S. would respond forcibly.

States usually pay a higher price to protect what they have than to increase their values, because possessions gain subjective and objective value over time and losses cause pain in excess of the joy brought by an objectively comparable gain.

Other states may correctly estimate the costs a state finds bearable yet misperceive the goals for which it will pay that price, as Britain and France overestimated Hitler's resolve on redressing Versailles grievances while underestimating his willingness to go to war to dominate Europe.

A state's behavior may not correspond to its basic intentions when it misperceives or miscalculates and undertakes dangerous actions it did not mean to risk, as the Soviets grossly mis-estimated the risk of putting missiles in Cuba and Hitler was reckless because he was certain the other side would back down rather than because he accepted a high probability of war.

States that use force to alter the status quo often differ from others less in their willingness to run perceived risks than in the fact that they perceive low risks in situations where others perceive high ones.

When analyzing another's policy, separate the state's willingness to run risks from its perceptions of the costs and dangers, because a cautious state that blundered into danger will not repeat the behavior once it understands it will meet strong opposition, whereas a state that knew what it was doing will not be deterred by a clearer picture, so strategies effective against one are inappropriate for the other.

A state may not see how far its actions will upset the status quo, because in an interdependent world limited moves can have large unforeseen consequences, as pre-WWI Germany's great strength and strategic location meant even small aggrandizements had large effects.

Whether a disruptive state acts from inadvertence or design matters only if others can alert it to the consequences and it would then modify its policy, and if that is not possible the distinction is immaterial.

It is often in an actor's interest to convince others that he will pay a high price on a specific issue but will not contest wider ones, yet this image is hard to project, since it is difficult to seem willing to go to war over a minor issue unless the stand is tied to more general principles, as Hitler disavowed demands beyond redressing Versailles so his vehemence did not read as unlimited aggressiveness.

A state's intentions, defined as what it will actually do, can differ from what its own decision-makers think they will do, so observers must predict how an actor will behave rather than how he thinks he will, and may sometimes predict his behavior better than he can himself.

Decision-makers often cannot predict their own behavior, because world politics outruns their imagination with unforeseen events or because they avoid thinking about a probable event when the reaction depends on unpredictable context or when the choice is politically or intellectually too difficult, as Germany could not formulate WWI peace terms without splitting the country.
People misjudge how much events will stir their emotions, so calm contingency plans may bear little resemblance to actual reactions, as most socialists expected to oppose World War I and did not.

Events can lead a decision-maker to re-think goals and values so that behavior departs from prior plans, and the common pattern is to plan a strong reaction but relent when the moment comes, as Kennedy withheld the planned strike on a missile site during the Cuban crisis, because people do not examine their basic beliefs until confronted with shocks and unpleasant choices.

A decision-maker may not act as planned when the actual context differs from the expected one, whether the event's own context, the international context, or the domestic context, as Britain backed away from aiding Denmark in 1864 once it realized previous behavior had alienated the French support its plans assumed.

Because decision-makers do not always know how they will act, others will disregard statements of intent when they believe their own prediction of the actor's behavior is more accurate, as the Joint Chiefs approved the Bay of Pigs partly believing Kennedy would reverse his stand against direct U.S. involvement if the invasion faltered.

Differing perceptions of the other state's intentions often underlie policy debates, and when the participants do not realize they differ on this crucial point the dispute becomes vituperative and unproductive, as much of the U.S. deterrence debate was really a disagreement about Soviet intentions dressed as clashing theories of international relations.

The central deterrence argument is that great dangers arise if an aggressor believes the status-quo powers are weak in capability or resolve, because he will test them starting with a small issue, and if they retreat they both lose the specific value and encourage him to press harder while making their later resolve hard to credit.

To avoid being tested to destruction, a status-quo state must display the ability and willingness to wage war and often cannot judge disputes on their merits, because issues of little intrinsic value become significant as indices of resolve, as Kennedy refused to trade away missiles in Turkey he had already ordered removed.

In a conflict resembling the game of Chicken, it can be safer to hew to the center of the road than to yield six inches on successive nights, provided one will really stop yielding before being pushed off, because refusing to play the game invites costly depredations.

A state under deterrence pressure often goes to extremes because moderation and conciliation are apt to be taken for weakness, fearing that admitting a willingness to make concessions will prompt the other to redouble its efforts for a further retreat rather than reciprocate.

The fear that concessions signal beatability inhibits even overtures that might end a conflict, as Japan would not call for mediation in the Russo-Japanese War lest Russia read weakness and Johnson feared that halting the bombing of North Vietnam would signal weakening resolve.

Even civility and a conciliatory tone are dangerous because aggressors often misinterpret them, as Chamberlain's pre-invasion note meant to show determination was read by the Germans as soft and as seeking a modus vivendi.

Deterrence does not require never changing position, since superior power must sometimes be recognized, legitimate grievances rectified, and enticing concessions made, but the other's friendship cannot be won by gratuitous concessions made without conviction of their justice or of equivalent return.

When the distribution of power is favorable, firmness can check aggression, because the high cost of war, the low probability the aggressor can win, and the value he places on what he already holds lead even a minimally rational state to refrain and to pursue its values peacefully once it sees the defender cannot be bullied.

In the deterrence worldview the world is tightly interconnected, so what happens in one interaction influences others as each state scrutinizes the others' behavior for indications of interests, strengths, and weaknesses.

The deterrence view often rests on the belief that the other's aims are unlimited, so yielding on one matter only encourages further demands with no end, as in Tojo's reasoning about the United States and Khrushchev's image of appeasing a bandit.

A less extreme deterrence view sees the other as having no plan but opportunistically probing where resistance is least and pulling up when it meets formidable resistance, as Palmerston characterized the United States.

The spiral model's root is the anarchic setting of international relations rather than a psychological flaw or defect of human nature, because in a Hobbesian world without a sovereign each state is protected only by its own strength and knows that others without current aggressive designs might later develop them.

Decision-makers, especially military leaders, worry about the most implausible threats and plan against currently friendly states, and such fears are not always paranoid, since Frederick the Great's belief in a conspiracy behind the Seven Years' War proved justified when the secret archives were opened.

The deeper spiral complication is that most means of self-protection simultaneously menace others, so as Rousseau argued, with no guarantee of security everyone is anxious to begin war at a favorable moment to forestall a neighbor, making even offensive wars unjust precautions for the assailant's own protection.

In extreme cases states seeking security may believe the best or only route to it is to attack and expand, as the tsars held that what stops growing begins to rot and pre-World War II Japanese leaders saw the alternative to expanding dominance as sacrificing their very existence.

The drive for security produces aggression especially when a state requires a very high sense of security or feels menaced by the mere presence of other strong states, as Leites argued the Politburo felt acutely threatened as long as major enemies existed.

Arms procured to defend can usually be used to attack, so what one state regards as insurance the adversary sees as encirclement, and any great power with worldwide interests inevitably has the power to menace others, as a British navy able to protect its trade routes could also cut Germany off from the sea even absent any specific conflict.

When states seek the ability to defend themselves they get both too much and too little, gaining offensive capability while provoking menaced others to arm, and unless the requirements for offense and defense differ in kind or amount a status-quo power's military posture resembles an aggressor's, so others cannot infer aggressiveness from military forces.

Because a state cannot read the other's intentions from its capabilities, states tend to assume the worst and treat the other's intentions as co-extensive with its capabilities, reasoning that whatever the other can do to harm them he will do, and so buy as many weapons as they can afford.

Because both sides obey the same imperatives, trying to increase security by standing firm and accumulating arms is self-defeating, since the symmetrical beliefs of the two sides produce incompatible policies with results in neither's interest.

Arms increases meant to produce a sense of security instead produce a consciousness of other nations' strength and a sense of fear, and fear begets suspicion, so each government regards its own precautions as prudent while treating every other government's precautions as evidence of hostile intent.
States sometimes warn others that their security policies upset others' sense of security, but this perspective rarely enlightens a state about its own posture.

The unintended, undesired consequences of actions meant to be defensive constitute the security dilemma, so the central theme of international relations is not evil but tragedy, since states often share a common interest yet the structure of the situation prevents them from reaching the mutually desired outcome.
Competition for ever more power springs from the instinct of self-preservation within the vicious circle of the security dilemma rather than from any innate power instinct or drive to dominate.

The security dilemma manifests beyond arms races, as it fueled the late-nineteenth-century scramble for colonies, where even states preferring the status quo preferred expansion to the risk of being excluded.

The desire for security may lead a state to weaken a potential rival, which can create the very menace it was meant to ward off, as France's policy of keeping Germany weak made the Germans less willing to accept their position and decreased France's long-run security.

The security dilemma can trigger war when technology and strategy give a decisive advantage to whoever strikes first, because a fully status-quo state may attack out of fear that the alternative is being attacked, and if each knows the other sees the first-strike advantage even mild crises end in war.
condition: when striking first confers a decisive advantage

statement: Spiral theorists see current world politics as a Prisoner's Dilemma, in which each state pursuing its narrow self-interest with a narrow conception of rationality leaves all worse off than if they cooperated, and cooperation would make each actor individually better off, not merely collectively.

Cooperative arrangements are unlikely to be reached through coercion, because threats and an adversary posture provoke counteractions that leave both sides worse off, so states must use ingenuity, trust, and institutions to develop common interests without undue risk to their security.

Once a state develops an image of another, especially a hostile image, ambiguous and even discrepant information is assimilated to that image, so behavior others would read as neutral or friendly is ignored, distorted, or seen as duplicity, and this cognitive rigidity reinforces the effects of anarchy.

Decision-makers often draw unwarranted inferences of aggressive intent from others' arms, so an increase in the other's forces makes a state doubly insecure, both because the other can now do more harm and because the buildup is taken as evidence of active hostile intent.

A state does not apply the same reasoning to its own behavior: a peaceful state knows it will use its arms only defensively and assumes that others fully understand this, as Dulles assumed Khrushchev needed no convincing of American good intentions.

Because a state believes its adversary understands it is only arming defensively, it concludes that strengthening its arms cannot be harmful, since an aggressor is merely made less able to attack and a non-aggressor will not react, so the state believes it need not exercise restraint in its security policies.

Others are not so easily reassured, because the distinction between preparations to attack and precautions against attack is clear to those who build the armaments but not obvious to others, so each government resents suspicion of its own measures while reading the other's identical measures as preparation to attack.

The Hobbesian fear is asymmetric in perception: a state vividly feels its own fear of the other but cannot enter into the other's counter-fear, because it knows it means no harm and forgets that, since the other cannot see inside its mind, the other can never have the assurance of its intentions that it has itself.

Statesmen are led astray in two reinforcing ways, because their understanding of their own policy's impact differs from that of disinterested observers and they fail to realize that other states' perceptions are also skewed, and both errors widen the gap between how a state sees its behavior and how others see it.

A state can fail to see that its own policy harms others, as the United States, in neutralizing Formosa at the start of the Korean War and advancing to the Yalu, did not grasp that it was depriving China of a central value and objectively menacing Chinese security.

A state's sheer size and power make it a potential menace regardless of its behavior, as Wilhelmine Germany was feared by all as a threat to the European equilibrium even had it changed its conduct, and postwar U.S. statesmen similarly failed to see that their country's huge power is a standing threat even when used for others' good.

If a state believes others know it is not a threat, it concludes that others will arm or act hostilely only if they are aggressive, since a genuine security-seeker would welcome or at least not object to the state's policy, as the United States read China's intervention in Korea as proof of aggression rather than legitimate security concern.

When a state believes the other knows it is not threatening the other's legitimate interests, disputes produce antagonism out of all proportion to the issue at stake, because the state sees no legitimate reason for opposition and reads even minor conflicts as unprovoked hostility.

If instead each side recognizes that its own policies threaten some of the other's values, it will not interpret the other's reaction as aggressive intent or total hostility and so will be better able to keep the conflict limited.

The other side's perceptions deepen the misunderstanding symmetrically, because it too assumes its adversary knows it is not a threat, so it reads the state's explanation as senseless and concludes the state is even more dangerous than thought, as the Soviets read the formation of NATO as proof of an ulterior American purpose.

When both sides claim to be peaceful and afraid, each side, knowing there is no real ground for the other's professed anxiety and assuming the other sees this too, seeks a darker meaning in the claim, so mutual reassurances are read as evidence of hidden aggression and the dilemma deepens.

A state that over-estimates a challenge and mobilizes against a threat the other was not posing risks a dangerous misunderstanding, because the other, assuming the state knew there was no danger, infers that the state has militant plans of its own or wants to humiliate it.

The security dilemma becomes overlaid by reinforcing misunderstandings, as each side comes to believe the other is not merely a potential menace, which it must be under anarchy, but an active enemy, so the inability to see one's own actions as menacing plus the belief that the other's hostility can only mean aggressiveness lets conflicts expand beyond what the objective situation requires.

The psychological emphasis of the spiral model has a cost, because it slights the role of the system in inducing conflict and tends to assume that security rather than expansion is most states' prime goal, so spiral theorists give a psychological explanation for threat perceptions without adequately asking whether those perceptions are warranted.

Boulding distinguished real incompatibility, where realizing one side's image of the future would prevent the other's, from illusory incompatibility, where a compatible condition exists but perverse dynamics and illusions create escalating hostility purely from the parties' reactions to each other.

There is a system-induced incompatibility that is neither clearly real nor illusory: even when both sides primarily desire security so their images of the future do not clash, an increase in one state's security can make others less secure because of anarchy rather than misperception, so calling this incompatibility illusory misunderstands the problem.

Understanding the security dilemma dampens some arms-hostility spirals but cannot change the fact that some policies aimed at security genuinely threaten others, so not all conflict can be dissolved by the parties seeing themselves and others more objectively.

The crucial question with a self-fulfilling prophecy of hostility is the degree to which a state's actions based on an initially false image have actually transformed the other's intentions, because once the prophecy is thoroughly self-fulfilling the conflict is no longer illusory, overtures that earlier reduced tension are read as weakness, and a policy fit for an aggressor becomes appropriate.

The spiral perspective reveals a drawback of incrementalist policy-making, because a state's policy not only probes the environment but can alter it, and as long as basic beliefs about the other's intentions are wrong, minor remedial steps lead down a blind alley and the information they produce is of slight value at a high price.

The error of treating a status-quo power as aggressive is self-sealing, because self-correcting information may never appear unless the other goes to unusual lengths to demonstrate its peacefulness, since the incrementalist decision-maker tinkers only within his accepted assumptions and reads the ambiguous feedback as calling for only minimal change.

Deterrence and spiral theories give opposite answers on negative sanctions, with deterrence holding that power must be met by power, that aggression can be contained only by building and intelligently manipulating sanctions, threats, and force, and that the greater the aggressor's relative strength the costlier the concessions required.

Because it is easier to defend than to alter the status quo, as long as an aggressor lacks a preponderance of power even hasty and biased calculations should convince him not to press his challenges to the point of war, and once he learns the defender is strong he may become reconciled to the status quo.

Deterrence acknowledges that threats do not always work: they fail if not believed, they can fail even when credible if the adversary prefers war to retreat as North Vietnam preferred the punishment to abandoning the South, and they fail if the other side has situational advantages and can design around them to reach its goal without the proscribed action.

Threats can fail and also increase the other's hostility by revealing great conflicts of interest, but when this proceeds by increasing the accuracy of each side's perception it is not a spiral, because the aggressor is hostile only because its expansion is blocked rather than from unfounded fear and the rising arms and tensions are a completely rational response to a real incompatibility present from the start.

The spiral model argues that it is often not to a state's advantage to seek a wide margin of superiority, because in situations resembling the Prisoner's Dilemma rather than Chicken coercion is unlikely to produce the desired results.

An increase in an adversary's military strength may lead not to greater assertiveness but to a more conciliatory stance, because if the adversary mainly seeks security the added strength can give it the confidence to be reasonable, as the 1894 French minister told Germany that the stronger France felt the less distrustful it would be.
condition: when the adversary is mainly seeking security rather than expansion

statement: Threats and negative sanctions are often self-defeating, setting off a costly and unstable cycle, so short-run victories prove Pyrrhic if they convince the other that the victorious state is a threat that must be met by force.

If the spiral theory is correct it is partly because actors do not understand it or follow its prescriptions, since acting on a crude version of deterrence theory brings about the results the spiral theory predicts, so understanding either model lets statesmen behave in ways that undermine its validity and those who grasp the Prisoner's Dilemma play more cooperatively.

Scholars should not casually label an actor's threat perceptions as paranoia or misunderstanding without exploring whether the perceptions are accurate, because sometimes the feared conspiracy is real, as Frederick the Great's fears proved justified.

The security dilemma cannot be abolished but only ameliorated, by developing bonds of shared values and interests, since if actors care about what happens to others and believe the caring is mutual they will develop trust and cooperate for mutual benefit.
The first step out of an arms-hostility spiral is the realization, by at least one side and preferably both, that they are, or at least may be, caught in a dilemma that neither desires.

To break a spiral, one side must take an initiative that increases the other side's security, which invites reciprocation because it both reduces the state's capability to harm the other and provides evidence of its friendly intentions.

Spiral-reducing initiatives are most effective as part of a general strategy that shows respect for the other's legitimate interests rather than as isolated gestures, and may not work unless the state first explains that it believes much of the incompatibility is illusory, giving the other an alternative to the conflict framework.

A properly executed spiral-breaking move should be framed not as a concession or a trade but as a step toward a mutually beneficial relationship, so the state does not appear to retreat under pressure and both sides shift from a competitive to a problem-solving perspective.

Perceptions of friendship, like perceptions of enmity, can be made self-fulfilling, so treating another as an enemy helps turn it into one and handling it as a potential partner can make it more pacific, though the friendship version is equally true but far less believed.

Understanding the other's position is not always sufficient for a solution, because a state must still hedge against misplaced trust or a rival's later development of aggressive intent, so even when both sides seek only protection they may find no mutually satisfactory level of arms, and conciliation can sometimes invite greater demands.

Both spiral and deterrence theorists stress making intentions clear, but deterrers worry that aggressors will underestimate the defenders' resolve while spiral theorists worry that each side will overestimate the other's hostility, so the policies each recommends are exactly what the other says will backfire.

Neither the deterrence nor the spiral model is confirmed all the time, since there are many cases where increasing arms and deterring aggressors produced gains without setting off spirals and many where using force failed or led to mutual insecurity that harmed both sides.

The most obvious embarrassment to the spiral model is an aggressive power that will not reciprocate conciliation, because minor concessions, treating issues as separate, or even an offer to negotiate can convince an aggressor that the status-quo power is weak, as Russia stiffened its Far East position in 1903 after Britain expressed interest in negotiating.

Once an aggressor believes the defenders are weak, it may be impossible to change that image short of war, because unambiguous indicators of resolve are infrequent and the aggressor expects the defender to back down at the last minute.

Concessions made in the mistaken belief that the other is a status-quo power are especially likely to be misread when the other does not understand that the state's policy rests on a false image, because aggressors think their own intentions are obvious and so read concessions as fear and weakness, as Hitler concluded Chamberlain lacked resolve rather than thought Germany would be sated.

Even an adversary aiming for less than domination will raise new demands if it concludes that the state's desire for better relations can be exploited, as Germany increased pressure on France after France turned conciliatory in the first Moroccan crisis and the United States met Japanese concessions in 1941 with more extreme demands.

Even a status-quo power may read conciliation as evidence that the other is weak enough to expand against at little risk, because trusting someone and giving him the chance to gain at your expense can awaken his acquisitiveness, so a lowered level of arms can tempt the other to raise rather than lower its forces.

Returning conciliation for hostility can be the rational best policy under some circumstances, because a state unable to afford high arms and hostility, whose central values are not directly threatened, is apt to retreat, and even large states cannot afford too many enemies, as Japan dropped its opposition to the U.S. annexation of Hawaii in 1897 to husband strength for a crisis nearer home.

There are many cases where hostility checks an aggressor without unintended bad consequences, because a high level of real incompatibility existed to begin with, so the exercise of power either left the underlying conflict untouched or lowered it by showing one side that its interests were better served by abandoning hostility, as with Bismarck's Balkan deterrence and British firmness at Fashoda.

A state can deliberately increase hostility to make the other both retreat and become more friendly, by foreclosing the other's preferred course and forcing a choice between friendship on the state's terms and costly hostility, as Bismarck made a pact with Austria to drive Russia back into alliance.
Hostility can also succeed when the other believes the state can be satisfied with small concessions, which was part of why Britain and France gave in to Hitler.

A decision-maker will not feel he must match the other's arms and hostility if he believes the other's behavior is caused by insecurity, because if a state believes it and its adversary are in a security dilemma, the adversary's use of threats and power will not be self-defeating.

Cases where statesmen perceive that others are unduly afraid of them are rare but real, as the 1907 British foreign secretary credited genuine Russian apprehension in Central Asia and Cold War figures read the Soviet bomber build-up as a defensive response to the American atomic monopoly.

Perceptions grounded in the security dilemma rarely dominate policy and are usually a marginalized minority position, as Kennan's cable explaining how the Soviets might be frightened by NATO was ignored, showing how hard it is to convince most people that they may be inadvertently threatening others.

Neither spiral link is universal, because decision-makers sometimes see the other as acting from insecurity or the real incompatibility as limited, and even when they see extreme hostility they usually weigh, however roughly, the costs of a hostile response against the gains of conciliation and compromise, so while no one country fully controls the level of tension, statesmen often manipulate it successfully to reach their goals.

Hostility can be self-defeating and conciliation does not always lead to further demands, and appeasement often works even when there are major conflicts between countries, as Britain cemented American friendship by making many concessions around the turn of the century.

The successes of concession are largely invisible because conflicts settled by one side's retreating lack drama and pass unnoticed, and many major disputes might have been avoided by small concessions withheld only for fear that conciliation would be mistaken for weakness.

Memories of Hitler obscure that most statesmen are unwilling to pay an exorbitant price for a chance at expansion, so more moderate leaders tend to become defenders of the status quo once they receive significant concessions, because the appetite does not always grow with the eating.

Whether an adversary's appetite grows depends on how the concession is gained, since concessions wrenched from a state by dire threats are more apt to produce an image of weakness than concessions that appear freely given, and concessions on issues important to the receiver but not the giver are especially self-limiting.

Deterrence theory is not embarrassed by threats that fail because they are disbelieved, designed around, or insufficient, but what counts against it are cases where threats fail and conflict develops in a way and degree the original conflict of interest cannot explain, so that hostility, far from containing the enemy, creates him.

Judging whether the spiral model explains a case requires difficult analysis of how much real incompatibility was present at the start, because a conciliatory policy can succeed only if solutions exist that both sides prefer to war.

Coercive moves can produce limited spiral effects that fit neither model cleanly, backfiring by leading the target to reduce its vulnerability or find alternative partners, as Bismarck's cut-off of Russian bonds pushed Russia to borrow from France and German invasion rumors led Britain and the United States to build navies rather than align with Germany.
When threats lead the recipient to believe the sender is highly aggressive, the classic spiral of arms and hostility is apt to be set in motion, as in pre-World War I Anglo-German relations.

Gratuitous interference in another's vital interest backfires by signaling malign character, as the German attempt to frighten England into the Triple Alliance with the Kruger Telegram convinced British opinion that a state which would gratuitously interfere was unprincipled, reckless, or unreasonably hostile.

Demanding payment merely for refraining from meddling in an area where the other has won the right to act reads as unusual greed and presumption that goes beyond accepted self-interest, as when Germany demanded the Samoan and Caroline islands from the United States in 1898.

Persisting in a hostility strategy despite mounting evidence of its failure and despite no intrinsic conflict of interest manufactures an enemy, as sustained German pressure moved British policy from wanting to curb German excesses, to seeing Germany as a menace to France, to seeing it as a direct threat.

Each side in an escalating conflict reads its own hostility as a morally and pragmatically justified response to the other, as Germany saw Britain's alignment with France as harming it and thus saw German firmness as justified while dismissing British protestations of non-hostility as beside the point if not hypocritical.

Mutual first-strike advantage was an immediate cause of war in 1914, because each continental power believed the side that struck first would gain a major advantage, so waiting to clarify the other's intentions risked defeat and even a status-quo state felt great pressure to attack.

Neither theory covers all cases, and each has roots in an individual paradigm case, since the spiral model draws its inspiration from the origins of World War I while deterrence theory derives from the failure of appeasement in the 1930s, so deterrence says little about World War I and spiral theorists rarely discuss the 1930s.

Even the theorists do not apply their models universally, since deterrence theorists discuss World War I's mobilization races in spiral terms and a major deterrence contribution was stressing that mutual first-strike capability creates a reciprocal fear of surprise attack that is highly destabilizing.

Both deterrence and spiral theorists agree that Hitler could not have been conciliated, and even spiral theorists apply their prescriptions to adversaries they judge reasonable while excepting a genuinely unlimited aggressor like the Nazis.

The central and hardest question is what conditions make one model rather than the other appropriate: when force will work versus create a spiral of hostility, and when concessions will be reciprocated versus lead the other side to expect further retreats.

In a dispute between a large and a small power, the larger must calculate the reaction not only of the small power but of third parties, weighing whether conceding to a small state on a supposedly vital question signals that it would yield much more to stronger states on other issues.

Decision-makers repeatedly face the firmness-versus-conciliation choice whose right answer turns on the adversary's type and on third-party inferences, as Western leaders in the 1958-1962 Berlin conflict had to predict whether concessions would beget further Soviet demands or call forth reciprocation.

Aid and commitments to an ally can either restrain or embolden it, and because these calculations are hard they often yield bad policy, as Britain's 1902 alliance with Japan, meant to make Japan less likely to fight Russia, in fact removed Japan's remaining doubts about the safety of going to war.

Threats are more apt to work and the deterrence model to apply when the other side sees the costs of standing firm as very high, which holds when the other is relatively weak or vulnerable, places an especially high value on its citizens' lives and property, is highly risk-averse, or has a short-run perspective.
Threats work better when the other side believes that the state making the threat sees its own costs of standing firm as low.

Threats work better when the other side sees the costs of retreating as relatively low, which holds when its central values are not at stake, the issue does not involve principles applying to other cases, it can retreat without breaking important commitments, the threatener's goals are seen as limited, and the other believes the demands stem from the state's desire for security and that the state may see the other as a menace.

A threat is far less likely to trigger a spiral when the actor making it refrains from humiliating the other, inflicting gratuitous punishment, raising demands that lack legitimacy, or asking for something worth much more to the other than to itself, because these behaviors lower the other's fear that retreat will bring further demands and preserve the lines of salience separating present from future demands.

Concessions are more apt to encourage new demands when a retreat takes the state past a salient point, when the adversaries lack a common conception of fair play and reciprocation, when the concession signals that the state would sacrifice a great deal to avoid war, or when the state retreats even though the costs of doing so are very high.

A major determinant of a threat's effect is the intention of the other side, because when faced with a genuine aggressor threats and force are necessary and concessions, however useful tactically, will not meet the underlying sources of dissatisfaction.
Concessions made under pressure, or made when the aggressor thinks the status-quo power has no illusions about the conflict between them, are likely to quicken the pace of future demands.

When a state believes the other has responded to its conciliation by claiming the state retreated only because of the other's superior force and by raising new demands, it will infer that the other is an aggressor who must be dealt with firmly.

When the status-quo state stands firm and the aggressor responds in kind, the spiral model does not apply because the parties correctly perceive real incompatibility, but when conflict erupts between two status-quo powers the spiral model probably gives the correct explanation and prescription, since threats become self-defeating because neither side realizes the other is afraid of it.

Basic intentions are not the only variable governing reactions to threats and concessions, because the details and context of the moves, each side's operational code, and the specific goals held and attributed to others must also be examined, and not all status-quo or aggressive powers behave or interpret alike.

A conciliatory move can be read as weakness by more than a state seeking to overthrow the status quo, since that interpretation can spring from a contingent analysis of the alternatives available to the other, and an attempt to increase power can add illusory incompatibility even where real incompatibility is high.

The argument between spiral and deterrence theorists is not over a general model of international relations but over which model applies to a specific case such as the Cold War and, decisively, over what the adversary's intentions are.

Perceptions of intention explain the opposite attitudes toward minor issues, because spiral theorists see minor issues as opportunities to reduce tension while deterrence theorists fear that what is really in dispute is not the issue of the moment but everyone's expectations about how a participant will behave in future.

When one state sees another as extremely hostile it finds most compromises on specific issues unattractive, because the other's demands seem illegitimate, any compromise is expected to be only temporary, and yielding a defensible principle can place the state on unstable middle ground, so what is really at stake is each side's image of the other's values, strength, and resolve.

The belief that the other is highly aggressive leads a state to refrain from reciprocating even when the other modifies its demands, because if the other is out to dominate then true compromise is impossible, as those Finns who favored standing firm against Russia in 1939 were unmoved when the Soviets eased their position.

Policy debates often center on whether what is at stake is a specific matter or the wider question of security, as at Munich Chamberlain accepted the principle that no power should be allowed to dominate Europe by force but argued it did not apply to the case at hand, while the anti-appeasers were sure the great issues were at stake.

Major difficulties arise when one side thinks an issue can be treated in isolation while the adversary believes all matters are interrelated, because attempts to treat individual issues on their merits then appear to the linkage-minded adversary as indications of general weakness.

When one side treats an agreement as limited to the specific issue while the other reads it as promising a general settlement, charges of deception and bad faith arise as soon as either acts on its belief, so the underlying conflict is not merely postponed but exacerbated, as the papered-over Stamp Act compromise heightened Anglo-American incompatibility.

One's image of the adversary does not fully determine how small issues are handled, because tactical considerations such as buying time or uniting one's own side by making the other show its aggressiveness can dictate treating a small issue as isolated even when the other is seen as aggressive.

Small issues can grow into large conflicts for reasons other than the adversary's image, including moral values that make retreat prohibitively costly, coalition dynamics in which allies support a member's stake lest the alliance break up, and both sides believing that only a little more effort will bring victory.

Astute strategy and tactics let an actor treat one issue as separate, decline challenges, and limit the damage to his image when backing down, by re-interpreting positions, justifying retreats through the special circumstances of the case, and explaining non-contest by temporary disabilities, so that his behavior reads as context-bound rather than trait-revealing and concessions are less likely to invite future demands.

People differ in their propensity to perceive aggressiveness and in their general views on the effect of threats, often rooted in differing predispositions to see politics as characterized by conflict or by cooperation, so the same situation yields high-threat firmness readings from some observers and low-threat conciliation readings from others.

Deterrence theorists applied their model to the Cold War because they believed the Soviets were aggressive rather than the reverse, so although the Law of the Instrument is real, overstating it obscures the more important underlying disagreement about the adversary's behavior.

Disagreement over deterrence versus conciliation policies is not evidence of differing values, because the two sides disagree about the probable outcomes of each policy, so value differences could be inferred only by asking what each would favor with the empirical facts held fixed.

Both deterrence and spiral advocates avoid acknowledging the trade-offs in their analyses and imply their strategy is dominant, better no matter what the adversary is like, as deterrers assume that if they are wrong to see Russia as a threat their policy costs only money, a confidence the arms-hostility spiral shows to be misplaced.

Conciliatory gradualism toward an adversary can lead the state's allies to conclude it will settle with the adversary regardless of their interests, leaving it to face a hostile opponent with a weakened alliance system if the conciliatory assumptions turn out to be wrong.

Two major powers may cooperate once or twice at their allies' expense but then feel they must strongly back those allies in the next crisis lest the allies permanently defect, a danger compounded when either power expects the other's cooperation to continue, as Anglo-German Balkan cooperation in 1912-1913 did not recur.

The most important danger of conciliatory gestures is that the adversary may form an image of the state as one that can be bullied, because the very separability of military capability from psychological gesture means a state can decrease its security without changing the military balance, so in a world driven by resolve and perceptions of resolve a 'we are no menace' signal can be read as 'we will back down.'

Spiral theorists commit the same error they attribute to deterrers, underestimating the difficulty of projecting a desired and accurate image and forgetting that the adversary interprets behavior in light of what it thinks the state knows of its own intentions, so if the adversary is in fact aggressive, initiatives are especially likely to be read as a face-saving signal that it is free to expand.

Instead of claiming a dominant strategy, a policy advocate should aim for the more modest goal of policies that have high payoffs if the assumptions about the adversary are correct yet tolerable costs if those premises are wrong.

One robust move that breaks out of the security dilemma is to procure weapons useful for deterrence but not as effective for aggression, favoring survivable retaliatory systems over counterforce first-strike systems, though it is hard to tell what inferences an adversary will draw from any given posture.
condition: requires that offensive and defensive capabilities be distinguishable in kind or amount

statement: Because the effect of initiatives and threats depends on the adversary's intentions and perceptions, debaters should ask themselves in advance what possible adversary behavior they would take as evidence against their own interpretation, especially those who see the other as aggressive, since almost any evidence can be read as consistent with that image.

A limited-aims adversary finds it very hard to prove its ambitions are limited, especially if it fears the first side is aggressive, so the more it believes the state reads friendly overtures as weakness the more hesitant it is to take unambiguous conciliatory actions, and the state should therefore be more sensitive to evidence of the adversary's willingness to support the status quo.

Decision-makers should worry if the only actions that would convince them the adversary is not aggressive are measures they deem too risky for their own state to undertake, and those who think the adversary non-aggressive should ask what behavior would distinguish an aggressive but cagey state from a peaceful one caught in the security dilemma.

The common argument for empathizing with an adversary is insufficient, because one must empathize with a variety of possible outlooks, estimating how the other would respond under each of several possible intention-sets rather than only under one's best guess, while remembering that the other likely thinks you understand it and so reads your policy as designed for its own policy as it sees it.

The fog of foreign policy-making, the great difficulty of telling what others are up to, inferring their predispositions, and predicting their behavior, forces decision-makers to use shortcuts to rationality, often unawares, and these shortcuts produce systematic errors that increase conflict.

Belief structures tend toward consistency or balance, so people tend to believe that countries they like do good things and countries they dislike do bad things, though consistency is not the same as clear coherent thinking and comes in degrees.

Scholars too often apply the labels of closed-mindedness and cognitive distortion without appreciating the necessary role of pre-existing beliefs in perceiving and interpreting new information, even though recognizing that role does not mean people strike an optimal balance between openness and retaining useful beliefs.

People's belief structures tend toward consistency or balance, so they believe that countries they like do good things and that enemies make proposals that harm them, and they learn balanced configurations faster, remember them better, and interpret new information to maintain balance.

The key question about consistency-driven thinking is not whether it follows formal logic but whether it yields perceptions as accurate as other processes would and, at minimum, whether it is rational, since a logician would object only if the person believed his balance reasoning proceeded by strict logic.

Deduction cannot answer most of the questions that concern decision-makers, such as estimating intentions, predicting the consequences of one's own actions, and drawing inferences from ambiguous information, so they must employ less certain intellectual tools judged by accuracy and rationality rather than logical necessity.

Rational thinking means interpreting evidence by the generally accepted rules of drawing inferences, while irrational methods violate those rules and would be rejected by the person if he were aware of using them.

Rationality is only a loose constraint that cannot designate a single conclusion, since contradictory inferences can be equally rational, which makes calling a thought process not rational a strong statement.

Balanced attitude structures are not irrational when the consistency reflects well-grounded beliefs about consistency that actually exists in the environment, so expecting two of one's friends to like each other is rational if friends in fact tend to share values, and the halo effect can make perceptions accurate at low cost when traits really are correlated.

Viewing an adversary's proposals with suspicion is rational rather than merely emotional consistency, because believing the other aggressive implies by the very definition of an adversary that one should be skeptical of its suggestions, reinforced by knowledge of prior deception.

For decision-makers there is usually no independent affective dimension, because whether a statesman likes another state is largely determined by his beliefs about the degree of conflict between that country and his own, as U.S. leaders liked Russia more in the 1970s than the 1950s when they judged Soviet policies more compatible.

Decision-makers often recognize that states whose interests coincide with theirs have as many undesired characteristics as their enemies, as the Chinese saw the United States as no less selfish than Japan and Churchill offered to favorably reference the Devil if Hitler invaded Hell.

When political judgment displays cognitive-affective consistency, the reason is usually that the liking of another state and views of its specific characteristics are both linked through the third factor of the actor's beliefs about the other's interests and intentions.

Consistency between one's attitude toward a message's source and its truth value is often rational, and one should consider separately, as most intelligence services do, the source's reliability from its track record and the message's inherent credibility from its compatibility with other evidence, with the final judgment resting on both.
Judicious reliance on those believed to be experts brings benefits in excess of the costs, even though one can over-rely on authorities by blindly accepting whatever they alone say.
A source's credibility, and the influence of its later messages, is diminished if an initial message is too discrepant from the recipient's beliefs.

When a source is shown to be wrong on one issue, it and its other views are judged more severely, so advisers and experts proved incorrect lose influence, as U.S. leaders discounted Westmoreland's sanguine accounts after the 1968 Tet offensive and Jellicoe ignored correct Admiralty intelligence at Jutland because earlier reports had been baseless.

The reputation of a source matters less when the components of its argument are open to independent analysis, since a message that makes sense is accepted regardless of attribution while a message with questionable content is accepted only from a respected source.

In political communication an actor must inquire about the source's conflicting perspectives and interests, its biases, and the likelihood of deception, and such skepticism, while it sometimes discredits valid information, is on balance beneficial, as Kennedy rightly discounted Republican reports of Soviet missiles in Cuba given the Republicans' interest in exaggeration.

A source's interest can add force to its message, since participants accept from a mediator arguments they would reject from the other side and a hostile message is more likely to be believed when the agent conveying it is felt to be friendly.

Source influence on the interpretation of a message is irrational only when the person excludes other legitimate influences or lets irrelevant beliefs about the source contaminate perception, since a scientist's competence is relevant to his experiments while his private conduct is not, and authority based on the power to reward or punish rather than on cognitive correctness is an illegitimate influence.

The tendency to perceive relations as balanced derives from experience and is at minimum rational, because social structures really are more likely to be balanced than chance would produce, and patterns of alliance and hostility often approximate balance as states with shared enemies join forces.

Because many real-world structures are balanced, perceiving balance often serves people well but leads them astray when the stimuli do not fit the pattern, as U.S. decision-makers were slow to recognize that two of their enemies, Russia and China, were hostile to each other.

Perceiving the environment as more consistent than it is does not mean people should perceive it differently, because as the a priori probability of a characteristic rises it is rational to keep perceiving it despite increasing discrepant information, just as one should always bet on the more likely outcome rather than probability-match.
Judging a stranger by inference from the subgroup to which he is thought to belong can be more accurate than trying to use specific cues from his behavior, which can actually reduce accuracy.

The tendency to perceive consistency is not strong enough to make perceptions of inconsistency unusual, since when evidence is abundant and clear people recognize that friends dislike each other and admired people behave badly, and the tendency is stronger in cognitively simple than in cognitively complex people, so balance findings do not show that people deviate from accurate perception.

People believe, probably correctly, that knowing a person's view on an important and controversial issue tells much more about him than knowing his view on a trivial one, because important issues carry more disagreement and relate to more of the person's character, so shared opinion on a significant issue grounds liking while a shared newsmagazine does not.

People employ different schemas for different relationship types, expecting a hierarchical pattern for influence or dominance relations and a balanced pattern for friendship, and they learn which schema fits which situation, so reasoning and experience largely account for when they perceive balance and when they do not.

One type of consistency is genuinely irrational: people who favor a policy usually believe it is supported by many logically independent reasons, expecting a policy that serves one value to serve several others even though the world has no reason to be so neatly helpful.

The proliferation of independent reasons is a tell of motivated consistency rather than logic, because each belief would separately suffice to justify the preference, as opponents declare the end unattainable, the means harebrained, and the cost staggering, all at once.

Belief systems display overkill, clustering logically unrelated beliefs, as test-ban supporters believed testing was a medical danger and would not improve weapons and raised tension while opponents took the opposite view on all three, though the health risks are unconnected to the military advantages.

The model of treating goals as constraints, in which an actor strives not to fall below a minimum on any goal rather than trading off, is often appropriate but cannot apply when the necessary information is absent or highly ambiguous, which is exactly the case in important foreign-policy choices, so trade-offs are then avoided by more severe irrational methods.

Irrational consistency makes choices feel easier because all considerations seem to point to the same conclusion and nothing must be sacrificed, but since the real world is not so benign, values are in fact sacrificed and important choices are made inadvertently.

Once the goal is agreed, all that is logically needed to affirm a strategy is the belief that it is most likely to work at lowest cost, but people go further by placing a very high estimate on their own plan's success and a very low estimate on the alternative's, as the WWI Easterners and Westerners disagreed on both the odds of a Western-front breakthrough and the gains of offensives elsewhere.

People rarely differ about the value of an objective without also disagreeing about the probability it can be attained and the costs involved, so those who disapprove of a movement's goals also tend to believe its tactics are ineffective, and a project's supporters estimate lower costs and higher benefits than its opponents.

An inverse relationship between a goal's importance and its expected cost pervades foreign-policy disputes, so opponents of aid to Nationalist China thought aid futile and a communist China harmless while supporters thought Chiang's victory both possible and important, a pattern repeated over pre-Pearl-Harbor aid and Vietnam withdrawal.

Morality is rarely seen to conflict with other values, so advocates claim their policy is best on economic grounds, leads to international harmony, and serves security all at once, as both free-trade and protection advocates each claimed all three benefits.

A common way trade-offs are avoided on national security is to argue at once that those calling for greater defense spending overestimate the threat and that, if the threat did materialize, the cheaper proposals would still cope with it, as interwar Britain argued about Japan.

Beliefs about specific policies show the same overkill, as MacArthur supported his stand with several independent claims and pro-bombing officials in Vietnam argued the bombing would cut casualties, raise the North's costs, and push it toward negotiations without risking Soviet or Chinese entry, so that there were more reasons than were required.

Both sides of many disputes claim their policy will both minimize the danger of foreign domination and maximize the chance of peace, even parties directly targeted by demands, as the 1939 Finns who thought concessions would only invite more demands also thought the Soviets would back down to firmness.

Logic would link the belief that an adversary will fight for its demands to the belief that it has threatening long-run intentions, since it would incur war's high costs only for extensive gains, yet motivated consistency lets people hold these two beliefs apart.

The pairing of beliefs that an adversary will not enter a conflict and that if it does the actor can easily defeat it is not necessarily irrational, because if the actor believes the adversary shares his perception of their relative strength, expecting to win is itself a cause of his low estimate that the enemy will act.

Actors commonly claim to have a dominant strategy that is best no matter what the other side does, as Schuschnigg felt about his German policy and Bundy argued the bombing of North Vietnam would be worth it even if it failed, but the world is rarely so benign that such strategies occur as often as they are claimed.

American leaders show irrational consistency on many issues, driven by economic plenty that encourages the belief that choices can be avoided by expanding the pie, by a liberalism whose harmony-of-interests emphasis discourages examining value trade-offs, and by an advantageous geography that has given the country free security and fewer hard choices.

Decision-makers do not simultaneously estimate how a policy affects many values, but first look at only one or two salient values, come to favor the policy that seems best on those, and then alter old beliefs and form new ones so that as many reasons as possible support the choice, so policy preferences precede and shape the supporting arguments.

The strongest evidence that a preference comes before its reasons is cases where inconsistent premises support one conclusion, as the U.S. Navy argued for a longer-range plane so carriers could stay far out at sea yet also for many missile ships to protect carriers against short-range planes.

Supporting beliefs change to preserve a fixed conclusion, as Haig first said the Flanders offensive depended on a French attack and later said the possible French collapse compelled him to keep attacking, and Daladier rated the French air force terrible when he felt France could not fight and fine, even inventing 5,000 Russian planes, when he felt it must.

Because preferences form on one or two values that dominate a particular situation and the same value does not dominate every situation, a decision-maker acts on one value in one context and another in another, which ensures no important value is entirely neglected but gives no reason the values are optimally combined and further reduces the effectiveness of each separate policy.

In irrational consistency a decision-maker buys psychological harmony at the price of neglecting conflicts among his own values and sets his priorities by default, unknowingly sacrificing some values, so unless balancing values is prohibitively costly it is in his interest to choose explicitly.

Awareness of the costs and conflicts hidden by irrational consistency would let a decision-maker examine his values and evidence more carefully, extend his search to additional alternatives, and seek creative solutions, whereas the belief that a single policy served multiple goals inhibits the study of better options.

Excessive consistency is sometimes driven by the prohibitive political cost of openly facing a choice, as the pre-World War I British cabinet knew a frank discussion of politico-military policy would bring the government down.

Irrational consistency makes decision-makers maintain a policy past its usefulness, because believing it best on all dimensions they react slowly to evidence it is failing some goals, whereas appreciating its costs makes them more sensitive to evidence that other policies would be more effective.

Irrational consistency often produces a policy that reaches no goal because it attempts too many, spreading resources too thin and leaving contradictions unrecognized, as the United States at Yalta wanted both free elections in Eastern Europe and governments thoroughly friendly to the Soviet Union.

Failing to see the conflict between one's own goals forces a hostile reading of the other, since as long as the United States could not see that free elections would produce anti-Soviet governments, the Soviet position had to be perceived as ideologically driven unreasonableness rather than an understandable demand for security.

Seeking too many objectives often means making too many enemies, as Wilhelmine Germany failed to rank its goals and choose which quarrels mattered, so a reckless attempt to do everything at once forced Britain, France, and Russia, who had little in common, together.

When a decision-maker fails to see the trade-off between advancing his interests and harming others', he does not believe his policy creates legitimate grievances, so he underestimates the opposition it provokes and reads resistance as unprovoked hostility that signals aggression, adding illusory to real incompatibility and fueling the spiral.

Value trade-offs occur less often than the logic of the situation dictates, and are least likely when the values are vague, when money is not involved to aid comparison, when effects are hard to predict, when values are deeply held, or when any policy entails major sacrifices, so irrational consistency is especially likely when trade-offs are easy to avoid or especially painful.

The same inference process that produces rational consistency also makes people fit incoming information into pre-existing beliefs and perceive what they expect, which is not irrational distortion but is necessary for understanding and characteristic of scientific investigation.

People preserve their images against what in retrospect was clear contrary evidence, ignoring information that does not fit, twisting it to confirm, or denying its validity, while confirming evidence is quickly and accurately noted, as Dulles readily accepted information about Soviet failings but demanded overwhelming evidence before crediting anything that contradicted his views.

Discrepant information is often simply not noticed, as analysts not expecting Soviet offensive missiles in Cuba did not pause over ships with wide hatches riding high in the water, and a wartime analyst expecting a rail-launched rocket paid little attention to an erected V-2 he saw as a column.

When actors do not spontaneously perceive evidence as conforming, they explicitly reinterpret it as compatible with their beliefs, as the United States gave an absurd explanation for the evacuation of Soviet civilians from Syria before the 1973 war because it was certain the Arabs were too weak to attack.

Outright refusal to believe reports that contradict a firm belief is common, and the telling reaction is not that the report is incorrect but that it must be incorrect, as Soviet headquarters replied 'You must be insane' to a front-line unit reporting attack on 22 June 1941 and the Navy Secretary insisted the Pearl Harbor message must mean the Philippines.

Expectations, or perceptual sets, are standing estimates of what the world is like and hence of what one is likely to encounter, creating predispositions to notice some things and neglect others, to draw certain inferences unconsciously, and to find alternatives hard to consider, and this way of perceiving is rational because intelligent decision-making is impossible unless significant information is assimilated to pre-existing beliefs.

The more accessible a category, the less input is needed to trigger it, the wider the range of inputs accepted as fitting it, and the more likely that better-fitting categories are masked, so a statesman's general expectations about the links between other states' characteristics and their intentions shape the images he forms.

General predispositions shape specific perceptions, so Western statesmen see a state as aggressive more readily if a dictator has just come to power than if it is a stable democracy and need only slight ambiguous evidence to see a communist-dominated state as an enemy, which makes understanding a decision-maker's general predispositions a key step in explaining his specific perceptions.

Perceptual predispositions grow out of experience and readiness is largely based on what the past led one to expect, but familiarity matters not in itself but as a factor giving reason to expect the stimulus in the particular situation, so one becomes predisposed to perceive even a rare stimulus when preceding events indicate it is likely.

The more familiar a phenomenon, the more quickly it is recognized, so rare objects are mistaken for usual ones and expected things may be seen when nothing is shown, and by the same process a state that has frequently attacked its neighbors will have ambiguous evidence read as renewed aggression even when other explanations are known to be possible.

Much of what people think they perceive is supplied from memory and expectation rather than the actual stimulus, as William James observed that we overlook misprints and hear little of foreign speech, so perception is heavily expectation-supplied.

Perception is shaped by cultural background, so an American and a Mexican viewing a stereoscopic pair of a baseball game and a bullfight each see mainly the image matching their culture, and observers hear foreign-language sounds closest to those of their own language.

Seeing is not a theory-free task, because the newly sighted at first see only blooming, buzzing confusion, and seeing involves learned conceptualization that makes us sensitive to common configurations but leads us to misperceive rare or unexpected ones, as a forest-dwelling Pygmy saw distant buffalo as insects.

A description or cue that a stimulus is likely makes a person quick to see it even if he has never seen it before, as subjects told what anomalous playing cards to expect recognized further anomalous cards much faster.

Explicit labels and instructions shape perception independently of familiarity, so subjects set for animals saw 'duck' and 'seal' where those set for travel saw 'dock' and 'sail', a speaker described as cold was seen as cold, and weapons have been misused because their names shaped perceptions of their potential uses.

Background and culture create perceptual predispositions just as instructions do, so UFO sightings match the science-fiction technology of their era, Tibetan materialized devils resemble the devils in Tibetan books, and a tribe saw the tracks and animals specified by its mythology, because shared cultural templates make ambiguous stimuli take the expected shape.

Predispositions are established by the immediate context in which a stimulus is placed, so a broken B is read as the number 13 by those primed with numbers and as the letter B by those primed with letters, and an ambiguous cat-or-bird figure is seen according to the prior series.

Context shapes even attributions of others' traits, so a fast decisive player who wins is seen as a quick thinker and astute while the same style when he loses reads as impulsive and careless, because perceptions are shaped not only by the behavior but by its presumed effects, without the observer's awareness.

Context-induced predispositions operate outside the laboratory, since politically sophisticated viewers saw the same 1952 convention footage very differently depending on which network's framing they watched, one seeing a delegation huddle as arguing and another as a strategic conference.
Context is supplied not only by the situation but by the concerns and information that dominate a person's thought at a particular time, known as the evoked set.

Whatever creates the predisposition, an actor who expects a phenomenon perceives ambiguous stimuli as that phenomenon, so when sure an object will be present it takes very little information, even information barely resembling it, to convince him he sees it, as Fleet Air Arm planes hunting the Bismarck attacked the two-funneled Sheffield and analysts took folded tents to be V-2 launch platforms.

There is an obvious danger of a self-fulfilling prophecy in intelligence, because when an analyst tells field agents that a phenomenon is likely, the agents are more apt to report ambiguous stimuli as that phenomenon, which makes the analyst more certain and feeds the belief back to the field.

Expectations aid decision-making when the environment conforms to what it is thought to be, but mislead when the regular pattern is absent or when a deceiver exploits the expectations, as people shown anomalous cards initially saw them as normal and an object of slightly off color is reported as the expected color.

Although it seems obvious that ignoring, misremembering, or twisting evidence to preserve old ideas is irrational distortion, it need not be, because such processes would reduce accuracy only if data were unambiguous or all states of the world equally probable, whereas since evidence always permits multiple interpretations and prior theories must guide new information, the influence of expectations is consistent with rationality and essential to the logic of inquiry.
