One can be too open-minded as well as too closed, because adjustive behavior requires the stabilizing keel that strong cognitive structures provide, so the balance between flexibility and stability requires revising attitudes on a preponderance of evidence rather than being swayed by an isolated fact, since losing memory makes an actor drift like driftwood while losing openness makes it fly straight like a bullet.

The flexibility-versus-stability conflict exists at the organizational level as well, because organizations must develop standard operating procedures for recurring problems yet maintain the openness needed to recognize and creatively handle new issues.

Fitting data into a pre-existing framework, even when it does not do justice to all the facts, is not merely a psychological drive and does not necessarily reduce accuracy, because theories are built on facts while at the same time giving them significance and even determining what counts as a fact.

A scientific paradigm sets the framework for research by bounding what explanations make sense, marking which phenomena matter and which are to be ignored, and even shaping instruments so they may be unable to detect unexpected phenomena, so normal science solves problems within the paradigm and does not aim at novelties.

A paradigm leads scientists to reject flatly evidence fundamentally out of line with its expectations, so such an experiment is ignored by its author, rejected by editors, or disregarded by colleagues even without a flaw being found, at the cost of missing major discoveries, as astronomers repeatedly recorded Uranus as a fixed star before it was recognized as a planet.

One's estimate of a hypothesis's validity depends not only on the evidence bearing directly on it but on how well it fits well-confirmed theories, so it can be rational to reject one hypothesis and affirm another even with equal facts for each, as it is rational to disbelieve in UFOs, which would require rewriting basic laws of nature, while tentatively crediting a creature whose existence would not.

Rejecting discrepant information can lead to wrong conclusions but is a necessary part of theory-building, because pure empiricism is impossible, facts do not speak for themselves, and every step of inquiry from identifying what needs explaining to judging an explanation satisfactory is governed by the theory's fundamental conceptions.

The world is not so cleanly built that all the evidence supports a single theory, since there is no such thing as research without counter-instances, so no parsimonious explanation of a complex set of cases is completely satisfying and some aspects of the truth simply do not make sense.

Because it is rare that all facts fit one conclusion, the closer one looks at a case's details the greater the chance some will contradict the accepted explanation, so in high-attention cases like political assassinations those dissatisfied with the official account fail to appreciate that even the correct explanation will not tie up all the loose ends.

Explaining away deviations as experimental error is indispensable to research, because a scientist knows this practice may one day make him miss a genuine discovery yet continues it, since taking every anomaly at face value would degenerate research into a wild-goose chase after imaginary novelties.

Institutions must likewise refuse findings too discrepant from prevailing theory, because only such refusal prevents the contributions of cranks, frauds, and bunglers from flooding and corrupting scientific institutions.

Resistance to theory-changing data is often reasoned rather than mere obscurantism, because an established theory earned acceptance by economically explaining a wide range of events, is backed by much evidence, has survived challenges, and has pointed to fruitful research, as the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic and phlogiston systems were comprehensive explanatory structures.

Because an established theory has explained so much, its proponents both see the loss in abandoning it and are confident it will absorb troublesome new findings, and this faith is usually vindicated, since in almost all cases reiterated efforts produce a solution to even stubborn problems within the paradigm.

It would be irrational to drop a well-established theory for a small amount of discrepant information, so one must follow the weight of the evidence, which necessarily involves ignoring or twisting bits that seem to contradict the theory, because the alternative is to abandon any attempt to understand the world.

Choosing among competing images of world politics is easier than choosing scientific paradigms, because foreign-policy analysts can usually use previously developed alternative images rather than create a new framework, and competing images share more in common than competing paradigms, so interpretation of specific evidence is less dependent on prior beliefs.

Evidence about another state's foreign policy cannot make sense without some framework of beliefs and most information will not easily fit one explanation, so a statesman who wants even minimal coherence must refuse to give full weight to evidence others would see as discrepant, and unlike a scientist he can also account for discrepant information by believing the other is trying to deceive him.

The label placed on an event shapes how it is seen, because once an object is categorized the person sees further resemblances between it and others in the same category, as the British navy, once it categorized WWI convoying as defensive, grouped it with mine defenses and could not see that convoys destroyed more submarines by drawing them to the escorts.

A piece of information's later availability depends on whether it was filed under the categories for which it is eventually seen as relevant, as the British navy could not compare convoy and patrol effectiveness because reports classified submarine kills by vessel type rather than operational task, and the 1950 U.S. ambassador's alarming report on the North Korean army was filed with aid appeals and could not be found when war broke out.

Because an actor files information under the concepts he holds when it is received, new ideas are hard to develop and test even when they do not require recasting the elementary facts, since the old filing cannot be reordered by a new scheme.

Different people look at the same information and see different things according to their theories, so one analyst saw a column where another expecting a smaller mobile rocket saw an upright V-2, and visitors' reactions to a controversial country are better predicted by their prior views than by what they see during the visit.

Different people use the same event to support opposite policies, each seeing it as confirming, so both supporters and opponents of collective security thought the 1938 Anschluss proved their view and the 1941 embargo confirmed both the militant and conciliatory factions inside Japan.

Old paradigms lose their hold as they fail to solve more and more important problems, but much of the evidence for a new paradigm seems persuasive only after people see the world through it, so observations that in retrospect discredit the old theory are misinterpreted while it still holds sway.

The mere presence of the facts from which a correct inference could be drawn does not mean it will or should be drawn, because if no one is listening for signals against an improbable target the signals cannot be heard, and there is no route from experience to a theory even though a theory can be tested by experience.

Laymen exaggerate the empirical nature of science, since in some cases the most convincing or only evidence for a theory appears after the new theory dictates what experiments to run and how to interpret results, as the law of multiple proportions became recognizable only once Dalton's theory was accepted and the data re-ordered by relative weights.

Accepting a new theory alters perception both consciously and unconsciously, so scientists immediately see things they had overlooked, as Western astronomers began to see celestial change only after Copernicus even though the Chinese, whose cosmology permitted change, had recorded new stars and sunspots much earlier.

Once a new image of another state is established, the other's actions look very different, with new behavior noticed, old behavior dismissed, and other acts reinterpreted, as the onset of the Cold War gave Americans an entirely different view of Soviet conduct during World War II.

A single piece of behavior can crystallize an image that will not return to its original state even after the actor reverses his position, as the image of Japan as a menace solidified by the Tripartite Pact was little affected by later Japanese moves to draw back and its offer to negotiate a withdrawal was dismissed as worthless.

A new image changes what is considered obvious and what requires special explanation, so viewing Russia as a status-quo power makes its restraint self-explanatory and its Cuban missiles puzzling, while a security-seeking image makes an observer sensitive to Soviet concessions and differential treatment of Eastern European states.

Because established theories give a coherent, interrelated view, contradicting facts cannot be appreciated until the theory is displaced, and more radically the facts later seen as vital support can be seen only after the theory is accepted, as Galileo's Ptolemaist observers looked through the telescope yet could not see that Jupiter had moons.

New facts are often discovered by abandoning established authority rather than the other way round, as Vesalius first assumed Galen's channel through the septum was merely invisible and only years later, his faith in authority shaken, declared it did not exist, so one can reverse the saying to 'I'll see it when I believe it.'

Belief change is gestalt-like and batched rather than incremental, because a consistent attitude structure inhibits piecemeal change among interconnected elements, so change comes in large batches with several elements shifting almost simultaneously, much like the flip from seeing a drawing as a vase to seeing two faces.

Sometimes a new perception is so overwhelmingly satisfactory that it is accepted the moment it is pointed out, without argument, and then seems so natural that the person cannot understand how he missed it or return to his earlier disorganization, as a photo interpreter, once shown a rocket, went back over prior photographs and easily detected more missiles.

More often the interaction between theories and facts makes debate on the merits of opposing paradigms or images difficult, because what counts as an important fact in one framework may not in another, both sides find bits the other cannot explain, and the same information can be cited for conflicting conclusions.

Disagreements are rarely settled by appeal to one or two facts, because interpreting a document is conditioned by one's overall view of the actor's character and policies, so each side reads an ambiguous document as support for a view already formed from much other evidence, as with the Ritter-Fischer dispute over Bethmann-Hollweg.

In most political questions it is impossible to separate judgments about specific inferences from the larger merits of the contending images, because a state's acts are not neatly labeled aggressive or peaceful like colored balls drawn from a jar, so the interpretation of each act is unavoidably conditioned by the hypotheses held.

Because both sides can reasonably draw on the same facts to support opposite conclusions, an interpretive dispute cannot be settled by discussing the most recent behavior, so the general images that lie behind the specific interpretations should be debated instead, as when Finland twice had to judge whether Russia was planning an attack.

Ignoring discrepant information or assimilating it to prior beliefs perpetuates inaccurate images and poor policies, yet these processes are necessary if decision-makers are to act at all, so an actor who refuses to alter his image when some evidence does not fit cannot automatically be condemned, and irrationality is detectable only when the assimilation violates generally agreed-upon rules for treating evidence.

One failure mode is not even beginning to grapple with a large body of information indicating one's views are wrong, or, absent an open dispute, failing to notice events of obvious import, as Haig took no account of Russia's withdrawal from the fighting or the American declaration of war.

Another failure mode is rejecting information because considering it is too painful, as Baldwin waved away a report on German rearmament saying that if he read it he would not sleep, and some decision-makers refuse to receive emotion-laden information to avoid being influenced by it.

A further failure mode is refusing to engage opponents' arguments or being unable to grasp simple but powerful considerations against oneself, as Dowding, even after the fact, could not acknowledge the logic of the large-fighter-formation proposal despite having the intellectual ability to see it.

Because intelligent decision-making involves actively seeking information and not merely weighing what is brought to one's attention, the failure to look for evidence that is clearly available and significant is itself an irrational way of processing information.

Decision-makers repeatedly fail to seek the crucial information behind a vital prediction, as the 1915 Dardanelles plan assumed the fleet's arrival would spark a revolution in Constantinople with few arguments sought, and the 1956 British assumed the Suez Canal would close without ever checking how little training its pilots actually required.

The failure to seek important information is even more striking when it persists for years, as the interwar British and American air forces built war plans on the effectiveness of strategic bombing without gathering or evaluating evidence on whether the necessary targets could be located and hit.

Not every case of ignoring or stretching information deserves condemnation, because for every signal there are usually several plausible explanations, so selecting the one that fits a popular hypothesis is reasonable as long as that hypothesis is popular because it has successfully accounted for a great deal of data, since a theory is necessary to see any pattern in a contradictory mass of evidence.

Understanding a complex situation requires the right theoretical framework, as one could grasp the complexity of Soviet policy toward China only by seeing it balance national against ideological interests and immediate against long-range considerations, which Hurley's naivete and optimism prevented him from even beginning to tackle.

Observers who lack a theoretical framework are strongly swayed by the most recent data or the latest short-run trend and show marked instability of opinion, and an experiment found that people given training in judging personalities became less accurate because it destroyed their confidence in naive but powerful modes and made them attend to individual differences they could not interpret accurately.

Because evidence and images interact necessarily, it is hard to find general differences between how those who are right and those who are wrong draw inferences, since one could take an event that did not happen, act as though it had, and find many clues pointing to it that officials had ignored or explained away.

Those who turned out to be right usually showed no more openness to new information than those who were wrong, as Vansittart fitted each ambiguous bit of evidence into his own hypotheses about German aggressiveness just as Chamberlain did, so a correct hypothesis is often reached by methods indistinguishable from those of people who were mistaken.

Those who are wrong may only seem more stubborn because they receive more discrepant information, and the right may seem open-minded only because their initial views were correct, so instead of a person being wrong because he is stubborn, he may be stubborn because he is wrong.

It is difficult to specify when a person is too closed-minded, because there is no sharp line between the degree of holding to beliefs and disparaging discrepant information that is necessary for intelligent comprehension and the degree that maintains beliefs all fair-minded people should reject, and sometimes the stubborn man is vindicated.

The correct explanation is often not supported by the bulk of the evidence, and in politics an incorrect belief frequently makes the most sense of the available data, as the true facts of Watergate were highly implausible until behind-the-scenes access allowed the flow of events to be reconstructed.

Those who reach the right conclusion may be less reasonable and treat information in less justifiable ways than those who are wrong, because hunches, luck, and an accurate general analysis often explain a correct prediction while those who disagree are often truer to the particular facts, as a correct grasp of the general situation leads to doing injustice to specific facts.

Those who are right are rarely distinguished by superior ability to judge specific bits of information, since their expectations and predispositions simply provided a closer match to the situation, as those who quickly inferred Nixon's guilt in Watergate did so because they already distrusted him rather than from close observation of the immediate events.

People learn and remember accurately when the schema they apply fits the arrangement of the stimuli, so cognitively simple people can make fewer errors than complex ones when their simplifying hypotheses match the social structure they face, meaning complexity is not always functional.

Successful detection of a military or diplomatic surprise is less explained by an intelligence service's skill in piecing together arcane bits of information than by the degree to which its predispositions and expectations happen to fit what the other is actually planning.

An actor trying to surprise another should find out what the other expects him to do and then do something else, rather than try to alter the other's predictions, because it is better to exploit the fact that people assimilate discrepant information to prior beliefs than to fight it, as the Normandy deception succeeded largely because Hitler already believed Calais was the target.

A correct prediction can be a lucky match between a person's predispositions and the situation, as the anti-appeasers' predispositions were appropriate in the 1930s only because Hitler came to power, since under most leaders Germany could have been appeased and many now-wise Englishmen would have been dangerous warmongers.

Predispositions produce accuracy when they fit the environment, so a statesman sensitive to security threats perceives correctly if his state is often menaced, and job-training programs and job selection try to create such matches, though there is no guarantee that threat-sensitive people will staff only the insecure states.

Unless one realizes that the difference between accurate and inaccurate perceivers does not lie in ability to examine specific facts, one will over-credit those who were right with superior intellect, promote them, and adopt their views, holding an unwarranted faith that they will keep perceiving accurately under changed circumstances.

Not being aware of the inevitable influence of beliefs on perception makes a decision-maker who thinks an event yields self-evident inferences grow overconfident and prematurely exclude alternatives, because he concludes the event provides independent support for his beliefs.

People frequently fail to realize that evidence consistent with their hypothesis may also be consistent with others, and since the vital data when choosing between hypotheses is what only one can account for, they treat data that also supports alternatives as confirming their view and see their interpretations as compelling rather than merely plausible, as Britain and Norway read German ship movements as confirming an Atlantic breakout when the same path was equally consistent with the invasion that occurred.

Believing an inference is based only on the event itself, a person assumes a reasonable holder of a different hypothesis would still admit the event best supports his own view, so when others do not he grows more intolerant of their positions and stops attending to them.

Many experiments show people do not understand the impact of their beliefs on interpretation and attribute their judgments to the stimulus itself, as the same man was rated less favorably when labeled a union organizer than a business leader while subjects believed they had judged by his physiognomy, and convention viewers thought they had seen the events for themselves.

Mistaking belief-driven interpretation for independent confirmation is self-reinforcing, since reflecting on a stereotype-shaped impression strengthens the stereotype through false independent support, and taking cues from one's party is rational only until one's trust in the party is inflated by finding that its position agrees with a view one derived from it.

Continuing involvement with an issue decreases the ease with which a person can change his mind, because changing at a later stage carries the high cost of admitting error and is inhibited by the increased amount of apparently supporting evidence, an effect amplified when prior beliefs make him mis-remember the facts.

An irrational double standard is not merely giving the same behavior different meaning depending on who does it, since theory-laden perception makes some of that legitimate, but is constituted when a person uses the same behavior as compelling evidence for opposite images, as a woman read an identical gait as pompous for a disliked professor and humble for a beloved teacher.

Decision-makers commonly reason as if any reasonable person would agree that an event independently confirms their image, failing to see that their perception is colored by that image, unable to understand how others draw different inferences, and so growing more confident, as both sides did in the 1939 Finnish debate over Soviet intentions.

Most important internationally is that a state takes as evidence of another's hostility actions that, had it done them itself, it would have seen as consistent with its own peacefulness, as the United States read the Soviet rejection of the Baruch Plan as hostility even though any suspicious state would have found the plan unacceptable.

The mirror image is that a state does many things it believes are consistent with its own peacefulness which the other sees as compelling evidence of aggression, as Kennan blocked a Pentagon step near the Soviet frontier that he realized a Soviet leader would read as preparation for war within six months.

Decision-makers often assume the context is different and read the other's actions as inconsistent with non-aggression, solidifying their hostile image, while being unable to understand how others could draw the same conclusion from their own similar actions, which is a dangerous double standard, as the United States condemned North Vietnamese resupply during a truce while itself moving record supplies.

Actors often fail to communicate their messages and images because they rarely realize that what matters is not how they would understand a message but how others will, so unless an actor understands others' beliefs about international relations and about himself he cannot see what inferences they draw from his behavior, and if he mis-estimates their beliefs he will be confidently wrong about how the other sees him.

Actors are more apt to err on the side of being too wedded to an established view and too quick to reject discrepant information than to alter their theories too quickly, so people often undergo premature cognitive closure.

Judging closed-mindedness is complicated because the choice is often not between the prevailing image and a single alternative but among several competitors, so an actor may rationally hold an image whose probability is below one-half yet higher than that of any single alternative, and while political strategy explains some apparent rigidity it cannot explain why decision-makers keep even their private images past appropriateness.

The initial organization of stimuli strongly structures later perceptions, because once a belief takes hold new information lacks the impact it would have had earlier, so a person who was experimenting with interpretations now automatically perceives new information as having a fixed meaning, as a dominant percept suppresses inharmonious cues and enhances harmonious ones.

The hardest mental act is to rearrange a familiar bundle of data and escape the prevailing doctrine, so people may sense something is wrong without specifying why and, even knowing an image is incorrect, still find it hard to see something else, just as optical illusions persist after one is told what he is seeing, because the established perception is so hard to lose.

Being too closed to discrepant information is closely linked to forming a hypothesis too soon, because perceptual hypotheses fixate after receiving a minimum of confirmation, and once partial confirmation occurs almost nothing changes the person's report.

Initial incorrect hypotheses delay accurate perception for a long time, since subjects who watched a slide from its most blurred stage held their usually wrong early image far past the point where others exposed only to the clearer later stages identified the object, so exposure to early ambiguous information impairs the extraction of information from later evidence rather than giving a head start.

Premature judgment poisons later analysis, because a judgment made after reading a small amount of data makes new data harder to assimilate, a partial-support hypothesis seduces a problem-solver into keeping a false approach, and inexpert early interrogation can spoil witnesses for later examination by pressing them beyond their observation and biasing them toward the first officer's preferred explanation.

In most experiments the later information is more valuable, as when a slide progressively clears, but political and social phenomena do not automatically become clearer over time as if a fog were lifting, so if early bits of information are as valuable as later ones the resulting images will not be as misleading as those produced in the experiments.

Premature closure increases the stability of policy because perceptions are slow to change, and since people assimilate feedback to prior beliefs, all but the most unambiguous feedback is seen as confirming the established policy, so incrementalism's promised self-correction fails and actors proceed longer down blind alleys before revising their basic assumptions.

Satisficing applies to perceptions as well as decisions, because people do not compare many images to see which best explains all the evidence but adopt the first that provides a decent fit and examine alternatives only when it fails badly, so once an independent variable is believed powerful its presence is credited with important effects without rigorous analysis.

Perceptual satisficing is not conscious cost-minimization, because the cost of trying a new interpretation would be low were it not for the strong hold of the already-formed image, as a student who expects to be mistreated because of her sex reads all slights as discrimination without testing whether her student status explains them.

Rough estimates of another's intentions, meant at the time to be merely tentative, exercise a powerful lasting influence, as a British admiral read one of two wartime objectives as overriding and held it despite later clarifying messages, and the Czech leadership stayed confident of no Soviet invasion in 1968 because early ambiguous measures fit its war-of-nerves image.

Any policy of gradually increasing pressure on an adversary carries a hidden danger, because the common claim that less belligerent measures leave stronger options undamaged overlooks that the first actions set an image that cannot easily be altered.

Two kinds of people tend to have accurate perceptions: those whose predispositions match the stimulus, and those who avoid forming initial estimates until a lot of data is available, so it is often in a decision-maker's interest to keep his early judgments vague and the slow pace of the State Department contributes to this.
An image is formed on little information when the evidence closely resembles a well-known pattern, as incongruous playing cards were quickly seen as normal because they resembled real cards.

An early and incorrect perceptual set forms when an actor has unusual intentions whose behavioral manifestations resemble those of more common aims, so the widespread misperception of Hitler's intentions is largely explained by the belief that any defeated, proud, and powerful state would merely seek to regain a legitimate place, a belief Nazi behavior was designed to fit.

Because information highly compatible with an established belief is quickly assimilated to it, that belief masks the perception of similar alternatives, so Admiral Kimmel dismissed the Japanese code-burning report because it fit his expectation of an attack on British and Dutch territory, and generally the belief that the other is bluffing masks the perception that it will actually fight because the two behaviors resemble each other.

An image forms on little information under pressure to reach a quick conclusion, and since the pressure to quickly form an image of another actor rises with the other's importance, even a state that is studied more carefully because it matters more may be perceived no more accurately than a less important one.

Policy-makers underestimate the cost of forming preliminary hypotheses because, while they know an incorrect image leading to an incorrect policy is costly, they do not realize that an incorrect image also delays the development of accurate perceptions, so they form images more quickly than they would if they understood the process.

The tendency to assimilate information to a pre-existing image is greater the more ambiguous the information, because ambiguity is defined by the ease with which evidence can be read in several ways, so the more ambiguous the evidence the less likely it is to embarrass the established image.

A confident actor believes his image is supported by much data, so he will and should be slow to modify it for discrepant bits, but certainty also lets him perceive a pattern in what would otherwise be a meaningless blur, as subjects held an image far past the point where a slide had gone out of focus.

Image flexibility is an inverse function of the extremity of the belief's level, and since sureness of belief yields a resistant image, images of another actor as very aggressive or very peaceful tend to be strongly entrenched.

A person is less apt to reorganize evidence into a new image if deeply committed to the established view, where commitment means not only power and prestige stakes but how satisfactory and internalized the way of seeing has become, so training and experience are functional when the environment is stable but costly when it changes.

Success with one method inhibits developing new ones when needed, as subjects who learned a formula were much slower on similar-looking problems it could not solve even after realizing it would not work, and this rigidity strengthens with stress and method complexity, so countering it requires prior exposure plus explanation, warnings that solving may require breaking a set, or a pause before beginning.

Scientific and technological breakthroughs are often made by the young or by people trained in another field, because they can more easily free themselves from the established framework, as most major innovators in the early steel industry, including Bessemer, Kelly, and Carnegie, had no experience in the iron trade.

Domain experts can be the worst at anticipating discontinuities, since the professional military experts all failed to predict the shape of World War I while amateurs such as novelists came closest, and the strategic usefulness of railways in war was first realized by civilians.

Inexperience can be an asset for seeing the anomalous but real, as pulsars were partly discovered because a graduate student did not appreciate the risks and was willing to contemplate as a serious possibility a phenomenon all past experience suggested was impossible, which a more knowledgeable investigator would not have explored.

The link between being an outsider and innovating has alternative explanations, since leading firms may rationally minimize change and innovators may have creative personalities that lead them to reject long training and the accepted framework, so lack of training may be an intervening variable between personality and inventiveness rather than an independent cause.

Because commitment to an image inhibits developing a new one, those most involved in carrying out a policy guided by the old image are the least able to innovate, which is part of the rationale for a policy-planning staff freed from immediate problems and for expecting perceptual openness from individuals newly assigned to a problem or country.

Review committees are more apt to see problems in a new light and recommend non-incremental change if their members have not previously worked on the problem, and since most policy reviews lack imagination, the risk of missing constraints known to insiders is usually worth running.

Distance from implementation buys the ability to ask basic questions, so congressional foreign-policy committees may gain perceptual and political independence by remaining less involved in carrying out policy, even though their detailed suggestions will be less valuable.

Perceptions are influenced by immediate concerns, or evoked sets, as well as by deeper expectations, so a person interprets stimuli in terms of what is at the front of his mind, and familiarity alone is not enough because he must also expect the object to be present.

The evoked set shapes perception even without communication and even when the phenomenon thought about is no more likely to be present, so preparing a contingency plan increases the probability that decision-makers will see future events as resembling the situation they contemplated and as calling for the plans they developed.

People interpret incoming information in terms of their current concerns without calculation, so two scientists independently misread the same drug side-effect according to their main research interests, one admitting that thinking in terms of muscle blinded him to the changes taking place in the cartilage.

The evoked set can be strong enough to make a person ignore information not relevant to his immediate concerns even when it later clearly merited attention, as a McGovern aide did not follow up Eagleton's report of hospitalization for exhaustion because it came as an answer to the alcoholism charge that was what they were looking for.

Perceiving another's messages through one's own evoked set is reinforced by the belief that the other shares one's concerns, so a message sent from a different background produces misunderstanding unless a party knows the other's perspective, and receivers attuned to subtleties are worse off because searching for subtleties increases the impact of their own expectations.

These barriers afflict even the basic ability to understand what message the other is trying to convey, so the Spanish in 1898 scrutinized McKinley's message not for indications of American intentions toward Spain but for effects on rebel morale, and thereby missed his warning of further action in the near future.

Differences in information, perspectives, and time lags produce misperception even with complete common interest, no deception, and both sides wishing to communicate accurately, as Washington's warning to General Short to expect hostile action, meaning external attack, was read as sabotage because each side wrongly assumed the other shared its information and neither realized they were not communicating.

The failures behind the charge of the Light Brigade were caused by unrecognized differences in evoked sets from geography, time lags, and contrasting experiences, since Raglan on the heights could see the guns being moved while Lucan below could see nothing, the courier leapt to a vengeful reading from his own concerns, and Raglan's prior restraint of the cavalry made a cavalry-alone attack unthinkable to Lucan.

A message is interpreted in light of events not foreseen when it was written, and a time lag lets the receiver's context change, so Grey's 1914 warning reached the kaiser just after he learned of Russian mobilization and predisposed him to see it as part of a plot.

Uneven distribution of highly classified information within a government, including information about the state's own behavior, leads different parts of the bureaucracy to different perceptions of others' actions, as Crowe, restricted to what was printed, read an Anglo-German convention as German aggression while an official who knew Britain's own position interpreted the German behavior more accurately.

The interpretation of an adversary's act depends on who holds the relevant classified context, so the Gulf of Tonkin attack looked different to those who knew the ship had been gathering electronic intelligence close to shore and that South Vietnamese commandos had raided the coast two days before.

An ambassador who is unaware of the messages passed between his home government and the one he deals with is apt to misinterpret both nations' behavior, which is why the State Department requires that reports of conversations with foreign diplomats in Washington be sent to the relevant American embassy.

Facts that would make a third party's behavior comprehensible may be withheld even by allies, so Britain read German demands in the 1905 Moroccan crisis as aiming at continental domination only because it did not know France had secretly offered Germany territorial compensation.

Uneven information about the adversary within a government produces failure even when all the pieces are present, as a British convoy was destroyed because those who knew a German force was out did not know the convoy schedule while those who knew the convoy route did not know of the German ships' movements.

When vital information is unevenly distributed within both governments, a receiver can go astray by knowing certain information and wrongly assuming the sender knows it too, so those who knew of the U-2 flights may have read Soviet behavior less accurately if they assumed their counterparts knew of them.

Differences in what most concerns an actor are a major cause of misperception, because an important issue absorbs so much of a decision-maker's attention that he sees most events in its terms and cannot realize others do not share his preoccupation, so he assumes others are focused on his concern and believes that producing effects on it was their goal.

Actors see themselves as central to others' behavior, so an actor's knowledge of what he wants, fears, and has done frames his perception and he sees others as orienting themselves toward his concerns and as helping or hurting him, as a Chamberlain supporter read the German takeover of Czechoslovakia as Hitler being unhelpful to Chamberlain.

Even harder than believing the other sees you as an opponent is realizing the other is playing an entirely different game, as an official read a traffic cop's use of his first name as a racial slight when it was the cop's standard practice for asserting dominance over any suspect, because the identity most salient to him he assumed was equally salient to the cop.

A dominant concern makes an actor read the other's every act through it, as the Allies after 1917, preoccupied with the war against Germany, read everything the Bolsheviks did as German-influenced and could not see the Russians cared only about preserving the Soviet regime rather than about helping or hurting the Allies.

Egocentricity about one's own dominant concern is symmetric, since an embattled democracy attaches absolute value to its cause and cannot understand any other contest, but the Bolsheviks were equally unable to believe their revolution did not appear to everyone else as the most important world event.

Even actors with a history of communication and cooperation may misperceive each other because prior experience makes each assume more quickly that the other shares its concerns and understands its messages, as Dulles privately meant the Cape route by appropriate action at Suez while Eden read it as an invitation to force the canal.

People perceive incoming information in terms of the problems they are dealing with, and re-orienting attention is difficult, as the crew of the Libyan airliner, immersed in finding the Cairo airport, could not grasp even after warning shots that they faced Israeli fighters ordering them to land.

Actors fail to send appropriate messages or draw accurate inferences because they wrongly assume the other shares their evoked set, as the Israelis assumed the Libyans knew the fighters' nationality and chose to flee, never imagining they were too engrossed in their task to grasp the situation.

Actors overestimate how much each understands what the other is trying to say, not by overestimating common interest but by rarely accounting for how much the other may be concerned with different tasks, so each overestimates the extent of a shared agenda and rarely sees how far its own and others' perceptions are shaped by a particular combination of concerns and information.

History genuinely shapes perception rather than being a mere grab-bag from which advocates pull lessons to prove points they already hold, because if history only reinforced beliefs, people with different outlooks would not draw the same lessons from an event and historical experience would not alter decision-makers' views.

History gives a statesman a range of imaginable situations and lets him detect patterns and causal links, but its lessons are not on the surface even though the surface lessons are learned most easily, so a too-narrow conception of the past and a failure to appreciate changed circumstances produce the tyranny of a misapplied analogy.

Some events, especially wars, leave such an impression that equally dramatic developments are required to displace them, so having overlearned from a traumatic event decision-makers become insensitive to incoming information, flying straight like a bullet.

An analogy often precedes and drives the analysis rather than merely illustrating an independently reached view, as Truman's analogy to the 1930s preceded his analysis of Korea and shaped his later perceptions, encouraging him to see the aggression as unprovoked and to expect further attacks if this one went unmet.

Learning from history is often not conscious, since a decision-maker need not explicitly identify the present with a past situation to be influenced, as Royal Navy officers who said World War I held little lesson because it was all so different now were nonetheless deeply influenced by it.

The lesson a statesman draws is contingent on the accidental shape of his formative era, because had the 1930s displayed tension-hostility spirals, an erratic Hitler, or diversionary small attacks, Truman would have read the Korean attack quite differently.

Analogies provide a useful shortcut to rationality but obscure the ways the present case differs from the past, so a dramatic experience often hinders later decision-making by supplying an analogy applied too quickly and widely, and an actor would sometimes perceive more accurately had he not undergone the earlier experience, so more knowledge does not necessarily increase the ability to cope.

For some purposes the biased selection of events people learn from does not matter, because knowing that an outcome has occurred teaches an important lesson when the outcome was previously believed impossible or never considered, as 1914 revealed that inflexible war plans could rule out desired political options.

When decision-makers already know the candidate categories and are uncertain which known possibility is correct, a dramatic event misleads by shifting their perceptual thresholds too much, so leaders became more apt to read ambiguous evidence as showing world-domination ambitions after Nazi Germany even though Russia or China are no more likely to seek domination because Germany did.

The prescriptive force of learning from the 1930s is weaker than believed, because it did not take Hitler to teach that appeasing an aggressor is dangerous, which was always known, so the crucial question is always whether the particular other side in this encounter must be stopped by force, not whether appeasement is generally unwise.

The pressure to apply one salient situation's lessons to resembling others is so powerful that even those aware of the pitfall succumb, as Nicolson criticized Castlereagh for estimating future stability by the factors of the just-concluded war yet later added lessons meant to guide the next peace treaty, overgeneralizing without analyzing whether the key variables differed.

To know what lessons a person will learn from an event one often needs more than general learning principles and a description of the event, because what he learns at a given time is influenced, sometimes decisively, by the outlook he already held.

An organization's definition of its role and identity can block it from learning the obvious disconfirming lesson, as the British navy, defining its mission as fighting the enemy's main fleet, was so dominated by the memory of Jutland that it forgot the nearly decisive anti-submarine fight and had to relearn all those lessons in the next war.

The same historical event yields divergent lessons shaped by prior beliefs and sometimes at odds with the objective history, as Munich led scholars to conclude that deterrence of Hitler was impossible while U.S. statesmen drew that success feeds the appetite of aggression, and the belief that Vietnam proved conventional forces cannot beat guerrillas ignores that U.S. troops crushed the Viet Cong and the South was defeated by a conventional invasion.

The link from lessons learned to later behavior is only probabilistic, so learning from history biases but does not determine perception and can be outweighed by other motives, as Munich made British decision-makers sensitive to the dangers of appeasement yet their fear of nuclear war led them to favor conciliation in the 1958-1962 Berlin crises.

A formative lesson can fail to transfer even where it obviously applies, as Pearl Harbor should have sensitized American decision-makers to the danger of surprise attack yet until the mid-1950s the United States barely guarded its strategic bombers and nuclear stockpile, operating only four part-time radar stations in 1947.

Interpretations of past events are not unmoved movers, so to show that history shapes present perception one must demonstrate that causality flows from the interpretation of the past to present perceptions, ruling out both spuriousness and the possibility that current preferences shape memory.

Current policy preferences can shape memories of the past, shown most clearly when a shift in memory follows a shift in preference, as Roosevelt's beliefs about why the League of Nations failed changed as his trust in the Soviet Union waned and new information about the postwar world arrived.

Even where beliefs about history clearly did not determine policy, they may still have supplied the available analogies and excluded other models that would have been salient had the earlier events been different, so history plays a role even when it does not dictate.

When an interpretation of the past is strikingly incorrect, it was likely shaped by current preferences rather than the reverse, as French advocates of the offensive doctrine blamed their 1870 defeat on a defensive posture in great distortion of the war's history, so unless a general learning principle explains the belief the preferred contemporary strategy probably caused it.

When the same factors cause both current preferences and the memories drawn on, the correlation between lessons and later perceptions is spurious, as liberals and conservatives gave contrasting versions of the World War I economy when debating postwar price controls because each perspective drove both the stand and the historical analysis.

Spuriousness is most likely when the initial and later situations are most similar or when the person chose to place himself in the initial situation, whereas an experience probably had a genuine impact when an early response is repeated in a situation that people who did not undergo the experience see as very different.

Whether the person chose to be in the formative situation is a test for spuriousness, since when he chose the situation the same belief or personality that explains his initial response likely explains later ones, but spuriousness is not plausible for formative experiences he did not seek, as with Rusk's unsought wartime service in the China-Burma-India theater.

Spuriousness is unlikely when people with different personalities and beliefs learn the same lesson from an event or when an experience changes a person's mind, because then his pre-existing outlook cannot account for the lesson, so its later application to a different situation shows the past playing an independent role.

There are two kinds of generality in learning, and the more general and abstract the previous learning about the properties of an object or method, the more it helps and the less it hinders future problems, so history should make one wise for always rather than clever for another time.

Decision-makers learn broad general lessons of the wrong kind, applying an analogy in its broad outlines to too many disparate cases and to too many aspects, because the learning did not involve understanding the causal relations, so it is not general in the sense of grasping the crucial characteristics likely to recur.

Decision-makers usually fail to strip away the ephemeral, context-bound facets of a past event and mistake situation-specific features for general characteristics, because they assume the most salient results were caused by the most salient aspects of the preceding situation and attend to what happened rather than why, so their learning is superficial and post-hoc.

Productive analysis penetrates to the underlying mechanism rather than surface resemblance, as scientists seeking a cancer treatment studied what about cancer-cell surface proteins lets a substance make them clump rather than searching for similar-looking substances, paralleling Darwin's shift to discovering the mechanisms that impose order whether or not that order is conspicuous.

Decision-makers rarely test a causal attribution, because their search for causes is quick and oversimplified, they make few comparisons to judge a variable's causal efficacy, and once they think they know a cause they rarely look for other cases where the variable was present or additional instances of the same outcome to see whether other causes could produce it.

Decision-makers are rarely misled by small oddities but instead see causes that are as dramatic as the results, as the outcome of the Franco-Prussian War was attributed to the different forms of the armies while less dramatic factors such as Prussian staff planning, railways, and artillery were at least as important.

An account that stresses a few overriding variables yields rigid rules that do not guide a changing world, because one event can serve as an analogy to many others only if a major cause was correctly identified and other factors are unimportant or constant, whereas if the outcome depended on interacting factors, applying the lesson without analysis makes the world seem more unchanging than it is.

Learning a noncontingent rule from a context-dependent outcome causes error, as Britain and France, having learned that militias were ineffective without understanding why the rule held in 1871, wrongly discounted German reserves in 1914.

A behavioral pattern learned in one context does not transfer to a changed context, so the German surprise attack on Norway succeeded partly because the Norwegian foreign minister expected Hitler to issue demands first, as in peacetime, overlooking that once war began the incentives shifted sharply toward attacks without warning.

Axioms applied without understanding their conditions fail when the conditions change, as Halsey chased a Japanese decoy fleet at Leyte Gulf because it contained carriers, guided by axioms that had been useful earlier but were no longer valid once the enemy's carriers were unimportant.

Copying a policy without studying its enabling conditions attributes too much generality to what was actually a product of a combination of variables, as Nigeria chose railways over highways because railroads had aided Western development while overlooking the conditions, such as the lack of substitutes and absence of ethnic conflict, that had made them effective elsewhere.

Categorizing an outcome as a success leads decision-makers to over-credit the policy, paying little attention to its costs, to whether another policy would have worked even better, or to whether success was largely luck, and rarely asking whether the favorable outcome occurred in spite of their choices, so successful policies are too quickly repeated.

On failure, decision-makers assume the rejected alternatives would have done better and often that they should have known this, rarely leaving room that a policy, though not the best, was the best choice given the information available, so appeasing Hitler was a bad policy that there may have been no way to recognize as such at the time.

People preserve a prior belief by attributing an anomalous success or failure to special factors, as cavalry proponents argued the Boers would have done even better fighting in the traditional manner and air-force officials attributed the Korean air-war success with obsolescent aircraft to factors peculiar to Korea.

Because an actor's own actions loom large to him, overgeneralizing often means believing his behavior was a major influence on the outcome, so he underestimates variables outside his control, sees very different cases as similar, and fails to notice or denies changes in the context in which a policy is to be reapplied.

In continuing issues people remember that they hold a value but forget why, so when conditions change they discuss policy in the old terms without considering the ends it now serves, as many liberals were slow to consider that segregation sought by a weak minority might differ in its consequences from segregation imposed by the dominant race.

Inappropriate learning is explained not by a lack of mental ability but by the complexity of the subject, the small and biased sample of cases available, the conditions under which learning takes place, and the decision-makers' failure to realize how much they are influenced by their views of the past.

Because decision-makers start from dramatic outcomes and lack explicit theories of what is surprising, they learn little from negative outcomes such as aggression that does not occur, crises that are avoided, quiet compromises, and slow peaceful transformations.

People learn most from events they experience firsthand, that influence their careers, or that have major consequences for their nation, which produces an idiosyncratically biased sample driven by the accident of what one happens to experience or which dramatic event occurs in one's lifetime.

The available sample of cases is not only biased but small, so the few high-impact events are overworked as analogies and decision-makers are insensitive to changes in variables that were constant in the familiar cases, as those gauging interwar naval strength had little choice but to extrapolate from the single battle of Jutland.

Decision-makers have few occasions to verify a lesson, because unlike physical-environment cues that are checked many times a day, foreign-affairs cues cannot be readily checked and an analogy is applied rarely with little unambiguous feedback, so infrequent validation increases reliance on preferred, less-than-certain cues and stabilizes cue use too soon at a suboptimal level.

High-drive conditions inhibit the most flexible principle-type learning, so overwhelming events produce overgeneralized and oversimplified lessons, meaning decision-makers are often too involved in the highest-impact events to derive the most useful information from them.

Because they are pragmatic and unaware of the past's influence, decision-makers treat the study of history as an interesting diversion, whereas if they understood the impact of the lessons they have learned they would take greater care that those lessons were correct and applicable.

When an event affects the predispositions of many members of an organization, its lessons become institutionalized in textbooks, rules, and even language and outlive their applicability, as the Royal Navy Staff College in 1934 spent three days studying Jutland while ignoring the 1917 U-boat crisis and the methods devised to contain it.

Over-correcting for the last failure can lose the next opportunity, as after stiff resistance at Salerno the Anzio landing was given a strong defensive component, a cautious commander, and conservative instructions, so the Allies' caution forwent an easy victory when the road to Rome lay open.

Success consolidates the power of a policy's advocates while defeat strengthens dissenters, so Japan's initial success in World War II reinforced the dominant group that believed it could win a limited victory and made it harder for dissenters to ask what Japan would do if the Allies refused a short war.

Four variables determine how much an event affects later predispositions: whether it was experienced firsthand, whether it occurred early in adult life or career, whether it had important consequences for the person or nation, and whether the person is familiar with a range of events that facilitate alternative perceptions.

Firsthand experiences exercise too great an influence on predispositions, so the main problem is not that too little is learned without direct experience but that people under-learn from others and over-learn from themselves, as it took the Bay of Pigs to drive home for Kennedy a lesson about scrutinizing expert advice that he already knew.

Learning from an event varies with the actor's time, energy, and ego involvement, so participating teaches more than witnessing and witnessing more than reading, but since most situations must be learned about indirectly, events seen and participated in leave disproportionate impressions and the lessons drawn from them are overgeneralized.

A firsthand experience creates an over-predisposition driven by luck rather than representativeness, so a person bitten by a snake is quicker to see snakes and mistakes branches for them while his equally-at-risk unbitten friends are far less affected, and a diplomat who saw a reform movement go communist perceives peaceful change elsewhere differently even knowing of the other case.

Not only the event but the position a person held within it shapes his perceptions, so someone whose job was to get troops into Korea remembers the war differently from someone deciding what messages to send China, each retaining specific sensitivities the other lacks.

Knowing about an experience is not equivalent to having it, since experiments show active participation influences later behavior more than passive spectating and that merely knowing of deception without experiencing it has the same effect as being ignorant of it.

Nations remodel their defenses from their own experience and rarely from foreign wars, and they over-generalize their own failures, as the British concluded from Gallipoli that amphibious operations could not succeed while the uninvolved Americans developed the amphibious tactics that proved successful against Japan.

A firsthand failure with a technology, even one caused by misuse, blocks its later adoption, as the French and Germans discounted machine guns after France misused an early version as artillery in 1870 while the uninvolved British saw the gun should not be judged by a misuse and pushed its development.

One learns little from another's experience even with high incentives and much in common, since in wartime it is one's own battles that change one's tactics, so the Americans were slow to learn the British lessons about combatting U-boats and about the intolerable losses of unescorted daylight bombing until they suffered them themselves.

Firsthand experience powerfully fixes images of other actors, so a person is slow to detect changes in an actor with whom he had prior firsthand contact, as Curzon was blinded in 1919 to the reversal in which Persia now feared Britain and looked to Moscow.

Firsthand experience makes a person insensitive to variables that change from one situation to another, as Trygve Lie judged Iran's handling of Soviet troops by Norway's positive experience of a Soviet withdrawal despite the very different circumstances.

Predispositions created by firsthand experience shape perceptions of other actors too, since dealing with one kind of adversary increases the chance others are seen as similar, as a South African governor who had served in the West Indies saw the settlers' reaction to abolition as a greater threat than the border friction that soon led to war.

A trauma one side experienced but the other did not breeds mutual incomprehension read as bad faith, as the Soviet demands on Finland in 1939 rested on a civil-war-derived view of protecting Leningrad the Finns could not grasp, so the Finns concluded the arguments were disingenuous and aimed at destroying their independence.

The desire to see for yourself and judge by direct observation is often a mistake for a complex problem on a short visit, because the masses of available information carry less weight than personally witnessed but unrepresentative incidents, as Churchill came away from one successful exercise too optimistic about sonar.

A summit participant gives undue weight to firsthand impressions of his counterparts, so a statesman seeking to avoid relying on others' judgment may acquire information whose impact is out of proportion to its validity and thereby decrease his own accuracy, a danger compounded by excessive confidence in judging others face to face.

An actor learns most fruitfully from events he knows well enough to analyze in detail but that are not so close they dominate his future perceptions, so decision-makers may learn best, though not most, from reading history or observing other states, whose larger range of cases forces more thought before seizing on an analogy.

Part of the impact of direct involvement is the rational gain of information depth, because a participant obtains far more, though not necessarily representative, information than dispatches can convey, since not all the nuances and subtleties of events can be transmitted secondhand.

If firsthand impact were merely rational information depth, it would make a person slow to see other situations as like his case and lead him to draw only careful limited conclusions, but since people instead use their experiences as sweeping analogies, the information-depth explanation for firsthand impact is probably wrong.

The claim that a state should learn most from what happened to it because that best indicates its future cannot account for the magnitude of learning differences or the absence of similarity analysis, as European soldiers dismissed the American Civil War and the Russo-Japanese War as irrelevant to European warfare yet could not afford to neglect the firepower and trench countermeasures those wars displayed.

Actors are influenced by their own experience even when analysis would not sustain a claim for its greater relevance, as West German generals avoided close air support because Goering's air force had failed after 1943 and 1972 NATO unit leaders were casual about enemy air attack because Western forces had enjoyed air superiority since 1942, even though which side one was on should not govern beliefs about future tactics.

The correlation between participating in a situation and later perceptions may be spurious if self-selection is present, so spuriousness is unlikely only when the actor did not choose to enter the situation, when all who had the experience learned the same lessons, and when the experience changed the participants' views.

Nations have less choice than individuals in the situations they face, so self-selection rarely explains why a state's predispositions correlate with its previous experiences, but because a state's environment such as its geography is more constant than an individual's, the repetition of perceptions and policies may instead be caused by common situational variables.

When different people learn different lessons from an event, both a person's analysis of the event and his later perceptions may be determined by his pre-existing beliefs rather than by the event, as Stimson's hard line toward Japan may have flowed from a general belief in force rather than from his personal participation, since others did not draw the same lessons.
One can be fairly confident that an event exerts an independent influence on perception when large numbers of people with a range of characteristics and beliefs all learn the same lesson from it.

Events occurring early in a person's adult life have an especially great impact on his perceptual predispositions, because at that stage people are open to new ideas that, once rooted, maintain influence for life, while later events are seen within a more established framework and leave a reduced impression shaped by the earlier ones.

The ways of performing that brought a person success when he first emerged as a distinct individual become a persistent style, so a new president may turn to the strategies that worked as he became a man, as the way Nixon won his first race for Congress set his style.

The political issues and stands that advanced a person's early career and marked him as talented provide analogies that he applies with little discrimination, so a man who first made his mark by calling an adversary's bluff will later be more prone to stand firm, and three British Foreign Secretaries of the 1930s had made their reputations by appeasing Indian demands.

The diffuse values and ways of thinking that dominate a person's gripping early career supply the mental frame he brings to later and different problems, as some of Churchill's naval mistakes came from addressing naval problems with a soldier's mind because his first careers were as a soldier and a land-war journalist.

People absorb the values and beliefs dominant when they first begin thinking about politics, and because that first orientation is not easily replaced but structures the interpretation of later events, all who come of age at the same time are affected similarly, producing a generational or cohort effect.

To find a person's basic political ideas one must often go back to the events that demanded attention in his early life, which he sometimes uses as explicit analogies but more often as the basis of a general outlook, as contending French diplomatic generations of the 1870s favored conciliation or assertiveness according to the climate of their early adulthood.

Elite attitudes show cohort break-points rather than smooth aging trends, so younger politicians are less hostile to the opposition, as older British Tories saw Labour as a sinister intruder while younger ones saw it as merely the other side.

The formative lessons are fixed by the age at which a person first pays serious attention to politics rather than by his birth year, so Truman, only two years younger than Roosevelt, drew far less on the Treaty of Versailles because he became interested in politics later in life.

Substituting the time of first political concern for chronological age reintroduces spuriousness, because when a person first attends to politics is partly determined by his internal characteristics, which could independently explain the predispositions he later displays, especially through the role of his first success.

Early success is not all-or-none, since it can reinforce pre-existing habits or the situation itself, rather than deep personality, could have led to the first-success approach, which is then maintained even after the variables that were its immediate cause have ceased to operate.

It is hard to establish a causal role for early experiences when a person learned lessons that others did not, as Vansittart's early anti-German impressions cannot be explained without reference to pre-existing beliefs, since the incidents were not objectively distinguishable from others and many who shared them formed different impressions.

The correlation between early experience and later behavior is less likely to be spurious if the independent variable is the situations the person faced rather than the strategies he chose, because the experiences, actors, and challenges are more out of his control than his choice of strategy.

Spuriousness is rarely a plausible explanation for generational effects, because the people did not choose the experiences they were exposed to and many people with different characteristics learned the same lessons.

Sharp break-points and reversals in an opinion-versus-age curve rule out simple aging and point to generational effects, since a life-cycle process would produce a smooth single-slope curve that is the same whenever the data are collected, whereas differences among Cuban worker cohorts toward the revolution can be explained only generationally.

For elites one must also consider selection effects, since a generation of leaders may show distinctive beliefs because holding those views made a person more likely to become a leader, as Churchill was excluded from power in the 1930s for not sharing the dominant view of Germany, though this applies only to elites and only when many are excluded for inappropriate views.

Because a person rarely gains power until twenty or thirty years after his formative events, their political impact is long delayed, so a major war's lessons may have less impact in the immediate postwar years than twenty years later when those most strongly stamped by the war take power.

The strength of delayed generational effects depends on how long the event dominated the political climate and how wide the ruling age-band is, so the world wars embedded deep lessons by holding attention for years, and when a government is dominated by people who shared the same formative experience, as often follows a revolution, the effect is much stronger.

Events also have immediate effects on those in power, because important events change a state's leadership by bringing to power those whose views fit the earlier event, bring younger people into government for whom the recent event is formative, and can change the predispositions of established people.

Immediate and delayed effects together produce generational cycles in policy, because a new orientation forms in reaction to a trauma and is learned especially well but in oversimplified form by the younger people who will govern later, who then misapply it, are slow to abandon it, and thereby make its failure dramatic enough to set the next generation on its course.

Within firsthand experiences an event's influence varies directly with its importance for the person and the groups to which he is loyal, so events with major national consequences both socialize the previously unconcerned and change the predispositions of many people with established views.

Just as people believe that big events must have big underlying causes, they act as though events with major consequences contain more information about how the world works than less dramatic happenings, so the resulting lessons are salient enough to be passed down to those who did not experience the events.

The way a state gained its independence or made its revolution shapes the concepts and strategies its leaders later apply to ruling their country and dealing with the world, with those who participated most affected.

Impressed by their own success, leaders are vigilant to the possibility of opponents using the very tactics that brought them to power, so the Bolsheviks' rapid conspiratorial rise fed an almost paranoid fear of domestic opposition and Stalin, haunted by how quickly a returning exile had taken power, intensified the purges as war approached.

Revolutionary leaders project their own success-recipe onto very different situations, so the Bolsheviks saw other countries' internal politics through their own triumph and prescribed their 1917 tactics of defeatism, national self-determination, and uncompromising radicalism to parties working under hugely different conditions.

A leader's read of foreign adversaries mirrors his domestic opponents, so the Bolsheviks, having been saved by the tolerance of liberals and socialists at home, concluded that such groups were essentially weak and showed little respect for social-democratic or liberal regimes abroad, seeing in them the images of the Mensheviks and Kadets.

A formative event shapes perception even in areas where prior ideology was silent, which shows the influence is not spurious, since nothing in Marxism required the stress on national self-determination adopted by communist parties after it succeeded in Russia, and later perceptions followed the revolutionary rather than the Marxist heritage.

A fortuitous formative association can become a rigid lifelong category, as Nkrumah equated federalism with feudalism and tribalism because his most obstinate independence foe happened to be the federal-demanding Ashanti, and later equated obstinate heads of state defending their sovereignty with Ashanti chiefs.

Leaders over-prescribe the narrow set of tactics by which they won power to unlike contexts, as Communist China's leaders supported a narrow range of revolutionary tactics not required by their heritage nor clearly appropriate for the varied contexts for which they were prescribed, limiting local revolutionaries' freedom to think in terms of their own situation.

A founding experience is projected far beyond its applicability, even implausibly, as American support for a united Europe drew on memories of its own regional cooperation and Roosevelt urged the Articles-of-Confederation analogy on British India, which Churchill called an act of madness.

The last major war deeply shapes the perceptual predispositions of most citizens through its associated diplomacy, methods of fighting, alliances, and termination, and it so dominates national life that all old enough to remember it will in a real sense have experienced it firsthand.

What is believed to have caused the last war is considered likely to cause the next, so generals prepare to fight the last war while diplomats prepare to avoid it, as the League of Nations was built with a cooling-off procedure for the seemingly sudden outbreak of World War I that failed in the 1930s because Italy simply used the cooling-off months to prepare for war.

The last war's lesson governs the current threat read, so the belief that World War I could have been avoided by conciliatory diplomacy made 1930s statesmen alert to hostility spirals and to illusory incompatibility, while beliefs about World War II's origins made the West apter to see Russia and China as aggressors.

The latest armed conflict retunes threat perception and mis-fits the next case, so after Vietnam's guerrilla nature became unmistakable it became the model for the future and ambiguous cases such as Cambodia were seen as guerrilla warfare when in the 1950s they would have been read as a conventional invasion resembling Korea.

A specific last-war lesson is often applied without re-examining changed conditions, as Stalin demanded a Gulf of Finland base from the memory of the Russian Civil War and would not budge even when the Finns showed the gulf was too narrow for a modern naval assault if either shore was defended.

The recent-war lesson aids decision-making only if the next confrontation resembles the last, and since the general truths, such as that overestimating hostility can cause an unnecessary war and that one should not concede to a system-overthrower, were already known, another instance of a well-known phenomenon should not drastically change the estimate of its recurrence probability unless it represents a trend, yet it produces drastic changes that decrease later accuracy.

It is usually the last major war rather than earlier ones that has the most impact, because major wars come rarely and most people have firsthand memory of only the most recent, so a wider range of remembered analogies dilutes the influence of any one, which is why elder statesmen are less swayed by the most recent war and often exert a moderating influence.

The presence or absence of alternative analogies strongly shapes interpretation, because a decision-maker whose framework is dominated by a few categories fits events into them quickly and on little information, while those familiar with multiple possibilities are less influenced by any single historical case.

Decision-makers who are amateurs, who have experienced few types of situations, or whose nations have a short history of important international politics are especially influenced by a few dominating analogies, so Americans tend to see situations in terms of the relatively few major events important to their country and are slow to appreciate the variety of goals and strategies other actors can pursue.

People living in a period characterized by a particular kind of actor tend to see a new and different actor as fitting the familiar pattern, which helps if the original conditions persist but makes it harder to recognize and cope with change, as China's well-developed tribute system made its adjustment to the West much more difficult.

If an actor's environment consistently presents certain problems and opportunities, he becomes predisposed to see later situations as fitting the earlier pattern, so U.S. officials approved the 1972 Soviet grain deal without foreseeing the price effects because their whole lives the problem had been disposing of surplus crops.

A protected geography shapes a distinctive and limited worldview, so the physical separation of the United States and Britain from strong neighbors let them keep small armies, avoid entangling alliances, view foreign policy in terms of freedom and morality rather than compulsion, and react to threats only in their later, clearer stages.
