Not realizing their interests and perceptions were shaped by their unusual geography, the United States and Britain could not understand why others felt their security required extreme suspiciousness and quick reaction to distant threats, so they under-grasped international anarchy and the security dilemma and tended to categorize others as completely friendly or completely hostile.

A secure power under-attributes security motives to others and to itself, so when others took threatening actions Britain and the United States were less apt to consider a security motive, and even less sensitive than others to the risk that their own actions inadvertently endangered others, as Britain viewed German reactions to the 1904 entente as unprovoked.

A power is slow to perceive the loss of a former structural advantage, so Britain was slow to abandon its splendid isolation and America withdrew from world politics after World War I and might have done so again after World War II had Soviet behavior not been so precipitous and the Munich analogy so strong.

Contact with another actor on an important issue can establish so firm an image that it is very hard to dislodge, misleading the actor if that behavior was a biased sample or if the other later changes, and this overgeneralization is compounded when observers overestimate the other's internal characteristics and underestimate the context, as the French in the 1920s underestimated Mussolini's hostility because Italy had joined the Allies in World War I.

Means-to-an-end behavior is misread as a permanent trait, so Bismarck was mistrusted for years because observers saw his willingness to launch aggressive wars as a permanent characteristic without realizing those wars were a means to unifying Germany and would stop once that goal was reached.

A state that was expansionist under one set of circumstances or leaders is likely to be seen as a continuing threat whose aggressiveness is attributed to slow-changing factors like geography and national character, but this is rarely the product of considered judgment and there is usually little effort to ask why the other was aggressive and how far its behavior was caused by short-term conditions unlikely to persist.

A state benefits when a series of encounters establishes others' predispositions, because if images of resolve and friendship overgeneralize, an actor who stood firm or was friendly in one case gains the advantage of others expecting that behavior from him in other contexts.

A common lesson is to avoid policies that failed in the immediate past by keeping the goals but trying tactics opposite to those that failed, which is sometimes sensible but usually pays insufficient attention to whether alternatives would have worked or whether the new situation resembles the old, so those who remember the past can be condemned to make the opposite mistakes.

The over-correction error resides in the perceptual stage rather than the policy choice, because avoiding a failed strategy is coupled with an increased readiness to see a wide range of situations as resembling the ones that previously caused the most trouble, as Louis XIV recognized James II's son as King of England in 1701, alert to an earlier Stuart-restoration surprise, though 1701 was very different and there was no support for James.

American post-World-War-I peacemaking failures systematically shaped the opposite policies in the next war, so because the failure to demonstrate that Germany's army had been smashed had let the stab-in-the-back myth flourish, the Allies pursued unconditional surrender, and because German grievances had been fed by a sense of being tricked into a violated armistice, commitments to the Axis were avoided.

Correctly diagnosing the last failure's causes does not justify assuming the new situation resembles it in mechanism or detail, so there was no clear reason to expect the power defeated in the last war to start the next one, and if the real danger was a falling-out among former allies then other lessons were relevant.

When a policy has brought notable success, actors apply it to later situations seen as resembling the past one, but paying insufficient attention to why it worked they do not scrutinize the new situation for the attributes that made success possible, and because they overestimate their policy's role in the earlier success they are especially insensitive to situational variation.

A successful policy is over-applied across cases, so Japan believed a limited war with the United States was possible in 1941 because Russia had earlier settled for a limited defeat, and the success of the 1954 Guatemala operation likely emboldened the proposal for the Bay of Pigs.

Success undermines its own preconditions, because a successful policy alters the environment as others change positions or pay high costs to avoid another defeat, yet the actor preoccupied with his winning strategy is slow to see this, as Hitler expected Britain and France not to fight for Poland as they had not before, missing that his string of triumphs had convinced them his ambitions were unlimited.

Repetition of a policy may reflect the decision-making process rather than the outcomes it produced, because having once made the major effort of thinking through a line of action, actors later apply it without careful re-examination, and only the most dramatic and obvious aspects of a case, such as a Balkan crisis, are used to judge whether it resembles the one the policy was designed for.

Before crediting an earlier success as the cause of a later policy, one must consider that both may be caused by the same independent variables such as the objective situation, the operational code, or national style, as Japan used largely the same argument to the throne in 1904 and 1941.

The claim that a similarity of responses reflects a similarity of stimuli is doubtful when the initial and later decision-makers differ, when the ideological climate has changed, and when the two objective situations have little in common, and when the perception of similarity is not shared by outsiders or later scholars.

A first flaw in learning from history is that the events providing analogies are usually not chosen because they are the best guides to the future, since there is often little reason why the last war rather than earlier ones should most resemble the current situation or why what happened to one's own state should be more relevant than the fates of others.

A second flaw is that because outcomes are learned without careful attention to causation, lessons are superficial and overgeneralized and are applied across events with little sensitivity to variation, so people use a major event to explain a general situation rather than seeing what smaller and less dramatic aspects of the past case would help.

A third and fixable flaw is that decision-makers do not examine a variety of analogies before selecting the most illuminating one, but instead see the present as like recent dramatic events without considering alternative models or the implications of that framing.

A decision-maker draws, often without realizing it, on his knowledge of his own domestic political system to understand other states, and predispositions are most influenced by domestic practices so deeply ingrained that people do not realize alternatives exist, which is most prevalent in homogeneous or isolated societies.

A nation's own political history bounds what it can understand abroad, so the American framework, conditioned by never having had a social revolution, makes it hard for Americans to understand Europe's social question and the deeper struggles of Asia.

Under-grasping foreign social conflict leads to underestimating the difficulty of exporting one's own institutions, so Americans failed to picture the passions of the Russian civil war and believed that a little pressure could make real democracies out of strife-torn states, thereby underestimating the costs of intervention.

When one believes another state generally resembles one's own, one overestimates the congruence between the two states' structures, norms, and behavior, so where differences are less obvious each side generalizes from its own domestic politics, as Americans underestimated the importance of the Treasury in Britain.

The particular role a person played in his own domestic politics does not seem to shape his perceptual predispositions, because any predispositions from familiarity with one part of the system are overwhelmed by broad knowledge of the country's politics, so the shared and accepted view of one's own system is more useful for understanding other states than particular political experiences.

Training shifts a person's perceptual threshold, so advanced police-administration students perceived more scenes as violent than beginners, meaning training makes a person quicker to detect the real thing but also more prone than the untrained to see it when it is absent and to act inappropriately.

An analyst's training biases him toward false positives on the very thing he is trained to catch, so British anti-appeasers differed from appeasers mainly in their close professional acquaintance with foreign affairs, and diplomats, being sensitized to aggressors recognized too late, may rarely mistake an aggressor for a status-quo power but more frequently see threats that do not exist.

A person's professional background supplies his default explanatory frame, so Ambassador Joseph Kennedy, a former Securities and Maritime commissioner, explained German aggressiveness in economic terms because the revolutionary character of the Nazi regime was not something he could easily grasp.

People do change their minds even on questions that matter deeply, so the extreme view that minds never change cannot be sustained, and uniform movement of opinion in one direction along a continuum is as significant as the absence of shifts across the midpoint, since the punishment of Japan changed the intensity of beliefs even where it made no converts.

People change as little of their attitude structure as possible, so when they must change something they first alter the beliefs that are least important, least supported by information, and tied to fewest other beliefs, and the first mechanisms invoked preserve all of the person's original attitudes.

Because beliefs are interconnected, large-scale change is avoided only if a person limits the implications of his initial response, which explains both the prevalence of incremental decision-making and the far-reaching cascade of changes that occurs when central beliefs are finally altered.

The first belief-defense is failing to see information as discrepant, so the person dismisses it, does not notice it, evades it by simply not understanding the message, or takes it as valid but not contradictory, and even when an alternative interpretation is pointed out he may claim the evidence actually supports his view.

A second defense is to see the information as discrepant but explicitly reject its validity, concluding that because one's general beliefs are certainly correct the specific contradicting event must not have occurred, a move that is easier to invoke the greater the inconsistency, as the French in 1914 concluded the German attack through Belgium must be a feint.

A third defense is discrediting the source, which is most readily used against opponents and least against trusted advisers, so true warnings from disliked sources are dismissed, as happened with Keating's warning about missiles in Cuba and Panikkar's warning that China would enter the Korean War.

A fourth defense is to admit puzzlement, acknowledging the information as correct and embarrassing but claiming it cannot yet be explained, which quarantines the anomaly so it has no immediate impact on other beliefs, as Maxwell Taylor admitted he could not explain the continued strength of the Viet Cong yet did not modify the view that led him to expect the contrary.

A fifth defense is bolstering, seeking new information and considerations that support one's views to drown out the imbalance, which underlies the use of shifting rationales for the same program, as Korean strategic bombing was justified first by interdiction and then, as results disappointed, by raising the war's cost to the enemy.

Bolstering can overshoot because it has a momentum of its own, so an attack strong enough to mobilize a person's defenses without overwhelming them can set off a backlash that leaves the belief stronger than it was before.

A sixth defense is undermining, the opposite of bolstering, in which additional elements are adduced to weaken the discrepant information itself, as a smoker points to methodological faults in the studies linking cigarettes to cancer, with discrediting of the source contributing to the undermining.

The first several defenses cope with discrepant information without any attitude change, either by not recognizing it as discrepant or by neutralizing its impact, so only when the evidence is too significant for these must some pre-existing views be sacrificed.

When change is forced, the least-change route is often differentiation, in which the person splits the object and sloughs off the parts causing conflict, a common form being to separate an individual's personal qualities from the policies he is implementing so one can remain friends with a person of a different political persuasion.

Another form of differentiation separates what a person is doing from what he normally does or would do with more freedom, as Germany read Italy's support for the Ruhr occupation as the product of unavoidable circumstances rather than voluntary action and so did not react with hostility.

Creating exceptions to a generalization is a form of differentiation, so one can resolve believing the Soviet Union is a status-quo power while seeing its recent Middle East actions as aggressive by deeming that policy unique and thus condemning it without revising the general evaluation.

In extreme differentiation a person redefines whole categories to hold different attitudes toward things no longer seen as alike, as Southerners supported both the American creed of equality and the institution of slavery by placing slaves in the category of nonhumans.

A less frequent mechanism is transcendence, the opposite of differentiation, in which elements are built up and combined into larger superordinate units, as a person who dislikes both Russia and China but knows they are in conflict resolves the incongruity by grouping them together as powers that hold abhorrent values.

When defenses fail and views must change, the least central and least important parts of an image change first, following the same minimal-change rule as scientists who make the smallest possible alteration of prevailing hypotheses, so avoiding change to the basic aspects of an image need not be a pathological attempt to protect a satisfying worldview.

To predict what a person will resist changing, one must identify his central beliefs in advance, and a cursory knowledge of a belief system reveals which substantive beliefs underpin much of his worldview, as opponents of evolution who held orthodox religious beliefs preserved the central role of the Creator by developing a theory of special serial creations.

When one country believes another is its enemy, the perception of hostility is usually more central than other aspects of the image, so restraint by the other is more likely to change the actor's view of the other's strength than of its intentions, as most Americans read Russia's building of fewer missiles than predicted as weakness rather than friendship.

A person's view of himself is usually highly central and is maintained at the cost of altering many other beliefs, so people who believe they are just conclude that if evil was done they cannot have done it and that if they did it, it cannot be evil, and those whose self-image involves succeeding externalize blame for failures, as MacArthur attributed the Chinese surprise in Korea to the Truman administration.

National self-images are similarly central, since not many people are willing to see their own state as aggressive or even as inadvertently threatening, which increases the danger of spirals of hostility.

The tendency to preserve central beliefs explains why people often miss the basic causes of undesired events and instead blame the idiosyncratic acts of a few individuals, as the communist takeover of China was blamed on individual officials rather than on a fifty-year policy doomed by its inherent contradictions.

Conspiracy theories are prevalent because an unexpected and undesired event need not alter many important attitudes if it can be attributed to the machinations of a small evil group, so the more important the subject and the more beliefs a deep-seated cause would force to change, the greater the acceptance of conspiracy explanations.

When conspiracy theories are inappropriate, people attribute failure instead to temporary and removable obstacles, so the ineffectiveness of cavalry in the American Civil War was blamed on unusual terrain and poor training, letting European observers avoid recognizing the growth of firepower that would appear in their own future wars.

Central beliefs are also shielded when internal causation is attributed to a factor that need not operate in future, such as not having worked up to capacity, so for the first year after Pearl Harbor naval officers blamed U-boat losses on a lack of planes and ships rather than on the defects of their antisubmarine strategy.

When conspiracy and special-condition explanations are unavailable and beliefs are tightly connected, people are led to strange, ramifying conclusions by using deduction to find the only explanation that reconciles undeniable fact with immovable premises, as the Soviets, unable to credit the Marshall Plan's apparent altruism, concluded its real aims were military.

A tightly connected belief system changes incrementally only while the no-change mechanisms suffice, after which either maintaining central beliefs forces far-reaching peripheral changes or the central beliefs themselves change and set off a cascade, so the system is incremental until it is not.

The strength of the connections among beliefs governs the pressure-response curve, since people with more centralized belief systems change fewer opinions under low pressure to change but more than others under high pressure.

Compromises involving central beliefs are unstable, because a person may breach a principle without realizing it and then bring other attitudes into line, and drastic changes can occur unforeseen as he develops the implications of what seemed a minor innovation when accepted, so a small accepted step later forces changes he would have rejected up front.

Because people can anticipate that one step down a slippery slope invites further steps, those who wish to take a limited action justify it, to themselves as well as to others, by arguments and principles that cannot be applied to a wide range of other cases.

Minimum attitude change is rational only if the central elements are substantiated by a solid base of theories and data as well as supporting many beliefs, but it is irrational when the central elements receive their power of resistance merely from the fact that changing them would require changing many other perceptions and plans that rest only on them.

Where the elements of an attitude structure differ in centrality, one should expect not the fewest total elements to change but several peripheral elements altered instead of a smaller number of more central ones, thereby minimizing the magnitude of the eventual change.

The rationality of minimum change depends on the evidential basis of the central belief, so finding limited explanations for discrepant information is rational when the central assumption rests on careful analysis, but irrational when the assumption rests on weak evidence and gains its resistance only from the many other beliefs and plans that rest on it.

A useful rule of thumb is that cases in which policy remains constant while circumstances change drastically are apt to involve irrational resistance to change, since the same policy can suit many situations only rarely, and in such cases no analysis is made of whether the old policy fits the new circumstances.

The rate at which discrepant information arrives matters as much as its amount, because a large batch makes the contradiction with the prevailing view obvious while a gradual trickle lets each bit go unnoticed, be dismissed, or be handled by adding an exception, so the actor never perceives that discrepant information is accumulating.

A slowly changing object can show no perceived movement despite a great cumulative shift, so sudden events influence images more than slow developments, as the 1948 Czech coup hit the United States harder than the gradual consolidation of Soviet control elsewhere.

An adversary can disguise an image-contrary change by increasing it gradually below the detection threshold, as the Germans lengthened their radar jamming slightly each day during the Channel dash until British operators reported it as ordinary atmospherics.

Reviewing the whole series of information rather than each item in isolation reveals the pattern, so American officials derived little from the Tokyo-Washington intercepts because each was returned as soon as it was read and no one ever reviewed the entire series, though a pattern would have been detected.

Receiving information in large packets rather than a steady stream aids detection of flawed assumptions, so a decision-maker's lack of day-to-day involvement can put him in a better position to see inadequacies in prevailing formulations, as Johnson's distance made it easier to reverse policy on the multilateral force.
Decision-makers can capitalize on this by deliberately increasing the degree to which information comes to them in sizable chunks, which makes them more sensitive to discrepant evidence.

The inherent bad faith model of another state is unfalsifiable in practice because it can explain almost any behavior, since hostility needs no special explanation and conciliatory actions can be read as an attempt to lull the perceiver or as evidence that the other responds only to power and that pressure should be continued.

The belief that the other is trying to help but must contend with powerful internal opposition is highly resistant to change because it accounts for both friendly and unfriendly behavior, as a friendly-Stalin image was undisturbed by hostile Soviet acts attributed to a militant faction in the leadership.

An image resists change to the degree it yields no deductions that can be checked against the evidence, so the belief that internal opposition would topple the other's government as soon as invaders appeared was easy to maintain before the Dardanelles, Suez, and Bay of Pigs because reliable indicators of a regime's strength are rare.

A sharply defined proposition that observations can contradict is vulnerable even if it is a central element of the belief system, as the comet of 1577 cutting through the supposed crystal spheres led even the conservative Tycho Brahe to declare his disbelief in them.

A belief that can be disconfirmed only by an event that cannot occur until it is too late is dangerously self-protecting, so the conclusion that the other side is bluffing can be disproved only when war starts, since a bluffer aims to behave exactly as a country willing to go to war would behave.

A belief's disconfirmation rate reflects how it was established, so a belief past-confirmed by information arriving infrequently and irregularly is not disturbed by long gaps, while one confirmed on a precise schedule is more impacted by non-appearance.

Seeking evidence that cannot disconfirm one's hypothesis wastes effort or breeds unwarranted confidence, as people looked out their windows to check whether Martians had invaded without realizing that nothing they saw could have reassured them.

Dismissing an actor's signals as having no predictive value makes reassurance impossible, so once British decision-makers before the Boer War were convinced any Boer pledge would be violated as soon as pressure relaxed, no agreement could be satisfactory, and because an actor feels least bound by his word when other payoffs are high, perceivers discount his claims most in crises.

Confidence that one understands an actor and the objective situation makes one discount his explicit signals without any suspicion of deception, as Macmillan mispredicted American behavior at Suez because conclusions from his longstanding knowledge of America outweighed Eisenhower's contemporary warnings.

Images of other states are especially resistant because behaviors that do not fit can be dismissed as deception and because, unlike a distorted room that action corrects, other actors are neither unchangeable nor passive, so it is rarely possible to establish clean tests of others' intentions and the clearest evidence that an image is wrong is a policy disaster, by which time it may be too late.

A common misperception is to see others' behavior as more centralized, planned, and coordinated than it is, a manifestation of the drive to squeeze complex and unrelated events into a coherent pattern, because people are unable to accept a random situation and read order into random data.

People resist explanations that involve several independent elements and prefer unitary explanations to conjunctive ones, both in accounting for their own behavior and in explaining others', where they minimize the number of causes by overestimating the degree to which behavior can be explained by consistent and powerful personality factors.

People see as many events as possible as linked to a minimum number of causes, so they are slow to perceive accidents, unintended consequences, coincidences, and small causes leading to large effects, and instead see coordinated actions, plans, and conspiracies.

Encompassing another's behavior under a few rules is reasonable and parsimonious, but fuller later information usually shows the behavior was the product of more numerous and complex forces, and the predictions the oversimplified model yields are often misleading.

Awareness of anarchy makes decision-makers alert for dangerous plots, so if another's behavior seems innocuous they look for hidden and menacing significance, and because threats and plots are common in international relations the search for a devious plan behind seemingly spontaneous behavior cannot easily be labeled pathological.

The perception of an evil plan behind disparate events is much more common than the reality and is usually spontaneous rather than a deliberate decision to play it safe, and decision-makers tend to be uncomfortable with explanations that point to the importance of chance or blunders.

Coincidence in time, space, and sequence produces an involuntary and indivisible experience of causality, so men are hesitant to believe that rapid-sequence events affecting them could have occurred by chance, as slamming a door just as a light burns out feels causal even when one knows it is not.

It is far more common to see coincidental events as part of a plan than planned events as coincidental, so the movements of military forces are almost always seen as supporting foreign policies, as other states read British fleet maneuvers that coincided with a diplomatic message as designed to reinforce it even though the two acts were causally unrelated.
Because decision-makers know that others are not apt to believe in coincidences, they may delay or change their behavior to avoid appearing to be influenced by other events happening at the time.

Because chaos and confusion are not satisfying explanations, actors seek hidden manipulations, so many believed the German fifth column was largely responsible for the Allies' mobilization difficulties in World War II when later investigation showed the fifth columnists had done very little and the incidents were caused by Allied disorganization and natural disorder.

Like confusion, stupidity is rarely given its due, so otherwise inexplicable behavior is seen as part of a devious and usually hostile plan, as the escape of the Goeben from a superior British force seemed so unlikely as a blunder that the German leadership concluded Britain was unwilling to strike heavy blows.

The view of an individual or a state as a single billiard ball is often invalid, because each pursues a variety of goals in a complex environment without recognizing the trade-offs among them, so behavior may be self-contradictory as the actor furthers one value in one context and another value in a different situation.

Because of the drive to unify and achieve closure, people overestimate the unity of personality, and because observers overestimate the influence of the other's internal characteristics and underestimate the situation, they expect greater constancy and are surprised when the person behaves differently under changed circumstances.

Decision-makers generally overestimate the degree to which their opposite numbers have the information and power to impose their desires on all parts of their own governments, so they see the state's behavior as centrally controlled and use weapons procurement as an index of coherent strategy, as an inefficient first-strike system and very large Soviet missiles were read as showing the Soviets must be contemplating aggression.

If a state's military budget reflects the outcome of parochial inter-service conflicts, then procurement tells little about its foreign-policy intentions, which will be determined under a different power distribution, or by different people, or by the same people acting on different values.

Over-centralizing the other government causes dangerous misreadings of its signals, as the Chinese decision to enter the Korean War was partly caused by Peking ignoring the pluralistic Western political process and giving authoritative spokesmen in Tokyo equal or greater weight than Acheson and Truman.

Decision-makers overestimate the centralization of another's policies even when familiar with its domestic politics, as the U.S.-British Skybolt dispute was exacerbated because each failed to understand the other's internal bargaining despite years of intimate cooperation, so such distortions are only more pronounced between less familiar states.

Even the apparent exceptions to over-centralization perceive only a minimum of confusion, since wartime Allied statesmen who explained rapid Soviet shifts by the mysterious Politburo still pictured two factions vying for control of a centralized policy rather than genuine disorder.

Alliances usually appear more durable and binding from the outside than from the inside, as many believed Germany and Italy had conducted a concerted, carefully planned policy since 1936 when in fact they developed no joint plans and were often unsure of each other's intentions.

Overestimating the adversary coalition's unity drives self-defeating choices, as Japan overestimated Anglo-American cooperation and believed America would enter the war if Japan moved against British and Dutch territories, forcing Japan to choose between forgoing those resources and attacking the United States.

Domestic groups in conflict see the other side as more unified than it is, so in labor-management disputes each believes the other is controlled from above and each political campaign pictures the other as well organized, purposive, and intense in a way incompatible with what one feels inside it.

The tendency to see the other side as centralized and Machiavellian is especially strong in some actors, so the Soviets, whose operational code holds that nothing is accidental, believe all their enemies' moves to be carefully planned, and the French, who plan with long-range calculations, often see others as operating the same way.

Some individuals project their own propensity to plot onto others and so see them as centralized and Machiavellian, as Holstein consistently read ambiguous events as elaborate English plots to trap Germany, and people with low tolerance for ambiguity and low cognitive complexity are especially likely to perceive more centralization than is present.

Over-perception of centralization is stronger when two sides are in conflict, because cooperating actors have detailed information that reveals diversity while adversaries lack it and can explain plan-incompatible behavior as deception, a perception reinforced by the conservative desire to assume the other's hostility will be implemented with great skill and efficiency.

Actors tend to perceive the behavior of the other side's subordinates and agents as carrying out official policy, underestimating how often agents violate the spirit and letter of their instructions, so De Gaulle was persuaded that a consistently insulting American general could not have acted without orders from higher authority.

Although decision-makers know their own state is not monolithic and that policy is bargained, they overestimate the centralization of their own state's implementation of policy and assume, absent contrary evidence, that their agents act as instructed, so when this is wrong they are misled about the actions taken in their state's name.

Being misinformed about one's own state's behavior makes the other's reactions incomprehensible, because the other state's behavior is partly a function of what one's own state does, so a decision-maker who does not know what was done in his name will think the other is responding to a different set of events than it actually saw.

Even when subordinates faithfully implement instructions, a decision-maker's beliefs about what was done may be inaccurate because the actions rested on false premises or did not produce the reported effects, as Washington believed a 1965 raid on North Vietnamese anti-aircraft sites had demonstrated determination and killed Russian technicians when the sites were dummies and no one was killed.

Imprecise instruments can make each side read collateral effects as the other's deliberate policy, so the restraints on bombing civilians in World War II broke down because neither side realized it could not bomb accurately enough to avoid collateral damage, so each thought the bombs that fell on its own civilians reflected the other's policy.

Agent disobedience creates two problems, since the decision-maker does not fully control foreign policy and undesired impressions and commitments are given, and when the agent does not report his actions accurately the decision-maker is misinformed about what the other side knows about his state.

Agents disobey when their values, payoffs, and tactical judgments differ from those at home, a divergence created by selection, by capture in which ambassadors come to identify with the state they deal with, and by a negotiator's incentives to reach an agreement that those at home do not share.

The man on the spot almost always feels he knows more about the local situation than his superior and believes his instructions out of touch, so agents of both sides in a negotiation often form an alliance to convince their home governments to scale down expectations while each assures his own side that he is standing firm.

The commonest form of agent distortion is to twist instructions by transmitting the official message alongside a private opinion that contradicts it, as Henderson protested the takeover of Austria while adding that the Austrians had acted with precipitate folly and told a German leader he had no sympathy for the Czechs.

An agent's unofficial remarks can affect the perceiving state's image in three ways, being read as a deliberate disavowable signal, as representing strong internal trends that will become policy, or, least likely, as views likely to influence the agent's own government, so in 1939 Germans were warranted in paying more attention to Japanese ambassadors' private comments, which reflected the army's views, than to their instructed messages.

Being misinformed about one's own agent's behavior increases conflict, because each side then proceeds on different beliefs about what was done in the state's name, as the pre-Pearl-Harbor Japanese ambassador's report that Hull had sponsored a draft, rather than merely called it worth discussing, inflated Japanese expectations so that the later official note read as an American stiffening.

When both sides' agents distort messages, direct talks produce divergent expectations, since each side is told the other originated the proposal and so each expects the other to take the initiative and make further concessions, so that even an acceptable initial proposal can break down as each holds out for more.

When a nation has worldwide interests and both sides' agents disobey and deceive their home governments, each state assumes both sides' agents are obeying instructions, so each thinks its own agents are cooperating while the other's antagonistic agents represent official policy, and rejects the other's protestations of being the aggrieved party as deceitful hypocrisy.

It is not always the agent who is to blame when the home government does not know what he has done, because those at home sometimes give unclear instructions or ignore the agent's reports, as Bismarck read British intransigence over African colonies as hostility while never carefully considering the information he had transmitted or that his agent might not have acted as instructed.

Taking the other's behavior as the product of a centralized actor with integrated values, inferring the plan behind it, and projecting that plan forward misleads if the behavior was the result of shifting bargaining and ad hoc decisions, because a transient phenomenon is endowed with enduring qualities and isolated actions by scattered agents are read as a menacing multi-stage plan, as China read ad hoc American decisions on Korea and Taiwan as designed schemes for aggression against its homeland.

Because the importance of the other's internal conflict is underestimated when it is seen as centralized, the state devotes insufficient resources to learning about the other's factions, bureaucratic structures, and domestic preoccupations, which reduces the effectiveness of attempts to influence its policy.

Illusory incompatibility is created because duplicity rather than confusion is perceived when the other's policy is inconsistent, so the friendlier segments of an erratic policy are seen as deceptive and the whole judged two-faced and treacherous, and when the other's agent is more hostile than its final position the agent is taken to represent the other's true, temporarily thwarted hostile intentions.

When one state reacts with anger to what it wrongly believes was a double cross, the other, knowing its own behavior was unexceptionable, reads that anger as a bargaining tactic or a smokescreen for devious plans, which deepens its image of the first as not only hostile but unreasonable.

The belief that the other acts as though it were centralized, though inaccurate, may be a useful assumption that yields relatively accurate predictions when the interests and power of the contending elements in the other's government are fairly stable.

Even if predictions from the assumption of centralization are not very accurate, they may be the best possible, because it does not follow that predictions based on incomplete and unreliable information about the other's factions will be more accurate than the simplifying assumption.

When a decision-maker cannot tell which method best fits each individual case, he should always use the method of prediction that works in the largest number of cases rather than distribute his guesses in proportion to the outcomes, because probability-matching, though common, is not rational.

Decision-makers should not jump to the conclusion that the other is a centralized actor implementing a well-developed plan, but should remain sensitive to alternative explanations involving internal conflict and lack of coordination, and when it seems that only hostility and duplicity could account for the other's behavior they should not immediately assume a coherent policy lies behind it.

Actors exaggerate the degree to which they play a central role in others' policies, so when the other behaves as desired the actor overestimates his policies' responsibility, but when the other's behavior is undesired the actor sees it as internally derived and believes the other is trying to harm him rather than that the effect was an unintended side-effect of his own actions.

People alter their perception of causality to protect self-esteem, seeing their own actions as a more important cause of their successes than of their failures, so supervisors and teachers claim credit for good work but blame workers and students for bad.

When a decision-maker is misinformed about his own agent's more extreme private remarks, his home government is denied a key input into the other's image of it, as British leaders who knew Henderson was more pro-appeasement than the official line still did not know the extent of his remarks and so wrongly believed their resolve was clear to Germany.

Actors almost always feel responsible for exerting influence when the other acts as they wish, a belief that is often incorrect, and there are almost no cases in which an actor underestimated his influence in producing a desired outcome.

Actors sometimes perceive that the other is responding to them personally rather than to the state they serve, as several American agents in post-revolutionary Russia each believed a Soviet action resulted from his own individual representations though later research showed their urgings had little to do with it.

A common exaggeration of influence is the belief that one has thwarted the adversary's evil intentions when the adversary was planning nothing, so when generals act vigorously and no attack comes they credit their action with disrupting an offensive, and an actor is especially apt to believe his threats affected the other's intentions rather than its capabilities.

Deterrence is self-confirming, because lacking the historian's knowledge of the other's intentions the decision-maker freely selects a pleasing interpretation of why the adversary has not harmed him, is more apt to believe deterrence worked than that it was unnecessary, and if the other does act hostilely can still believe it would have done even more damage but for his stance.

The correlation between adopting a deterrence policy and perceiving credit for its success is spurious, because both are explained by the original perception of the other's intentions, so those responsible for the policy see it as more efficacious than do observers who did not share the belief that the other would otherwise have acted.

Attributing a valued outcome to one's own efforts is an exception to the general tendency to see others as autonomous origins of their own behavior, because if an actor tried to influence the other and the other acted as desired, the actor sees the other not as an origin but as reacting to him, and so attributes the other's friendly action to his own power rather than to the other's goodwill.

Tension-reducing initiatives are less effective because the perceiver is likely to believe they show not that the other is friendly but that his own policy of firmness is working, as the kaiser read any British slackening in the naval race as proof that German pressure was effective and should be increased.

When an actor uses rewards and over-credits his influence, he decreases his future offers, so if he has overestimated his influence the rewards become insufficient, no agreement is reached, cooperation is limited, and he is surprised and attributes the failure to the other's unfriendly intentions.

When an actor uses threats and attributes success to them, he is not tempted to decrease their magnitude but instead has his belief in the other's hostility reinforced, relies still more on negative sanctions, and may overreach himself, further increasing the chances of war.

Overestimating one's successful influence is explained partly by ego gratification and, more importantly, by an information asymmetry: the actor is familiar with his own efforts to influence the other but knows much less about third parties' actions and the other's domestic processes and internal conflicts, so absent strong contrary evidence the most parsimonious explanation is that he was influential.

At a turning point where the other is poised between greatly helping and greatly harming the actor, the actor overestimates his potential influence and ignores the other's autonomous and permanent sources of conduct, as Britain and America each thought its Spain policy would have great impact though Franco was mostly guided by his fear of German domination and his beliefs about who would win the war.

A naive stimulus-response philosophy leads manipulators to take for granted that the other's actions depend on nothing but the momentary stimuli they control, so the enemy's own deep-rooted loyalties and spontaneous assessment of his interests are not taken into account when trying to foresee and influence his conduct.

When others' actions hurt or threaten the perceiver, he overestimates the degree to which the behavior was a product of internal forces aimed at harming him, over-personalizing the other's policy, because if he overestimates his own influence he concludes the other must have had strong motives.

If the other's behavior injures the actor, he is apt to believe that injury was the other's purpose, because perceivers assume that people always intend to do what they do and intend it to have the effect it has, so in coalition wars each actor overestimates the fraction of the enemy's resources devoted to fighting him.

The aggrieved side assumes the injury was the other's main goal and projects that motivation forward, foreseeing greater harm unless it reacts strongly, so it reads internally-motivated acts as centrally aimed at itself, as Kennedy took Khrushchev's promise of support for wars of national liberation, likely aimed at China, as an authoritative exposition of Soviet intentions.

An actor overestimates the degree to which the other's undesired behavior is a product of the other's autonomous desires and underestimates the degree to which it is a response to an action of his own, so he sees himself as the object of the other's unprovoked and inner-directed hostility and is slow to see that his own actions may explain the other's behavior.

Even more common than failing to see that the other's undesired act flows from one's own unintended invitation is failing to appreciate that the other's hostility may be a product of his fear of oneself, so Washington was strangely resistant to the idea that the Soviets might be reacting to features of American behavior.

Each side in a conflict tends to believe the other's motives are fixed and independent of its own behavior while its own motives are a varied response to the other, as both England and Germany before World War I failed to appreciate the extent to which the other's unfriendly acts grew out of the belief that the hostility it was receiving was unprovoked.

If the other's hostility is seen as rooted in autonomous drives, there is no reason to examine one's own policies as self-defeating, no need to demonstrate a willingness to reach settlements, and further concessions are thought unable to alter the other's behavior, which neglects the possibility of favorably affecting the other by moderating one's own actions and increases illusory incompatibility.

A related belief is that the other's decision to go to war is highly autonomous, so that the other will attack when and only when it is ready and can be neither appeased nor provoked, a belief that removes agency from one's own actions.

Actors injure others more than they mean to because they do not see how far their policies conflict with the other's interests, and because the actor does not understand that the perceiver reads harm as intended, he wrongly believes that even inadvertent damage will be recognized by the other as not his goal, failing to see the other will perceive more hostility than a disinterested observer would.

Self-righteousness blocks the conclusion that the other's undesired behavior was provoked, because such a conclusion would imply an unfavorable self-image, so Anglo-German relations before World War I deteriorated partly because the British did not like to think themselves selfish and the Germans did not like to think themselves aggressive.

It takes great insight to realize that actions one believes are only the natural consequence of defending one's vital interests can appear to others as directed against them, as a former British undersecretary observed that to a foreigner the British Empire must appear as a huge giant sprawling over the globe that cannot be approached without eliciting a scream.

An actor who believes he is not a threat assumes the other knows he is not hostile, reversing his usual identification of others' intentions with the effects of their actions, so his failure to understand that he may not have communicated his non-hostile intentions feeds spirals, because if he believes the other is hostile yet perceives him as peaceful, he concludes the other is clearly aggressive and must be met with firmness.

Strong feeling deceives perception, so as Aristotle noted the coward under fear sees his enemy in a trifling resemblance and the lover sees his beloved, and while Clausewitz held that timidity in battle makes everyone more inclined to believe the bad than the good, the more common claim is that men perceive what they want to perceive.

Most experiments on wishful thinking omit the incentives for accuracy that operate in real life, where a person's welfare strongly depends on accurate perception, so the absence of this constraint may permit the wish-fulfillment effects found in the laboratory, while incentives to be accurate produce more accurate responses.

When the costs of the two possible errors are asymmetric, biased perception is rational, so if mistaking A for B is cheap but mistaking B for A is costly, an actor is well-advised to perceive an ambiguous stimulus as B, and experiments show people do this as a difference in perception rather than a conscious decision to play it safe.

Much affect research showing that coins are seen as larger or that deprivation makes ambiguous stimuli look food-related does not demonstrate wishful thinking, because these perceptions do not fulfill the wish and carry no implications for action, so they have little relevance for decision-making.

Expectations rather than affect may explain many wishful-thinking findings, since subjects are slower to recognize taboo words because of less familiarity rather than affect and food deprivation changes the subjects' evoked set by bringing thoughts of food to mind, so what looks like desire-driven perception is often an expectation effect.

Much of the influence of expectations is unconscious rationality, because different perceptual thresholds for different words project into the future the relative frequency with which a person has seen them, which the subject would have no grounds for rejecting as an explicit strategy.

Seeing one's own candidate as agreeing with oneself is better explained by expectation than by desire, because a person who finds he and a candidate agree on many issues overestimates their agreement on all other issues, and strong partisans expect such agreement more than weak ones do.

When desires and expectations coincide, analysis should not stop at concluding that expectations explain the perception but should ask whether desires influenced the expectations, since affect can act indirectly through expectations, as college ties helped establish the expectation through which students each saw the other team commit more infractions.

It matters whether desires influence perception directly or only through expectations, because if they act only through expectations their impact is diluted by their further remove from the outcome, since many non-affective factors also influence expectations and variables other than expectations influence perception.

Some studies show that affect can influence beliefs directly, as hypnotically induced changes in affect toward an object led to changes in beliefs about its instrumentality, though the artificial manipulation limits the relevance, since real decision-makers who oppose a policy are not disgusted by it but believe it conflicts with their interests.

Desire inflates the estimated probability and confidence of a desired outcome, since subjects overguess the frequency of desired outcomes and underguess undesired ones and hold their guesses of a desired outcome with greater confidence.

People attribute power to the person favorable to their desire, as most boys hoping for a ticket perceived the friendly, approving interview-board member as the powerful and influential one, though higher motivation increased this distortion under some conditions and produced more accurate perceptions under others.

People bias their beliefs toward expected gain and away from expected loss, being more tolerant of inconsistency when a cognition promises gain than loss and rearranging beliefs to maximize expected gain even at the cost of imbalance, though real-world constraints dampen this effect.

The rated desirability of a statement and its rated truth value are highly correlated, but logic can override wishful thinking, since subjects are quicker to accept information that increases logical consistency at the expense of wishfulness, and awareness of the bias reduces it on re-testing.

Making a question salient and inducing a person to think about his answer reduces, though does not eliminate, wishful thinking, so the reflection that most political decisions permit can partly counter it, since explicit syllogisms are less congenial to wishfulness than the ambiguous evidence surrounding most decisions.

The experimental evidence for the existence of wishful thinking is not as strong as is usually believed, because controlling for third factors is extremely difficult, alternative explanations such as expectations are not always excluded, and even the suggestive experiments lacked incentives for accuracy.

Wishfulness often predicts the same behavior as the more general expectation hypotheses, so an analyst should not attribute a perception to desire when the strong tendency to see what one expects already explains it.

It is hard to draw specific propositions about what a decision-maker will think or do from the general concept of wishful thinking, because wishfulness gives no clue to the content of beliefs and can equally predict opposite behaviors.

Wishful thinking can imply either persisting in a policy because one sees it succeeding or abandoning effort because one believes the goal is already reached, so it does not by itself predict which a decision-maker will do.

Wishful thinking can imply either overextension, trying to accomplish more than is possible, or passivity in the belief that a benign world will protect one's values even if one does nothing, so labeling a policy as wishful requires more than the outcome.

Wishfulness may lead a decision-maker to overestimate the chances of success of the policy he has adopted, but it does not tell an analyst which policy he will select or which means he will judge most productive.

When the content of perceptions cannot be generalized, look for covariance, and the most conclusive evidence of desire's influence is a case where a shift in desires was followed by a shift in perceptions, as when Californians' stereotype of Chinese immigrants worsened once economic competition made exclusion advantageous.

Covariance evidence for wishful thinking must be checked for spuriousness, because changes in desires are often caused by factors that could rationally lead to altered estimates of probable outcomes, making unambiguous cases rare.

One can look for rationalization, where a shift in desire follows rather than precedes a shift in estimates of what will happen, but not every such shift is rationalization, since an actor forced to examine a situation more carefully may genuinely learn how to make the best of it.

When an outcome is highly desired and not improbable, decision-makers may fail to explore what they will do if it does not occur, yet on facing the need they often design a new policy and do better than they had thought possible.

Correlations between desires and perceptions holding other factors constant are weaker evidence for statesmen than for experimental subjects, because a statesman's desires are linked to many other variables and decision-makers from the same well-integrated political system tend to share both desires and other determinants.

Asking merely whether statesmen are over-optimistic is a weak test, because some correlation between beliefs and desires is expected even without wishful thinking, since people can be optimistic for unrelated reasons and decision-makers choose a policy precisely because they think it will succeed.

Finding that decision-makers overestimated the probability of desired events does not by itself demonstrate wishfulness, because in an uncertain world random or non-affective errors would often coincide with desires, and it is not established that errors toward desires outnumber errors away from them.

Statesmen frequently err against their desires by overestimating others' hostility and by being too cautious, underestimating that a decisive stand could achieve a highly desired goal, so error is not reliably biased toward what is wished.

The historical record is biased toward recording wishful thinking, because wishful errors produce policies that dramatically fail and attract notice while opposite errors of excessive caution produce inaction that goes unrecorded.

Expectations hold primacy over desires, because when a person's expectations conflict with his desires the expectations usually prevail, as when an admiral who wished a report of the enemy's course to be true instead concluded his experienced observer had erred because the reported behavior made no sense.

Differing perceptions of another state can rarely be explained by differing desires, because opponents in a policy debate typically share the same goals of peace and security, so a person who accuses another of wishful thinking usually shares the other's wishes but not his perceptions.

Even if desire-perception correspondence were no greater than chance, that would not show desires have no influence but only that their influence is outweighed by other factors, since two variables working in opposite directions disguise the weaker, as fear-driven overestimation of a threat can mask a wishful overestimation of one's ability to cope with it.

The soundest working conclusion is that one's stereotyped image of the world is not the world one would wish for but the world one expects, so perception is governed more by expectations than by desires.

Whether a person is vigilant or defensive toward a danger depends on his belief about his ability to take effective counteraction: if he can avoid the pain by recognizing the stimulus and acting, his perceptual threshold is lowered (vigilance), but if nothing can avert the pain, his threshold is raised (defense).

The vigilance-versus-defense proposition reconciles seemingly contradictory findings, since people are sometimes highly alert to noxious stimuli and sometimes insensitive to them depending on whether corrective action is possible.

Avoidable punishment can alter perception without the person's awareness, as subjects shocked for certain settings shifted their adjustments to avoid the shock while still consciously perceiving the original percept and without realizing they had changed their pattern.

It is hard to tell whether such effects change perception or only response, because even an uncertain person has an incentive to act as though he perceives a noxious stimulus whenever the cost of doing so is low.
Whether high fear produces more attitude change than low fear has no invariant answer and depends on whether the message tells the audience how to cope with the threat.

When people are told how to meet a threat, high fear produces more attitude change than low fear, but when they believe few effective steps are available, high fear produces less change, because fear aroused but not relieved motivates the audience to ignore or minimize the threat.

Reactions to warnings of natural disasters follow the same rule: vigilance increases when signs indicate that self-initiated action is needed for protection, while people who feel ineffective become less sensitive to the information and a feeling of immunity is strongest when nothing can be done to ward off the danger.

How a near-miss is interpreted determines later vigilance or defense, because a near-miss read as proof of hopeless vulnerability produces extreme or defensive reactions to future warnings, while one read as showing the person is not vulnerable if he takes feasible precautions produces reactions more realistically attuned to the evidence.

Wild rumors and pleasing but inaccurate beliefs flourish only where action is impossible or not contemplated, whereas people prepared to act on what they learn do not shun undesired news, and involvement with material decreases distortion in its transmission.

A sense of efficacy and belief that one can control one's environment are associated with effort and striving, and people prefer information opposing their position over supporting information when the opposing information will be useful, as in preparing to debate or serve on a jury.

Undesired information is shut out most readily when there are no incentives for accuracy, because if a person can do nothing to avert a danger there is no psychological or rational payoff in detecting it, just as there is no point building an early-warning system a state cannot act upon.

The best evidence for this proposition in international relations, cases where a change in an actor's belief about his ability to cope with a danger was followed by a shift in his perception of the danger, is scarce, because the belief is hard to isolate and a changing environment makes it hard to exclude externally induced changes in threat perception.

There is some evidence that weaker states perceive a given country as less of a menace than stronger states do, even though the weaker states are more directly threatened, as the United States consistently saw Russia as more aggressive than its smaller allies did and less capable French leaders sought less information about a future war's costs.

At the individual level, a person's estimate that a threat will materialize varies with the expected efficacy of countermeasures, so a statesman who believes himself powerless to change policy on detecting a threat will perceive such threats less readily than one who believes his views will matter.

Actors are slow to recognize dangers when even a policy based on accurate perception would be inadequate, as decades of American 'unfounded hopes' about China reflected that, absent willingness to commit the necessary resources, little could be done even with a correct diagnosis.

People are conservative in probability judgment and avoid extreme estimates, so even under overwhelming evidence they keep estimates near .50, thereby underestimating very likely events and overestimating very unlikely ones.

When an outcome's payoff is great but its probability slight, decision-makers tend to overestimate that probability, not through simple wishfulness but because the high stakes bring a normally dismissed proposal into consideration where the conservatism bias then inflates its estimated chance of success, as with Allied plans to reopen an eastern front and with Vietnam.

An alternative to the distortion account is that decision-makers may recognize a slight chance of success yet judge a policy worth pursuing because the potential gain is huge, so when payoffs are very high, small differences in success estimates can tip the choice and the necessary fine distinctions may be impossible to make.

The conventional wisdom that wishful thinking pervades political decision-making is not supported by the evidence, and affect has the most impact on perception when accurate perception matters least, when the person has no incentive to perceive accurately because he cannot act on what he expects to happen.

Two cognitions are in a dissonant relation when, considered by themselves, the obverse of one would follow from the other, as knowing a rejected car is better than the one a person bought is dissonant with having bought the lesser car.
Dissonance is psychologically uncomfortable, so a person is motivated both to reduce existing dissonance and to actively avoid situations and information that would likely increase it.

Dissonance theory rests on the postulate that people seek strong justification for their behavior, wanting to believe the reasons for their decision were overwhelming rather than merely adequate, which makes it an ego-defensive theory unlike theories of cognitive balance or congruity.

To reduce post-decision dissonance a person rearranges his beliefs to better support his action, seeing more drawbacks and fewer advantages in the rejected options and more merits in the chosen one, seeking out confirming information, and avoiding, distorting, or derogating dissonant information.

After a decision there is a spreading apart of the alternatives, meaning an increase in confidence in the decision or in the perceived gap in attractiveness between the chosen and rejected options, or both.

Because a decision-maker usually has more unambiguous evidence about the consequences of the chosen alternative than about the hypothetical effects of rejected ones, dissonance reduction in political cases is typically accomplished by denigrating the rejected alternatives.

Dissonance effects apply only to post-decision situations and require both a definite commitment, meaning the decision unequivocally affects subsequent behavior, and a felt-free choice, since a person who had no real alternative finds sufficient justification in his lack of freedom and so feels no dissonance.

A decision sharply changes how a person processes information, because before deciding he seeks conflicting information and forms a compromise judgment, but once committed he cannot compromise and instead must minimize the extent to which the evidence pointed in opposite directions.

Post-decision dissonance reduction occurs outside the laboratory, as racetrack bettors grow more confident their horse will win immediately after betting and a decision-maker's prior doubts often dissolve once the choice is made.

Dissonance reduction does not always imply wishful thinking, because reducing dissonance can alter desires themselves and confirming that a decision was wise can run counter to one's wishes, as deciding to build a bomb shelter can lead one to tune out reassuring evidence while still hoping for peace.

Applying dissonance theory to politics requires drawing a line between pre- and post-decision phases, which is hard because there is often no clear moment of decision, but one can still contrast an actor's obviously undecided early stage with the later stage in which he is committed to an established image and carrying out a policy.

What counts as consonant or dissonant is unclear for complex questions, so the workable rule is that a dissonant cognition is one the person would have counted as a reason against the course he later chose, which means what is dissonant varies with the person's own beliefs.

Evidence that a policy is failing is dissonant with having chosen it only if the person feels he could have predicted that outcome from the information available at decision time, because dissonance reduction wards off the perception that the decision was unwise, not the recognition that an unpredictable world produced a bad result.

A person can admit in hindsight that a decision turned out wrong without believing he decided badly given what he knew, so how strongly dissonance operates depends on how much foresight the decision-maker thinks he should have had.

The magnitude of dissonance effects is uncertain and may be small relative to real-world forces such as institutional interests, political incentives, and feelings of duty, since even in the laboratory dissonance shifts the relative attractiveness of alternatives by only a few percentage points.

Dissonance reduction changes the premises of later deliberations, so its most important effect is to add psychological force to inertia, making a tentative decision hard to reverse beyond what bureaucratic and reputational costs alone would explain.

Policies persist despite discrepant information for reasons that need no psychology, because the domestic and bureaucratic costs of change are high, subordinates hesitate to flag current failures, and breaking an international commitment damages the state's reputation for keeping its word.

The selective-exposure claim that a person avoids dissonant information and seeks consonant information is a weak effect, easily overcome by the potential usefulness of the dissonant material, curiosity, and confidence that one can cope with it, so avoidance appears only when other reasons for exposure are absent.

The stronger mechanism by which dissonance prolongs policies is the post-decision spreading apart of the alternatives, whereby decision-makers come to feel certain they chose correctly even though before the decision the chosen policy had not seemed obviously best.

The rapid, large shift toward the chosen alternative that participants and scholars rarely attribute entirely to political considerations is evidence that dissonance reduction rather than post-decision regret is the dominant post-decision process.

Dissonance analysis of a decision is irrelevant when the decision itself changes the environment and destroys the availability of alternatives, as after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor viable alternatives to fighting on may not have existed regardless of dissonance.

Decision-makers commonly report that their doubts vanished and the situation seemed clearer once they committed, and they reject evidence they would have weighed carefully beforehand, as Madison stood by an equivocal French offer even as evidence of deception mounted that the British, with the same information, readily perceived.

A leader's vehement rejection of a proposal that actually accords with his own ideals can signal dissonance reduction, as Wilson resisted a late change that would have brought the peace treaty closer to his principles because admitting the change was needed would have been dissonant with the concessions he had already made to obtain the League.

When a chosen policy previously believed to carry very high costs is later confirmed, decision-makers reduce dissonance by revaluing the outcome, as American leaders who feared a domino collapse abandoned the deterministic domino theory after deciding not to intervene in Vietnam in 1954, a belief change larger than the new information warranted.

Spreading apart the alternatives increases inertia by raising the amount of discrepant information needed to reverse a policy, and continued dissonance reduction leads decision-makers to ignore policy-questioning information whenever they believe they should have foreseen the negative consequences.

Acting on a value in one case increases that value's potency over future cases, because dissonance reduction replenishes rather than depletes it, so refusing a bribe or a rival job offer strengthens later resistance by raising the value placed on integrity or on one's current position.

A statesman's post-decision revaluations propagate to other decisions, since inflating the dangers of the situation he acted against makes him more likely to act similarly elsewhere, and downgrading a rejected goal means he will not pursue it even if circumstances later permit, which is one reason an actor who has prepared a fall-back position fights less hard to hold his original stand.

The degree of dissonance, and thus the strength of efforts to reduce it, is proportional to the attractiveness of the rejected alternative, the qualitative dissimilarity of the alternatives, and the importance of the choice, so the greater the pre-decision conflict the greater the subsequent drive to justify the decision.

The same factors that make new evidence most valuable to a state generate the greatest psychological pressure against openness, because close and vital decisions most need reconsideration yet also arouse the strongest dissonance-reduction efforts, though a hard decision can paradoxically be reversed more easily since its alternatives start closer together.

Expending resources on a policy increases dissonance and thus the pressure to believe the policy is succeeding, because a person who wants to see his decisions as wise must believe his gains are proportionate to what he sacrificed, so sacrifice raises the value placed on the goal.

The main effect of costly effort is to inflate the perceived success of the goal, since experiments show that people who undergo an embarrassing initiation to join a group rate it more favorably than those admitted easily, though a person can alternatively justify meager results by the mere chance of a large success.

When a policy has high costs, decision-makers are prone both to overvalue what has been achieved and to perceive failures as successes, altering both their evaluation of outcomes and their estimate of the factual situation.

Correlating the resources a person spent on a policy with the value he places on it is spurious, so the sound test compares people who initially held the same views but expended different resources, predicting the person who sacrificed more will later evaluate the decision more favorably.

The actor most heavily invested in a policy is the most committed to its continuance and the most resistant to disconfirming information, which is why an official who staked his career on a course reacts with anger to news it is failing while less-invested colleagues change their minds more easily.

Negotiators tend to value the agreements they make more highly than do the less-involved members of their home governments, because the effort they invested in reaching the agreement raises its perceived worth.

The costs of war raise the valuation of winning and the estimated probability of success, so a negotiated settlement leads both sides to value their gains more highly than if the war had been cheaper, and acute awareness of a war's costs can make its outcome look like a success.

A state that expected to win but finds itself losing justifies its original decision by rating the concessions it forwent more negatively, revising upward the cost of a settlement negotiated from weakness, which increases its willingness to keep fighting so long as it sees even a slight chance of eventual victory.

The winners of costly wars develop inflated estimates of the fruits of victory, perceiving the same specific outcomes as bringing more desirable consequences, which is one reason costly modern wars are seen by participants as producing a much safer world.

Dissonance reduction inflates the value placed on specific objectives gained through sacrifice, making it hard to reassess their real worth once the fighting ends, as Britain could not take a fresh look at the slight postwar importance of the Straits it had fought so hard to hold.

Heavy peacetime expenditure also pressures a decision-maker to believe he has reached his goal, as German leaders judged Britain would stay neutral in 1914 because having spent so much to build a deterrent fleet was dissonant with Britain fighting anyway.

Effort expended on a means can transform that means into an end, because as a difficult undertaking gains momentum and engages people's personal commitment, suspending it for a wider goal becomes progressively less acceptable.

Spending resources acts as positive feedback that makes sunk costs, which a rational actor would ignore, drive further commitment, since the raised valuation of the goal and the need to justify prior sacrifice generate pressure to invest still more, as Tojo refused to withdraw from China because of the men, casualties, years, and money already spent.

In a more extreme form of positive feedback a person expands his objectives rather than merely trying harder, which is likely when the price already paid is too high to be justified by the original goal even when its value is exaggerated.

Whether a person reduces dissonance by trying harder or by perceiving success depends on which route is open: if he can do no more he inflates his judgment of his accomplishments, but if failure is unambiguous and the situation is not hopeless he increases his efforts.

By the psychology of insufficient reward, the incentive offered for behavior a person would not otherwise perform is inversely related to the attitude change that follows, because a large reward already justifies the act while a small one leaves dissonance to be reduced only by bringing attitudes into line with the behavior.

A decision-maker who feels he had no choice but to act is less prone to avoid or distort information than one who acted freely, because strong external compulsion or negative sanction supplies sufficient justification and leaves no dissonance to reduce.

The greater the positive and negative incentives for endorsing a policy, the less the pressure on officials' private attitudes, so strong rewards, loyalty norms, and pressures for a facade of unity actually preserve a wider diversity of private views within an organization.

Believing one had a real opportunity to influence a decision increases the feeling of free choice and therefore the dissonance, so unusually open deliberations can leave participants more strongly committed to the outcome and more resistant to new information.

The sense of compulsion is subjective and can itself serve dissonance avoidance, because a person who reaches an undesired but avoidable outcome tends to feel he had little choice, so a decision-maker's belief that he had no alternative but war may reflect a wish to escape the dissonance of its costs rather than a straight analysis.

A test of whether no-choice belief reflects dissonance avoidance rather than analysis is whether less-involved people who favor the same policy nonetheless see a wider range of options, since genuine analysis usually reveals more alternatives rather than fewer.

Dissonance is unlikely to homogenize views across a whole government but poses a real danger of it within the decision-maker's personal staff, because aides who owe loyalty to their chief and lack job security and independent organizational support tend to bring their opinions into line with their behavior.
