Counterattitudinal behavior with insufficient justification changes attitudes only if the person believes his action had significant consequences for which he is responsible, so an act that influences no one gives him no reason to seek justification.

Introducing discrepant information can produce a boomerang effect, because evidence that arouses enough discomfort to trigger dissonance reduction but is not convincing enough to change the mind leaves the person holding his original view even more strongly, the opposite of learning.

Boomerang or anti-learning is most likely when both the person's position and the dissonant information are resistant to change, so that the only way left to reduce dissonance is to pile up further support for the existing belief, as a failed prophecy led the surviving believers to proselytize more.

Political anti-learning appears when failure leads an actor to hold his policy more strongly, as leaders redoubled commitment to an approach after it had already produced a setback, though such cases are not conclusive because a stable predisposition could drive the repeated behavior.

The central contribution of cognitive dissonance theory is that people rearrange their perceptions, evaluations, and opinions to justify their own behavior, and by spreading apart the alternatives and heavily weighting sunk costs they entrench inertia and incrementalism, so each step in a policy adds psychological pressure to take the next.

Dissonance reduction introduces an unintended continuity into policy because altered values carry into later decisions, so the drive to see oneself as a more rational decision-maker ironically reduces rationality by impairing one's ability to use new information and re-examine one's own values.

Awareness of common perceptual errors and safeguards against unwarranted confidence can reduce the discrepant information needed to re-examine a belief, but no formula eliminates misperception or reveals which image is correct, since with ambiguous evidence even the interpretation that best fits the evidence may be wrong.

To interpret another's behavior and to shape one's own so the other draws the intended conclusion, an actor must try to see the world as the other sees it, or when unsure of the other's perspective examine the situation through several possible perspectives.

An actor should at minimum avoid assuming that his own view of the world is the only possible one and avoid believing the other sees his actions as he sees them, because assuming one's peaceful intentions are self-evident leads to reading the other's arms increases as unprovoked aggression.

Because people underestimate how strongly established beliefs shape perception, they change their minds more slowly than they think and therefore overestimate both how sensitive they are to variations in others' behavior and how easily they can change others' image of them.

An effort to make others accept a desired image succeeds in direct proportion to how compatible that image is with what they already believe, so an actor should design his behavior to work with the other's expectations, and altering those expectations requires prolonged or dramatic behavior that may be misperceived for a long time.

Decision-makers usually benefit from making their beliefs and values explicit, and it is often more fruitful to debate two opposed images or theories as complete wholes than to argue over the interpretation of each individual incident.

Many crucial policy failures occur not because decision-makers reach the wrong answers but because they ask the wrong questions, taking the most important matters for granted and failing to scrutinize basic assumptions.

The beliefs most in need of being made explicit concern the higher end of the means-ends chain, because the most general goals cannot guide action so actors adopt subgoals but often fail to analyze why attaining a subgoal would actually produce the desired higher end, as when planners assumed taking a capital would topple a hostile leader without scrutinizing the prediction.

A policy can outlive the belief that justified it, because when the environment changes in a way that removes a key premise, decision-makers often keep the old policy even after they have revised the belief that supported it, as happened before Pearl Harbor.

Subgoals tend to harden into ends valued for their own sake, especially once their pursuit has consumed much time and effort, so as circumstances change decision-makers keep striving for now-wasteful subgoals instead of asking whether new ones would better reach the end.

Because new information is interpreted within an established framework rather than calling the framework into question, a person who has not worked on a problem before or who has been away from it is often best able to see that an old subgoal no longer needs to be attained.

Irrational cognitive consistency keeps a policy constant despite drastic environmental shifts, and unless the consistency is covering a weakness too painful to face, it can be partly diminished by re-examining and making explicit the reasons the policy was originally adopted.

Decision-makers should decide in advance what evidence would confirm and, more importantly, disconfirm their views, because an actor who has thought about which events his hypothesis excludes is far more likely to notice and react to those events, whereas one who has not lets a wide variety of events pass without disturbing his faith.

Pre-designating what would be surprising cannot reveal when an image is wrong or which image is right, but it sensitizes the actor to discrepant evidence so that small contradictory bits call the image into question instead of being assimilated to it, which is why opponents ask proponents to state exactly what they expect a policy to achieve.

Trying to specify disconfirming evidence can reveal that an image is in fact invulnerable to most events, as with an unrecognized inherent-bad-faith model of an adversary, and a warning sign is when the opposite of an observed event would have been read as supporting the same conclusion.

Explicit prediction has severe limits, because individual facts admit multiple interpretations so no single embarrassment should overturn a theory, good theories yield only probabilistic predictions in complex international politics, and precise negative expectations require a level of theory that international relations rarely provides.

People may fail to update even when they witness the very events they had earlier said would count against their hypothesis, as a foreign minister who cited an adversary's silence as proof it would not fight did not reconsider once the adversary went public.

A single operative hypothesis with no competing alternatives is too readily confirmed, so decision-makers should encourage the formulation of alternative images and play with the evidence in the context of unpopular as well as popular hypotheses.

Rather than seeking unbiased analysis, decision-makers should deliberately structure conflicting cognitive biases into the process by using multiple devils' advocates, since one person cannot see the evidence as an opponent would when the difference in frameworks is basic, making a devil's advocate who is not a true devil of limited value.

An adversarial debate need not produce the correct image to be valuable, because it forces the decision-maker to exercise explicit judgment among competing interpretations and surfaces implicit assumptions that an individual rarely has the ability or incentive to expose on his own.

The diversity that exists naturally within a large organization is often insufficient, because shared assumptions make doubters seem unsound, long-standing issues are not reopened, homogeneity is strongest among a leader's personal assistants, and small secret high-level groups escape both departmental bias and built-in expertise and conflict.

Institutionalizing a devil's advocate can backfire, because labeling opposition as a devil's-advocate role signals resistance and makes a minority view easy to dismiss, and a decision-maker who exposes himself to token opposition may gain false confidence from the incorrect belief that he has been especially open-minded.

A decision-maker should give special weight when subordinates who previously held differing views converge on the same conclusion, particularly one against his own position or against their own interest and reached despite sanctions, while discounting conversions that could be produced merely by the role the subordinates were placed in.

It is dangerous to let those with an interest in maintaining a policy judge its effectiveness, so the party that negotiated an agreement should not be the one that monitors compliance with it, since doing so invites a one-sided interpretation of the evidence.

Individuals and organizations should not let their tasks, prospects, and identity become tied to a specific theory or image of another actor, because once they do, the subgoals bound up with that identity take on value of their own and information about alternative routes to the higher goals goes unconsidered.

A research or critical arm meant to keep an organization flexible loses its value when it internalizes the parent body's beliefs and depends on it for funding, because it then conducts inquiry to prove the established theory rather than to find the facts, avoiding or ignoring disconfirming tests.

An organization tends to avoid rigorously testing the doctrine on which its existence rests, as the RAF neglected the photographic reconnaissance that could have shown strategic bombing would not work at acceptable cost, because a negative result would have forced a new and subordinate mission.

Commitment to an organization's central mission distorts even technical and procurement choices, as air forces underestimated bomber vulnerability and starved long-range escort development because escorts and alternatives did not fit the doctrine of independent strategic bombing.

A mission can narrow from a general goal into a specific means that is then defended for its own sake, as an air force came to define its mission not as strategic bombardment but as strategic bombardment by manned bombers, resisting missiles and drones that threatened that means.

Even an intelligence agency excluded from policy-making and tied to no particular hardware has an organizational stake that biases its estimates, because it can develop a view of the world that maximizes the importance of its own distinctive competence and interpret information to imply its continued necessity.

A basic safeguard is for decision-makers to take account of how perception produces common errors, so awareness that belief systems display irrational consistency and that images form too quickly should lead them to examine their supporting evidence, suspend judgment longer, and consult people less involved with the issue.

Knowing that evidence consistent with one's existing beliefs is often wrongly taken as disconfirming alternative views should restrain a decision-maker from the unwarranted confidence that comes from the incorrect belief that events are proving his image correct.

Because people select historical analogies by rationally irrelevant features such as whether their own nation took part, and because most learning from history is superficial, a decision-maker should search the past more widely and study the causes of previous outcomes to judge which cases are actually relevant.

Decision-makers should watch for the specific recurrent distortions of perceiving the other side as highly centralized and carefully planning its moves, and of attributing the other's friendly acts to one's own behavior while attributing its unfriendly acts to unprovoked hostility, because these errors systematically inflate the other's apparent hostility.

Finding that one misperception is more common than its opposite does not by itself show the error distribution is suboptimal, because the right response depends on comparing the cost of that misperception with the cost of the opposite error, so an asymmetric cost can justify tolerating the cheaper error to avoid the catastrophic one.

The cost of overestimating another's hostility is itself frequently underestimated, because decision-makers wrongly assume a nonaggressive other will recognize their peaceful intent and overestimate how easily a suspicious but nonaggressive state can prove it seeks no expansion, so they should correct for a tendency toward excessive vigilance.
